title: Long-term allies and verifiable reality must make way for Saving Private Nige | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Has Farage’s brain been hacked? Has he started talking in his sleep? There’s no shortage of explanations for this scandal
Author: John Crace
Headline: Has Farage’s brain been hacked? Has he started talking in his sleep? There’s no shortage of explanations for this scandal
Content: Nigel Farage has said he ‘wasn’t even listening’ during a meeting where evading the law on accepting donations from overseas was discussed.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage has said he ‘wasn’t even listening’ during a meeting where evading the law on accepting donations from overseas was discussed.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchNigel FarageLong-term allies and verifiable reality must make way for Saving Private NigeJohn CraceHas Farage’s brain been hacked? Has he started talking in his sleep? There’s no shortage of explanations for this scandalSun 6 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTShareWe’ve all been there. It’s a lovely summer’s day and you just want a bit of me time. A quiet lunch of champagne and oysters. As you do. Anything to get away from having to pretend you are interested in the people of Clacton. Hell, it’s bad enough being expected to actually visit Clacton – who in their right mind would want to do that? – let alone having to talk to the little people who live there.So, you’re just minding your own business when who should turn up but two of your closest mates in politics – or contractors who you’ve barely heard of, as you prefer to call them – saying they have been having meetings with an American donor and his son who have already given you more than £30,000 for an opinion poll you have commissioned and now want to bung you another £500,000. And these guys would like to meet you.The cheek of it. Two strangers, one of them even a foreigner, who want to take up an hour of your time. And all you’re going to get for it is half a million quid. Who do they think you are? Don’t they know the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne stumped up a £5m gift? Admittedly,several hundred Cameo usershave bought you for £80 a pop, but that was at least a few months ago. Things have changed. Besides, that wasn’t really being bought. More a short-term rental.These wasters are basically insulting you. But you’re a tolerant kind of guy. You choose to indulge them. If you have a fault it’s that you’re never chippy and are unfailingly polite. Everyone tells you that. So you go along with them even though they have nothing of value to offer you. Yes, Yes. That’s fascinating. Thank you so much. But all along, you’re not really listening at all. You’re just zoning out. Trying to chill out in the sun. All you’re really thinking is of getting the first train out of Clacton.Over the past few days, Reform have been in a tailspin over theChannel 4 News stingthat appeared to show the party was intensely relaxed about breaking the law by taking money from overseas. First, they tried to style it out. It was a hoax. Nothing to see here. It was an establishment plot carried out by anti-establishment climate protesters. Go figure. Then, as the net closed in, they started to panic. No one had a clear line on anything. Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s long-term protege, and James Orr, the lawyer turned Cambridge academic turned Reform head of policy, left the party. Anything to buy some breathing space. All that mattered now was Saving Private Nige. Everyone else was expendable.So for his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that was recorded on Saturday but broadcast on Sunday morning, Nige was keen to distance himself from any allegation of wrongdoing. That person in the film that people said was him? It was actually an avatar. Who knows how many versions of Nige might be in play at any one time? He’s a very busy man.View image in fullscreenLaura Kuenssberg conducts an interview with Nigel Farage for the BBC.Photograph: BBCBut whichever Nige it had been, he was certain that he hadn’t been listening as the people around him were discussing in some detail not only how they exactly planned to break the law but how they had done so in the past. I mean, that was just pub talk. Who doesn’t like to boast about apparently criminal behaviour over a couple of drinks?Laura K seemed rather taken aback by this. She wasn’t the only one. Because it turns out Nige is capable of holding down his part in a conversation when he isn’t even listening. What a gift that must be. Most of us distinctly remember him saying, when the talk turned to the polling, that Nige insists he had no idea he had been funded by foreign money, that the polling had been “amazing”, had provided “bang for buck” and “it had worked – boom”. Perhaps he was just talking in his sleep. Or had had his brain hacked by the establishment. He even made a point of thanking the donors.Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform broke lawRead moreNot that they were donors, of course. Maybe that was the bit that hurt the most. The realisation that the offer had never been genuine. Then came the distancing. Jukes and Orr had been “injudicious at best”. That would suggest that at worst they might have been … maybe that’s one for the lawyers.What you had to remember was that Nige had never been close to Dan. Had never really liked him. Come to think of it, he had no idea why he had allowed him to be his right-hand gofer for the last 10 years. As for James, he was just an ingenu. A dreamer. It was totally unreasonable to expect someone who had trained as a finance lawyer to know anything about … er, the law concerning party funding. And it was just daft to think that a Cambridge ethics professor should behave ethically. Orr’s thesis had been on “divine lawmaking”. Perhaps breaking the law had been God’s will.Dan and James had just been freelancing. They didn’t really work for Reform. So any alleged law breaking was one step further removed from Nige. Besides, as Reform leader, it wasn’t his job to be the compliance officer. Even though no one apparently knew the rules governing party donations better than him. He was the world’s leading expert. That was by the by. His job was just to be the frontman. To smile and shake a few hands. He had just been doing what he had been told.Yes, said Laura, by now totally confused. But you did appear to be up to speed as the potential donor outlined how a scheme like that would be breaking the law and told him, “it’s all above board”, she said. Worried that she might be losing the plot. No, said Nige. What he had said was: “Is it all above board?” Except he hadn’t. He had definitely said it as a statement. Still, that cleared up one thing. The reason he hadn’t been listening was because he had hearing difficulties. One that made him turn every sentence on its head. Hopefully the police will take that into consideration if they get round to starting an investigation. Nige could do with a break.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageThe politics sketchReform UKParty fundingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Reckless review – this breathless thriller about siblings in a hit-and-run is a masterpiece | Television | The Guardian
description: The Australian retooling of Neil Forsyth’s excellent Guilt sees a brother and sister deal with the aftermath of accidentally killing a stranger. It’s a fast-paced, impressive ride
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The Australian retooling of Neil Forsyth’s excellent Guilt sees a brother and sister deal with the aftermath of accidentally killing a stranger. It’s a fast-paced, impressive ride
Content: Always listen to your elder sister! … siblings June (Tasma Walton) and Charlie (Hunter Page-Lochard) in Reckless.Photograph: SBSView image in fullscreenAlways listen to your elder sister! … siblings June (Tasma Walton) and Charlie (Hunter Page-Lochard) in Reckless.Photograph: SBSTV reviewTelevisionReviewReckless review – this breathless thriller about siblings in a hit-and-run is a masterpieceThe Australian retooling of Neil Forsyth’s excellent Guilt sees a brother and sister deal with the aftermath of accidentally killing a stranger. It’s a fast-paced, impressive rideLucy ManganSun 6 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust do what your elder sister tells you. That’s all there really is to leading an easy life. As a senior female sibling myself, this has always been my belief and now, as a viewer of Australian comedy-drama-caper-thriller Reckless, I can report it as absolute fact.I mean – first things first. Ideally, do not hit a pedestrian out walking late at night in his pyjamas while you’re driving under the influence of a joint you smoked at a family wedding, as record shop owner Charlie (Hunter Page-Lochard) does. But if you do, and if the older sister you are taking home tells you to keep driving – well, at least give it some consideration? Especially before you get your fingerprints all over the corpse’s wallet and start dragging him out of the road in front of his neighbours’ houses, then putting him back into his home. And if you do do all that, at least start listening to her thereafter. Follow her lead, after she finds a letter in the dead man’s house about the terminal cancer he was suffering from, in thinking that you just saved him months of agony, then go about the rest of your life with your mouth shut.Alas. Charlie is too sweet and chaotic a soul to do as his rigorously – not to say ruthlessly – logical sister June (Tasma Walton) suggests, nor to follow her damage limitation strategies thereafter. Which is bad news for them but good news for viewers, because what follows is a seamlessly preposterous-yet-plausible-under-the-suspended-disbelief-rules-of-the-genre that delivers a lot of bang for its four-hour buck.Reckless is a retooling of Neil Forsyth’s excellent Leith-set series Guilt, which examined the descent of two brothers into a morass of moral and other horrors after they kill a man in a hit and should-have-run. Here it has been relocated to Fremantle, Perth and infused by its Indigenous (re-)creator Kodie Bedford with additional racial tensions that up the stakes and give a fresh spin to the whole.The siblings are a First Nations family and part of June’s reaction comes from knowing that the odds will be unfairly stacked against them if they turn themselves in. More immediately, she does not want to lose the law firm she has built (and whose proceeds enabled her to buy her bumbling brother the record shop that keeps him afloat, becauseolder sisters are great), nor Charlie to lose contact with his daughter and become “just another absent Black father in prison”.Unfortunately, she neglects to tell him not to drop his wallet in George’s (for so is the dead man named) house, so Charlie ends up going to the wake to try to retrieve it. Whereupon he becomes enmeshed with George’s one remaining living relative, his English niece Sharne (Jessica De Gouw). June, learning to work with what she’s got, advises him to stay close to her until she’s signed all the estate paperwork and gone back to the UK.Alas, Sharne is of an enquiring mind, and is perturbed both by the police report’s mention of bruising on the body and by the damage to her uncle’s pyjamas and other inconsistencies that start to accrue. This is when June introduces Roddy (Clarence Ryan) into the narrative mix – a shambolically drunken private investigator she recently fired but who she insists to Sharne is the best of the best (“Comes from a long line of bush trackers,” she says, as he stares blankly at the torn PJs before falling over). June’s assumption is that Roddy will be useless and/or report what they tell him to report. But Roddy seizes on the case as a chance for redemption, sobers up and starts running down every lead he can. And then there are the neighbours.The lies, obfuscations, porch cameras, contradictions, complications, near-misses arrive at pace. Only one episode was available for review but I can see that you might start wishing for a little breathing room, a bit of a gap before the next eccentric character or villainous twist comes into play – but this is to quibble. Reckless is a fantastic, fun ride grounded by a realistically fractious but at heart loving relationship between the siblings, the light but piercing commentary on the wider racial and socioeconomic dynamics at work in Australia that illuminate rather than halt the action, and a cast of credible, however idiosyncratic, characters whose size makes the tonal consistency all the more wildly impressive. Many balls juggled, none dropped. Reckless is, underneath its flourishes, a masterpiece of control.Reckless aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now in the UK, and is on SBS on Demand in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Let your mind wander, don’t retire and stop worrying: surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliff | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: In his new book The Brain Cliff, Dr Norman Swan outlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive decline
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In his new book The Brain Cliff, Dr Norman Swan outlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive decline
Content: Broadcaster and author Dr Norman Swan says that ‘mental time travel’ – reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future – is good for brain health as we age.Photograph: Ekaterina Demidova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBroadcaster and author Dr Norman Swan says that ‘mental time travel’ – reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future – is good for brain health as we age.Photograph: Ekaterina Demidova/Getty ImagesHealth & wellbeingLet your mind wander, don’t retire and stop worrying: surprising ways to help save your brain from the cognitive cliffIn his new book The Brain Cliff,Dr Norman Swanoutlines the science of brain ageing and strategies for staving off cognitive declineGuardian staff speak to Dr Norman SwanSun 6 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou write that instead of fearingcognitive decline, “changing the way you think about the brain cliff can literally change the way you think and remember”. How?Dr Norman Swan:There are three things you need to know which are not widely known.Think cognitive change not cognitive decline: one way people think about our cognitive function is by comparing it to what it was like when we were in our 20s and it’s not a valid comparison. It leads to an assumption that we’ve declined into deficit. That’s not actually what’s happened, especially when we’re in midlife (40s and 50s). Our brains have changed, not deteriorated. Focusing on what that “change” looks like can make the task of maintaining cognitive function and perhaps even improving it, much clearer. Sure, our fluid intelligence – which is about speed and problem-solving – peaks in our 20s, but unless you’re a maths whiz or a gun lab researcher, that is less important than what’s called your crystallised intelligence, which can actually improve with age. It’s the wisdom of knowledge and experience.Secondly, as the years pass, our thoughts move address.The experts: neurologists on 17 simple ways to look after your brainRead moreThis is about a phenomenon in the brain called scaffolding. To protect our cognitive abilities and perhaps even enhance them as the years pass, our brains build out networks of nerves which act pretty much like the scaffolding inside a skyscraper. It’s the infrastructure around which the brain works. The more successfully we scaffold, the further away we push the brain cliff. This scaffolding initially moves across the brain then into the frontal lobes – the all-important prefrontal cortex which brings our thoughts and memories together and is involved with judgment, decision-making and emotional control.The third idea is that we should do as much as possible to encourage the scaffolding and as little as possible to get in its way.For The Brain Cliff I interviewed seven cognitive super-agers, who are as different as you could imagine – from the illiterate 95-year-old shoemaker to the woman who taught Mick Jagger statistics and the 94-year-old woman who still works in McDonald’s in Kyushu, Japan. But underneath, they’re remarkably similar and they’re all protecting their scaffolding in several ways. One example is how they respond to stress. They get over it. They problem-solve. They don’t ruminate. And where do you think we ruminate? Yes, in our prefrontal cortex. So you’re occupying valuable brain space for cognitive function with unproductive circular thoughts. As we move through life, the prefrontal cortex becomes more and more important and anything that distracts or damages it potentially brings the brain cliff closer. Depression affects the prefrontal cortex. Alcohol does too.You mention that the time to start helping our brains adaptis in our 40s and 50s. What should you be doing at that age and is it ever too late to start?It’s never too late to start.Exercise enhances our brain plasticity, which in turn encourages brain scaffolding. An anti-inflammatory diet – with low amounts of red meat, high diversity of vegetables including leafy greens, fermented foods such as yoghurt and fruits such as berries – can change the microbiome and aid direct absorption of bioactive compounds, both of which support brain scaffolding.View image in fullscreenBroadcaster and author Dr Norman Swan: ‘I’ve no intention of retiring. Retirement is bad for your brain. So the ABC will have to sack me.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianWhat’s also thought to be part of scaffold building is what’s called the default mode network – what our brain gets up to when it’s supposedly at rest. When the default mode network fires up, parts of the brain that don’t normally talk to each other make connections. How do you know if your default network is at work? Your mind wanders. Mind wandering looks as though it’s good for your brain.The battle to boost our deep sleep – and help stop dementiaRead moreAn associated activity is mental time travel: reliving the past, being well anchored in the present and imagining the future. When you’re in midlife you’re in a good place when it comes to mental time travel. When you’re young, there’s not much past; when you’re much older, the past tends to dominate. Mental time travel and mind wandering seem to encourage our scaffolding.What was the thing about cognitive super-agers which most surprised you, having interviewed so many of them?One of the important findings from research has been that genes don’t play a large role in whether we’re on a journey to the brain cliff or when we might reach it. That means the environment and how we live matter hugely and that’s what the cognitive super-agers I interviewed illustrated.There was only one of them where you could convince yourself that his family history mattered, and even he – a neuropsychiatrist from New Jersey aged 100 – was doing the things that maintain your brain. He had learned a new skill – pencil drawing – and through the classes had made new friends and was well connected with other people beyond his family.View image in fullscreenThe Brain Cliff by Dr Norman Swan.Photograph: HachetteWhat have you changed in your own life or daily habits since going on this deep dive into cognitive decline?I’ve become much more aware of when I might be ruminating and how I respond to stress. I work hard at problem solving and “getting over it”. I’ve really cut back my alcohol intake – not that it was ever high. I’m much more assiduous about my coronary risk factors like cholesterol and blood pressure. Leafy greens, berries and yoghurt are more prominent in my diet, and moderate to vigorous exercise is not an optional extra in my life. Oh … and I’ve no intention of retiring. Retirement is bad for your brain. So the ABC will have to sack me.You say that rumination and stress may accelerate cognitive change. How, and how can people best try to counteract this?For some people these are disabling and it’s hard to change by yourself. There are variations on cognitive behavioural therapy which can help in the hands of a well-trained clinical psychologist.You have a chapter titled “Don’t Retire”. Should we all be working until we drop?Work is mostly good for our brains. The evidence is strong that cognitive decline speeds up after retirement. Now some people with hard physical jobs simply can’t keep them up. The point here is what retirement means. If you move from your job to other work such as volunteering, new leisure activities, learning new and complex skills, then that’s actually not retirement. You’re still at work. Retirement to the couch and Netflix is a bad idea.The Brain Cliff by Dr Norman Swan (A$34.99, Hachette Australia),is out 8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingNeuroscienceDementiaAustralian booksAustralian lifestyleHuman biologyHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier life | Food | The Guardian
description: We all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshed
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: We all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshed
Content: Choosing the ideal diet can be a minefield, especially when you’re tired.Illustration: Moritz Wienert/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChoosing the ideal diet can be a minefield, especially when you’re tired.Illustration: Moritz Wienert/The GuardianFoodThe sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier lifeWe all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshedRachel DixonSun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstudy published in the journal Nature Healthlast month found that food choices and meal timings have “immediate and measurable effects” on sleep. It was just the latest in a growing body of research into the link between diet and rest. Here is the latest science on what to eat for better sleep – and how sleep deprivation can affect your dinner the next day.What should I eat for a good night’s sleep?While there isn’t “a special sleep diet” that will guarantee eight undisturbed hours, a Mediterranean-style diet comes closest, says Dalhia Campbell, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for theBritish Dietetic Association. She describes it as “a balanced, varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, lean proteins and healthy fats to help stabilise energy and support the hormones involved in sleep”.Prof Marie-Pierre St-Onge is the director of theCenter of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Researchat Columbia University in New York, and the author ofEat Better, Sleep Better. Her research into“plant-forward” diets, includingthe Mediterranean diet, is investigating why they are beneficial for sleep. She says this could be due partly to the phytonutrients in plant foods, which have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds, and partly to nutrients that feed the gut microbiome and are involved in gut-brain communications. “That could play a role in improving sleep through helping people quiet their minds,” St-Onge says.Are there any specific sleep-promoting foods?View image in fullscreenGive kiwi fruit a try.Photograph: Flavia Morlachetti/Getty Images“It is best to look at your overall diet rather than focusing on one particular food,” says Campbell. “The latest UK diet and nutrition survey shows that fewer than 17% of adults meet the ‘five a day’ recommendation. Improving fruit and vegetable intake supports general healthandsleep.”But once you’ve nailed your five a day, are any fruit and veg better than others? “There’s quite a bit of research showing tomatoes, tropical fruits such as bananas and pineapples, and oranges have benefits for sleep,” says St-Onge. “Nuts and seeds, especially pistachios and walnuts, and wholegrains can contribute to better sleep as well.”Emerging studies show that kiwis may have some benefits, says Dr Sammie Gill, a senior nutrition scientist at theBritish Nutrition Foundation,but the evidence is limited so far. There is also early research into tart cherries: “A recentsystematic reviewindicated that consumption may help improve sleep duration, sleep efficiency or sleep onset time,” she says. “That said, the science remains limited and inconsistent.”Do I need more protein?View image in fullscreenGet your protein from a range of sources.Photograph: fcafotodigital/Getty ImagesDiets higher in protein have alsobeen associated with better sleep. “Proteins are important because they provide a source of tryptophan, which is essential for producing serotonin and melatonin, which are important for sleep,” says St-Onge. Tryptophan is one of the nine essential amino acids that your body can’t make on its own, so it has to come from your diet. All animal proteins and many plant proteins contain tryptophan. “In the US, people talk about turkey all the time, like, ‘That’s why you fall asleep at dinner on Thanksgiving,’” says St-Onge. “But food is not an instantaneous process – it’s not like you pop a pill and two hours later it gets to exactly where it needs to get.”If you do want to try tryptophan-maxxing, Gill says other sources are “dairy, eggs, fish, seafood, meat, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and legumes. Tryptophan-containing foodshave been linkedwith improved sleep outcomes – such as total sleep time and sleep efficiency – compared with controls.” So having a warm milky drink before bed makes sense? “There isn’t strong research showing thatwarm milk helps with sleep, but that shouldn’t stop you from having milk as a bedtime option,” says Gill.What foods will keep me awake?“Foods that are low in nutrients and high in fats and sugars are less likely to support good sleep,” Campbell advises.St-Onge conducted research on this topic in France. “We showed that people who consumed more ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of insomnia symptoms. We’ve also shown that women who consume foods that have a higher glycemic index – the types of foods that tend to raise your blood sugars to a greater extent than others – have a higher risk of developing insomnia.” According to Diabetes UK,high GI foodsinclude refined carbohydrates such as white bread, potatoes, doughnuts, bagels, sweets, sugar-sweetened breakfast cereals and sugar-sweetened drinks. As well as added sugars, St-Onge would avoid foods high in salt.Does caffeine help or hinder?View image in fullscreenCaffeine tolerance can decrease with age.Photograph: Curly_photo/Getty Images“Caffeine is a double-edged sword,” says Gill. “Plenty of studies have shown that caffeine in moderate doses [up to 400mg/four cups of coffee a day] can have a positive effect on cognitive performance, memory and alertness. But at higher doses, it can trigger anxiety, irritability and restlessness.”Four coffees may sound an awful lot to some. “The effects of caffeine vary from person to person – some people are more sensitive to its effects. How you respond to caffeine is partly determined by your genetics,” she says. But however much you drink, the main thing is to do so in the morning. “Caffeine has a quarter-life of around 10-12 hours, meaning that if you consume it at lunchtime, a quarter of the caffeine is still in your body close to midnight, which can disrupt sleep.” Cutting it out by lunch “can lead to noticeable improvements in sleep quality and quantity”.As you get older, you may find the after-dinner espresso you once enjoyed is now keeping you awake. “Your ability to metabolise caffeine changes as you age,” says St-Onge. “It’s important to keep track and evaluate every so often. If you’re starting to see that your sleep is changing, you might want to make adjustments related to intake of caffeine or timing of the last caffeinated beverage.”How about alcohol?View image in fullscreenAvoid ‘one for the road’ …Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesMany people think a drink or two helps them fall asleep – and they are right. But that doesn’t mean it’s a sleep aid. “Alcohol is a sedative – it does not prompt natural, ‘true’ sleep,” says Gill. “While it may help you fall asleep faster, it significantly disrupts the quality of your sleep. Alcohol, even in low amounts,reduces REM sleep, which is important for emotional processing and memory consolidation.”What’s more, “alcohol interacts with several neurotransmitters that are important in the regulation of sleep and can trigger awakenings during the night, which can make you feel tired the next day”. It can also make acid reflux worse, adds Campbell. So much for the trusty nightcap.How long should I leave between dinner and bed?View image in fullscreen… and the late-night cuppa.Photograph: Daniel de la Hoz/Getty Images“Studies have foundthat later meals are generally linked to lower-quality sleep,” says Gill. “A recent trialfound that eating dinner one hour before bedtime was linked with reduced sleep continuity and stability.” And you may find it harder to drop off in the first place, says Campbell, as your body is busy digesting your meal.St-Onge cautions that going to bed on a full stomach also increases your risk of heartburn and acid reflux. “As a general rule, wait two to three hours after a meal,” she says. If you already suffer from acid reflux,NHS adviceis to avoid food for up to four hours before bed. Beware of that late-night cuppa, too, says St-Onge: “If you’re drinking much too close to bedtime, you’ll need to wake up to use the bathroom.”But I hate going to bed hungry!“It’s OK to have a light snack after an early dinner if you’re feeling hungry – going to sleep on an empty stomach can disrupt sleep, too,” says Gill. “The key message is: don’t go to bed too full or too hungry.”“Choose a light, nutritious option such as yoghurt with fruit and nuts, or wholegrain toast with nut butter and banana,” says Campbell. “That’s better than grazing on biscuits and chocolate.”Why am I ravenous when I haven’t slept well?View image in fullscreenSugary cereal is tempting when you’re tired, but it’s not ideal.Photograph: Kinga Krzeminska/Getty ImagesThis is partly down to your body’s hunger signals. “Some research suggests that sleep loss can alter appetite hormones such as leptin [which signals fullness] and ghrelin [which stimulates appetite],” says Gill. “One study showedthat one night of inadequate sleep can increase ghrelin levels and decrease leptin levels.” As a result, “poor sleep is associated withincreases in energy intake, mainly from snacking, especially on foods higher in fat and carbohydrates.One review foundthat people who are sleep-deprived consume an average of 385 calories extra the following day compared with controls.”St-Onge’s research has found this hormone effect varies by sex: “Ghrelin tends to rise before a meal, signalling hunger. We’ve shown that it increases to a greater extent in men who haven’t had sufficient sleep.” In sleep-deprived women, on the other hand, leptin – “the satiety signal” – is suppressed. But the result is the same: overeating.It’s not just about ghrelin and leptin. “I always tell people that we don’t necessarily eat because we’re hungry, right? People have many reasons to eat, and eat despite lack of hunger,” says St-Onge. She says our brain reward centres are affected by how much sleep we’ve had the night before, and the “hedonic signals – the things that make food more appealing – tend to be more intense after a period of short sleep. So you’re more susceptible to reaching for appetising or pleasurable foods.” Who hasn’t chosen the pain au chocolat over the porridge after a bad night?Does this mean poor sleep will make me gain weight?In the long term, it certainlyincreases the likelihood. “Studies showthat people who regularly sleep less than six hours tend to gain more weight over time, and increasing sleep to seven or eight hours can help with appetite regulation,” says Campbell. As well as disrupted hunger hormones, there are a number of explanations. “Observational studies show those who don’t get enough sleep tend to eat less fruit and vegetables, more sugar, less protein and less fibre. Staying up late at night also means that you might get peckish and be more tempted to snack. And when tired, we may be less motivated to be active and to cook from scratch, relying more on quick, less nutritious foods and fizzy, sugary drinks.”Does the time I go to bed affect what I eat the next day?View image in fullscreenEarly birds may have it easier than night owls.Photograph: Flashpop/Getty Images“Most ofthe research focusis on chronotype [your body’s natural preference of when to sleep and wake] – if you have a late chronotype versus an earlier chronotype,” says St-Onge. So is it better to be an early bird or a night owl? “Typically, people with earlier chronotypes tend to have more healthful diets and exercise more,” she says. Plus, “people who have an earlier chronotype have an easier time getting adequate sleep duration because their sleep is more aligned with the societal clock”. Unfortunately for late risers, chronotypes are thought to be largely genetic.I do shift work – how can I eat and sleep well?“Shift workersreport less healthy dietscompared with day workers, andshift work is associatedwith increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes,” says Campbell. She suggests “eating the main meal before a night shift, and choosing lighter, nutrient-rich foods overnight”. This is easier said than done, says St-Onge. “It’s difficult because it’s a whole culture that needs to change – people tend to bring in treats to have in the middle of the night.”Should I take magnesium?View image in fullscreenSome studies show supplements help.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty Images“Try science-backed sleep strategies first, focusing on regularity, timing, temperature and lighting,” says Gill.Campbell agrees: “Rather than looking to supplements, it’s more helpful to look at the bigger picture. Take a look at sleep routine, stress levels, alcohol and caffeine intake, activity levels, and any underlying health issues that might be affecting rest, such as sleep apnoea, menopause symptoms or frequent night-time waking.”If you’ve sorted your diet, exercise, sleep hygiene and general health, however, there is some weak evidence that magnesium may help. “Observational studieshave linked magnesium with sleep-promoting effects, whereas limitedgold-standard trialsreport mixed results,” says Gill. “A recentrandomised controlled trialin adults with self-reported poor sleep quality supplemented with magnesium glycinate found modest improvements in insomnia severity.Another studyshowed that supplementation with magnesium threonate improved sleep quality and daytime alertness in people with self-reported sleep problems.”Do I need added vitamins?B vitamins and vitamin D are also commonly believed to help with sleep – are supplements advisable? “B vitamins are abundant in the diet – typically, people don’t have any deficiencies in those,” says St-Onge. “Vitamin D is something that could be problematic, especially if you don’t drink fortified dairy products. We can produce vitamin D from sunlight, but in some populations the sun is not sufficient, so that could be something that could be supplemented.” In the UK,government adviceis to consider taking vitamin D in autumn and winter.What about melatonin?“Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles,” says Gill. “It’s often called the ‘hormone of darkness’ because its levels increase as evening approaches, signalling to your brain and body that it’s time for sleep. Rather than acting like an on-off switch, melatonin works more like a dimmer switch – preparing your body for sleep without directly causing it.” So should insomniacs take supplements? “Melatonin supplements are most effective for shifting the timing of your sleep, rather than as a routine, everyday sleep aid,” says Gill. “Melatonin can also be really helpful for managing jet lag. When used at the right time, melatonin can help fool the brain into thinking it’s night-time.”Explore more on these topicsFoodSleepHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mind games and a ‘toss master’: world stone skimming contest returns to Scotland after cheating scandal | Scotland | The Guardian
description: More than 400 competitors battle windy conditions on Easdale, a year after tampered-with stones made headlines
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: More than 400 competitors battle windy conditions on Easdale, a year after tampered-with stones made headlines
Content: Easdale is home to stone skimming’s colosseum: a former slate mine flooded by a ferocious Atlantic storm in 1881.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldView image in fullscreenEasdale is home to stone skimming’s colosseum: a former slate mine flooded by a ferocious Atlantic storm in 1881.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldScotlandMind games and a ‘toss master’: world stone skimming contest returns to Scotland after cheating scandalMore than 400 competitors battle windy conditions on Easdale, a year after tampered-with stones made headlinesPatrick GreenfieldSun 6 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Want to touch it?” Jonny Jennings asked, clutching the World Stone Skimming Championship trophy in his arms as he waited for the ferry. The mind games from the 2025 men’s champion had started hours before this year’s competition had even begun. The 38-year-old had travelled from Kentucky to Easdale island just off the west coast ofScotlandto defend his title. He was not giving it up without a fight.On Saturday, more than 400 of the world’s best stone skimmers descended on the tiny island in the Inner Hebrides, normally home to just 60 residents. From Argentina to India, Hong Kong to Jamaica, more than 30 countries were represented, ferried over in groups of 10 from the mainland.Easdale is home to stone skimming’s colosseum: a former slate mine flooded by a ferocious Atlantic storm in 1881, forming a natural amphitheatre for the tournament. Competitors get three throws across the 63-metre (207ft) stretch, which is marked off like a swimming lane. Stones must be made of Easdale slate and can be no wider than 7.6cm (three inches). The ultimate aim is to hit the back wall, the equivalent of a nine-dart finish that sends the crowd into raptures.View image in fullscreenOfficials check the stones used are made of Easdale slate and are no wider than 7.6cm.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldFrom the “skim of destiny”, the stone plinth from which all skimmers have to throw, the back wall of the quarry does not look far away. But looks deceive on Easdale. The wind, the rain and shadows in the water combine to make it one of the toughest places to compete for skimmers in the world. Many elite male skimmers can throw more than double the distance of the quarry in calmer conditions. But at the world championships, they often crumble.The World Stone Skimming Championship takes place on Easdale island“It’s the magic of Easdale,” said Lucy Wood, the six-time female champion. “It’s different, very different. You have got hundreds of people watching you throw. It’s completely insane. Some people say that the island is not the best place to host the competition because of the back wall, and you cannot really throw that far. But most of these skimmers have never even hit it.”On Saturday, a vicious wind played havoc with the competition, blowing stones off course as it swirled around the quarry. To combat conditions, many skimmers changed their style to try to avoid the gusts. Some bent their knees more than usual, others wound up their arms and used brute force for their throw. But nothing seemed to work. Stones whizzed off course in all directions, disappearing into the depths of the quarry far short of their intended target. By the halfway stage, just one competitor had hit the back wall.View image in fullscreenAbbey McDonald prepares to throw during this year’s championship.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldLast year, the competitive spirit boiled over. Two competitors were caught cheating after fashioning stones into perfect circles in an attempt to improve their chances of a better throw. The scandal madeinternational headlinesand organisers had a geologist on hand this year to check stones if any questions were raised.“To win at Easdale, you need to have guts,” said Dr Kyle Mathews, the competition organiser, known as the “official toss master”.“You need distance, consistency and accuracy. You need to be able to stand up and throw when it counts. We are often put in the same category ascheese chasing down the hillor theconkers championship. But these skimmers have genuine sporting talent. The world record for the javelin is nearly 100 metres. The record for stone skimming is much further than that,” he added.View image in fullscreenLast year’s men’s champion. Jonny Jennings, from Kentucky, waves to the crowds.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldWhen it was time for Jennings to throw, the packed crowd around the colosseum fell silent with expectation. Dressed in his signature colour, the “Green Giant” finished his pint of beer before taking the plinth, still wearing sunglasses. “Now that’s aura,” one young spectator whispered.Jennings had to hit the back wall if he was going to retain the title. His first attempt was superb, delighting the crowd, but the stone disappeared into the water just before it could produce a satisfying “clink” with the back wall. The second skewed left, caught by the wind. He waited for the gust to die down for his final attempt. Bending his knees, the champion unleashed the throw with all his might. But it was short again: 2026 would have a new men’s champion.View image in fullscreenThis year’s winners Abbey McDonald and Liam Knight show off their trophies.Photograph: Patrick GreenfieldBy late afternoon, Liam Knight from North Carolina was still the only competitor to hit the back wall. Nobody could beat him. “I came here two years ago and I got the bug. I had to use a technique that nobody else was using to get it out past the wind. It was brutal. It ruined everyone’s day,” said the 32-year-old. “It was kind of a trick shot really. But it worked.”At the award ceremony, Jennings had to watch from the crowd as Knight lifted the trophy. He would return to the mainland empty-handed. But he would be back next year to try again.Explore more on these topicsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority | Germany | The Guardian
description: Projections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Projections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted
Content: Ulrich Siegmund, pictured arriving to vote on Sunday, had said his goal was to gain 45% or more.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund, pictured arriving to vote on Sunday, had said his goal was to gain 45% or more.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersGermanyFar-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majorityProjections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being countedKate Connollyin BerlinSun 6 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, securing a historic result and more than doubling its support. The AfD now appear on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.Germany’s far-right AfD thanks Elon Musk as France warns state election win a ‘serious moment’Read moreInitial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, anddecisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations. The party, an offshoot of Die Linke, has agreed to cooperate with the AfD on issues such as energy price reform.Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority – the condition it has said is central to it taking power, given its refusal togovern with another party.The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as aBrandmauer,or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.Addressing jubilant supporters, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said: “We have made history in this country”. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, he said his party was ready to ⁠reach out ​to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change.“We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue ​better policies,” a beaming Siegmund,35, said after ⁠exit polls had been published. He said themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with the AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Siegmund on Sunday evening called Merz “a very good campaigner for the AfD”.Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how the AfD could rule.About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents.Final polls had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support,and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSiegmund celebrating with the AfD’s co-leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right) after polls closed on Sunday.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersThe Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.Explore more on these topicsGermanyAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision
Content: Activists staged a demonstration in Westminster, London last September in anticipation of the government’s changes to the Send system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenActivists staged a demonstration in Westminster, London last September in anticipation of the government’s changes to the Send system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianSpecial educational needsPupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for supportSchools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provisionRichard AdamsEducation editorSun 6 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools and councils acrossEnglandare expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.Some parents of special school pupils in England spending £5,000 on EHCPsRead moreBill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million haveidentified special needs, according toofficial data.The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid manylocal authorities becoming technically bankrupt.Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to itswhite paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Gould, the schools minister, on a visit to a school in Colchester, said she families have been let down by the system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”Send plan for England gets cautious welcome amid workload concernsRead moreIpsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.Madeleine Cassidy,Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchoolsSchool fundingLocal governmentChildrenEducation policyEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport | Florida | The Guardian
description: Three people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a halt
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Three people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a halt
Content: An Amazon cargo plane after it crashed at Miami international airport on Sunday, in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Amazon cargo plane after it crashed at Miami international airport on Sunday, in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesFloridaAt least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airportThree people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a haltMaya YangSun 6 Sep 2026 17.49 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami international airport inFloridaon Sunday afternoon after the flight, which was arriving from Puerto Rico, overshot the runway, striking several vehicles and resulting in at least five deaths.The plane erupted in flames as dark smoke billowed into the sky, bringing operations at one of the busiest airports in the US to a halt. The pilot and copilot were trapped in the cockpit as a result of the crash, said the Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah.The mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade county said at a news conference on Sunday that in addition to the five people who were killed, five others were injured. Miami-Dade fire rescue confirmed during the same conference that ten total people were involved, with five deaths, three people in critical condition and two taken to a local hospital.Jadallah, described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.The National Transportation Safety Board has assembled a team to investigate, the agency said in asocial media poston Sunday evening. They are scheduling a media briefing for Monday.Videos posted online show heavy plumes of smoke surrounding an aircraft bearing theAmazonarrow logo on its tail. Unconfirmed reports suggest there may be casualties, but details about injuries or fatalities remained unclear.The plane was a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Prime Air.The Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) confirmed the crash in a statement to the Guardian, saying: “21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 pm local time on Sunday, September 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.”The plane overran the airport’s diagonal runway and was disabled at the north-west end of the airport, a spokesperson for Miami international airport said.An air and ground stop has been issued at the airport, preventing all other flights from landing or taking off at the busy south Florida hub. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.“All runways and taxiways at MIA are currently closed as of 3pm and a ground stop is in effect,” the airport said, adding: “Miami-Dade Fire Rescue has responded to the scene.”About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.More than 60 units from the Miami-Dade fire rescue services appeared on scene, with units arriving “to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”, the fire departmentsaid, with the post adding that the plane had struck multiple vehicles near the airport.Firefighters were “working on extinguishing the fire and assessing patients”, the post said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS transportation secretary Sean Duffysaidon social media that responders would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.“If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,” he added.Meanwhile, the Miami-Dade sheriff’s officeannouncedstreet closures due to the crash, saying: “NW 67th Avenue between NW 25th Street – NW 36th Street is currently closed. Expect delays and seek alternate routes.”Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today.”Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”Explore more on these topicsFloridaMiamiAmazonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 75% of A&E staff in UK face violence or aggression daily or weekly | A&E | The Guardian
description: Survey finds long waiting times and overcrowding have made abuse ‘routine’ part of working on hospital frontline
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Survey finds long waiting times and overcrowding have made abuse ‘routine’ part of working on hospital frontline
Content: In a survey of more than 2,000 workers, 63% of respondents also said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia.Photograph: Nick Moore/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn a survey of more than 2,000 workers, 63% of respondents also said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia.Photograph: Nick Moore/AlamyA&EAlmost 75% of A&E staff in UK face violence or aggression daily or weeklySurvey finds long waiting times and overcrowding have made abuse ‘routine’ part of working on hospital frontlineJosh HallidayNorth of England editorSun 6 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly three-quarters of A&E staff experience violence or aggression daily or weekly, according to a survey highlighting the “appalling” abuse ofNHSworkers.The Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) said understaffed and overcrowded emergency departments were contributing to increased targeting of medics.In a survey of more than 2,000 workers in the UK, 63% said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia, while 73% said violence or aggression of all kinds was a daily or weekly occurrence. Almost all (96%) said they had experienced abuse from patients or members of the public.Dr Ian Higginson, the president of the RCEM, said: “No one should go to work fearing or, worse, expecting to be attacked, intimidated or abused. Nor should they lack confidence that their employers have their backs, or that the judicial system will kick in.“Yet that’s the reality faced by the majority of my colleagues in EDs [emergency departments] across the country. They often do not feel safe to care for patients. It is an appalling state of affairs which is contributing towards many people seriously considering whether emergency medicine – or even healthcare in general – is for them.”Senior nurses said in January that abuse of NHS staff had become a national crisis.In the survey, emergency department workers said long waiting times and overcrowding had made violence and aggression a “routine” part of working on the hospital frontline. Staff shortages and corridor care – patients being treated in non-clinical spaces because of overcrowding – were also cited as main reasons behind the abuse.One anonymous resident doctor said: “Working in the ED, you brace yourself for a lot, but nothing truly prepares you for direct, hateful verbal abuse, especially when it’s racially charged.”A senior emergency doctor told the survey they had been kicked in the face by an aggressive patient lying on a trolley.Ministers have pledged to get key waiting times across the NHS back on track before the end of this parliament in 2029. However, the leaders of professional bodies have called for faster action after aseries of targets were missedat the end of the financial year in March.The NHS was told to ensure 78% of A&E patients were treated within four hours by March. While it came close to that target – 77.6% of patients were treated within four hours that month – the proportion has since slipped.Higginson called on the government to accelerate its drive to reduce waiting times and overcrowding. “Much has been said by us and other organisations over the years about violence and aggression towards healthcare staff. But the problem seems to be getting worse, not better,” he said.“It’s time for action, time for governments, employers and organisations stand up for NHS staff, and time to ensure that those who intimidate, abuse or assault those who are trying to care for them face meaningful consequences for their actions.”The worsening conditions in A&E would have “devastating” consequences for the workforce if they continued, the RCEM added.Only 4% of those surveyed said they always felt safe working in A&E, while 75% reported short-term stress and anxiety, 40% said they had experienced burnout and 28% long-term stress or anxiety.In January, dataobtained by the Guardianrevealed that more than 295,000 incidents of physical violence and aggression by patients against staff had been recorded by 212 NHS trusts in England between 2022 and 2025.Hospitals records showed the number of violent incidents, which ranged from violent threats to attempted and actual assaults, had risen from 91,175 in 2022-23 to 104,079 in 2024-25. This was equivalent to about 285 cases being reported every day in the most recent year.A Department ofHealthand Social Care spokesperson said: “Any acts of violence, abuse or harassment towards NHS staff are completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated. Everyone working in our national health service has a fundamental right to be safe at work, and it is deeply concerning that so many emergency department staff continue to experience this behaviour.“That is why this government recently introduced new NHS staff standards, which set out the steps that every NHS employer across the country must take to prevent and reduce violence and abuse against their staff and help ensure they can do their jobs safely.”Explore more on these topicsA&ENHSViolence against women and girlsRaceHospitalsDoctorsNursingShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmoil | John Healey | The Guardian
description: John Healey speech on Monday will stress links between fiscal discipline and growth amid concerns his cautious approach jars with Burnham’s radical plans
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: John Healey speech on Monday will stress links between fiscal discipline and growth amid concerns his cautious approach jars with Burnham’s radical plans
Content: John Healey, pictured at a gathering of G20 finance ministers last month, will set out how the government plans to boost regional economies.Photograph: Sam Wolfe/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey, pictured at a gathering of G20 finance ministers last month, will set out how the government plans to boost regional economies.Photograph: Sam Wolfe/ReutersJohn HealeyChancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmoilJohn Healey speech on Monday will stress links between fiscal discipline and growth amid concerns his cautious approach jars with Burnham’s radical plansPippa CrerarPolitical editorSun 6 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey will argue the government’s plans to boost growth across the whole country will enable the British economy to “turn a corner” despite anxiety over volatile bond markets derailing Labour’s crucial first budget.The chancellor is expected to argue that fiscal discipline is “indivisible” from good growth, especially at a time of difficult global headwinds, amid concerns that hiscautious approachjars with Andy Burnham’s more radical policy plans.In a speech in the West Midlands on Monday, Healey will set out how the government plans to boost regional economies by easing Treasury bureaucracy and giving more powers to local leaders to drive business investment, innovation and skills.But public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, driving up government borrowing costs, resulting inHealey putting Britain on noticefor a tough 28 October budget.Economists have predicted that the chancellor – who has said he wants a “buffer against uncertainty” – will have to put up taxes or cut spending to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom his predecessor Rachel Reeves had last year.“Fiscal credibility is indivisible from good growth,” the chancellor is expected to say. A Treasury source said this was “true at any time, but especially at a time of global uncertainty” amid warnings that Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East would push up inflation and hit public finances.Healey will say that, despite the bleak global backdrop, pursuing growth across every region will help unlock “huge latent potential” and show Britain is “turning a corner”, with people, businesses and communities ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies.UK long-term borrowing costs could halve chancellor’s budget headroomRead moreThe prime minister argued at the weekend that it would be impossible to build a dynamic economy on crumbling infrastructure, with businesses needing affordable energy and reliable transport, and so more investment would be needed.But in a move that will undermine Labour’s efforts to reindustrialise, the UK’s biggest carmaker,Jaguar Land Rover, which is based in the West Midlands, was expected to announce thousands of job cuts.During a speech at a manufacturing site on Monday, Healey is expected to reiterate that Britain’s growth must extend beyond its biggest cities.“The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past,” he is expected to say. “The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places. The next chapter of Britain’s growth story will be written in more places.”National government must work with the new No 10 North on a “dual mission” to remove obstacles for local leaders and businesses, he is expected to say. “Instead of getting in the way with complexity and red tape, we need a strong, strategic centre wired to enable local leaders and their ambitions.“I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.”View image in fullscreenHealey wants national government to work with No 10 North on a ‘dual mission’ to remove obstacles for local leaders and businesses.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHealey will announce that the British Business Bank will allocate £150m to scale up businesses across the north of England. The pot will offer investments from £5m to £15m to help university spinouts and the expansion of other innovative companies.He will underline the government’s commitment to “place-based” growth, building on Reeves’s attempts to move the focus of the Treasury away from the south-east. “Ask an economist what growth is and you’ll get a number,” he will say. “But ask the country and you’ll get a different answer.“A young person getting a new job in a company that’s on the up. A sole trader winning a new contract that pays for a holiday with their kids. A business winning a new export order, giving the community around it a new lease of life.”However, businesses are braced for what they fear will be higher taxes to fill a fiscal hole caused by rising borrowing costs and Burnham’s new spending plans. In an interview with the Financial Times on Saturday, Healey refused to rule out increasing levies on bank profits.Taxing the banks: what Europe’s windfall levies brought in as Burnham eyes his next moveRead moreHealey has also been under pressure over the timeline to hit defence spending targets, after quitting Keir Starmer’s cabinet over the issue. On Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, indicated the government would spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence by 2030.“We’ve made some clear movements early on to show that direction of travel … [Healey] has not moved away from the target you’ve said. He said the fundamental target is the 2035 3.5% of GDP on defence spending that is ourNatocommitment. The trajectory to that covers the 3% but that is the principal target,” said Reynolds.View image in fullscreenHealey, pictured in June, the day before he resigned from his post as defence secretary over military spending plans.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPARobert Jenrick, Reform UK’s economic spokesperson, said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff. Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy.”Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, described Healey’s speech as a “policy-light word salad”, saying it would do little to comfort families and businesses who were worried about more tax rises or the rates of government borrowing.On the BBC on Sunday, Griffith, who was a Treasury minister at the time of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, said there had been “lots of good things” in that fiscal statement – including tax cuts and cutting regulation – attracting criticism from Labour.Explore more on these topicsJohn HealeyEconomic policyBondsAndy BurnhamJaguar Land RoverUnemploymentTax and spendingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens | Bristol | The Guardian
description: Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute
