Content: Redevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRedevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianBristol‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opensTemple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commuteSteven MorrisSun 6 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone.On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of thatcrumbling Royal Mail sorting officenext door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public.The proximity ofthe Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC)to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot affordBristol’s expensive property and rental marketto commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings.The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been.View image in fullscreenThe former Bristol Royal Mail sorting office next to Bristol Temple Meads train station was demolished in 2019.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes,Bristol Temple Quarter, which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’sfirst prime minister’s questions.Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city.“We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students.“It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.”View image in fullscreenThe Sloane Robinson building is the £241m centrepiece of the University of Bristol’s Temple Quarter campus.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies.It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space.But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens.A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added.Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations.Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised.View image in fullscreenThe Sloane Robinson building is named after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student Hugh Sloane.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianMembers of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.”The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m.The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths.The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m.Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market.View image in fullscreenMembers of the public will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThough the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it.Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said.Martin Booth, editor of the independent magazine and websiteBristol 24/7and author of111 Places That You Shouldn’t Miss in Bristol, said the new site looked as if a “gigantic spaceship” had crash-landed next to the station. “But it is a manifestation of the university’s efforts to be a more visible part of our city – not just in their privileged position on top of a hill in Clifton,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBristolUniversitiesHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Georgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in future
Content: Georgia Gould, the minister for school standards, believes the Send model used by Thomas Lord Audley school in Colchester represents future best practice.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorgia Gould, the minister for school standards, believes the Send model used by Thomas Lord Audley school in Colchester represents future best practice.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianSpecial educational needsAnalysis‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provisionRichard AdamsEducation editorGeorgia Gould says moving system towards inclusion will mean parents ‘don’t need to fight’ for support in futurePupils with Send plans in England likely to double in rush for supportSun 6 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTShareGeorgia Gould is in a race against time. And the minister responsible for overhauling England’s special educational needs provision is hoping that a state school in Colchester will help her beat the clock.Gould visited Thomas Lord Audley secondary school last week to see the secrets of its success in persuading local parents that it can help children with special needs thrive in a mainstream setting.Under the government’s proprosalsannounced in February, more funding and universal support are to be given to mainstream schools to accommodate children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send).The schools minister told the Guardian that institutions such as Thomas Lord Audley are doing many things that will become national policy under the new system.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Gould wants the approach taken at Thomas Lord Audley to be followed by all schools in the UK.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian“What they are doing here is a really powerful example of best practice,” Gould said, explaining how the school engages with families and pupils a year or more in advance of entry, and draws up bespoke plans for pupils’ needs similar to the government’s proposed digital records to track and share day-to-day support for children with special needs, called individual support plans.Gould said: “Part of the work we are trying to do, to transform the system towards inclusion, is to take the best practices from schools like this, and make sure that people can see the evidence and the impact they have on things like attendance … And then we want to spread that practice.Labour’s Send reforms get this right: disabled children in mainstream schools is transformative for everyone | Frances RyanRead more“Of course, schools want to do everything in their power to support children and it’s important that they get a blueprint to be able to do that.”The hope is that the new tiers of support and national standards will be in place by 2030, when the government wants education, health and care plans (EHCPs) – which many families now use to access support – to be narrowed down to those with the most profound educational needs and disabilities.But the government’s white paper will allow existing EHCPs to remain in place after 2030. In doing so it may have created a surge of applications from families who fear missing out if they don’t get in before that deadline. That surge means the legacy of EHCPs will absorb funding desperately needed by the new system of support that does not require parents to jump through legal hoops.English councils need to hire 1,400 more educational psychologists, says reportRead more“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight and battle and go through a bureaucratic process,” Gould said, highlighting evidence she has seen from Rochdale schools that offer early intervention for speech and language difficulties.“They’ve seen an 85% reduction in referrals for speech and language support because they were able to meet much more of that need at a universal level earlier on, and then those children who did go for an assessment were ones who really needed that specialist extra support. There are models that show this is possible, so we want that early support to be available to everyone.”View image in fullscreen‘We want that early support to be available to everyone’: Georgia Gould chats to a Thomas Lord Audley pupil.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianSimon Essex, the executive head ofThomas Lord Audley, said the school had earned the trust of parents in Colchester so that it is now oversubscribed.“We want to serve our community,” he said. “We don’t want any young people who live nearby who can’t come here because we can’t meet their needs.“That’s our goal, and if that attracts others then we will work hard with the local authority to make it work. That’s why I’m hoping that the funding the government will bring will enable all schools to have the same mindset that we have for these young people.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchoolsEducation policySchool fundingChildrenanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war? | Australian military | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here
Content:
Australian facilityAustralian facility with US military accessAustralian facility with US access unresolvedUS facility with Australian accessUS corporate accessRAAF Base AmberleyRAAF Base AmberleyRAAF Base TindalHarold E. Holt Communication StationPine GapScroll downVideo credit: The Australian Ministry of DefenceIn the near pitch blackness of a wet June morning, a US B-2 Spirit stealth bomber 
                swoops from the sky, touching down on the outskirts of Brisbane to swiftly refuel – 
                engines still running – at one of the US air force’s key allied bases. 
                Before the sun is up, the nuclear-capable warplane is back in the air.RAAF Base Amberley, about 50km south-west of Brisbane, is a vital staging point for 
                US military operations across the region. But it is hardly alone.This map shows every military base in Australia, which includes US- and Australian-run bases.Analysts warn of a “saturation” of the continent by the US military, and argue that Australia’s 
                most important security ally could drag the country unwillingly into war.Amid the red dirt of Katherine, the runway at RAAF Base Tindal is being expanded to be able to better accommodate massive American B-52 bombers, the so-called “Stratofortresses”. These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask.On the remote coast of Western Australia, a cluster of highly technological assets – deep space radar, space surveillance telescope, and the Harold Holt naval communication station – provide vital information to enable US submarine and space warfare.The naval communication station is designed to reach submerged submarines. Its antenna array broadcasts on very low frequency radio.The US-run Pine Gap, in the centre of the country, is regarded by some as the US military’s most valuable intelligence site outside the continental United States.The satellite tracking and signals intelligence base detects missile launches, intercepts military communications and provides targeting information for US forces around the world.Essentially incorruptible – difficult to access, physically or otherwise – in a desert valley in the centre of a massive continent, it downloads and transmits masses of data from powerful US satellites constantly monitoring vast swathes of the globe.For the US military, Australia represents, in the words of one now-retired general, “location, location, location”.Australian militaryThe US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?Exclusive:US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them hereUS military presence in Australia, mapped – videoWhy can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcastBen Doherty,Andy BallandNick EvershedSun 6 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTShareUS militaryinterests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. TheUS militarycontrols 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”The US military-industrial complex in AustraliaEach square represents one facilityUnited States-controlled facilities with Australian access (17)Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access (24)Australian facilities with US military access (51)Australian facilities with US corporate access (18)Australian facilities with no significant US access (41)Australian facilities with US access unresolved (17)US access to Australian defence facilitiesAccess levelFacilitiesUnited States-controlled facilities with Australian access17Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access24Australian facilities with US military access51Australian facilities with US corporate access18Australian facilities with no significant US access41Australian facilities with US access unresolved17Guardian graphic‘Aligning ourselves completely’The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.Training, including for2,500 marines on dry-season rotationin the Northern Territory.Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth ofpre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.7:00US military presence in Australia, mapped – videoBeyond the military’s presence, at least 42Australian militaryfacilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.Lockheed Martinassembles guided missilesin Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to buildrocket motors for guided weaponsat Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperabilityand provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access,Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.View image in fullscreenWorkers with a missile at the Port Wakefield facility.Photograph: Lockheed MartinThe Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.TheForce Posture agreement– “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base –rather a “rotation”– but there is little contestation of its actual implication.double quotation markThis is a massive institutional failure in AustraliaProf Richard TanterArguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence ministerChristopher Pynetold a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it:Aukusis also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and anhonorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.Is Australia at war with Iran? The fine line between ‘defensive operations’ and complicityRead more“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations withChina, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”View map of military facilities by the numbers‘Waltzing its way into a war’At apress conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.View image in fullscreenUS defense secretary Pete Hegseth meets Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAMarles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.Earlier,the minister toldthe Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s2026 national defence strategyreiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.Australians’ fragile faithGovernment ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship isbroader, deeper and more enduringthan thetenures of prime ministers and presidents.But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.ALowy Institute pollshowed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.a graphicJust more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.Other findings are more damning: apoll for the Australia Institutefound more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.Explore the US military's footprint in AustraliaAustralian facilityAustralian facility with US military accessAustralian facility with US access unresolvedUS facility with Australian accessUS corporate accessAll basesAustralianUSFacility type: All types▾Guardian graphicThis represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that theTrump administrationhas repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you canliterally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”Secret documents reveal preferred Australian nuclear submarine base – and warn it could be a military targetRead moreShe cites theMarch attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”Scappatura says the phrase“empire by invitation”was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”TheAustralian bases & US involvementdatabase is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

title: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?
Author: Daniel Susskind
Headline: A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?
Content: Daniel Susskind: ‘We should try to be imaginative.’ All photographs: Lydia Goldblatt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDaniel Susskind: ‘We should try to be imaginative.’ All photographs: Lydia Goldblatt/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AIA Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?Daniel SusskindSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy. But my dad, who has the same thought as them, sees the disappointment on my face that morning – and decides to risk it. We set off. And when we arrive, the park is completely empty. Nobody else was brave enough to visit. We have everything – the rides, shows, food – to ourselves.I loved the idea of writing that story. But, as so often happens, we were too busy to do anything about it. Life ran away from us. I grew up, and we both forgot about it.Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. I told my oldest about it – and she wanted to hear the full thing. We turned to ChatGPT, gave it the vague outline and asked it to have a go at writing the story in the style of Dr Seuss (one of our favourites). Within a few seconds, we had it. She read it out – and we laughed.Of course, what this AI generated wasn’t perfect. A few lines didn’t quite make sense; a few Americanisms had slipped in (“sneakers”, “cinnamon buns”). But that night on the sofa we had great fun together tweaking the prompts, refining the story, adding more scenes, working with this strange new creative partner to do something that had escaped my grasp for decades.For the last 15 years, I have been exploring the impact of AI on work and society. But becoming a dad of three small people has made these disruptions far more personal: it is clear that their future is going to look wildly different from my past.For my wife, that realisation really sunk in a few weeks ago, on a journey to her parents’ in Suffolk. Three children, confined in a car, stuttering along the A12, is a combustible setup. So we were thrilled to find a rare podcast that everyone miraculously enjoyed: History’s Not Boring, a series of 15-minute bursts of conversation, on a kaleidoscope of subjects, narrated by two children.double quotation markWe are letting children down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabitView image in fullscreenAs we listened, we started to speculate in the car about who these whiz-kids might be. Where were they from? How were they selected? How did they juggle this job with school? Eventually, I went to the website to find out. All our answers were wrong. The kids did not, in fact, exist. The entire podcast seemed to be generated by AI. None of us had realised.It was a strange moment, learning that people we had grown fond of were not actually people at all. It was also remarkable that AI could create such high-quality educational content. But for my wife, a podcast and documentary maker, it was an unsettling moment as well: here was something that would have taken her and a talented team several days to make, and now it was being done without people.My work on AI has taken me to boardrooms and conference halls, classrooms and government buildings. But wherever I go, one question is now asked more than any other:what should my children do?Today, we are floundering. Teachers worry that the way they teach no longer seems to work. Parents, watching their children use AI to solve problems and answer questions, wonder what they really know. Employers doubt whether traditional educational achievements, awarded in time-honoured ways – coursework, exams, assessments – are still a useful guide to what young people can do.Yet reacting to these new technologies by putting barriers up, as many instinctively want to do – banning, admonishing, punishing – just cannot be right. To begin with, this is the water in which the next generation will swim: we are letting them down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit.How often, for instance, have you heard people accuse students of cheating if they use AI to help them with their work? But at what point are we cheating them by failing to overhaul the way we are educating them? If AI is making education “too easy” for young people, at what point does the burden shift on to us, the adults, to make their education more testing, to push them on, to stretch them?More importantly, this dismissiveness of AI is also unimaginative. It stops us appreciating the astounding possibilities AI could create for the next generation as well. Of course there are risks. But at the same time, if we use this technology wisely, what difficult ideas might the next generation now grasp, ones that were beyond us when we were in their shoes? What hard problems might they now solve, ones that once required years of training and experience – if they were solvable at all?Forget future-proofing skillsA big part of the challenge of AI is that our traditional response to technological disruption in the working world – the idea of “future-proofing” people – no longer works. In 2013, the then prime minister David Cameron announced that England would become the first place in the world where all children in primary and secondary schools wouldlearn to code. This, in the words of education secretary Michael Gove, would “equip every child with the computing skills they need to succeed in the 21st century”.The idea seemed bold and clever: in the years that followed, it was hard to find an advanced country that did not follow our example.Fast-forward to today. What does it turn out that the latest AI systems, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are best at doing? Writing code. In January 2026, Anthropic reported that90% of the codefor Claude Code – their AI-powered coding assistant – was itself written by AI. Skills that were meant to protect kids from technological disruption for their entire lives were largely redundant before they had even left school.double quotation markWe must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiotFor politicians and policymakers, it is tempting to dismiss the coding saga as an unfortunate blip. But this is a mistake. The reason they slipped up was because they had believed in the idea of “future-proof” skills, the thought that there exists some valuable set of skills that AI will not be able to do for some time – and that by thinking deeply enough about the future, we can accurately identify them.The truth is that we know only two things about what lies ahead. One is that it will be full of technologies that are far more capable than today. And the other is that we know little else. But rather than attempting to resolve this uncertainty, we have to accept it and instead ask a different question: how do we prepare the next generation to flourish in a future that we actually know surprisingly little about?View image in fullscreenGet back to basicsThe first step is to get back to basics. Since 2009, literacy and numeracy have been falling among young people around the world, according to the OECD’s programme for international student assessment (Pisa); the same holds true for adults. In itself, this is worrying. But given the uncertainty that we face about the future, these trends are a disaster.Why such a calamity? To begin with, while it might be hard to say precisely which more advanced skills will turn out to be most valuable in the future – creativity, judgment, something else – they will rely in some way on these basic skills. They are the foundations for everything else.What’s more, AI systems are far from flawless. They make mistakes, often on simple problems; they hallucinate, providing confident and plausible answers that are completely made up. They are, as the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton put it, “idiot savants”. That means we must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiot.So, with both those reasons in mind, we should be focusing intensely on teaching literacy and numeracy, even if AI does them better, as it increasingly seems to do. Getting back to basics is what an economist would call a “no-regrets” strategy – we will never regret improving these basic skills, however the future turns out to be.double quotation markI have used AI to respond to my five-year-old’s bedtime-delaying tactic of asking vast questions just as I turn down the lightsAnd we should try to be imaginative. When my eight-year-old grew bored learning her times tables the traditional way – long lists, learned by rote – I turned to ChatGPT to create various computer games, designed by her, to test what she knew. (Unicorns and rainbows featured in all versions.)Then there was the time my five-year-old was tired of reading his standard-issue phonics books after school – there really is only so much Biff, Chip and Kipper a human being can take – and instead we used AI to generate some custom stories together, carefully tuned to his reading level and much closer to his favourite topics. (At the time of writing, HMS Belfast, TNT explosives and Bukayo Saka.)Experimentation is important and we can learn so much from the creativity of others. Take Chris Moran, for instance, head of editorial innovation at the Guardian. His daughter had beenreading Draculaat school but was struggling to place the sprawling novel in the real world. Together, with the help of AI,they built an app–PlotLines– which placed the story on an interactive 1890s Ordnance Survey Map, plotting the key scenes and character journeys around Europe, with the help of AI. (They have done it for many other books now, too.)These are precisely the sorts of innovations we should be testing and embracing throughout education – rather than banning.View image in fullscreenTeach both, test bothDespite the uncertainty we face, there is still one thing that we do know about the future: it will be full of technologies that are vastly more powerful than today. With that in mind, we must teach the next generation to use them. To do this properly will require us to dedicate a serious chunk of time to teaching people how to use AI.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe challenge, though, is how to do this without also setting them up to forget crucial basic skills. An important,growing fearis that AI is making us stupid. Why bother reading a book if AI can summarise it? Why bother completing maths homework if AI will do the sums? And in my view the answer here lies not in Silicon Valley, but with a forgotten British maths professor, Wilfred Halliday Cockcroft, half a century ago.In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 theCockcroft Reportwas published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPTRead moreIt is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).Cockcroft was realistic: “all candidates”, he expected, “will have access to a calculator by 1985”. And his proposal was revolutionary: overhauling mathematics education by splitting it into two parts, spending part of the time teaching students to use a calculator and the rest of the time learning to cope without one – and crucially, testing both. It caught on. Learning maths without and with a calculator is now the gold standard around the world, the former nurturing the basics and the latter applying them to more fiendish problems.We should also be realistic and revolutionary, adopting this tried-and-tested principle – what I call “teach both, test both” – for AI now. Every subject, from history to English literature, should be divided in two: teach students to use AI in one part, teach students to flourish without it in the other – and, crucially, examine both. A teacher cannot monitor whether or not a student uses AI in the quiet solitude of their bedroom. But nothing can replace the feeling of sitting in an exam, looking at the paper, and feeling that cold sweat when you realise you haven’t prepared for both parts.View image in fullscreenNot all screens are badOne of my worries is that we allow a legitimate sense of concern about the impact of social media on children’s lives to seep into how we think about AI, allowing good restrictions on the former to turn into kneejerk bans on the latter. Social media and AI are not the same thing, and whereas the former often dehumanises and distracts us from the real world, AI – used in the right way – can make our lives go far better.There is another way to think about this: a debate is now under way about the “Goldilocks” amount of screen time for children – not too much, not too little, just the right amount. But this is not the right argument to be having. What matters is not so much the amount of screen time, but what is actually on those screens, what we are using this technology to do.This distinction matters not only for thinking about what we teach, but how we teach as well. Consider a further example: personal tuition. It is often said an average student who receives one-to-one tuition willoutperform almost all their peersin a traditional classroom setting. I saw this first-hand, as a tutor in Oxford for years, teaching mathematics and economics.The problem, though, is that human tutors are too expensive to provide to everyone. But now, AI can finally provide high-quality personal tuition, tailoring the way material is taught to the unique strengths and weaknesses of each student, mimicking interactions with a human tutor but at a far lower cost.In all honesty, AI provides a level of tailored instruction that I – and many other teachers I have watched over the years – have struggled to achieve. In part, it is the breadth of AI that is striking. I have used it to respond to my five-year-old’s bedtime-delaying tactic of asking vast questions just as I turn down the lights (in response to, “Daddy, where did the first human come from?” it drew up a short story about evolution), as well as to create step-by-step instructions to help graduate students solve hard mathematical problems in economics, such as the Ramsey growth model.“I don’t think anyone has ever paid such pure attention to me and my thinking and my questions,” a student was reported as sayingin The New Yorkerin April 2025. “It’s made me rethink my interactions with people.” AI never gets tired or distracted. It doesn’t have fixed office hours or limited classroom time. It will always answer one more question, always provide one more explanation of a problem you don’t understand.View image in fullscreenDaniel Susskind: ‘In the 21st century, the best ideas are likely to come from capable AIs instead of the heads of clever human beings.’Focus on problems, not the jobI am not surprised that students have beenbooing tech titansduring recent US graduation ceremonies. The most resistant groups I have spoken to over the last 15 years are young professionals: they have spent a big chunk of their life, and sunk huge amounts of money, preparing to be a lawyer or doctor or whatever it might be, and they are understandably furious when they are told, just as they cross the finish line, that the world they were preparing to enter is over.There is so much advice I would want to give them, worried at the start of their careers. But one of the most important bits is to choose a profession because the problem interests you, not the job. Bluntly, if you go into medicine because you like the look of doctors on House, or law because of Suits, or marketing because of Mad Men, then you are going to be disappointed. These jobs are soon going to look very different.But the problems themselves – improving health outcomes, providing legal advice, selling products? They are not going away. It is the way we solve them, and the skills required to do so, that will look very different.You could glimpse this well before the arrival of generative AI. Backin 2017, a team at Stanford University announced they had built a system that could tell whether or not a freckle was cancerous from a photograph as accurately as leading dermatologists. It was a remarkable moment, a lurch forward in AI-enabled diagnostics. Yet what was particularly interesting about this work is that the final co-author on theNature articlethat announced this achievement was Sebastian Thrun – not a medical doctor, but a leading computer scientist who developed the world’s first driverless car. Here was a man who knew very little about medicine at all, yet with the skills that he had was able to build a system that could rival the expertise of the finest doctors.Run towards AI and scienceWhat would I actually do if I were at the start of my career, back in the starting blocks of life? Without hesitation, I would run towards AI and science – not because it is protected from automation, but because it is where the most excitement is likely to happen in years to come. In the 20th century, the best ideas we had about the world came from the heads of clever human beings. In the 21st century, I expect they are likely to come from capable AIs instead.We could catch a glimpse of that in late 2024, when the creators of anAI built by DeepMind– AlphaFold2 – won the Nobel prize in chemistry for solvingthe “protein folding problem”(one of the greatest unsolved challenges in biology, critical for understanding how diseases work and how to treat them). At the time of writing, frontier mathematics is next in line, new discoveries appearing at an impressive rate.Imagination, imagination, imaginationThe more time I spend with AI, the more I realise the main constraint on its use in the world is the limits of our imagination. Even if we were to press pause on progress in the technology today, there would be vastly more uses for it than we have currently dreamed up.Part of the imaginative task falls to us. But that night with my eight-year-old, crafting that story, reminds me that part of it falls to the next generation as well. “We look at the world once in childhood,” wrote the poet Louise Glück, “the rest is memory.” In that spirit, we need the next generation, with their sense of adventure and open-mindedness, their lack of world-weariness, to help us think wisely and freely, together, about what we can use these extraordinary technologies to do.What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind is published by Penguin at £20. title: Meera Syal looks back: ‘South Asians weren’t seen as funny. We sold you fags or served you curry’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The actor, comedian and writer on idolising Victoria Wood, being fuelled by rage and injustice after a sexual assault, and ​t​he life-changing impact of Goodness Gracious Me
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The actor, comedian and writer on idolising Victoria Wood, being fuelled by rage and injustice after a sexual assault, and ​t​he life-changing impact of Goodness Gracious Me
Content: FlashbackFamilyMeera Syal looks back: ‘South Asians weren’t seen as funny. We sold you fags or served you curry’The actor, comedian and writer on idolising Victoria Wood, being fuelled by rage and injustice after a sexual assault, and ​t​he life-changing impact of Goodness Gracious MeHarriet GibsoneSun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlack and white photo of Meera Syal standing smiling in 1968 and recreating the image in 2026Meera Syal in 1968 and 2026. Later photograph: Simon Webb/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman, assisted by Freya Redman. Hair: Narad Kutowaroo at Carol Hayes Management. Makeup: Aarti P. Archive photograph: courtesy of Meera SyalBorn in Wolverhampton in 1961 and raised in Bloxwich, also in the West Midlands, Meera Syal is an actor, comedian, novelist and playwright who was awarded a damehood in the 2026 new year honours. Her first novel, Anita and Me, won the Betty Trask award in 1996. She rose to prominence as a writer and performer on Goodness Gracious Me and starred inThe Kumars at No 42. She has two children and is married to the actorSanjeev Bhaskar. Her memoir,Vigilauntie: A Memoir – Innit?, has just been published, and sheis starring in The Children, at the Lyric Hammersmith, London, until 3 October.I have no idea why I was posingwithmy hand on a pillarin a professional studio in Wolverhampton. My parents must have thought, “Let’s preserve the era of the only child before her brother comes along.” As it was the late 60s, I’ve got marriage-age shoes on and a slightly uncomfortable, sticky-out skirt. As for the hair, my mother clearly cut it with the kitchen scissors.This was not a typical look for me. I spent most of my days in trousers and a T-shirt, rushing around Bloxwich on my bike. I had total freedom – if only my parents knew the things I fell off, climbed up, cut myself on, nearly drowned in or got impaled on.We were the only Asian family in Bloxwich, and I was the only Asian girl in my school. There were a couple of Asian boys, who got bullied horribly, but I had a protective bubble around me because my mum was a teacher at the infant school. It got harder as I got older. It was the 70s and we were the visible wave of immigrants, so the reception wasn’t always friendly. I’m not proud of it, but I did have a brief fighting period. The school bully was a psychopath. If you looked at her the wrong way, she’d say, “I’m going to mash you out.” She’d stand at the side and let one of her little minions scrap instead – mostly hair-pulling, punching. I realised that being timid and running away made it much worse. The fact that you stood up for yourself made people think twice. They didn’t expect self-defence from a little brown girl.My imagination came alivein my teen years, because I felt so out of place. I was surrounded by images of beauty in Jackie magazine – girls who were exclusively white, thin and blond. I had a culturally multifaceted life – at home I was very Indian, very cosy and warm, eating with my fingers, speaking my language. I’d code switch the moment I left: adopt a different persona, different accent, different walk. It’s no wonder I became an actor.My one-woman play, One of Us, was a huge turning point. I developed it with my friend Jackie Shapiro at the University of Manchester, mainly because I thought, “If people knew half the stuff in my head, maybe they’d think differently about how they saw me, and people like me.” It got picked for the National Student Drama festival, then it went to the Edinburgh festival, where it won some prizes. Two weeks before I was due to take up an MA at Leeds to do drama and psychotherapy, a director walked in and said, “I’m about to do a new play bySue Townsend. Would you like to be in it? And here’s an Equity card.” Until then, I had no idea how a person like me would get a foot in the door.double quotation markI wish I could save that seven-year-old from the fear ahead – and tell her she'd meet Donny OsmondAt the start of my career, I wassexually assaulted by somebody in the industry, somebody whom I trusted. That kind of behaviour was part of the culture in the 70s, 80s and even into the 90s. From remarks such as “Cheer up, darling” to the bum pinch, to what happened to me, everything was accepted as normal. But the sense of betrayal and shock almost made me give up. I thought, “I don’t have thick enough skin. If this is the way it’s going to be, I can’t do it.” Instead of being defeated, I got angry. Instead of shrinking, I tried to get bigger. It led me to meeting a bunch of women at the Asian Women Writers’ Collective who lifted me. I found my tribe. I got politicised. I started writing properly. I was fuelled by so much rage and injustice, and realised the corrosive part of assault is the silence around it. It was an awful thing to go through, but it changed the trajectory of my life.I’d been working in theatre for years when I got my first TV job. It was on The Bill and I had to run down Whitechapel High Street in London shouting, “There’s a bomb in the restaurant!” My uncles and aunties thought my career was a waste of time, so for me to be able to tell them I was on television – even for 10 seconds – was the marker of something.Victoria Wood was my absolute idol. I looked up to her completely. Then one day I got a call, “Victoria is doing a new sitcom called Dinnerladies. She’d like to see you.” I rehearsed the part a million times; I knew it inside out. And yet … I did the worst audition of my life – just a bad Mrs Overall impression. I learned that when you want something too much, you’re going to screw it up.Shobna Gulatiwent on to play the role of Anita and she was brilliant, but I couldn’t watch it for a long time as the memory was too painful.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom 1991 to 1996, I worked on a series called The Real McCoy. It was a black sketch show, a huge success, and undoubtedly opened the door forGoodness Gracious Me. We decided to approach Jon Plowman at the BBC about the concept, who said, “I don’t really know what south Asian humour is.” Neither did we. It was hard to explain as we were never thought of as funny: we were the people that sold you fags in the corner shop or set your bones in a hospital or served you curry in a restaurant. We weren’t seen as observant or ironic or absurd. But we knew what made us laugh, and we were given a chance. We assembled a team of writers and actors, and threw together a night at the Riverside Studios. The roar of the audience who finally felt seen was intoxicating. We had to hold on to that feeling throughout the commissioning process, which took years. But it eventually transformed our lives.Lena Headey looks back: ‘I told Harvey Weinstein where to go. A decade of possibilities disappeared’Read moreIn my 60s, I’ve realisedthis career is a marathon, not a sprint. The actors I admire most are the women who have survived through the dead zone where you’re not considered attractive or relevant. There was a time when you hit 50 and had to get the slippers out, because there was going to be very little work until the batty old grandma parts came up. That has changed over the last few decades, thankfully. It’s not perfect but it is better – and the juicy roles for women come more from theatre than television.Sometimes I wish I could save that seven-year-old version of me from the fear and insecurity that’s ahead. I also wish I could tell her: when you are 39 you are going to meet Donny Osmond – the boy whose poster you kiss every night. Most of all, I wish she could know that one day other Desis will come up to her and say, “I grew up watching you. You made a difference to the way I walked down the street and felt about myself.” All of the loneliness, the bad experiences, will transform into stories – stories that change people for good.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackMeera SyalTelevisionPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kindness of strangers: A hall-of-fame athlete helped my 94-year-old mum buy a vacuum cleaner | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A woman in the queue said she was happy to drive an hour, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house. I was worried – but how wrong I was!
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: A woman in the queue said she was happy to drive an hour, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house. I was worried – but how wrong I was!
Content: Composite: Victoria Hart/Alamy/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Victoria Hart/Alamy/Guardian DesignKindness of strangersLife and styleKindness of strangers: A hall-of-fame athlete helped my 94-year-old mum buy a vacuum cleanerA woman in the queue said she was happy to drive an hour, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house. I was worried – but how wrong I was!Read more inthe kindness of strangers seriesAndrea Malone as told toKatie CunninghamSun 6 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a 94-year-old woman, my mother is still very busy and active. So when a vacuum cleaner she liked the look of went on sale at a national electronics chain, Mum drove herself to the nearest store to buy it.Unfortunately, the shop in her area had sold out by the time she got there. The sales assistant told her it was still available in another Melbourne store – but that store was an hour’s drive away. As active as she is, Mum pointed out that at her age she really could not manage a drive of that length. She asked the sales assistant if they could transfer the vacuum to this store and was flatly told no.Just as Mum was feeling a bit taken aback by the poor customer service, the woman in the queue behind her interjected. She told Mum that she was happy to drive all that way, pick up the vacuum, then bring it to Mum’s house for her.The kindness of strangers: My car had been towed and my kids had no shoes, then a man made a wonderful offerRead moreThe woman in the queue seemed to be a genuinely nice person, so Mum allowed the vacuum to be ordered for her and gave the woman her address.As Mum recounted this story to me later, my heart sank. I couldn’t envisage a good outcome. But how wrong I was!The stranger was as good as her word. The next day, she drove all the way to pick up this vacuum cleaner and bring it to my mother’s house. Finally, having delivered the vacuum, the stranger asked if Mum was OK with putting it all together. Of course she wasn’t, so the woman did it for her.They kept in touch and even later went out for coffee – Mum doesn’t let anyone go that quickly! It was only later that Mum discovered the woman was actually a very well-known Australian sportswoman: basketballer Michele Timms.Neither my sister nor I live in Melbourne, so Mum relies on friends and family there for help. That a stranger would step up like that made me feel that there is real hope for the world. The generosity of it is mind-blowing, and something that is unexpected in this day and age.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
