title: Woman Unknown review – postwar paranoia with some deliciously dastardly Du Maurier touches | Movies | The Guardian
description: A nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival
Content: Tested to the limit … Mathilde Arcel in Woman Unknown.Photograph: courtesy Venice film festivalView image in fullscreenTested to the limit … Mathilde Arcel in Woman Unknown.Photograph: courtesy Venice film festivalMoviesReviewWoman Unknown review – postwar paranoia with some deliciously dastardly Du Maurier touchesVenice film festivalA nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survivalPeter BradshawSun 6 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 16.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an elegantly appointed drama-thriller from May el-Toukhy, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, with something ofAlfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca, which it consciously recalls. As director and co-writer, El-Toukhy has created a shrewd and painful movie about the terrible things you need to do to survive, and what it takes to forget those things afterwards.The scene is a prosperous, upper-middle-class apartment in Copenhagen just after the second world war, when the Danish resistance was permitted the powers of a secret-police militia to detain and interrogate those suspected of having given assistance to the Nazis. Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund) is a ageing factory owner and widower who has evidently fallen in love with his infant daughter’s nanny: this is Marie (fiercely and convincingly played by Mathilde Arcel). Or at any rate, he sees that the child needs a new mother, finds Marie attractive and appreciates her submissive attitude. They are now engaged.As for Marie herself, her fellow servants do not appear to resent her counter-jumper prominence as the new lady of the house; very indiscreetly, she sleeps with Christian in what will shortly be the marital bed. Marie has a reasonable working relationship with housekeeper Esther (Marina Bouras) who would otherwise be Rebecca’s stern Mrs Danvers figure but is in fact pleasant enough, though she disapproves of Marie’s friendly relationship with single-mother neighbour Mrs Berg (Sofia Nolsøe), whose worldly, sophisticated air she finds disagreeable.But poor Marie’s ability to cover up her own secret fears and sins is tested to the limit when she is expected, in a pure Daphne du Maurier touch, to wear the wedding gown of Christian’s late wife at the ceremony. She has to carry it on public transport to the dressmakers to get it altered (another Hitchcockian display), which leads to a disastrous encounter with someone from her past.Oasis, auteurs and seven hours of Bertolucci: 12 unmissable movies at the Venice film festivalRead moreAnd all the time, Danish women who are accused of having consorted with Germans are shamed in the street; their heads are shaved and swastikas painted on their back. The film also shows the great and underacknowledged truth of this, in postwarDenmarkas in postwar France: shaming women was a convenient way for men to divert attention from their own far more substantial and far-reaching Nazi collaboration. This includes Christian, whose factory would have gone broke without Nazi customers.The shadow of suspicion closes in on their well-appointed household as the wedding day approaches and, as various ruses occur to her to make sure that the past does not rise up to overwhelm her, Marie discovers a new strain of cunning and ruthlessness and self-pity in herself. This is a very watchable, expertly managed drama about the return of the repressed.Woman Unknown screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsSecond world warDenmarkVenice film festivalThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A part-time musician and an office manager disagreed on benefits and work-life balance, but ​where did they stand on community responsibility?
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: A part-time musician and an office manager disagreed on benefits and work-life balance, but ​where did they stand on community responsibility?
Content: Henry and Lynn. All photographs: Sonja Horsman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHenry and Lynn. All photographs: Sonja Horsman/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’A part-time musician and an office manager disagreed on benefits and work-life balance, but ​where did they stand on community responsibility?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howSam WollastonSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenHenry, 33, ManchesterOccupationWaiter and musicianVoting recordGreen. He describes himself as “left leaning”Amuse boucheJumped into a canal for one of his music videos. In JanuaryView image in fullscreenLynn, 61, BuryOccupationOffice managementVoting recordConservative in the UK. Democrat when she lived in the USAmuse boucheWon the French prize at school, though she’s rubbish at FrenchFor startersLynnThe restaurant has beautiful views of rolling hills. I had roast chicken and potatoes, panna cotta and a couple of glasses of red wine.HenryI ordered an old fashioned, and some white wine with the meal. I had a lovely peach salad, then a pizza. I told Lynn I grew up in Dubai, went to a French school, then uni in Paris with my final year in Bristol, which was my first taste of life in the UK.LynnHenry looks like a Green voter: flip-flops, pink trousers, bushy beard, earrings. My daughter might have voted Green when she was 16, because you think everything is free, but as you get older you realise someone has to pay. It’s unicorn politics.HenryLynn definitely had more facts and figures than I did, and is more opinionated. I’m still building my thoughts and opinions.View image in fullscreenThe big beefLynnI’m a huge proponent of the benefits system for people who need it, but it is exploited. A business owner I know looking for a labourer offered someone £35,000 a year. The guy flat-out said, “Sorry mate, with my housing benefit, my child benefit and everything else, that’s not worth me getting out of bed for.” There’s something seriously wrong with that.HenryI work in a restaurant, but when my hours go down I reapply for universal credit. I looked for other jobs, but ultimately didn’t find anything. Along with work, time for yourself and socialising with friends and family are the cornerstones of living. Without that, I wouldn’t have made my album, which is my passion.LynnI was raised on a poor council estate, and everybody worked and everybody’s gardens were nice. Go to those estates now and there’s no pride. People scream poverty, but they’ve got new iPhones, Sky TV, they’re getting their nails done. How can it be that you can’t afford to feed your children if you’re getting all that? The problem with Britain today is that it’s more about quality of life than working really hard, and Henry is part of that.HenryI’m more likely to volunteer, help out a community, if I’m in a good place. Having a social life is also important to maintain mental health. I did feel there was a generational difference between us. I don’t know if it’s the optimism of youth.View image in fullscreenSharing plateLynnWe agreed politicians need to stop chasing votes and stand up for what they believe in. And there needs to be more pride in the country. Look at Europe: people there are clearing the streets. We have none of that here.HenryThere can be a lack of community. And I do agree cheating the system isn’t right. On immigration, Lynn did somewhat sway me that there might be a physical limit to the number of people we can take in.View image in fullscreenFor aftersLynnI don’t agree with the full face coverings for Muslim women. It stops integration. How is it OK that someone on a motorcycle has to take off their helmet in a petrol station because you have to be able to see their face, but then you make different rules for different people? If you’re coming to a country, you have to assimilate.HenryYou should respect the culture of where you move to, but it doesn’t mean you have to ditch your own. Whether women should cover up is a different question, but they’re not a threat. Maybe because of where I grew up, I’m more comfortable around Muslims in full veils than a group of British lads in hoodies and tracksuits.View image in fullscreenDining across the divide: ‘I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”’Read moreTakeawaysLynnHenry’s lovely. He lives in an idealistic world and wouldn’t it be lovely if we could all live there? I don’t agree with his politics, but it’s good to hear other people’s points of view. We had a hug and went our separate ways.HenryLynn might have got more out of it if I’d had more facts, more debating power. There were a couple of times it got a bit animated – I said something and she repeated it, saying, “Are you serious?” But we had a nice dinner and a nice chat. A good, one-off experience.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeLynn and Henry ate atTre Ciccioin Ramsbottom, BuryWant to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ – but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Our US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Our US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Horse play … the Welsh Mari Lwyd procession at Chepstow Castle.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHorse play … the Welsh Mari Lwyd procession at Chepstow Castle.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS newsSome Americans call us ‘Europoor’ – but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly richEmma BeddingtonOur US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff …Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 14.43 EDTShareI’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) arecalling us Europeans, mocking us for ourlow salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.GB news presenter Tom Harwooddeclared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan.There are massive, obvious caveats. GDP is a wholly inadequate proxy for quality of life or even prosperity: theUN’s proposed alternative dashboard of 31 indicatorsincludes the likes of “respect for the planet” and wealth inequalities, against which the US would surely take a beating.US mortality rates are higher than European onesandlife expectancy is lower, so, when a medical diagnosis or accident could bankrupt you, how rich do you really feel?But, actually, this Europoor stuff is hitting me where it hurts: my New York-based grad student son out-earns me, and his junior nurse girlfriend is paid six figures – that’s more than I made in a city law firm. Quite right – nursesshouldearn more than corporate lawyers – but it’s hard to imagine them ever choosing to live here in the UK (an NHSnurse’s starting salary is £32,073).To console myself as I contemplate years of getting even Europoorer, flying long-haul to hug my son, I’ve been counting the ways we’re Eurorich. Sure, healthcare, social protections, holidays, blah blah – but what about thereallyimportant stuff?Cheese“The United States offers over 1,000+ cheese varieties and styles,” theCheese from the USA website claims, to which I would counter: “But do any of them taste of anything?” I doubt a single Freedom Cheese can clear a train carriage like a ripe époisses.BikesApparently, Americansbuy 130m bicyclesa year, but I suspect that’s thanks to a handful of legmaxxing California billionaires. Anyway, 130m also feels like the number of bikes parked outside Amsterdam Centraal station on any given day (in 2019, 41% of Netherlanderssaid the bike was their main mode of transport).SaintsThe US has 11 saints– pathetic. I’ve seen the remains of more than 11 saints in a single European mini-break;Ireland alone has an estimated 1,000.Wholesome foodLet’s take stock ofthis summer’s US food safety scares. Lettuce,blueberries,jalapenos,fruit bars,granola,eggs,alfalfa sprouts,mangoes,sourdough,tofu… basically anything healthier than Flamin’ Hot Cheetos is a gamble; Gwyneth Paltrow is probably claiming asylum in Puglia as I write.Weird rulersSure, they have their stable genius, but nothing can match absolute monarchy and centuries of inbreeding for floridly unhinged leadership.Charles VI of Francethought he was made of glass; the future Peter III of Russiacourt-martialled a ratfor eating one of his toy soldiers.Characterful teethThe US has, I read, “entered the age of veneer regret”, with people rueing their decision to drop big money on massive, gleaming, Hollywood teeth. Not over here! We’ve still got teeth Breugel the Elder would recognise (in the UK it’s partly because wecan’t access affordable dentistry, but sssh).Disturbing folkloreScratch the surface of any European country and some weird, sinister custom emerges. At Belgium’sMatî l’Ohê festivalthey mourn a bone by waving celery; Austria’s demon-chasingPerchten festivalinvolves dressing like a horned haystack; in Wales’sMari Lwyd, peopletake a horse skull on a pole from door to door singingfor midwinter. In the name of carnival, wethrow herringin northern France,execute a pretend marein Czechia and huntpeople dressed as bearsall overthe place. And really, what’s better – purchasing power or an annual opportunity to wave celery at a bone? I know my answer.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionEuropeHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: It felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquiet | John Harris | The Guardian
description: This young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edge, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: This young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edge, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Geese at the End of the Road festival in Dorset, 3 September 2026.Photograph: End of the Road festivalView image in fullscreenGeese at the End of the Road festival in Dorset, 3 September 2026.Photograph: End of the Road festivalOpinionGeeseIt felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquietJohn HarrisThis young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edgeSun 6 Sep 2026 06.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShare“If you want me to pay my taxes,” sang the 23-year-old man on the stage, loudly accompanied by the thousands in front of him, “You better come over with a crucifix/ You’re gonna have to nail me down.”Last Thursday night, I stood in a field in Dorset, and watched the headlining attraction on the first night of the End of the Road festival. Geese are a rock group from New York, led by the extremely talentedCameron Winter,who has a lot to say, and an often gnomic, veiled way of saying it. But the meaning of the most celebrated lines on his band’s most recent album – Getting Killed – might be clearer than a lot of the rest.There are hundreds ofdifferent interpretationsonline of a song simply called Taxes, from death and martyrdom to the avoidance of responsibility.He may just, I suppose, be telling the Internal Revenue Service to go away in the cause of small-state libertarianism. But at the risk of ridicule, I’ll opt for the most literal and crowd-pleasing reading: that Winter is inspirationally updating the idea of rock music sneering at the powers that be and rejecting whatever it is they want. When I first heard those lines, in fact, I imagined him being cornered by Donald Trump, JD Vance and some or other Maga goon squad, wearily exhaling and sending them on their way.For at least a decade now, rock – which is to say, stuff largely made with guitars and mostly delivered by bands – has been in an increasing state of cultural eclipse. Its presence in what remains of the singles chart is usually minimal-to-nonexistent; it tends to fare better in the albums rankings, but chronically lacks its old ability to push itself to the forefront of its era.It’s striking, then, that Geese’s somewhat belated rise has been powered by an album that consummately embodies its time, has received praise to match and is evidently loved by younger people who were supposed to have long ago become largely rock-phobic (for proof,see the footageof Geese’s performance at this year’s Reading festival). Their current high profile has been powered not just byGetting Killed, but Winter’s much more intimate solo album – titled Heavy Metal – and a one-man performance at Carnegie Hall in New York, about to be released as a film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson. Seemingly as a matter of contractual obligation, all four members of his group (including guitarist Emily Green) have hairstyles like those of the early-1970s Rolling Stones, but the music they now make – their first album came out in 2018 – usually suggests something immeasurably more contemporary.It is variously tender, soothing, angry and explosive, prone to tumble into lengthy improvisation, and sometimes shot through with knowingness that can be maddening, but is presumably the result of working in an artistic field now full of cliches that either have to be acknowledged or swerved around. But when they play live, power, ferocity and sudden snaps between loudness and calm take precedence. Some moments are redolent of Led Zeppelin, but taken somewhere completely different by the lyrical content. Radiohead are another oft-cited reference point, which feels more satisfactory, but only in the sense thatGeeselargely stay true to the idea that they should sound like no one but themselves and damn the consequences.This is an age in which a huge amount of popular music is tailor-made for audiences assumed to be in a constant state of distraction, so songs often have the briskest of intros and the crassest, most earworm-ish hook lines. Geese’s music, by contrast, is often gnarly and difficult, and entails friction between the musicians and their listeners. It took me six or seven plays to even start to get my head around Getting Killed, but in an occasionally masochistic way, I enjoyed every minute.And this, I think, is why. From its title onwards, Getting Killed is full of flickers and flashes of the volatile and frightening condition of both Geese’s home country and the wider world. Among the first words on the album, repeated five times, are “There’s a bomb in my car”, quickly followed by “My daughter is dead.” Otherlyrics seem – seem – to reference the crazed ringmaster who has led the US into both internal conflict and disastrous entanglements abroad: “All people/In times of war/Must go down to the circus,” Winter sings on a piece titled 100 Horses, following that up with “There is only dance music in times of war/But we have danced for too long.” What you really yearn for is a zinger akin to Bob Dylan’s “even the president of the United States/Sometimes must have to stand naked.” But Winter’s facility with words suggests he will soon get there, even if he is currently too keen on bathetically bursting his own lyrical bubble and thereby avoiding the “spokesperson for a generation” deadweight that Dylan found so irksome: “There were hundred horses dancing/Maybe 124,” he sings at one point, which isn’t even that funny.View image in fullscreenGeese performing on the Canopy stage at the Reading festival, 28 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PABut such slip-ups are rare. At the core of what Geese do is something that is also sharply generational. It’s surely one of the identifying features of people their age that even comparative material comfort (all four were privately educated) doesn’t make the anxiety that comes with being the canaries in the coalmine of digital capitalism unavoidable. The title track puts this point plainly: “I’m getting killed by a pretty good life,” wails Winter. “Getting killed by a pretty good life/I have been fucking destroyed by the city tonight.” A track titled Half Real suggests twentysomethings so understandably confounded that they just want to switch off. On Thursday, Winter sang with such ferocity that any lingering suspicions about archness or humour instantly vanished: “I’ve got half a mind/To just pay for the lobotomy/And tell ’em get rid of the bad times/And get rid of the good times too/I’ve got no more thinking to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn the face of it, there may be reasons to keep your distance: their comparatively privileged backgrounds, or aspurt of controversyabout the ubiquity and craftiness of their (very common) online marketing. But their empathetic kind of excellence makes those things almost irrelevant. What they excel at is reflecting their audience’s experiences, feelings, passions and furies back at them. At End of the Road, evidence of that connection was consistently there on the giant screen next to the stage. The younger members of the audience pressed against the barrier at the front rejoiced in every note of Taxes, and sang along most loudly to that eternal rebuke to the hypocrisies of power and influence: “Doctor, heal yourself.” But what was most telling was the ecstatic exchange between the band and their core crowd triggered by asimple linefrom one of Winter’s love songs, which seemed to take on quite another meaning: “I see myself in you.”They would doubtless hate me for saying so, but still: right now, Geese sound like the accidental representatives of a global demographic that may look sensitive and gentle, but that – in response to the impossibility of just about everything – may yet explode. In that sense, the simplest of messages is woven into what they do: look out.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGeeseOpinionPop and rockFestivalsIndiecommentShareReuse this content

title: There are three ways to shut down an annoying conversation – but are they too brutal? | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: We’ve all had meetings that could have been emails. Often, this also applies to casual chats with your friends, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: We’ve all had meetings that could have been emails. Often, this also applies to casual chats with your friends, writes Polly Hudson
Content: “Let me stop you there …”Photograph: Tetra Images/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreen“Let me stop you there …”Photograph: Tetra Images/Getty Images/Tetra images RFOpinionWork & careersThere are three ways to shut down an annoying conversation – but are they too brutal?Polly HudsonWe’ve all had meetings that could have been emails. Often, this also applies to casual chats with your friendsSun 6 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTShareThe last thing you need in a meeting that could have been an email is attachments. Sadly, it’s sod’s law that there’s one oblivious person in every work gathering who raises extra, unnecessary queries using as many words as possible, and holds everybody up. Now,Forbes magazine has helpfully suppliedthree phrases business leaders can use to stop rambling questions from hijacking or lengthening proceedings, without embarrassing the hijacking lengthener.But obviously it’s not only the office where we encounter those seemingly hellbent on derailing interactions, so can we steal Forbes’ gameplan for boring chat in real life?Many conversations are DOA, too dull to rescue, but others – at a party, the school gates, a random bump-into – can be going fine until a third party ruins it by asking for or providing superfluous details that stymie the story. Sometimes you’re not married to that party, so you can’t give them a Paddington hard stare or pinch them. What does Forbes advise?Could the right question bring some magic to your meetings? | Emma BeddingtonRead more“Phrase one: route the tangent somewhere else. Say, ‘Let me pause you there. That’s worth discussing, but it’s more than we can cover here … Send me the rest, and I’ll follow up after the meeting.’” Clearly too formal for a casual natter, but there’s still gold in them thar hills. “I’d love to hear all about this when there’s time – text me later,” may be the most artful get-out-of-chat-free card ever played. Next?“Phrase two: close a question you’ve already answered. Say, ‘We covered that earlier, so I’m going to keep us moving.’” Bit brutal, so IRL maybe reply, “But, anyway …” and then steer the convo in the direction you want to go (presumably towards the exit).And finally: “Phrase three: give the floor to someone else. Say, ‘I want to make sure we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet. Let’s take the next question from someone new.’” It was good while it lasted, but unfortunately every technique has its limits. There’s no way of saying this, whether in the pub or at the conference room table, that won’t be loudly and clearly received as STFU.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Burnham talks of radical change, but Treasury mood music says otherwise | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Bond market volatility means John Healey will have to take tough decisions, soon, if he wants to meet spending pledges
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Bond market volatility means John Healey will have to take tough decisions, soon, if he wants to meet spending pledges
Content: The chancellor, John Healey, left, talks to Andy Burnham during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, South Yorkshire in July.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey, left, talks to Andy Burnham during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, South Yorkshire in July.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAEconomics viewpointEconomic growth (GDP)Burnham talks of radical change, but Treasury mood music says otherwiseHeather StewartBond market volatility means John Healey will have to take tough decisions, soon, if he wants to meet spending pledgesSun 6 Sep 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTShareIn John Healey’s bright Treasury office, overlooking St James’s Park, the artwork has not changed since his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, selected a row of Bridget Riley printsin her feminist rehang. Judging by the signals emerging from No 11 about the chancellor’s 28 October budget, not much else has changed either.Voters listening toAndy Burnham’s promises to overthrow 40 years of neoliberalismand vanquish the ghost of Margaret Thatcher would be excused for expecting a radical policy reset. Early signs suggest they may be disappointed.Healey will give a speech about growth policy on Monday in his bluff, reassuring style, less than six months on fromReeves’s Mais lecture. He is expected to lean heavily on two of her favourite themes: investment and devolution.That’s hardly surprising. The UK economy has been held back by decades of underinvestment, and growth has been far too concentrated in London and the south-east.But the speech seems likely to be followed up six weeks or so later with a “steady as she (or rather he) goes” budget – with key decisions, including when the UK will be spending 3% of GDP on defence, deferred.When he resigned in June, Healey was adamant that the UK should set a “headmark date” of 2030 for hitting the 3% target. Treasury sources indicate that he has not changed his mind, yet he has made clear he intends todefer setting out a timelineuntil next year’s spending review.That suggests Reeves’s promise of one major fiscal event a year – the autumn budget – with a low-key forecast in the spring has been ditched.Usually, the budget before a spending review would set out the “envelope” – the broad path of future public spending – and, where necessary, the tax rises to finance it, leaving the details to be hammered out later. But the priorities for 28 October appear to be more immediate. Healey will fill in the gaps in the defence investment plan – the one he resigned over three months ago.There may be also modest further moves towards giving consumers “breathing space” from higher energy bills in January – though judging by themood music, it will not be funded, as the Trades Union Congress has urged, by awindfall tax on banks.Healey told the Financial Times this weekend: “People look at the banks largely as big profit-making multinationals, but their fundamental role is too often overlooked. That’s something that’s strong in my mind.”‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?Read moreThere is some logic for projecting what the chancellor has called “steadiness”. He has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, where volatility in government bond markets was a hot topic.Higher interest rates on the Treasury’s debt pile already appear to have wiped out up to half of the £24bn headroom Reeves left against her fiscal rules.Up to another £4bn is expected to have evaporated as a result of lower-than-forecast migration, andBurnham’s VAT cut on electricity billswill have to be paid for, too.It must be tempting to paper over the cracks and hope for the best. But the truth is that it will be all but impossible to raise defence spending to 3% by 2030 and avert the Whitehall funding squeeze pencilled in by Reeves for the back end of the parliament without raising taxes.Last year’s spending review was predicated on generous increases in spending for key departments including the NHS and defence for Labour’s first two years in power, followed by a much tougher three years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat means, as Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies told me, “things are so tight that if the government knows for sure, for example, that they want to increase defence spending to 3% by the end of the parliament, that would mean that to stick within the current plans, you’d have to hold all other departments, including the NHS, flat.” She added with typical understatement: “That seems pretty unlikely.”Miller said: “If you don’t want to do that, you probably want to find the money now, for the spending review next year. If you really want to get defence to 3%, that is a real challenge … the budget is the right time to be making preparations that would allow that to be possible.”That’s an extremely tough message to announce for a government that claims to be “bringing back hope”.One approach would have been to point to the fragility of the global environment – Iran, Ukraine, Donald Trump’s tariffs – and ditch some of Labour’s manifesto promises on tax and spend. But Burnham has already rejected that idea.There is no doubt more to be done on reforming welfare – so that more young people are encouraged into work instead of left without help, for example, as Alan Milburn’s forthcoming review is expected to recommend. And certainly, Burnham’s erstwhile friend Lord O’Donnell is right that the triple lock pensions promise should go.But that is unlikely to take Healey to the £10bn-ish additional spending he needs to get to 3% of GDP – let alone the 3.5% Labour has promised by 2035 – while still convincing the bond markets there is a plan for balancing the books.As the Resolution Foundation pointed out this week, the 3.5% targetlooks impossible to meet without tax rises on middle-earners– who still face less of a burden on average than in many other major economies, but may feel otherwise.Burnham’s choice of Healey as chancellor read like an endorsement of 3% defence spending by 2030. Postponing the decision will just unleash another six months of the destabilising speculation so depressingly familiar from Reeves’s tenure in No 11. Healey should bite the bullet at the budget and take the tough decisions now.Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)Economics viewpointLabourEconomic policyEconomicsJohn HealeyRachel ReevesAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: It’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we think, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: It’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we think, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A sit-in organised by the Cockroach Janta party, an Indian youth protest movement, Delhi, 6 June 2026.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenA sit-in organised by the Cockroach Janta party, an Indian youth protest movement, Delhi, 6 June 2026.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersOpinionMiddle East and north AfricaThe world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter futureSimon TisdallIt’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we thinkSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 08.43 EDTShareDon’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a trulyapocalyptic global outlookbegins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse.Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “new era of possibility” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’sglobal bond market upheaval, sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact hechose Ukrainefor his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, iseyeing UK defence vulnerabilities. These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged.Little wonder some analysts believe a third world war has already begun. Those who say this is over-dramatic should consider the following snapshots of the state of the world in 2026. From Kyiv to Khorramshahr, Kordofan and Kachin, conflicts flare and subside but never seem to end. All-out Russian aggression in Ukraine, now mostly comprising daily attempts to murder and terrorise civilians, is into its fifth year. Trump has lost his Iran bet, but keepskilling and bombingwith no end in sight. Insouthern Sudan, appalling atrocities go unchecked. InMyanmar,a people’s war against a brutal junta rages on. Israel’s response to the 2023 massacres has triggered an ongoing regional war embroiling Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Iran and the Gulf states. Worldwide,record numbersof people are displaced by conflict.Increasingly interconnected, these wars threaten to merge into one uncontrollable global conflagration. The alliance system, key pillar of the post-1945 order, is eating itself. Donald Trump taunts Europe andNatowith tariffs, troop withdrawals, barbs and insults at a time of acute vulnerability. Canada and the USare at daggers drawnas the White House bully fatuously threatens Venezuela – or Greenland-style annexation. Chinaaids North Korea, which also aids Russia, which aids Iran, which aids Hezbollah and the Houthis. In Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia, China looms menacingly as partnerships with Washington fray. In Taiwan, fears of invasion grow, aggravated by Trump’s obsequiousappeasing of Xi Jinping.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Xi Jinping in Beijing, 15 May 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Pool/APEverywhere you look, humanitarian crises caused by war, the climate crisis or natural disasters are producing chaotic mass migrations, malnutrition and disease. Increasingly, the suffering overwhelms a UN-led aid system crippled by US and UK funding cuts. In the fertile West Bank,900,000 Palestinians, their homes and farms besieged by settler extremists, are now food insecure, the World Food Programme says. In Somalia,millions go hungryamid record drought and predicted El Niño-related flooding. Colombia and Afghanistan face similar perils. Humanitarian and human rights outrages take individual form, too. In Hong Kong, for example, an ailingJimmy Lai, brave champion of free speech, languishes in 23-hour-a-day solitary confinement, a tortured casualty of Chinese communism’s hatred of democracy and civil rights.Skittish bond markets may be the least of the world’s economic and financial problems. Is a crash coming, reminiscent of 2008, only worse? The signs are ominous. The US just notched up a record$40tn in national debt. France, the UK, Japan and others are deep in the red, too. Unmanageable current-account deficits, rising inflation and the huge, draining diversion of investment into bloated AI tech companies all point to what market analysts cutely call a “disorderly correction”. By some estimates, the Nvidia chip-maker, plus Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, are “worth” about23% of the entire US stock market. Meanwhile, unaffordable northern-hemisphere energy and food prices loom this winter, exacerbated by Trump’s Middle East forever folly. In the worst case, all this could translate into global recession and yet more political instability. It’s a gigantic bubble waiting to burst.The existential hazards posed by the climate crisis and global heating should require scant elaboration after the terrifyingNepal-Tibet flood disaster. Similarly inimical to life on Earth, in an avoidable, human-made way, is the rapid proliferation of nuclear weapons, including so-called “battlefield” or tactical nukes that are more likely to be used in war zones such as Ukraine or Iran. All nine nuclear weapons states are expanding or modernising their arsenals, withChina in the lead. Countries such as South Korea and Saudi Arabia weigh their nuclear options. And now this atomic arms race is expanding into space. There really seems no limit to humanity’s relentless, doom-laden drive towards self-destruction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine MalikRead moreThe fundamental values of post-Enlightenment liberal societies are everywhere under siege. The rule of law is routinely flouted. While Putin and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu ignore war-crimes arrest warrants, Trump and his unctuous lickspittle,Marco Rubio, actively work to destroy the international criminal court. Across Europe, far-right racists, loons and bigots make political advances, seen again this weekend in the east German state ofSaxony-Anhalt. Next year, France will approach its own fateful national reckoning. In the US, Trump, enabled by a supine majority in Congress and dishonourable supreme court justices, is constructing a “constitutional dictatorship” to subvert future elections, symbolised by a gross, 250ft-tall “Arc de Trump”. Let alarm bells ring: US democracy and the entire western democratic tradition are in dire peril.What is to be done? Is any consolation to be had? First, key pillars of the post-1945 order, though badly battered, are still just about intact. The UN and most of its agencies, the international court of justice and collaborative, multinational western democratic alliances such as the EU, Nato and the G7 have so far survived the current tumult. Second, the age of tyrants is nearing an end. Theseangry old menare mostly headed for nursing homes, jail or the grave. May their legacies of fear and hate die with them. Last, younger generations in many “middle power” and developing countries, exemplified by India’sCockroach youth protest movement, are making plain their revulsion and rejection of the way the world is now. Like Burnham, they believe passionately in the power of possibility and change.The future lies not in the hands of political thugs and killers, of dictators and megalomaniacs, but in the hands of ordinary people everywhere. It depends on millions upon millions of individual daily acts of kindness, selflessness, faith and courage. So don’t lose heart. Keep your eyes open. Unblock your ears. And don’t look down!Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom | Nell Frizzell | The Guardian
description: I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect, says journalist and author Nell Frizzell
Author: Nell Frizzell
Headline: I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect, says journalist and author Nell Frizzell
Content: ‘I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic chairs as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders.’Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreen‘I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic chairs as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders.’Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAOpinionCareersAged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroomNell FrizzellI’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospectSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareYou know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.View image in fullscreenNell Frizzell in a homemade ladybird fancy dress costume, made while she was at school.Photograph: Nell Frizzell/The GuardianBut as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometresback home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the namethe Strokes, and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.I’m also far from the only person I knowhole-punching their way into a new careerafter decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years andthenwent into creative fields –Romesh Ranganathan,Philip Pullman,Joanne Harris,Greg Daviesand so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd this time I don’t even need to bring in my PE kit.Nell Frizzell is a journalist and authorExplore more on these topicsCareersOpinionTeacher trainingTeachingWork & careersSchoolscommentShareReuse this content

title: Air conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or not | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis
Content: ‘Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.’Photograph: Ay Moments/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.’Photograph: Ay Moments/Getty ImagesClimate crisisAir conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or notEduardo PorterGlobal AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisisSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareThe greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to“degrow”the economy and tocurb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation overair conditioning.If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts toreduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to theWorld Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world,according to the International Energy Agency(IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they aregenerally poorerand they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today,according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of40% to 50%of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.This is going to requirea lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciencesestimated thatin India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to aUnited Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.So what does one do? Apparently,58% of the Frenchwould rather “suffer from the heat than install an air conditioner in order to protect the environment”. But these sentiments cannot drive the world’s response to a warming world. To fight the battle against climate change requires, in fact, facilitating access to AC for billions of people who are now at risk of facing a hotter planet without the technology to protect themselves and their economies.This proposition doesn’t rest only on arguments from ethics – although there are plenty of those. For starters, there is substantial evidence that air conditioning reduces heat’s impact on health.One study of US datafound that the lethality of days hotter than 80F (27C) declined by about 75% from 1900 to 2004, almost entirely due to the adoption of residential air conditioning. Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.Another powerful reason is that limiting access to air conditioning will set back economic growth. There is abundant evidence that excessive heat in the workplacereduces labor productivityand that air conditioningmitigates the decline. Heat can also stymiestudent achievement,eroding human capital.Those living in India, Bangladesh, Indonesia or other unbearably hot places wherever will not heed the call to resist AC. Demanding unrealistic policies that are detrimental to their development is a straightforward strategy to ensure these countries do not cooperate with the effort to slow climate change.Campaignsfrom the west to stophydropowerin Africa, (even as westerners also called tostop developing fossil fuelson the continent) delivered little and engendered ill will. Trying to limit their access to AC would do the same.Whether it is to power industries, improve transportation, or cool homes and workplaces, achieving faster economic growth will require poor hot countries around the world to consume more energy. Their economic development is indispensable for the global battle against climate change.Just as fans of depopulation must understand that innovationneeds people, fans of shrinking humanity’s footprint on the planet to prevent climate change misunderstand how humanity has prospered despite environmental constraints: through innovation. The path to decarbonization requires figuring out how to produce zero-carbon energy on a vast scale everywhere. It will be easier to do thisin a rich worldwith AC and refrigeration than in a poor hot one.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisExtreme heatEconomicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they are
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they are
Content: Piazza del Popolo in Rome earlier this year. ‘Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe.’Photograph: Antonio Masiello/GettyView image in fullscreenPiazza del Popolo in Rome earlier this year. ‘Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe.’Photograph: Antonio Masiello/GettyOpinionExtreme heatThe Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us allEditorialWith thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they areSun 6 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.36 EDTShareThe numbers are now trickling in:nearly 2,900dead in the UK,at least 35,000dead across Europe. That’s how many people are believed to have lost their lives in this year’s early-summer heatwaves– the death tolls for the August heatwaves have yet to be counted. In a sense, these people died in a series of natural disasters, similar to the hundreds who died last month after flooding in Nepal, or during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain. And yet we do not process these events the same way. Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe, but they are rarely framed as such.There are some obvious reasons for this. Heatwaves by definition unfold over longer periods than other disasters, they are less dramatic, the majority of those who die are elderly or otherwise vulnerable, and their deaths often take weeks or months to be catalogued and reported, all of which make heatwaves seem less immediate and visible. But while heatwaves will probably never provoke the same visceral shock as earthquakes or tornadoes, it should still be possible to shift the way the public thinks about them, which could save lives and lessen their damage.The first and most obvious change is in the way heatwaves are reported on. The tendency to use images of“fun in the sun”should be balanced by serious examination ofdisrupted transitand thedangers of living in sweltering buildings. Perhaps the immediate fallout could be made more legible: heatwave deaths might be made more granular with personal detail. Ultimately, governments should report the death tolls and other fallout closer to the actual event – recall that during the Covid-19 pandemic the UK government statistics reporting wastweakedto reflect weekly Covid-specific deaths, which the media and public followed with close interest.More could also be done to make heatwaves feel like a major collective experience, similar to other disasters. Research shows that over time the British public have come to regard heatwaves as aserious problem, onelinked to the climate crisis. But at the same time, most people think that they arepersonally unlikelyto suffer any health consequences. Worryingly, work by the British Red Cross showed thata majority of thoseaged over 75 did not consider themselves vulnerable to extreme heat.It would help to better communicate the risks and potential adaptation measures to vulnerable people, but equally good would be fostering a sense of community responsibility. Currently, the UK government has an excellent system to warn specific sectors – such as medical and care services – about extreme heat. This messaging should be expanded, and voluntary and local groups should be further encouraged to help people at risk. Again the pandemic gives a model here – the Scottish and Welsh governments in particular fostered a sense that we were all in this together.At a society-wide level, a pilot project in Seville, Spain, toname specific heatwavesand give them a categorisation system like hurricanes made early warnings more effective, and also provided an important anchor for news coverage. This simple intervention should be considered in the UK. Changing the way we talk about extreme heat seems a minor thing. But if the public can be helped to recognise heatwaves as the major disasters that they are, lives would be saved and people would be convinced that the difficult work of adapting to the climate crisis is urgent and necessary.Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatOpinionClimate crisisHealtheditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Vital accountability mechanisms have withered as English devolution has evolved. The government should take note
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Vital accountability mechanisms have withered as English devolution has evolved. The government should take note
Content: The former offices of the Northern Echo newspaper, Darlington. An estimated 4.1 million people in Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe former offices of the Northern Echo newspaper, Darlington. An estimated 4.1 million people in Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionDevolutionThe Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutinyEditorialVital accountability mechanisms have withered as English devolution has evolved. The government should take noteSun 6 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.41 EDTShareAndy Burnham has criticised Britain’s “unaccountable state” that is at once too powerful and too distant from everyday life. He has made English devolution the central idea of his premiership, but his plan to give England’s mayors unprecedented power and money will have to confront a number of tricky realities, not least a landscape in which scrutiny of local government is vastly diminished.As England’s devolution map has evolved, vital accountability mechanisms have withered. The abolition of theAudit Commissionin 2015 deprived Whitehall of information about local government spending. The decision, taken by the then Tory prime minister David Cameron during his “bonfire of the quangos”, coincided with a period when cash-strapped councils were selling off assets and making risky investments. A succession ofbankruptciesandscandalshave since exemplified the dangers of governing in darkness, including the questions raised atTeesworks, the development led by Ben Houchen, a Tory mayor, where a “culture of excessive confidentiality” has prevailed, according to a damning 2024 government report.There is widerecognitionthat greater accountability is needed. But Westminster has tended to create top-down mechanisms where accountability flows upwards and local scrutiny is infantilised. The “trailblazer” deals in 2023, for example, gave the mayors of Greater Manchester and the West Midlands greater flexibility over spending, but made themanswerableto quarterlyselect committees of MPs. Under the current public accounting regime, the Treasury appoints an “accounting officer” to each government department, who answers to parliament for their department’s use of money, including that spent by local authorities. Located in Whitehall, these officers lack knowledge of the places such spending impacts.View image in fullscreenLisa Nandy.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAMr Burnham is right to try to wrest power back from the Treasury and recognise that those closest to a community best understand its needs. His government’srecent pledgeto appoint the chief executives of mayoral strategic authorities as “local accounting officers” is welcome. But its plans to give England’s mayors a share of income tax generated in their area (a power that Lord Houchen has said he will use tofund rebates) will demand deeper forms of accountability. The English devolution bill in 2026 created a new Local Audit Office and introducednew powersfor scrutiny committees. Both are improvements.A fine place to end up would be the creation of “local public accounts committees”, an idea suggested in the Starmer government’swhite paperin 2024. These could bemodelledon Westminster’s public accounts committee, whose reports have exposed flagrant misuses of public money. The prime minister wants to take a “place-based” approach to public service delivery. Such local committees, if properly resourced and empowered, could be integral to scrutinising these initiatives.Yet scrutiny isn’t solely the job of officials. The decline of local media poses another problem. Although new localreporting outletshave flourished in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, an estimated4.4 million peoplein Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet. A robust solution, oncemootedby the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, would be a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism. When mayor, Mr Burnham had a media capable of holding power to account. The same cannot be said for too many places in Britain.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Education in prison is key to tackling the crisis  | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: It would be better for the government to focus on rehabilitative programmes, rather than turning laundry rooms into extra cells, writes Jon Collins. Plus letters from Margaret Carey, Simon Hamilton and David Evans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: It would be better for the government to focus on rehabilitative programmes, rather than turning laundry rooms into extra cells, writes Jon Collins. Plus letters from Margaret Carey, Simon Hamilton and David Evans
Content: ‘Rather than investing in converting offices and laundries into cells, we should be properly funding education so that prisons can focus on rehabilitation.’Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Rather than investing in converting offices and laundries into cells, we should be properly funding education so that prisons can focus on rehabilitation.’Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianPrisons and probationLettersEducation in prison is key to tackling the crisisIt would be better for the government to focus on rehabilitative programmes, rather than turning laundry rooms into extra cells, writesJon Collins.Plus letters fromMargaret Carey, Simon HamiltonandDavid EvansSun 6 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareTurning laundry rooms into cells, as the justice secretary has proposed, will put even more pressure on our understaffed and overcrowded prisons (Burnham warned running prison capacity near limit is ‘big risk’, 1 September). This will, in turn, make it even less likely that people in prison will be able to access the education and training that will help them to turn their lives around.Education in prison is proven to reduce reoffending and get more people into work. But we’ve already seen provision slashed by a quarter in prisons this year. Just this week, an inspection of a prison in northern England found that there were not enough places in education and many men were frustrated at the lack of opportunity to progress in their sentence.Rather than investing in converting offices and laundries into cells, we should be properly funding education so that prisons can focus on rehabilitation. That would enable people to spend their time in prison purposefully and ensure they don’t come back.Jon CollinsChief executive, Prisoners’ Education TrustI have worked in prison-linked charities for over 30 years and am tired of saying that evidence proves that prison does not “work” in respect of preventing repeat offending, except, of course, when the offender is inside. Some offenders clearly need to be taken out of circulation, but building more prisons, at vast public expense, is not the answer to changing the behaviour of the majority of them.We should be using that money on structured and rigorous programmes, within the community, which promote behavioural change, personal development, literacy and employability, and maintain whatever family and community ties existed.Andy Burnham should think again. The government should spend the money on numeracy and literacy programmes, vocational and relationship skills, restorative justice, healthy living and keeping people in touch with their communities wherever possible. That way we won’t need to spend precious tax money on ever-more hugely expensive prison places.Margaret CareyHurstpierpoint, West SussexNowhere in the debate about prison overcrowding have I seen any discussion about a blindingly obvious solution: reform of drug policy. Many people in jail are there as a result of the relentless thieving required to support an opiate habit.So, isn’t it time to get rational, follow the evidence and start treating addiction as the health problem it so obviously is, rather than a moral failing to be punished? Decriminalise drug use as they did in Portugal in 2001 (without triggering societal collapse), and suddenly there would be plenty of room to lock up all the people who actually deserve it. Without building any more prisons. Incidentally, you’d also reduce crime and provide relief to thousands of addicts and their families.Simon HamiltonKington, HerefordshireZoe Williams (Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids, 31 August) states that “the purpose of prison itself has always been threefold – punishment, public protection and rehabilitation”. Not quite so. There is a fourth major purpose, which is deterrence. If a hard or lengthy sentence can be acknowledged to act as a deterrent, then it follows that a lenient sentence or very early release would have little deterrent effect, if any.David EvansMarket Harborough, LeicestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive  | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Letter: Areas will remain excluded, and nothing is gained from making local government units larger and more anonymous, write Steve Leach and Colin Copus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Areas will remain excluded, and nothing is gained from making local government units larger and more anonymous, write Steve Leach and Colin Copus
Content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham holds a National Economic Council meeting at No 10 North in Manchester.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenPrime Minister Andy Burnham holds a National Economic Council meeting at No 10 North in Manchester.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live News.DevolutionLettersDownside of Burnham’s devolution driveAreas will remain excluded, and nothing is gained from making local government units larger and more anonymous, writeSteve LeachandColin CopusSun 6 Sep 2026 12.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTShareJohn Harris correctly recognises that “England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance”, but justifiably points out how areas remain excluded from the new arrangements, or are at best a poor fit (Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?, 30 August).Allowing for a further batch of city region-based authorities over half of England’s population does not suit this model. Where are the city regions and “strategic authorities” in most of rural Devon, Surrey, Hertfordshire and much of Kent and Essex?IfAndy Burnhamgoes ahead with the local government reorganisation (LGR) he inherited from Steve Reed, we will be faced with vast tracts of non-place authorities with names such as Devon Coast and Countryside and North West Essex, which do not make sense as strategic authorities. They are what remain when the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has completed its long-term aspiration of reducing the number of English councils and councillors.We estimate that when this LGR is completed, 90% of councillors and 75% of councils across England could have disappeared, eliminating almost all authorities based on real places and communities. Germany, with itsBasic Law, much admired by Mr Burnham, operates with about 11,000 municipalities in a tiered county-municipality structure, and retains municipalities based on real places. The equalisation elements of the Basic Law, which sparks the PM’s interest, have been achieved without the introduction of huge anonymous unitary councils across Germany. England already has the largest units of local government across Europe; nothing is to be gained from making them larger and more anonymous.Steve LeachEmeritus professor of local government, De Montfort University;Colin CopusEmeritus professor of local politics, De Montfort UniversityHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
