title: No bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says minister | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government
Content: The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg the focus should be on making the carmaker ‘as ⁠competitive as possible’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenThe business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg the focus should be on making the carmaker ‘as ⁠competitive as possible’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAJaguar Land RoverNo bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says ministerCarmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and governmentRob DaviesSun 6 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job losses at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), after it emerged that the UK’s biggest carmaker isplanning up to 4,000 redundancies.Before crunch talks on Tuesday between JLR, union leaders and government officials, the business secretary,Jonathan Reynolds, said it was not his job to “intervene and run businesses”.JLR, owned by the Indian conglomerateTataMotors, told staff on Friday to expect a voluntary redundancy programme, as it tries to shore itself up against tough conditions with £1.7bn in cuts over two years.The Coventry-based company is expected to provide further details on job cuts as soon as Monday, which could include an admission that compulsory job losses are possible.The expected cuts, which represent almost 12% of JLR’s 34,000-strong UK workforce, threaten to provide an early reality check on Andy Burnham’s pledge to “reindustrialise” Britain.View image in fullscreenJaguar Land Rover staff check Range Rover bodies at the carmaker’s factory in Solihull.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersSources said they expect the redundancies, first reported in the Sunday Times, to be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shop floor production workers.JLR is understood to be responding to pressure from Tata to offset a slump in sales, exacerbated by thefallout from last year’s cyber-attackand the impact of Donald Trump’s tariff wars.Speaking on the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg show on Sunday, Reynolds signalled that the government was unwilling to put money into the business to limit job losses.Which UK carmakers will be hit hardest by Trump’s latest import tariffs?Read moreAsked if there could be financial support to protect the jobs, he said: “Not if it’s to bail people out.“If this is about making sure over time that workforce is right to make the business as ⁠competitive as possible, that’s the conversation we need to have,” Reynolds said, referring to the wider “challenging” environment for the auto sector.“We need to adapt to evolving global market conditions,” a spokesperson for JLR, which has its largest plant in Solihull in the West Midlands, said.Reynolds is expected to come under pressure to help staunch the number of job cuts from the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, during crunch talks with the JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, scheduled for Tuesday. Union officials will push for JLR to swerve compulsory job losses in favour of retraining or voluntary redundancy where possible.While Reynolds indicated that no bailout would be available, he hinted at other options to support carmakers.He refused to rule out watering downgovernment targets for UK automakersto reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035, pointing to an open consultation on the issue.Carmakers and unions have lobbied hard for a slower transition, saying the targets outpace actual customer demand.Reynolds also said that the government was sometimes prepared to invest “alongside” industry.In 2024, the new Labour government under Keir Starmer agreed to invest £500m in another Tata business, the Port Talbot steelworks, to build greener electric arc furnaces. However, the investment did not prevent 2,500 job losses at the south Wales site.View image in fullscreenStephen Kinnock, the secretary of state for Wales, and Andy Burnham at Tata Steel in Port Talbot – Keir Starmer’s investment in 2024 did not prevent job losses there.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetThe prospect of a jobs purge at JLR poses a challenge for Burnham, who has placed plans to “reindustrialise” Britain at the heart of his offer to voters since taking office less than two months ago.Last year, after JLR suffered the crippling cyber-attack, the government agreed to provide the company with a guaranteed loan facility of £1.5bn to help battle the impact on its supply chains and production.None of the loan has been drawn down.Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival planRead moreAs well as the cyber-attack, which halted production for several weeks anddented the UK economy, JLR has suffered the fallout from tariffs imposed by Trump, affecting the key American market for models such as the Range Rover and Defender.Trump initially slapped tariffs of 27.5% on British cars before reducing the figure to 10% as part of aUS-UK trade deal unveiled by Starmerto great fanfare at a press conference held at JLR’s Solihull plant in May last year.Competition from Chinese models such as ​the Jaecoo 7 – ​ranked third among Britain’s top-selling cars – ​has also eaten into sales at JLR, which makes more than 400,000 vehicles a year.JLR is not alone in being affected by these external factors. The German carmaker Volkswagen said last week itplans to cut a further 50,000 jobsas part of its turnaround plan as it faces US tariffs and Chinese competition.The Guardian has approached the department for business and trade for comment.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryJob lossesManufacturing sectorTataHackingJonathan ReynoldsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Britain’s Yellowstone’: restoration project aims to take the greed out of land acquisition | Rewilding | The Guardian
description: Investors in Emblehope Moor will get their financial returns – and then it will be given to community or charity owners
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Investors in Emblehope Moor will get their financial returns – and then it will be given to community or charity owners
Content: The vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m by Restore.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m by Restore.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianRewilding‘Britain’s Yellowstone’: restoration project aims to take the greed out of land acquisitionInvestors in Emblehope Moor will get their financial returns – and then it will be given to community or charity ownersPatrick BarkhamSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 05.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is difficult to find the most remote place in England. There is no public transport, no roads and no sign of any human habitation. Online route finders mistakenly direct cars up a grassy track. But miles along gravel forest roads in the far north ofNorthumberlandis the largest contiguous rewilding site under single ownership in the country.The vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m byRestore, a nature restoration company that works with landowners across Britain.The aim is to bring golden eagles, curlews, black grouse and beavers back to the moor which in former guises was a traditional grouse shooting and sheep farming estate and a dog-training ground.But the restoration project, which is still seeking to raise £4m to fund its 20-year scheme, also has a unique proposition: after delivering new biodiversity and abundance alongside financial returns for investors and repaying the crucial £4.5mTriodos Bank loanthat enabled the purchase, it will hand over the site to local community or charitable ownership.View image in fullscreenRestore’s first tasks will be to return water to desiccated peat moorland and remove swaths of non-native sitka spruce.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“We want to prove that the bank is paid back, investors get their two-times return but we don’t need to become the next for ever laird,” said Benedict Macdonald, an environmental writer and the founder and director of Restore. “We’re keen to leave a well-funded community project for the future. It’s not an aggressive land-holding model; it’s both a capitalist and community model and I want it to become the national model for the uplands – we’ve got to take the greed out of it for it to work.”The environmentalist Ben Goldsmith hails the burgeoning mosaic of increasingly wild estates in Northumberland as Britain’s Yellowstone.Close to Emblehope in the north of Northumberland is Rothbury, the largest estate to come on the market for 30 years, which theWildlifeTrusts are seeking to buy with an unprecedented £30m fundraising appeal that is nearing its target.Other private estates in the area, including 12,000-acreCollege Valleyand 4,000-acreHepple Wilds, are accelerating nature restoration while the vast 148,000-acreKielder Forestis increasingly managed by Forestry England for biodiversity.View image in fullscreenEmblehope already has exciting numbers of raptors, including merlin and visiting golden eagles.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“We’re not the size of Yellowstone but we’re in England’s largest wild landscape by a long factor,” said Macdonald.Emblehope, a site of special scientific interest (SSSI) which was managed for biodiversity byformer owners the Royal Kennel Clubfor a number of years, already has exciting numbers of raptors, including merlin and prospecting golden eagles. The site’s streams still have trout and salmon, and there are red squirrels and pine martens in the area.But Restore’s first tasks will be to return water to desiccated peat moorland and remove swaths of non-native sitka spruce.A hidden network of land drains have left what should be water-soaked peatland completely parched. Patches of sphagnum moss that are usually water-filled sponges even in summer are dry. Modelling suggests Emblehope’s rewetted peat could store an additional 100,000 cubic metres of water, equivalent to about 40 Olympic swimming pools.View image in fullscreenDried-out sphagnum moss, which is usually a water-filled sponge.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“It’s going to be a massive exercise to identify the exits of water from the land,” said Macdonald.In the future, they will call on beavers to help hold back more water. There are promising patches of birch and willow growing beside one stream – beaver food – but Macdonald has witnessed beavers making dams out of heather on even more treeless moors in Norway and is confident they will thrive.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images showRead moreBefore that, there is a more urgent task for the ponies that are to be introduced on to the site.The cattle- and sheep-grazing on the estate’s moorland was reduced by the previous owners on the advice of conservationists but Macdonald is alarmed by dry “thatch” beneath the thick tussocks of moorland grass. “It’s quite dangerous from a fire point of view,” he said. His priority is to get Exmoor ponies on to the site, because they will eat down the grassy thatch and reduce the fire risk.Opening up the site to more diverse grazing animals will reduce aggressive grass species and increase the diversity of the sward. The grass is also currently too thick and long for curlew chicks to survive and find food, and so other species will benefit from the grazing animals.Destined for the chop are dense sitka plantations, which harbour little life and raise predation to unnaturally high levels because goshawks lurk in them.View image in fullscreenBenedict Macdonald, the founder and director of Restore.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianOn Emblehope, the removal of the trees will hit a few species, such as long-eared owls and crossbills. But these will remain in the wider landscape because there are huge tracts of plantation forestry across neighbouring Kielder.Restore plans to leave patches of a few older trees but admits the problem with retaining any sitka – and the problem with its Forestry England neighbours – are what Macdonald calls the “little shitkas”, the baby trees that pop up all over the wilding moors from wind-blown seed.The solution is to plant broadleaved screens around the edge of the site to stop wind-blown sitka seed.While Restore’s promotional videos have tantalised people with glimpses of lynx, Macdonald is wary of being seen to endorse moves to bring back the lost predator, which many rewilders view as an ideal solution to Britain’s overpopulation of wild deer. While asurveysuggests 72% of local people are in favour of reintroducinglynx, many sheep farmers in the area are vehemently opposed to an animal that could make their working lives harder.“We have no funded plans for lynx, and we have no wish to be in the reintroduction party,” said Macdonald, although he conceded “the economic argument [in favour] is compelling”. Research to be published next year will quantify the potential tourism bonanza to Northumberland.Although there are proposals to release lynx into surrounding Kielder, one wasblocked by Natural Englandand a second, the Wildlife Trusts-backedMissing Lynx project, is still consulting. Emblehope is unlikely to be a key habitat for the forest-dwelling animal.View image in fullscreenGalloway cattle grazing the landscape. The estate’s farmer and gamekeeper are being kept on as part of the project.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianDespite Restore’s wilding manifesto, it is retaining the estate’s farmer and gamekeeper.“What surprises me is how surprised people are that we’ve retained staff who know so much about the land,” said Macdonald. “The farmer is a real student of the history of grazing here and he’s very open-minded. The gamekeeper has been looking after some of Britain’s highest densities of birds of prey. These guys work 18-hour days, they live and breathe the area.”Restore will fund the transformation of Emblehope via conventional income from forestry (removing the sitkas) and cattle, sheep and, in the future, education and carefully limited eco-tourism – as well as government environmental land management payments. But it expects most of its income to come from natural capital payments.These include carbon credits for the sequestration in restored blanket bog and “30x30Restore units” whereby corporations pay for the restoration of 30-metre by 30-metre patches of habitat. Restore’s vision is that corporations pay not for biodiversity outcomes but for conservation action on the land which provides more wildlife. Macdonald said: “It’s perfectly natural for large corporates to sponsor big sporting events across the world. In nature, in England, this is a big event.”Explore more on these topicsRewildingNorthumberlandNorth of EnglandConservationWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Zia Yusuf’s post about Camden council leader is ‘straightforward racism’, says minister | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Senior Reform UK figure has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Senior Reform UK figure has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee
Content: Yusuf asked on X: ‘Do you understand what’s happening?’ after pointing out that Abdi-Wali had been born in Somalia.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenYusuf asked on X: ‘Do you understand what’s happening?’ after pointing out that Abdi-Wali had been born in Somalia.Photograph: James Manning/PAReform UKZia Yusuf’s post about Camden council leader is ‘straightforward racism’, says ministerSenior Reform UK figure has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugeeJosh HallidaySun 6 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has accused Reform’s Zia Yusuf of “straightforward racism” after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection was not British.Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia and the leader of Camden council, has been tipped as an early favourite to contest theLondonseat for Labour after the former prime minister’s resignation.Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X last week: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”Sagal Abdi-Wali.Photograph: Camden LabourThe post, which has been viewed 8m times, drew sharp criticism from several senior Reform UK figures during the party’s conference in Birmingham at the weekend. Appearing on Sky News on Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, also condemned Yusuf’s post as “straightforward racism”.Asked by the presenter Jon Sopel for his thoughts on the message, Reynolds said: “Pretty straightforward racism, isn’t it? There’s a potential candidate referenced there; spent decades in this country, huge contribution to her local community, so I think that speaks for itself.”When Sopel asked whether it was “plain racism”, Reynolds replied: “Absolutely.”Yusuf has drawn significant criticism for his inflammatory comments on X in recent months, including from top Reform UK figures. Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative minister who defected to Reform UK last year, described the post about Abdi-Wali as “nasty”.“It was a nasty tweet. Zia Yusuf is a brilliant man, and he’s a genius actually, and he’s an incredible communicator. I wish he closed down his Twitter account,” she told Times Radio.View image in fullscreenDorries and Yusuf during a panel discussion at Reform’s conference in Birmingham on Saturday.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PALaila Cunningham, Reform’s candidate for mayor of London and the daughter of immigrants from Egypt, told the Standard: “I don’t know what he meant by that comment. I read it a few times.“I didn’t understand what he meant by that comment. Of course, you know, that woman is British. She’s the leader of Camden council. I didn’t understand what he meant by that.”Reform UK has been contacted for comment.Abdi-Wali arrived in Camden as a child refugee from Somalia. She has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour.She was first elected as a councillor in 2022 and became the leader of the council in May, when she said: “Camden has been my home for 35 years. It is the place that gave my family sanctuary, that welcomed us, and that has shaped so much of who I am, what I stand for and what inspired my commitment to public service and to working for the community that welcomed us.”Labour is expected to announce its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection by Wednesday. Labour faces a battle against the Green party to retain the seat as the latter is expected to confirm Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, as its candidate.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose | Mayoral elections | The Guardian
description: Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right
Content: Sadiq Khan (left) and Andy Burnham help to stack loaves of bread during a visit to a supermarket in London. Khan is yet to say whether he will seek a fourth term as London mayor.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSadiq Khan (left) and Andy Burnham help to stack loaves of bread during a visit to a supermarket in London. Khan is yet to say whether he will seek a fourth term as London mayor.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesMayoral electionsLondon mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to loseTories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the rightHelena HortonandAamna MohdinSun 6 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action.Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year.At the weekend, the former home secretaryJames Cleverlywas seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate.“I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even thoughLondonis a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.”View image in fullscreenJames Cleverly and the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAAlso standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.”But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment. A recent poll by Savanta UK for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, put Labour’s candidate in the mayoral race on 33%, the Tories 18%, Reform UK 18%, Green party 17% andLiberal Democrats9%,.The Conservatives’ bid to unseat Khan is complicated by the presence of Reform.Laila Cunningham, a former Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, is Reform’s candidate. She has been pounding the streets of London since the beginning of this year trying to drum up support.“I’m not stepping aside for the Tories,” she told the Guardian. “How many times have they tried to unseat Khan? They have failed.”View image in fullscreenReform’s Laila Cunningham: ‘I’m not stepping aside for the Tories.’Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersCleverly, she says, is “literally the establishment and he’s gone from one ministerial job from another”. She thinks he will be picked as the Tory mayoral candidate and said: “It will be two Sirs versus a woman. Sir Khan and Sir Cleverly.”Though the rightwing vote looks evenly divided between Tories and Reform, she is confident she can charm some of Khan’s voters: “It is not a left or right divide either, we won nine seats in Barking and Dagenham in the local elections, where the Tories wouldn’t dream of winning one.”Cunningham, the daughter of Egyptian immigrants, said she was “not your typical Reform person. People often see me and say they are surprised I am in Reform.”Akinbusoye is on the licensing committee of Westminster council, which is consulting torestrict “vertical drinking” in pubs– standing and drinking. Cunningham said: “That says it all. The fact they even call it vertical drinking is a joke.”View image in fullscreenDawn Butler, the Labour MP for Brent East, has said she would run if Sadiq Khan confirmed he would not seek a fourth term.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesThe Labour MPDawn Butlerhinted at her intention to run this week: a video of herself walking past a sign reading “a new Dawn for London”, captioned: “When London puts up signs saying ‘A New Dawn’ … what else was I supposed to do?”She first floated hermayoral ambitions in 2023, and has since confirmed to the Guardian that she would run as soon as Khan confirmed he would not seek a fourth term. Khan did not respond to a request for comment.There are no obvious contenders in sight for the Greens, with the party’s attention focused on its leader Zack Polanksi’s plan tofight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. A Green party source said: “We do have a number of people who’d be incredible candidates but no firm name. We feel confident after our latest local election results that Londoners will be excited by our vision for London.”Would Cunningham rather fight Butler or Khan? “[Khan’s] got incumbency. He may do better. It doesn’t make a difference because it’s what the party represents, she seems to think he was a great mayor so she seemingly wants more of the same.”Explore more on these topicsMayoral electionsLondonSadiq KhanJames CleverlyLaila CunninghamDawn ButlerLocal governmentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Councils in England and Wales accused of excessive fees to run outdoor classes | Local government | The Guardian
description: Report documents use of commercial licensing for free or donation-based exercise classes in parks and on beaches
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Report documents use of commercial licensing for free or donation-based exercise classes in parks and on beaches
Content: The Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life said some  of the fees ‘bear no relation to any money these classes make’.Photograph: Wirestock, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life said some  of the fees ‘bear no relation to any money these classes make’.Photograph: Wirestock, Inc./AlamyLocal governmentCouncils in England and Wales accused of excessive fees to run outdoor classesReport documents use of commercial licensing for free or donation-based exercise classes in parks and on beachesAmelia HillSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 6am on the beach at Westgate-on-Sea in Kent, Angela Brier-Stephenson used to meet a small group of about 10 people for yoga.The class lasted 45 minutes and participants paid what they could.Thanet council told her she would need to pay £1,200 a year as part of its seasonal licensing scheme. She has not run the class for the past two summers as a result.Councils acrossEnglandand Wales require hundreds of pounds in fees, dozens of pages of paperwork and first-aid certification from people running small, free or donation-based exercise classes in parks and on beaches, according to a new report published by the Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life.The report, titled Banned from the Beach: the Crackdown on Outdoor Community Sport, documents how licensing schemes first aimed at commercial personal trainers and bootcamps in the early 2000s now also apply to even small community gatherings, including a qigong class of seven people, and a mother-and-baby choir.Josie Appleton, the director of the Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life, said: “The fees bear no relation to any money these classes make and are frequently far larger than the cost of running the scheme.”Thanet brought the fee down to £300 for fitness activities before the 2026 season. “The licensing process allows the council to ensure that all current regulations are met. When an individual or organisation provides a service to the public that involves payment or donation, regardless of pricing structure, it remains a commercial activity,” a council spokesperson said. “All commercial operations require licences when trading on publicly owned land. Fees are set by business type and location and started at £300 for fitness activity in locations such as Westgate-on-Sea.”In Bristol, Julia Turner is resisting a £100 fee to run her £8-a-session, BYOB (bring your own baby) choir. “I am leading classes for new mothers in parks which have no clean working facilities; there are no bandstands to keep us dry and there is no way to reserve a spot. I would be happy to pay a one-off fee for the council to check my risk assessments but other than that, what are we actually paying for?” she said.Turner has staged a flash-mob singing demonstration inside City Hall. But she admitted that running the choir, which began as a passion project, was at risk of becoming “too difficult to bother with”.Also in Bristol, Chloe Broomby said the fees had made it impossible to run her weekly, donation-based qigong classes on the Downs.“I don’t make much money; some weeks I only had seven people turning up,” she said. “It really was for the joy of it.”Ailie Tam, who has taught community yoga in St George Park in Bristol for six years, was happy to continue running her classes at an occasional loss when only one or two people turned up. But she too has stopped the sessions since fees were introduced.Bristol city council said its scheme included discounted rates of up to 75% for small businesses and charitable organisations.“Licensing helps to ensure that businesses operating in these important public spaces are appropriately insured and act responsibly,” said Stephen Williams, a councillor and the chair of the public health and communities policy committee. “The licence fees cover the cost of administering the scheme, with any surplus money reinvested into maintaining and improving our city’s parks.”Appleton’s report identifies 19 councils with licensing schemes for outdoor exercise that also apply to free or donation-based classes. The councils, she said, used a range of legal mechanisms, from events-licensing schemes designed for large events, and others designed for commercial personal trainers in the early 2000s, to Victorian park bylaws.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the London borough of Richmond, running an unlicensed exercise class is a criminal offence – enforced by a private contractor, Parkguard, which issues fixed-penalty notices.“Our enforcement officers will seek to engage constructively and support park users in understanding and complying with regulations, using formal enforcement action only where necessary and proportionate,” said a council spokesperson. “Where an organised activity makes regular use of our parks, it’s reasonable that it makes a contribution towards managing and maintaining them.”Shouting and stroking ponies outlawed by rural councils in England as antisocial behaviourRead moreCouncils say they need to know who is using public land and to ensure activities are safe.In the London borough of Waltham Forest, a free outdoor fitness class was stopped mid-session by two park rangers. A council spokesperson said: “We ask for a small fee and completion of forms to provide vital information – even for free events – to ensure compliance with safeguarding and health and safety policies, and to help contribute to maintenance costs.”In Swansea, officials initially proposed charging Helen Wilson £24.15 a session for the free or donation-based weekly beach yoga classes she had been running for more than a decade. After hundreds of messages of support and a petition, the council withdrew the charge, saying the fees were to ensure public space was used in a safe way and that it had initially understood the classes to be commercial.Wilson said: “I think they saw it as an opportunity to make money and if that jeopardised what I was offering, then so be it.”Tam believed the main issues was that “the people being pushed out of parks by these fees are the very people helping to make those spaces more valued, cared for and actively used by their communities”.Explore more on these topicsLocal governmentCommunitiesEnglandWalesYoganewsShareReuse this content

title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending
Content: Stanley in the Falkland Islands. Ministers in the UK have condemned Javier Milei’s comments.Photograph: Rob Carter/AlamyView image in fullscreenStanley in the Falkland Islands. Ministers in the UK have condemned Javier Milei’s comments.Photograph: Rob Carter/AlamyDefence policyFalklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chairExclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spendingKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJavier Milei’s threats to theFalkland Islandsmake it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.Tan Dhesi said thecomments by the Argentinian presidentthis week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for thedrone incident[in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. TheLabourMP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.View image in fullscreenTan Dhesi asked Andy Burnham whether he backed the 2030 commitment to defence spending at Wednesday’s PMQs.Photograph: House of Commons/PA“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJavier Milei threatened oil sanctions against firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/ReutersHis comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows thatArgentinahas a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.Ministers in the UKcondemned Milei’s commentson Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyFalkland IslandsArgentinaAmericasLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian first | Australia news | The Guardian
description: The casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the process
Author: Jack Larkin
Headline: The casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the process
Content: The mushroom coffin, created by Loop Biotech, pictured at Sydney Harbour.Photograph: Loop BiotechView image in fullscreenThe mushroom coffin, created by Loop Biotech, pictured at Sydney Harbour.Photograph: Loop BiotechAustralia newsWoman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian firstThe casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the processFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJack LarkinSun 6 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has been buried in a coffin made from mushrooms inNew South Walesin an eco-friendly first for Australia.Carolyn, whose surname was withheld for privacy reasons, was laid to rest on Friday by friends and family at Springwood Cemetery in the Blue Mountains. She was aged in her 70s.The mushroom coffin, created by the Dutch firm Loop Biotech, was grown from mycelium – the root network of fungi – and hemp fibres.The coffin is grown in mould in a climate-controlled room, taking just a week to fully form. Once buried, it takes about 45 days to become part of the soil.The process is akin to composting, as the body and coffin gently biodegrade and transform into nutrient-rich soil in far less time than a traditional wooden casket, which can take up to 50 years to break down.View image in fullscreenThe biodegradable coffins weigh about 30kg.Photograph: Loop BiotechCarolyn’s husband, Donald, said picking the mushroom coffin aligned with his wife’s values of giving back.“She was always there to help others. It feels very true to who she was that even after her death, she can still do something for others while giving something back to nature,” he said.While Carolyn is the first to be buried in the coffin in Australia, Loop Biotech’s founder Bob Hendrikx said there had been thousands of others across Europe and the US.“Five years ago when I started, there was lots of interest from Australia,” Hendrikx said. “It was a little bit harder to ship overseas [at the time].”Hendrikx hopes the mushroom coffins, which weigh about 30kg each, could improve the sustainability of the Australian funeral sector by shortening the decomposition process.“It’s about giving back to nature: we have the mushroom, which is grown and dissolves into nature, but the actual benefit is that … it’s enriching the soil,” he said.“The body needs to just return to nature and let nature do what it’s done best forever.“If a kangaroo dies in the forest, it’s just going to be part of the cycle of life.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s enriching the soil’: Loop Biotech founder Bob Hendrikx in Sydney.Photograph: Loop BiotechDr Hannah Gould, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Melbourne, believes people are becoming increasingly interested inenvironmentally friendly farewells.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As people perhaps become less religious, other kinds of values or community groupings become more important, and one of those that we’ve seen is eco-death.Gone to a wetter place: the Queenslanders disrupting the death industry with water cremationsRead more“This idea that perhaps that you don’t go up to heaven after you die, you return to the earth, has been an increasingly popular narrative around death and dying.”While about 70% of Australians choose to be cremated, it has a substantial environmental impact: the emissions from a typical cremation are estimated to be equivalent to125kg of carbon dioxide.View image in fullscreenLoop Biotech’s mushroom coffin can be lined with moss.Photograph: Loop BiotechIn recent years options such asalkaline hydrolysis(a cremation-like process that uses water instead of fire), natural burials without embalming, and even shallow burials have become available. A natural burial uses a cardboard coffin with rope handles and will emit less than 10kg of carbon dioxide equivalent, according toPlanetMark analysis.Gould believes that as Australians are living longer and more people are dying from prolonged illnesses, more time is being spent thinking about how to depart and farewell loved ones.“They’ve maybe seen or organised a funeral for their parents and it hasn’t gone so well,” she said. “And they’re now deciding that they want to do things differently. So we’re seeing a huge rise in funeral planning.”This story was amended on 7 September 2026 to correct the name of Carolyn’s husband, Donald.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsNew South WalesConsumer affairsDeath and dyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands | Hawaii | The Guardian
description: Storm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane season
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Storm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane season
Content: A satellite image shows three storms, from left: Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie, in the Pacific Ocean on Wednesday.Photograph: CIRA/NOAA/APView image in fullscreenA satellite image shows three storms, from left: Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie, in the Pacific Ocean on Wednesday.Photograph: CIRA/NOAA/APHawaiiHawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islandsStorm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane seasonMarina DunbarSun 6 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHawaii has declared a state of emergency as powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands, with the first impacts expected as soon as Monday.The storm is the third system in just over three weeks to threaten Hawaii during an active hurricane season in the central Pacific. Lowell remained a category 3 hurricane early on Sunday morning, packing winds of 125 miles per hour while moving north-west at six miles per hour.According to the forecast, Lowell will reach Hawaii as a category 2 hurricane. Its center could pass roughly 130 miles west of Ni’ihau or 170 miles west of Kauai between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.The threat comes amid unusually intense hurricane activity across the Pacific.As of Saturday, Hurricanes Karina, Lowell and Marie were all churning in the Pacificat the same time, marking the region’s first triple-hurricane stretch in a decade. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) was also monitoring afourth potentialsystem off the coast of Mexico.The Pacific averages only eight hurricanes per year, according to the NHC, making three simultaneous hurricanes highly unusual.Lowell’s projected offshore path is expected to keep the storm’s most dangerous winds away from Hawaii’s islands. But heavy rain, high surf and dangerous coastal conditions are still expected.A tropical storm warning is in effect for Kauai and Ni’ihau, where wind gusts above 39 miles per hour are possible over the next 48 hours.Lowell is the third storm in a matter of weeks to hit Hawaii as the climate crisis continues to increase the intensity and frequency of storms and other weather events.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTropical Storm Moke poised to slam into Hawaii just days after Hurricane LalaRead moreTropical Storm Mokestruck the southern partof Hawaii’s islands two weeks ago, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. That came just days after Hurricane Lala hit the region.The Hawaii governor Josh Green said Lala alone had caused at least $43m in infrastructure damage on the Big Island, along with another $4.6m in damage to homes.The escalating storm activity comes as the UN warns that this year’s El Niño is forecast to become the strongest on record in four decades.Astatementreleased on Thursday described El Niño as being “supersized before our eyes”, adding that the world is in “the danger zone of extreme weather”.The latest data on the natural climate phenomenon shows a near 100% likelihood that the latest El Niño will continue through February 2027, the statement said. The stronger an El Niño becomes, the greater the chance it will significantly alter rainfall and temperature patterns around the world and help fuel extreme weather.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) haspreviously warnedthere is a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in 70 years.Explore more on these topicsHawaiiExtreme weatherHurricanesEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state
Content: Olivia Grange (right) said the petition’s request for Charles to seek legal advice from the privy council was critical to advancing Jamaica’s reparations claim.Composite: PA, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOlivia Grange (right) said the petition’s request for Charles to seek legal advice from the privy council was critical to advancing Jamaica’s reparations claim.Composite: PA, Getty ImagesCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaicaJamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King CharlesSlavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of stateNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentSun 6 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTShareA landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaica over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, theCaribbeannation’s culture minister has said.The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so,” she told the Guardian.First announcedin June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to theAmericasand sold into slavery.Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up theCaribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser forthe Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slaveryas the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbeanlaunched a manifestooutlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries werelegally obliged to consider reparationsfor the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmerresisted pressure from member statesto include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.A palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.”Later on Sunday, the delegation hosted a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”Explore more on these topicsJamaicaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceSlaveryKing Charles IIICaribbeanAmericasMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe | Aerospace industry | The Guardian
description: Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market
Content: The uncrewed Spectrum rocket successfully entered orbit after its launch from Arctic Norway.Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe uncrewed Spectrum rocket successfully entered orbit after its launch from Arctic Norway.Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/ReutersAerospace industryGerman startup sends first commercial rocket into space from EuropeIsar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch marketReuters in OsloSun 6 Sep 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continentalEurope, a milestone for Europe’s efforts to secure independent access to space.Isar Aerospace said on Sunday that it would rapidly ⁠expand satellite deployments after the ⁠first orbital launch of ​its uncrewed Spectrum rocket from ArcticNorway, marking a ⁠breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches.“Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry,” Isar’s co-founder and chief executive, Daniel Metzler, told reporters.Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, hailed Saturday’s launch in a ​statement, calling it “the beginning of a new era”.Merz visited Isar’s ‌launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s ‌efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under the administration of country’s president, Donald Trump.The EU defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, wrote on the social media platform X: “Europe’s independent access to space just got a major boost.”Blasting off from Andøya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment.It was Isar’s second launch, 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site.Isar has said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting about 40 launches a year.The German company ​is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.Global players ⁠in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the US, and the French firm ArianeGroup, ​a joint venture between Airbus and Safran ​that uses a spaceport in French Guiana, South America.Explore more on these topicsAerospace industrySpaceEuropeNorwayGermanySatellitesnewsShareReuse this content

title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth | China | The Guardian
description: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
Content: A Chinese national flag raised outside a bank’s headquarters in the financial district of central Beijing.Photograph: Kim Kyung Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Chinese national flag raised outside a bank’s headquarters in the financial district of central Beijing.Photograph: Kim Kyung Hoon/ReutersChinaChina prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growthBeijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reservesRob DaviesSun 6 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy isstruggling to escape weak growth.The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry ElliottRead moreThe People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries.The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans.Explore more on these topicsChinaEconomicsAsia PacificBankingInsurance industryStock marketsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of Thrones | Maisie Williams | The Guardian
description: After her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourself
Author: Simran Hans
Headline: After her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourself
Content: Maisie Williams: ‘I’m in love! That’s all I’ll say.’ All portraits: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaisie Williams: ‘I’m in love! That’s all I’ll say.’ All portraits: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianMaisie WilliamsInterview‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of ThronesSimran HansAfter her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourselfSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaisie Williams has dabbled in witchcraft exactly once. The actor was getting ready to audition for a part in a film. “I wanted it so badly that I went on to Etsy, and I paid a witch to manifest me the role,” she says, poker-faced.“It didn’t work, and that was where my days of witchcraft ended,” she adds, breaking into an infectious cackle.The spell may not have worked that time, but Williams will soon try her own hand at witchcraft on screen in Practical Magic 2. The sequel to the beloved 1998 romcom, about two supernatural sisters played by Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, it features Williams as Antonia, the youngest daughter of Bullock’s Sally Owens. She never did get her money back from her Etsy witch. “It was maybe, like, £16.50? Which is not going to break the bank, but good for her. Good for her, to be making money doing nothing!” Williams laughs again.We meet on a sweltering afternoon at a posh pub in Belgravia in London where women in expensive-looking sundresses are drinking Aperol spritzes on the terrace. Williams arrives from a busy day of appointments. She removes a pair of oversized grey headphones and sets them down on the table (she was listening to the US singer-songwriter Slayyyter on the walk over). “I’m in my business outfit because I’ve hadbusinessmeetings,” she explains. (It’s arguably a very gen Z take on corporate dressing: long, dark hair worn in a practical ponytail, white T-shirt, smart grey trousers with a matching grey miniskirt attached, chunky, don’t‑mess-with-me Prada boots.)Today’s agenda has included two jewellery fittings for a red carpet event, an “important producing meeting, with me as the producer” and lunch with her former Game of Thrones co-starHannah Murray. The pair were catching up and discussing Murray’s recent memoir,The Make-Believe, about her devastating experience with a wellness cult. The group promised spiritual healing through expensive, elaborate rituals; Murray experienced a psychotic episode and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder. “I knew something was going on, but I didn’t know it was that,” Williams says. “I felt really upset with myself for not asking sooner.”View image in fullscreenMaisie Williams as Arya Stark in Game of Thrones (above) and with Florence Pugh in The Falling (right). Photographs: Helen Sloan/HBO; AlamyView image in fullscreenWilliams says she hasn’t always been a sceptic regarding magic. “I used to indulge in the whimsy of the patterns of the universe and think, ‘Oh, it’s a sign that everything’s going to work out.’” She says, taking a sip of Diet Coke. But after reading Murray’s book, Williams decided that searching for symbols in daily life might not be so wholesome after all. “I realised it leaves your mind slightly malleable to seeing a sign because you think it’s a divine intervention, and not just a good, fun coincidence.”The 29-year-old actor is probably still best known as Arya Stark from Game of Thrones, the baby-faced assassin who shot her to stratospheric levels of fame at age 12. I remember first seeing her in Carol Morley’sThe Falling, in which she stood out as a prickly, stiff‑backed schoolgirl opposite a then unknown Florence Pugh. In the seven years since Game of Thrones ended, Williams has landed roles in Marvel spin-offThe New Mutants, in Danny Boyle’s miniseriesPistolas punk icon Jordan, and in Apple TV’sThe New Look, a glossy drama about Christian Dior and Coco Chanel in Nazi-occupied Paris. She has started her own production company, and co-hosts theFrank Film Clubpodcast with two of her friends. It has been a period of trying different things, of searching for light relief, after a long stretch dealing with some much darker stuff. Last year, she even got a new agent. “He was bringing me fun things and was calling me every day,” she says. One of those fun, unexpected things was Practical Magic 2.Williams had seen the original once or twice, but rewatched it before her audition. “The first movie has a lot of different beats to it,” she says diplomatically. That’s one way to put it: tonally, the film is all over the place. Based on an Alice Hoffman novel, it tells the story of the Owens sisters, two witches doomed by an ancestral curse: any man who falls in love with an Owens woman is destined to die. It is a cult classic, with fabulous 90s costumes, Bullock and Kidmandrunkenly dancing around their kitchento Harry Nilsson’s Coconut and a jarringly dark domestic violence subplot. The sequel is much slicker. Directed by Susanne Bier, it sends Sally’s more rebellious eldest daughter Kylie (Joey King) to England as she tries to break the family curse. Bullock and Kidman go after her, bickering the whole way, while Williams’s character, a trainee neurosurgeon, holds the fort at home.View image in fullscreenMaisie Williams as Jordan in Danny Boyle’s Pistol.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/FX“Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman are real movie stars – from a time in cinema that is escaping us,” says Williams matter-of-factly. “I went into this film seeing them as otherworldly.” She recalls meeting the actors for the first time at the read-through. Later that day she was heading to Glastonbury festival. “I got back in my car, and I wound the windows up, and I was just like … ” Williams claps both French-manicured hands to her face and lets out a high-pitched shriek. “I had my dog in the car. He was probably thinking, ‘What is going on?!’ And then I drove to Glastonbury.” On set, in between takes, the veteran Hollywood actors imparted important wisdom to their younger co-stars. But it wasn’t about the industry. “We spoke about how being friends with your ex is a fallacy,” she says. Who said that? Was it Kidman, who is recently divorced? “We all said that!” Williams demurs.In the film, Williams and King are an inseparable sister duo, snuggled under the covers at their mum’s house and whispering as if they’re at a sleepover. In real life, Williams has three siblings, including one sister who is five years her senior. “When we’re together it’s like no time has passed but we’re not … ” She pauses. “We don’t call every day,” she says. “We’ve had waves in our life when we’re a lot closer, but a lot of our connection now comes through the kids.” Williams takes her niece and nephew on camping trips. “We never went out partying together,” she says. And, anyway, when she would have been the right age, Williams was busy filmingGame of Thrones. “I was away most of the time, and I’d moved out as well.”Williams’s route to child stardom came via a curiously X Factor-themed school nativity play. “I played Sharon Osbourne, and had done such a good job that my friend’s mum felt compelled to tell my mum, ‘You should put her into classes.’ That was when I started taking it seriously, because they were taking me seriously.” Then things got very serious, with Williams barely in secondary school when she landed a role on Game of Thrones. The speed at which her career took off shaped her expectations of the film industry, she says. “I thought, oh! Whatever you want, you can get. Like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “That was how I thought the industry was.” Her naivety, she reckons, was a good thing. “It informed the way I see life, and the way I threw myself into what turned out to be a huge responsibility.”Those early positive experiences, she says, gave her the confidence to pursue her dreams. “I wasn’t knocked down as a child. I wasn’t knocked down by my mum. I wasn’t knocked down by teachers at drama school, and I wasn’t knocked down by the industry when I did start auditioning.” Williams wonders if she would have still been resilient if she hadn’t enjoyed early success. “I think that a lot of people have a gift, but they just don’t get cast in a huge TV show when they’re 12.”double quotation markI could access anger and fear because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of timeView image in fullscreenWilliams claims not to know about an Arya Stark spin-off movie that is reportedly in development with HBO. “I saw that, too! I was like, huh?” Would she be interested in returning to that character? “I don’t know, really. She would have to be developed in some way because I feel like I’ve changed so much, and I feel like what people loved about Arya is that she was always a child doing things that were quite grownup.”In person, Williams is warm but somewhat guarded; she sits next to me on the leather banquette but maintains a cautious distance. She is good company, with a beaming smile and a glorious, trilling laugh, but several times in our conversation I sense her weighing up her words. When asked about her early life growing up between Bristol and Somerset she becomes visibly uncomfortable. She settles on an honest, abridged answer. “My mum and my siblings and I spent a lot of time with my auntie,” she says, adding that she was mostly raised by the two women. “My auntie was a childminder with loads of other kids, so my life was vibrant and silly and fun and playful.”Williams describes herself as “not coming from a hugely privileged background”. I wonder how, on the brink of 30, she reflects on growing up with less. “When I reflect on myself as a child, I wish I could just tell her it’s going to be fine. It’s going to work out. I think the fear that I felt at that time was so defining for many years of my childhood. I didn’t know. I was so ambitious as a small child, and I think maybe that did come from wanting my life to be different.”In 2022, Williams spoke about the difficulties she faced back then on theDiary of a CEOpodcast. Her parents split up when she was a baby, and her father is no longer in her life. “I had a traumatic relationship with my dad, and ever since I can remember I have struggled sleeping,” she told host Steven Bartlett. She described a teacher noticing her struggling at school and asking if she ate breakfast in the mornings. Williams said she didn’t. She was eight. The teacher called her mum. “I would look around at other kids and be, like, ‘Why don’t they seem to understand this pain or dread or fear? Joy – when does that come for me?” she said on the podcast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markMy relationship to success was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?View image in fullscreen“I have very close friends that I had not told,” Williams says today. “What I said on that podcast was all I’ve said about it to a lot of people, other than my family and my therapist. I even had boyfriends who didn’t know. So my reluctance to want to talk about it again is because my relationship to fame, and my relationship to success, was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?” She winces.“I think it reached a lot of people who were in the same position, and I’m really happy that it did.” I’m curious to know why she chose that moment to finally speak about what had happened to her. “I always wanted to,” she says. “I think part of the reason why I was so good at playing Arya was because of how I’d grown up.”She says journalists would often ask her how she was able to access such difficult emotions as a younger, less experienced actor. “I always felt like it was something I couldn’t say. I could access these emotions because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of time.” What emotions? “Anger and fear.” She lets out a bitter laugh. “Stonewalling. I know that feeling of shutting down. These things that you don’t really start to understand about yourself until a lot later.” Being a teenager, she says, is already so fraught with emotion.By the time she recorded that podcast, “I had done a lot of therapy,” she says, “and so was feeling a lot clearer about a lot of things.” It was Bartlett’s initial question that cracked them open for her. “He said, ‘What happened to you as a child that defines how you are?’ or something. It’s literally the only question that someone would have to ask me for me to answer honestly.” I was struck by her candour and vulnerability in that interview, I tell her. “I just thought that by releasing it, it was the last step in being free from it. Which kind of turned out to be true,” she says.I wonder what she makes of Bartlett now. “Mmm,” she says, eyebrows raising, her mouth tightening into a horizontal line. In recent years, Bartlett has become a controversial figure, who has been criticised for amplifying medical misinformation and platforming manosphere-adjacent guests such as fellow podcaster Chris Williamson, who blamed declining birthrates on “women’s socioeconomic emancipation into the workforce”. Bartlett has aired the views of “experts” who claimed that Covid vaccines were “a net negative for society” and that cancer could be treated by a keto diet. It’s not a show that seems particularly aligned with liberal values.View image in fullscreenStyling: Magdalena Bryk at Art Dept, assisted by Vienna Divens. Hair: Clayton Hawkins at Frame Agency. Makeup: Kindra Mann at Frame Agency. Dress and shoes: Alexander McQueen. Tights: Los Angeles Apparel. Knit: Shushu Tong. Headpiece: Piers Atkinson. Blazer, skirt and shoes: Shushu Tong. Coat: Marc Jacobs“At the time, it felt like he had a podcast that felt fresh and different,” Williams says. “After, I felt slightly like I had been part of a podcast that gets a lot of views based on uprooting trauma. When I saw the trailer to the episode, I felt slightly icked out by how he had clipped it. But ultimately I can’t control that. Now I just feel like it’s quite dangerous, some of these conversations that are being had and taken out of context.”Still, speaking about her experiences publicly was “a huge, defining moment of change” for Williams. “The first half of my 20s was just hell, but I think maybe it is for a lot of people,” she says. “I think that has more to do with the fact that Game of Thrones was ending, and I didn’t know what I was going to do next, and I just needed a break, to be honest with you. And then it also has to do with delayed teenage awkward years, and figuring a lot of things out that I felt like maybe I couldn’t do much earlier than that. And also Covid, and also an industry strike,” she adds with a shrug. The pub is getting noisy, filling up with finance bros who have just finished work.“But post-2023, every day has been getting better,” she says. What happened in 2023? “I started seeing my friends again. I moved out of London. I was living alone. I was back with my dog. Everything was different,” she says. Williams is too discreet to confirm whether this change was sparked by the breakup of her long‑term relationship with fashion designer Reuben Selby. “At that point, it was time to … ” She smiles as if she’s got a secret. “Just choose myself,” she says. “What always comes into my mind is Kim Cattrall,” she adds, paraphrasinga quote the actor gave to the Guardianthat became a popular meme. “‘I don’t want to be anywhere, not even for an hour, where I’m not enjoying myself.’ That’s truly how I’ve been the last three years.”For Williams, choosing herself means “a lot of quiet, a lot of reading, and writing, and yoga, and running, and exercise, and swimming, and cycling, and walking the dog. Walking the dog for, like, hours a day.” In other words, being in her body. “Exactly, because then I know what I want. And that can be going out with my friends all weekend, or it can be a fun dinner in London where you miss your last train home, or it can be going to the cinema alone.” This summer, it has meant going to Primavera Sound and seeing singer Ethel Cain play, having barbecues with her friends and watching the World Cup in her local pub.When I ask Williams what her career ambitions are now, a misty, faraway look comes over her. She does say her dreams out loud, but she’d rather not say them in print, she says. “My ambition is to work with people who have proven themselves to be really talented,” she says. “I’ve worked in the industry for quite a long time, and even though I love working with debut directors, there’s a stark difference in our experience now, which is noticeable. Working with people who are more experienced brings a different atmosphere on set.” She’s also been pouring her time into her production company, Rapt. It has meant reading a lot of scripts. “I cannot tell you the amount of postpartum horrors that people are making,” she says. “Whenever there’s one great movie, you’ll get seven scripts like that on your desk.” She and her co-founder, Lowri Roberts, are having fun writing their own feature film, too. “It’s a dark comedy. It’s a satire about the end of the world,” she says.Williams has frequently been cast in dark, dramatic roles: “But I don’t really think that’s how I am most of the time,” she says. “I think when I’m in bad situations, I’d be more likely to laugh than to cry. I don’t know if I’m really in the camp of ‘plan for the worst’.
