I’ve had periods of my life where I’ve been so overcome by the fear of what could go wrong that, particularly now, I’m more in a phase of ‘anything can be fixed’.”Not that there’s much that needs fixing. She is dating and “so happy” about it, though she is coy when pressed about the details. Has she been enjoying playing the field? “No! I’m in love,” she says, smirking. “That’s all I’ll say.” Does it feel different from other times she’s been in love? “Yes, which is good. There’s lots of laughter,” she says, giggling. The vibe this summer, she says, has been “hot, in all senses of the word”. She grins. “I got myself a fan. I am a late adopter of the fan.” Before that, she says, she was “just sweating”. These days, she’s too busy enjoying herself a la Kim Cattrall to be constantly bracing for the worst. “Life is actually quite fun, but we all torture ourselves over the agony of what could be.”Practical Magic 2 is out in cinemas on 11 September.Explore more on these topicsMaisie WilliamsGame of ThronesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wim Wenders clarifies that he does not believe film-makers should stay out of politics | Wim Wenders | The Guardian
description: Director’s controversial comments earlier this year warned of films that ‘enter the field of politics’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Director’s controversial comments earlier this year warned of films that ‘enter the field of politics’
Content: Wenders said film-makers ‘are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is’.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenWenders said film-makers ‘are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is’.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersWim WendersWim Wenders clarifies that he does not believe film-makers should stay out of politicsDirector’s controversial comments earlier this year warned of  films that ‘enter the field of politics’Philip Oltermannin VeniceSun 6 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe director Wim Wenders has clarified personal views on the relationship between cinema and politics that caused controversy earlier in the year, saying at theVenice film festivalthat he does not believe film-makers ought to stay out of politics altogether.During the Berlin film festival, the veteran German director, who was acting as the jury president, hadsaid at a press conferencethat “we have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics.”The remark drew much attention amid criticism of the German government’s support of Israel over the war in Gaza, and incensed some fellow film-makers, with the Indian author Arundhati Roy calling the comments “unconscionable” andpulling out of an eventin the German capital.Berlin film festival defends Wim Wenders after Arundhati Roy attacked ‘jaw-dropping’ commentsRead moreAsked by the Guardian at a press conference in Venice whether he stood by the comments, Wenders said he “could repeat the same thing” but conceded he “could be more explicit”.“What I said then was, as film-makers, we are the opposite of politicians. We have empathy. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” said the auteur, who had come to the Lido to present a documentary about the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.“We have a very different thing. I’m not working with a mindset of politicians, we are working with a mindset of empathetic people. And we are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is.”The director behind Wings of Desire and Kings of the Road continued: “That’s what I said, and was quoted as: ‘We have to stay out of politics,’ and that is not what I said, because it’s not what I said now, and I said the same thing then.“The frame of film-makers is a different mindset than the mindset of politicians, and we should not work with that mindset. We work with a different set of rules. I said it again, and I hope you’re not misquoting me, and say we have to stay out of politics because we do the opposite. We are the antidote.”From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor is a 3D film exploring the Pritzker prize-winning architect’s philosophy through portraits of his most notable buildings. It follows similar portrayals of the Cuban musical ensembleBuena Vista Social Club, the choreographerPina Bauschand the artistAnselm Kiefer.The buildings shown include Kunsthaus Bregenz’s concrete cube on Lake Constance and the “amoeba-shaped” David Geffen Galleries of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, but also more practical structures such as shelters for a Roman archaeological site in Chur, Switzerland, and Alpine chapels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPraising the architect’s buildings, Wenders said architecture and politics were “linked in many ways”. He referenced the controversy over the site of the former Gestapo and SS headquarters in Berlin, which Zumthor was chosen in 1993 to turn into the Topography of Terror memorial museum, but whose plans were later scrapped by the the German capital’s senate due to funding problems.“They didn’t stop it because it was too expensive,” Wenders said in Venice. “They stopped it because [they] thought it was no more necessary, because they already had the Holocaust memorial and they already had the Jewish Museum. So what they did instead, they built something cheap.”The “political act” of Zumthor’s original building, Wenders said, was to make the historical structure “invisible” and “show documents” instead. The redesigned historical site that opened to the public in 2010, he said, “doesn’t speak, and politics don’t want places to speak, politics wants control over the show”.Explore more on these topicsWim WendersVenice film festivalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Possible Love review – a tale of two couples is finely judged study of exploitation and friendship | Movies | The Guardian
description: Acclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong returns with an inspired account of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Acclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong returns with an inspired account of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband
Content: A tale of two couples … from left: Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji, and Zo In-sung as Sang-woo in Possible Love.Photograph: Netflix/APView image in fullscreenA tale of two couples … from left: Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji, and Zo In-sung as Sang-woo in Possible Love.Photograph: Netflix/APMoviesReviewPossible Love review – a tale of two couples is finely judged study of exploitation and friendshipAcclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong returns with an inspired account of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husbandPeter BradshawSun 6 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKorean auteur Lee Chang-dong brings to Venice his first feature for eight years. It is a finely judged, beautifully acted and rather novelistic work, in which a character at one point actually compares her surroundings to something from a novel. It is expansive and diffuse in terms of storytelling scope and dramatic focus, rich in intelligence while paying its audience the compliment of treating them as intelligent also. There are moments of pure inspiration in the superb flashback scenes of two characters’ early lives, and I rather regretted that these flashbacks were phased out relatively early on and that more was not made of their relationship with the present. Possible Love is perhaps a little contrived and self-aware and unsure how much emphasis to lay on its moments of irony and comedy, but it is made with such fluency and verve.It is a tale of two couples. Jeon Do-yeon (from Lee’s Secret Sunshine) and Sul Kyung-gu play Mi-ok and Ho-seok, a deeply unhappy married couple from a blue-collar background with a young son. Ho-seok is angry, depressed and struggling with a drinking problem after a catastrophic end to a strike at the factory where he worked. While at the funeral of a colleague of Ho-seok’s, who has taken his own life, he and Mi-ok meet a fashionable and wealthy couple who are making a documentary about the injustice of the way the factory workers were treated. (This couple have a dog instead of a child.)Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) is the stylishly dressed director, earnestly seeking public grants for her issue-driven documentaries but clearly only able to make independent movies because of her rich hedge fund-guy husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). The film hints that he has something to do with the sale of the factory that treated poor Ho-seok so badly. Shrewd Ye-ji senses that this unhappy working-class couple could make a great story, and with insouciant ruthlessness sets out to befriend Mi-ok, invites them on double-date trips to restaurants and for a vacation trip to Sang-woo’s magnificent family home with its private beach. She also gets drunk with Mi-ok – all part of what Sang-woo calls her “method acting” approach to befriending interviewees, to which she indignantly replies: “I’m trying to love these people.”Ye-ji intrusively pokes her camera into every corner of the couple’s lives. Mi-ok grasps how therapeutic it could be for them both to talk about their experiences and to have a kind of ownership of what they’ve been through; Ho-seok is much more reluctant to talk, partly because it has been so horrible – and also, perhaps, because he can see that comparing their humble lives to these wealthy people will be intimately painful and destructive.There is a cool and judicious neutrality to the way Lee treats Ye-ji and Sang-woo, not immediately exploring the satirical potential of their exploitative and predatory pseudo-friendship with Mi-ok and Ho-seok. And in fact this film finishes well before it gets to where another on the same theme might wish to take it – that is, with the documentary getting made and Mi-ok and Ho-seok becoming unwilling celebrities and public figures. Possible Love is far subtler than that. Its hesitant, conditional vein is signalled in the title itself. It is possible that the love between Mi-ok and Ho-seok will rekindle; it is possible that the “love” that Ye-ji shrilly insists she is trying to feel for them will be real. Love is possible – in the future. It is a sombre, bittersweet, elegant movie.Possible Love screened at theVenice film festival. It is in cinemas on 23 October and on Netflix on 6 November.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSouth KoreaVenice film festivalAsia PacificFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: 1984 review – brings new meaning to the word Orwellian | National Theatre of Scotland | The Guardian
description: Orwell is himself a character in this frustrating but provocative adaptation of his dystopian classic, which seeks to refresh its metaphors and make its totalitarian nightmare seem real again
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Orwell is himself a character in this frustrating but provocative adaptation of his dystopian classic, which seeks to refresh its metaphors and make its totalitarian nightmare seem real again
Content: Welcome to Room 101 … Irene Macdougall as O’Brien and Jack Tarlton as Winston in 1984.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenWelcome to Room 101 … Irene Macdougall as O’Brien and Jack Tarlton as Winston in 1984.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicNational Theatre of ScotlandReview1984 review – brings new meaning to the word OrwellianCitizens theatre, GlasgowOrwell is himself a character in this frustrating but provocative adaptation of his dystopian classic, which seeks to refresh its metaphors and make its totalitarian nightmare seem real againKatie HawthorneSun 6 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat is there left to say aboutNineteen Eighty-Fourin 2026? By now, Orwell’s dystopian satire has been held as a mirror to everything from Trump to TikTok. But this co-production from a trio of Scotland’s leading theatres (Dundee Rep, Edinburgh’s Lyceum and Glasgow’s Citizen) is a new adaptation by Chris Hannan, and seeks to shine fresh light on one of our most overused modern-day shorthands.It’s framed by speculative biography about Orwell’s tuberculosis treatment in a hospital near Glasgow, and it feels cheap, at first, to correlate Orwell and 1984’s Winston so simply. Both are played by Jack Tarlton with the same petulance and hacking cough. But Winston’s childlike naivety, and his monologues pleading for genuine conversation (which reverberate emptily; a literal echo chamber) eventually make for jarring contrast with Orwell’s frosty dialogues with his doctor, who fought opposite him as a fascist in the Spanish civil war.Jumpsuited Thought Police patrol a towering set made of rusty scaffolding, amid blaring industrial noise and plunges into blackout darkness: the staging of totalitarian Oceania is as nightmarish as you’d expect. Directed by Dominic Hill, an eight-strong ensemble bring surrealism, physicality and flashes of warmth. Irene Macdougall is a fabulously unknowable O’Brien, and Jessica Hardwick brings grit and humour to Julia, Winston’s famously underwritten love interest, although the pair share barely a spark of chemistry.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mihaela BodlovicWinston’s torture scenes, using the same hospital bed and nurses (now blood-stained), contrast hammily with Orwell’s bratty attitude towards his own medical treatment. It takes the sting out of these precisely choreographed violent acts, replete with the dreaded trip to Room 101, but the comparison pays off when Orwell and his doctor take a scalpel to their own opposing views about extremism, and even the baseline “facts” of medical science.Nothing but the truth: the legacy of George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-FourRead moreThe implication is that, outside of Oceania, we are lucky to indulge in arguments at all: poor Winston couldn’t. But how far can agreeing to disagree take us? And is there not a real danger in fence sitting, when the stakes are so high? This is both a frustrating handling of Orwell’s classic, and a provocative reminder of the importance in saying: “I don’t agree.”Explore more on these topicsNational Theatre of ScotlandGeorge OrwellDundee RepreviewsShareReuse this content

title: King Lear review – Ian McDiarmid is a titanic, heartbreaking wonder | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive production
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive production
Content: From emperor to king … Ian McDiarmid as Lear at the Crucible theatre.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenFrom emperor to king … Ian McDiarmid as Lear at the Crucible theatre.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewKing Lear review – Ian McDiarmid is a titanic, heartbreaking wonderCrucible theatre, SheffieldThe 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive productionMark LawsonSun 6 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “nothing” is spoken four times in four lines in the opening scene of King Lear, among 30 uses across the play. This feels the key to Titus Halder’s Sheffield Crucible staging, which really makes something of nothingness, crowned by an unusually age-appropriate performer as the “fourscore and upward” English king: 82-year-oldIan McDiarmid.The dark pit of Richard Kent’s design might be a nuclear after-blast. Like Peter Brook’s mid 20th-century stage and film versions, in a previous era of existentialist international tension, the interpretation radiates terminal uncertainty. Characters address pleas and prayers to “the gods” in the direction identified with heaven but with a growing knowing that nothing is there.It is also clear that the kingdom Lear ruinously tries to divide between his three daughters is already past its rule-by date, probably due to his eccentric leadership. In a moment of apparent clarity during his mental decline, Lear says, “I will be jovial”, and this often unremarked line seems the base note to McDiarmid’s titanic performance.View image in fullscreenFode Simbo as Edmund and Katie Wimpenny as Goneril.Photograph: Johan PerssonGiggling dirtily when speculating about his daughters having “issue”, he grins manically out of sync with situations. His threat to inflict “terrors” on the world even though he “does not know yet” what they are is not, as often, the forgetfulness of dementia but political bullshitting that wins a knowing laugh from the audience. Leaving his court unsure what he will say or do next, the erratic head of state is also transactional, giving real chill to the dismissal of the banished Cordelia: “Her price has fallen.”But, while it might be no surprise if this Lear suddenly imposed tariffs on France, the portrait of power is much broader: this demagogue, unfashionably, admits fault and reaches forgiveness.The acting paradox of Lear is that the textual extreme physical frailty must co-exist with the ability to carry Cordelia’s corpse and the vocal depth to serve the dense poetry. Because of this, middle-aged actors are often cast.View image in fullscreenSimbo as Edmund with Harry Redding as Edgar.Photograph: Johan PerssonWhile birth-date realism raises obvious risks, McDiarmid perfectly combines bodily authenticity (the problem of transporting the dead daughter cleverly sidestepped) with absolute verbal clarity on the required range from explosion to self-reflective emotion. When Lear’s heart broke, so did mine.Fool – also seemingly a chief of staff cum carer to Lear – is Max Revell, a dancer with a background in breaking and popping. The result is a spectacularly gymnastic Fool, backflipped by the storm winds and illustrating the jester’s metaphor about a crab by twisting himself into one. Dramaturg Sophie Duncan’s skilled elision of variant texts emphasises Edmund, played by Fode Simbo with a manipulative charisma suggesting Gloucester’s bastard son as a cousin of Iago in Othello. Bebe Sanders’ dignified, wounded Cordelia highlights the bravery of this character in the dramatic scheme. Mark Holgate is powerful as a site-specific Yorkshire Kent.The production is uniformly impressive but the wonder is McDiarmid, topping a remarkable career that combines a popular culture summit – Emperor Palpatine in the Star Wars movie franchise – with, now, this classical peak.At theCrucible theatre, Sheffield, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWilliam ShakespeareIan McDiarmidreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘When there’s joy, there’s room for hope’: Eberechi Eze, Leona Lewis, and Yinka Ilori in conversation with Ezra Collective | Ezra Collective | The Guardian
description: Bandleader Femi Koleoso gathers the England and Arsenal star, as well as the musician and artist, to discuss hope, creativity and Black British culture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bandleader Femi Koleoso gathers the England and Arsenal star, as well as the musician and artist, to discuss hope, creativity and Black British culture
Content: Collective wisdom … Leona Lewis, Yinka Ilori, Femi Koleoso and Eberechi Eze.Composite: Dennis Leupold, Mariano Regidor/Redferns, Matt Alexander, Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCollective wisdom … Leona Lewis, Yinka Ilori, Femi Koleoso and Eberechi Eze.Composite: Dennis Leupold, Mariano Regidor/Redferns, Matt Alexander, Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesEzra CollectiveInterview‘When there’s joy, there’s room for hope’: Eberechi Eze, Leona Lewis, and Yinka Ilori in conversation with Ezra CollectiveBandleader Femi Koleoso brings together the England and Arsenal star, the musician and the artist to discuss adversity, creativity and Black British culture‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold onto hope‘Like painting with light’: photographer Temi Adegbayibi on capturing the energy of musicMy cultural awakening , featuring Ezra CollectiveSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFemi KoleosoI wanted to bring together people who inspire me and whose work I think evokes hope and joy. Yinka, the first time I saw your work I thought: this is exactly what joy looks like – it’s bold, colourful and the perfect embodiment of that feeling. Leona’s music has brought me joy ever since hearing you when you were on The X Factor. You’re one of the most iconic Black British singers we’ve ever had. With you, Eberechi, your transfer to the Gunners meant a lot to a lot ofArsenalfans, but personally it was a really beautiful way of seeing that things do work out for the good people. Can you tell me about your journeys to where you are now?Leona LewisI grew up in Hackney and I was surrounded by music because my dad was a DJ. He had a million records he would play all the time. I gradually discovered people like Whitney Houston, Chaka Khan and Oleta Adams mainly through my dad and I got really drawn to powerful female singers. I started singing all the time. When I was at school, I had a hard time because I was bullied – singing and writing music became a way to find my voice, my joy and my confidence. From then, I knew music was what I was going to do with my life: I didn’t know how I would get there but I knew I had to. It’s interesting that you do a lot of youth work, Femi, because I went to a lot of youth groups in north London while I was getting into music and then from 14 to 17 I enrolled in the Brit School. It helped me establish my voice and since then I’ve always been obsessed with music and it’s become my therapy: my joy, my pain, everything.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to bring together people who inspire me’ … Femi Koleoso of Ezra Collective.Photograph: Thomas Niedermüller/Getty ImagesYinka IloriMy journey started as a young kid from the Marquess Estate in north London. I remember always being the odd one out growing up there because I was really into design, architecture and anything creative while my peers were into playing football. My mum had like 11 jobs – in catering, as a hairdresser, in hospitality – and seeing her do so many different things ultimately inspired me to follow my own path. I loved art and when I was studying for my A-level, I got interested in how design and play can speak for communities and be a voice for their experiences. My A-level teacher, Mr Doherty, encouraged me to take art and design seriously and eventually I got my bachelor’s degree and applied for a £3,500 loan from the Prince’s Trust to start my practice.During that period, I was splitting my time between working in retail at Marks & Spencer and having a small studio in Hackney, and just experimenting with designing, looking at Nigerian folklore. I love telling stories through design as it gives me the power to touch people. I can tap into an emotion and it will connect with people and that’s what has driven me forwards ever since.Eberechi EzeWhen I was younger I was released by eight football clubs: eight clubs said no, including Arsenal. But I remember knowing for sure that this thing was going to work out somehow. I knew it was going to happen because it’s been pressed so intensely on my heart, and on my mum’s heart as well, without putting pressure on me. It was always: “We pray it works out.” So there’s always been that hope, there’s always been that feeling of believing that this thing will come.double quotation markWhen I design a playground, I think: how can I find the ray of sunlight in darkness?Yinka IloriMy wife was saying to me recently: “It’s crazy because you’re living your dream [of playing for Arsenal]. And a lot of people are doing things they like to do and enjoy doing.” So walking out at the Emirates [in 2025] and living that experience was, you can probably see on my face, it was just a moment of immense gratitude and thankfulness. To God for what he’s done and for fulfilling that promise that was made to me at eight years old. That thing that was in my heart.FKWith the new record, I’ve been interested in hope. I feel like you have a spectrum where on one side you’ve got pain and on the other side you’ve got joy. For you Leona, you mentioned going through bullying at school. What eventually allowed you to find a way out?View image in fullscreen‘Music was my hope’ … Leona Lewis.Photograph: NBC/Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal/GettyLLMusic was my hope, and through singing I found a light to guide me. It gave me something to work towards and it was a form of escapism. It also became my fuel to get better. I remember learning the piano because of it, so the negative situation turned positive. Much like what Yinka said about his work, when I would write music and perform it, I’d feel really connected to others and it seemed like I could tap into their emotions too. When you’re going through a situation like bullying in school, you can feel really isolated, so having something else to focus on is important. Music made me feel less alone.FKThat really resonates with me, since our album is all about the different kinds of music that have come from a painful place but that end up bringing people joy. Things like calypso music doesn’t make sense to me because it was born out of enslaved Africans who were transported to the Caribbean and who ended up making steelpans out of oil drums. It should be the most painful music you can imagine, but it’s so joyful. Even music like grime and garage coming from council estates in London makes people rave and dance. Similarly, Yinka, has your work ever been able to drag you out of pain?YISo much of my work is centred around being resilient. Growing up and being exposed to crime, seeing people lose their lives or seeing friends go to jail, you have to find a way to still see these people as people and acknowledge the beauty and joy in their lives. It made me think about embedding all these conflicting emotions into designing an object or a playground or pavilion – how can you find the ray of sunlight in darkness? I don’t want pain to be the main factor that shows up in my work; I want to lean into joy. When there’s joy in the work, there’s room for hope. Recently, I lost someone close to me and it’s been a real test of still being able to find joy through pain but I think I prevailed.double quotation markI hope my daughter’s generation will step into a kinder, more compassionate placeLeona LewisEEI would say being released by Arsenal was the most painful because I was 13 at the time. Arsenal was all I knew, all my family knew, we had been there for so long, since I was eight. And at that age, it is really all you know, that’s your identity, you’re wrapped up in it. I just remember after that almost feeling like the world was over and not knowing what to do. Anywhere I went afterwards would be compared to Arsenal. I was playing at Fulham and I would be thinking of my friends at Arsenal. When we faced Arsenal, it was like the biggest day of the year for me.YIWhen you’re someone who celebrates joy, you have to wear that mask all the time, but there’s also loss and pain and you have to navigate those emotions too. Still, when people tell me about the way my work affects them, it’s a reminder to keep going because I’m doing something that impacts people’s lives in a small way. It’s the same when I listen to [Ezra Collective’s] I Have a God in the studio, I sing it and it takes me right to church! It’s the same with Bleeding Love, Leona; that’s the anthem that takes me out of what I’m feeling and reminds me of my purpose.FKForget the national anthem, Bleeding Love is the anthem! But have there been any hopeless moments for you Leona?LLI remember being at the airport a few years ago and I was going through a bit of postpartum anxiety at the time after having my daughter. This woman came up to me and she just said: “Your songs saved me. They got me through a divorce and during some of the worst times in my life. I’d put your music on and sing it at the top of my lungs and it made me feel better.” She gave me the biggest hug and it felt like everything melted away. It still makes me emotional to think about it today. The less we can think about ourselves and connect with others and get ourselves out of our own way, the better.View image in fullscreen‘The hope is to be able to inspire people’ … Eberechi Eze.Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty ImagesFKA big part of why I love doing youth work and being around young people is that they are hope and joy machines. They consistently make you feel like everything’s going to be OK. Just this morning, I was spending time with some of the young people I work with as it’s A-level results day and even if they’re not happy with their results and feel like all hope has vanished, you’re only three sentences away from them feeling like they can take over the world again. That’s the beauty of young people: the dark times are never too long and the bright times are so bright. They give me real hope for the future. What are the things that give you hope?LLHope is so wrapped up with my four-year-old daughter; she embodies it for me. She has such light and love and so many opinions. She’s optimistic and it’s beautiful to see. When you have kids, so many things in life are put into perspective. The tiny things that you used to worry about vanish, since there’s no time to consider them. Instead, I’m just hopeful for her generation to step into a kinder, more compassionate and hopeful place for themselves, too. To keep that spirit with them always.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markI want to make people believe that they can do their own thing, their own success storyEberechi EzeYIFor me, it’s seeing what my peers are doing. People like yourselves, the [artist and director] Julian Knoxes and all the people around me. They’re flying the flag of hope and joy in different ways and it’s beautiful. I was also really inspired by watching Shakira and Burna Boy’s World Cup half-time performance. That has been on repeat ever since it aired and it’s given me so much hope and joy for the future. It was beautiful with the colourful artwork on the floor and having children there singing with them. It really gave me positive energy for life and it’s stuck with me since.View image in fullscreen‘I’m doing something that impacts people’s lives in a small way’ … Yinka Ilori on the basketball court he designed at Bank Street Park in Canary Wharf, London.Photograph: Matt AlexanderFKIt’s funny you mention kids, Yinka, as I discovered your work after a kid in my youth group asked me to take him to this coolbasketball court in Canary Wharffull of all these crazy colours. I remembered looking into it and realising you designed it! That was such a beautiful way into your art.YII need to give that kid a basketball!FKHe would love that, especially since he put me on to it. With you all being so established, what do you hope for yourselves going forward? What’s left that you’re aspiring to?EEIn line with my craft and the job I’m doing currently, and with [youth career mentorship charity] The Eze Foundation and the things that we’ve got going on around us, me and my family, the goal and the hope is to be able to inspire people beyond what I’ve done so far. I want to make people believe that they can do their own thing, their own success story.LLI’m finishing my next record at the moment and I’m producing it all and trusting myself to do the whole thing, which is really new for me because I usually collaborate. I’m allowing myself to explore musically and to play the bass, drums and a little guitar.FKYou’re playing drums on the record? Respect!LLIt’s nothing on your level! But I’m leaning into that and exploring a different side to my musicality and allowing myself a space to grow. Sometimes you can get stuck in a box and it’s important to punch those walls away to see where you can go. That’s what I’m doing at the moment – trying to push myself creatively and be as authentic as possible while staying true to my music. It’s important for everyone to do.FKWhat about you Yinka, what’s still on the list?YIWe’ve been working on a new foundation where the idea is to make play accessible for underprivileged communities. We want to create playgrounds, basketball courts and well-designed spaces that allow these kids to find themselves in creativity. We want to design in a global language that everyone understands. That’s what I want to focus my energy on for the next few years.FKI want to end by saying how much of a positive influence you’ve all had on me. You’ve encouraged a lot of growth in me, so thank you. Let’s all move forward with hope.Ezra Collective’s album Here Because of Hope is released on 18 September.Explore more on these topicsEzra CollectiveLeona LewisJazzR&BPop and rockDesignArchitectureinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold on to hope | Ezra Collective | The Guardian
description: The bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. He shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. He shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks
Content: Femi Koleoso … ‘There’s power in a happy story – it brings hope.’Photograph: Sergio PontierView image in fullscreenFemi Koleoso … ‘There’s power in a happy story – it brings hope.’Photograph: Sergio PontierEzra Collective‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold on to hopeThe bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. In his editor’s letter, he shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks‘Things work out for the good people’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso meets his inspirations‘Like painting with light’: photographer Temi Adegbayibi on capturing the energy of musicMy cultural awakening, featuring Ezra CollectiveFemi KoleosoSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy first thought when contacted about guest editing the culture section in today’s Saturday magazine was: this will elevate me into an intellectual bracket far beyond my wildest dreams. The first person I told was my dad. The second was my secondary school English teacher, Mr Pickering. I guess it was a subtle way of letting them know that the student is now in charge.It’s a truly wonderful feeling. Even if this entire takeover is trash, I’m still proud to have been given this wonderful opportunity. That said, I did get an A in my GCSE English and English Lit!To give some context: I am not a writer, nor an intellectual or a journalist. I am Femi Koleoso, a musician from north London. Born to Nigerian parents and raised in Enfield, a corner of London paved with gold, I started playing the drums at church (I know, typical). This became more than a hobby; it was a deep-set love, nurtured in the UK’s wonderful state school system and polished in powerful youth clubs. Today, I travel the world with my band,Ezra Collective, playing and producing music, DJing and broadcasting on BBC Radio 6 Music for a living. If there were a version of the “British-Nigerian dream” that didn’t involve becoming a lawyer, accountant or doctor, you could say my family and I got pretty close.double quotation markThere is reason to have hope for the future; perhaps in this guest edit, I’m building a case for a more positive outlookThere’s power in a happy story; it brings hope. Normal school, amazing career. That’s the dream, right? That said, joy is at the centre of who I am, and every day I am filled with hope for the future.But is there really reason to have hope for the future? Though I often only want to talk about Arsenal football club and playing the drums, I am well-informed enough to see the many reasons to lose all hope, not just for the future of the UK but the world. But while I acknowledge that, I believe there is a counter argument. I believe there is reason to have hope for the future of the UK and beyond; perhaps in this guest edit, I’m building a case for a more positive outlook on things.The word “hope” has many definitions, but as my dear friend, the actor Letitia Wright, wonderfully phrases it via spoken-word interludes on our new album, Here Because of Hope, hope also captures the belief that on the other side of pain there can be renewal. There’s joy after mourning. Beauty from the ashes. Even when you don’t know how or when things will change, there can still be something inside you that believes your feet will eventually land on solid ground.So on one side, you have pain; on the other, there will be joy. And hope is a marker on that spectrum that brings you from one end to the other; it makes you feel like getting to joy might be possible.Being a musician, I see that hope most eloquently articulated in songs. Songs born out of pain bring joy. Fela Kuti wrote a song about his mother being executed by the Nigerian government – and its bassline became a club anthem. The pain and hardship of life in poverty-ridden council estates gave us grime music, which has people sweating and smiling in clubs. Calypso even emerged out of the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade.The fuel for this wide-ranging artistic output, across continents and centuries is, for me, hope. In these features, you’ll be able to read about some people and stories that bring me out of pain and into joy; stories that bring me hope.Collective decisions: Ezra’s cultural picksView image in fullscreen‘Wagner Moura is incredible’ … The Secret Agent.Photograph: APFilm: The Secret AgentI watched The Secret Agent recently while on a long drive to a show in Italy. It’s an intense story and Wagner Moura is incredible. I love the way director Kleber Mendonça Filho so immersively takes you into 70s Brazil.TJ KoleosoAlbum: Rosa Passos – RecriaçãoRecriação by Rosa Passos is a beautiful album, with minimal instrumentation but used in the most perfect way. Especially the drumming. It’s often just kick drum, rather than the full kit, and it works incredibly well. Also, if anybody knows what synth they used on the record, please let me know.Joe Armon-JonesView image in fullscreen‘It was a “Best of London” feeling’ … Steelpans, as celebrated recently at the Southbank Centre.Photograph: Tomprout/Getty ImagesLive music: Southbank CentreRather than go the traditional album-film-TV-show route, I’m picking the Southbank Centre. As part of its 75th-anniversary celebrations, it chose to celebrate the steelpan, and I had the privilege of watching loads of young bands play. It was a “best of London” feeling just seeing so many different generations, cultures and people all dancing and celebrating the joy that togetherness and music can bring.Femi KoleosoView image in fullscreen‘It felt so raw and had so much cultural depth’ … My Father’s Shadow.Photograph: Mubi /PAFilm: My Father’s ShadowMy pick is Akinola Davies Jr’s 2025 film My Father’s Shadow, a Nigerian coming-of-age tale. I watched it recently and loved it. The storytelling was great and it felt so raw. It had so much cultural depth, which I could resonate with as a Nigerian.Ife OgunjobiView image in fullscreen‘She’s not confined to one thing’ … KeiyaA.Photograph: Jessica FoleyAlbum: KeiyaA – Hooke’s LawI’m really into Hooke’s Law by KeiyaA at the moment. Ife put me on to this record when we were on tour in Italy and I haven’t put it down since. I love it when artists take us on a journey through different sound worlds within one album, as I think it creates such a rich and beautiful piece of art. Throughout this album it feels as if she’s not confined to one thing, which gives it a really original energy and makes it a truly unique and captivating listen. She produced it all as well and, sonically, it’s really tasty.James MollisonExplore more on these topicsEzra CollectiveBlack British culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herself | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: The Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in music
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: The Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in music
Content: ‘It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.’Photograph: Roam ArtistsView image in fullscreen‘It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.’Photograph: Roam ArtistsBlack US culture‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herselfThe Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in musicMorgan JerkinsSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be, but at the same time enjoying the fact that there’s nowhere I’m supposed to be.” This admission might seem like the beginning of an existential crisis, but it’s a welcome, liminal space for the rising singer and songwriter Momo Boyd. Between her recently released debut EP, a second EP in the works, and two tours, the 27-year-old is being pulled in many directions. But she’s also enjoying the emotionally ambiguous position she’s currently in – it’s what characterizes much of her work.Boyd, who’s a part of Infinity Song, a pop rock sibling quintet that debuted in 2015, confesses that she’s nervous about striking out on her own as a solo artist. The demands are high: Her debut MissMichigantour just finished its US leg this past August and she will continue on throughout Europe in the fall, with a stop in London in November. She said that in comparison to Infinity Song’s sound, which can be characterized by guitar-driven melodies full of romanticism. “I’m doing my own thing and it’s a bit folksy, emotional and personal.” One might expect that Boyd being both a solo artist and an ensemble group member means that she runs the risk of producing indistinguishable bodies of work. But her moodier sound could not be more different from the family band’s more optimistic tunes. Nevertheless, the young singer is quick to say that the balance between the two lanes has been “pretty easy”.The challenge so far has been trusting herself to explore different sounds in an industry where Black women’s artistry is often flattened into categories. The alternative and indie rock artist Santigoldspoke about the industry’s narrow view of “Black music”during her 2022 Tiny Desk performance, and theGrammy award-winning artist SZA once saidthat her own music was only categorized as R&B because she’s Black. Being Black, female and gifted is often accompanied with being misunderstood–a consequence that Boyd has learned early on in her career.View image in fullscreen‘I’m doing my own thing and it’s a bit folksy, emotional and personal.’Photograph: Jakubaszek/RedfernsHer musical origins began with her father, John Boyd, who started multiple choirs in Michigan, where the family is from, so that the younger people of their community would have an activity after school. By the time Momo was seven, her family relocated from the midwest to the north-east. While going to school in the Bronx, Boyd recalled, a blonde-haired, blue-eyed girl said to the singer: “Where you from? You talk like a white girl.” The comment made Boyd acutely aware of the cultural shift from her slower, midwestern roots to a faster, city life. The suspicion that she was cosplaying whiteness would resurface years later when she released her debut single, American Love Song.Boyd’s melancholic, haunting voice about an ill-fated romance in American Love Song has made some listeners call her the BlackLana Del Rey, which Boyd considers a compliment. “She’s so emotionally interesting,” Boyd says about Del Rey. “I was drawn to her.” Boyd said that working through her own deep-seated sadness has allowed her to protect her inner child and to present herself to the world with intentionality and sensitivity. As the seventh of nine children who, Boyd said, didn’t get much attention growing up, she spent a lot of her formative years experiencing anxiety and temperamental attitudes. She decided to channel those feelings from childhood into her music.After high school, Boyd chose not to attend college and remained at home with her parents, where she learned and practiced the guitar and bass for hours daily. She describes the isolation of that period as “tough” but crucial. When Infinity Song’s Hater’s Anthem, a quirky, acoustic number about jealousy and prideful laziness, went viral in 2023, her family knew that their dedication came full circle. “We always knew something would happen,” Boyd said. “We were feeling a bit discouraged and very unsure. Around that time we were just coming together to see what could happen.”View image in fullscreenMomo Boyd of Infinity Song performs during the Boston Calling music festival at Harvard Athletic Complex on 23 May 2025.Photograph: Astrida Valigorsky/Getty ImagesThough Infinity Song has developed a cult following as a group, each member intends to go solo. So when Boyd released Miss Michigan in April, her siblings were in full support of her endeavors. Boyd’s velvety vocals float over the seven tracks as she processes her self-doubt, avoidant tendencies and lovelorn experiences. Fader called hervoice “moisturized”and The Sourcecalled Miss Michigan “reflective and deeply personal”.This emotional interiority of her music manifests through the visuals for the aforementioned American Love Song, where Boyd sings about the inability to love due to being too “independent” and “American” for commitment. The music video captures Boyd with a delicate touch that complements her soft vocals. She is introduced wearing two-tone chaps-style denim jeans as she pets a horse and stares off into the distance. The fashion is pure rockabilly and Americana – her softly coiffed curly hair, the fit-and-flare silhouettes, a vintage style wedding gown, and an American flag sweater.Boyd alternates between playing the guitar amidst wild grass and brush and running through an open pasture. The ease that Boyd exudes as she frolics through a pastoral landscape might seem incongruent to how such settings, which recall plantations and fields, would have been the historical sites of violence against Black people. “People were assuming that I was catering to a white audience. They were questioning my right to make a song on Americanism because of my race. For it to be twisted as if I’m sinister or an agent of propaganda, when I tell you–” Her voice trails off before continuing. “Sometimes I’m like, should I even bring it up?”The truth, Boyd said, is that American Love Song is not propaganda or even a product of her own imagination. It was her life. Boyd lived with her large family in Shay Lake,a rural oasis for working class and upwardly mobile Black peopleseeking rest away from their homes in Detroit and Flint. Her home was the renovated lobby of an old motel with huge pine trees wrapped around the entrance. She reminisced on her family’s crabapple tree, picnics and bonfires, the small Black church her family frequented, and the countless stars that illuminated the evening skies. “This is where my home is. Do I not exist? Is this not where my family has put in all these hours of work? It’s just the truth. But the truth was controversial.”View image in fullscreen‘This is where my home is. Do I not exist? Is this not where my family has put in all these hours of work? It’s just the truth. But the truth was controversial.’Photograph: Jeremychanphotography/Getty ImagesBoyd operates within a tradition of Black female artists who dare to center their experiences as integral to the American landscape as anyone else’s.In 2016,Beyoncé performed with The Dixie Chicks at the Country Music Awards and online communities argued whether or not she belonged in the genre. Despite her 2024 album Cowboy Carter topping the Billboard charts,she received no CMA nominations.In 2020, Mickey Guyton triggered a shockwave throughout the country music scene withBlack Like Me,a song that addressed systemic racism in the industry. Country music star Tanner Adellspoke about the underrepresentationof Black women in her genre and staked her claim as a glamorous Black woman of the south with her song, Buckle Bunny. Adell toldGrammy.com:“We, as Black women, have been fighting our whole lives. We’ve been fighting for space. I’m purposely trying to bring softness into the picture.”Although Boyd emphasizes that she doesn’t want to over-intellectualize her music, her sound and aesthetic choices are inherently political. “I had some not so pretty experiences in high school with colorism–how you’re perceived, how you’re ranked on the scale of desirability, and whether or not you’re seen. It lowkey radicalized me … My goal is to be a representation for Black women who desire freedom.”Freedom, to her, is the refusal to allow the fear of failure to eclipse one’s courage and the ability to be one’s self. When Boyd created She’s a Sweetheart, a tongue-in-cheek song about a woman who’s too accessible to others, she said she wanted to create a world where Black women were the moment and nothing else existed besides those who looked like her. Despite once feeling invisible because of the color of her skin, Boyd professes that she’s always been a lover of beauty and feminine archetypes. She’s a devotee of classic rom-coms like Love Jones, Brown Sugar, and Pretty Woman. She loves the effortlessness of women from the 1970s and 1990s. And though her wide-ranging interests may confuse some people, Boyd enjoys the variety. “It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.”Explore more on these topicsBlack US cultureMichiganPop and rockBeyoncéLana Del ReyprofilesShareReuse this content

title: RLPO/Manze review – all-British Prom features fiery theatrics and cheeky subversion | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Smartly programmed Prom included a nimble rendition of Britten’s Violin Concerto, the visionary masterpiece that is Vaughan Williams’s Ninth, and the world premiere of Carmel Smickersgill’s A Brick Thrown With Love
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Smartly programmed Prom included a nimble rendition of Britten’s Violin Concerto, the visionary masterpiece that is Vaughan Williams’s Ninth, and the world premiere of Carmel Smickersgill’s A Brick Thrown With Love
Content: Total identification … Andrew Manze conducts violinist Simone Lamsma and the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenTotal identification … Andrew Manze conducts violinist Simone Lamsma and the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewRLPO/Manze review – all-British Prom features fiery theatrics and cheeky subversionRoyal Albert Hall, LondonSmartly programmed Prom included a nimble rendition of Britten’s Violin Concerto, the visionary masterpiece that is Vaughan Williams’s Ninth, and the world premiere of Carmel Smickersgill’s A Brick Thrown With LoveClive PagetSun 6 Sep 2026 08.52 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver a century of British music was on display at this smartly programmed Prom in which the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic proved youdon’t have to hail from Berlinto hold a London audience spellbound. Principal guest conductor Andrew Manze bookended the concert with career-spanning works by Vaughan Williams, there was a world premiere from Carmel Smickersgill, and Simone Lamsma was a commanding presence in Britten’s Violin Concerto.Smickersgill’s A Brick Thrown With Love imagines an act of protest from three perspectives: the idea itself, the affected community and the person responsible for lobbing said brick. The opening movement featured a cheeky clarinet theme, mocked, distorted and ultimately hijacked by a subversive orchestra. A shiver of bells built to an elated climax in part two before shifty, syncopated brass propelled the third section to a brutal catharsis. The musical impasto was applied a little thickly in places but the imagination was impressive.Lamsma won the Britten International Violin Competition in 2004, and her interpretation of the composer’s angst-ridden concerto felt like an act of total identification. Silvery legato and fiery theatrics were the order of the day, ably supported by Manze (himself a violinist) who knew the importance of balancing soloist and orchestral forces. Imperious yet lyrical in the opening movement, Lamsma brought a whiff of brimstone to the whirligig scherzo with a cadenza that exuded pure witchcraft. The finale’s tortuous mood swings were nimbly charted through to the bleakly inconclusive final trill.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCManze has a deep understanding of Vaughan Williams, evident at once from the orchestra’s cushioned account of the Fantasia on a Theme of Thomas Tallis. It was a shame though that no real attempt was made to separate the antiphonal string groups as the composer intended, something the sonorous Albert Hall might have been made for. No cavils regarding his cohesive reading of the Ninth Symphony, which here emerged as the visionary masterpiece it most certainly is. Flugelhorn, cor anglais and a louche saxophone trio added baleful atmospherics to a dark and detailed interpretation that highlighted the work’s kinship with the Sinfonia Antartica as well as its terse interior drama and brooding orchestral weight.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsProms 2026PromsClassical musicRoyal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The twilight of Edna O’Brien: son chronicles novelist’s dedication to her craft and the dread of loss  | Edna O'Brien | The Guardian
description: Carlo Gébler describes mother’s doomed battle to complete a final book as age and infirmity sapped her powers – and his own feelings about her passing
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Carlo Gébler describes mother’s doomed battle to complete a final book as age and infirmity sapped her powers – and his own feelings about her passing
Content: The novelist Edna O’Brien, photographed at her home in London in 2019, blazed a trail for generations of Irish writers.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreenThe novelist Edna O’Brien, photographed at her home in London in 2019, blazed a trail for generations of Irish writers.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverEdna O'BrienThe twilight of Edna O’Brien: son chronicles novelist’s dedication to her craft and the dread of lossCarlo Gébler describes mother’s doomed battle to complete a final book as age and infirmity sapped her powers – and his own feelings about her passingRory CarrollIreland correspondentSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter visiting his dying mother in London, Carlo Gébler returned to his rural home in NorthernIrelandone night and encountered a hedgehog sitting on the doormat. A thought bubbled up: his mother had died and returned as this woodland creature.In fact his mother, the novelistEdna O’Brien, was still alive, and not reincarnated, but his mind insisted otherwise. “At that moment that’s what I believed. And then of course I stopped believing it because I knew it wasn’t true.”When O’Brien died days later in July 2024, at the age of 93, the literary worldmourned the passingof a singular voice who had scandalised her native Irelandwith depictions of female sexuality and blazed a trail for generations of Irish writers.Now her son has produced a chronicle of O’Brien’s final years, a twilight marked by her struggle to keep working despite illness and frailty, and of the impact of her death on his own life.Published on 11 September,No One Tells You: The Last Years of Edna O’Briendocuments the writer’s doomed battle to complete a final book about TS Eliot as age and infirmity sapped her powers.It was a painful fate for a woman so dedicated to her craft. “My mother’s strategy was basically to be a Stakhanovite, to keep on working. That was the elixir of life,” Gébler, a novelist, critic and biographer, said in an interview.View image in fullscreen‘The elixir of life’: Carlo Gébler chronicled his mother’s determination to keep writing in her dying years.Photograph: David Barker/Carlo GéblerO’Brien escaped a stifling and conservativeupbringing in County Clareby moving to Dublin and eloping with an Irish-Czech writer,Ernest Gébler, to England, where they raised two sons, Carlo and Sasha, before divorcing.The Country Girls, published in 1960, established O’Brien’s reputation, launching her image as a glamorous public persona in London: a convent-educated rebel who befriended Hollywood stars while penning novels, biographies, plays and poetry.Female desire and subversion populated O’Brien’s fiction decades before Ireland liberalised and legalised divorce, same-sex marriage and abortion, but that did not entitle Irish people to “co-opt” her memory for political ends, said Gébler.“In Ireland people want a narrative which emphasises the progressive journey, as if she planned all the political progress on the back of an envelope. She wasn’t antagonistic to progress but she was a writer. Writing is about the transcription of feeling into a narrative. That is not a political programme and you shouldn’t get the two mixed up,” he said.View image in fullscreenO’Brien, pictured in 1977, wrote about female desire and subversion decades before Ireland legalised divorce, same-sex marriage and abortion.Photograph: Jane Bown/The ObserverGébler said his mother endured many hostile reviews, initially by critics who deemed her work “unseemly” and later by critics who disliked her forays into the lives of historical figures, such as James Joyce’s museNora Barnacle, or thekidnapping of girls in Nigeria. “Her fiction changed its register, but the world isn’t very sympathetic to that. It’s kind of: ‘It’s not your gig, madam’.”He called a 2019 New Yorker profile a “hatchet job” and lamented that his mother was accused of cultural appropriation. “The dialogue on the left about what is and is not appropriate for writers to write about is chilling. It’s morally cramping and inhibiting.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEdna O’Brien in her own words – archive, November 1962Read morePosthumous acclaim for his mother validated the morbid joke about death being a great career move, said Gébler. “A living writer is sometimes overlooked because there’s so much other noise, but death is an even bigger noise, so you can get people’s distracted attention.”For Gébler, however, her passing brought loss, confusion and dread. “The awful thing about a parent’s death is that you move up to the cliff edge. Once they’re gone, you know you’re next. And then you start to have all sorts of terrible thoughts. Why did I do this to my children? They didn’t ask to be born and then they too are going to die.”View image in fullscreenThe cover of Carlo Gebler’s memoir, No One Tells You: The Last Years of Edna O’Brien.Photograph: New IslandThe impulse for the memoir came in her final weeks as he shuttled from his home in County Fermanagh to tend to her in London, said Gébler. “The unconscious is very patient and very clever, and it always waits until the right moment. And then comes this very strong sense, right, this is what I must write.”Asked if his mother would have approved of the book, Gébler replied: “I think she would have thought that that’s what writers do. She might have preferred a fictional iteration.”He opted for nonfiction. “Why not just tell it as it was? It is about my experience of the death of somebody to whom I was very close – it’s about what the effect someone’s slow annihilation has on the psyche of someone that continues living.”His response to the hedgehog on the doormat showed the “strange things” that the mind is capable of. “Although you are reasonably rational, there are deep wells of irrational belief.”The finality of death is unconscionable, said Gébler. “There’s no way around the fact: one’s own extinction is disgusting to contemplate, as is the extinction of other people.”Those who are close to a dying person have an obligation to let them feel seen and heard, he said. “Human being to human being, you listen. That’s your most important duty.”His other advice is to impose order on the chaos of loss by writing about it, no matter whether in scribbled notes or a published book. “If you just let things fester in the basement of the psyche, they just get bigger and darker and huger and more and more terrible. You have to get it up into the light. And then you can come to some sort of accommodation with it, or a truce.”Explore more on these topicsEdna O'BrienBiography booksIrelandLondonTS EliotJames JoycefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It leaves holes inside of you’: graphic novel aims to remember the history and horror of genocide | Comics and graphic novels | The Guardian
description: Dana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to Palestine
Author: David Smith
Headline: Dana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to Palestine
Content: An image from Dana Mashoian Walrath’s studio.Photograph: Dana WalrathView image in fullscreenAn image from Dana Mashoian Walrath’s studio.Photograph: Dana WalrathComics and graphic novels‘It leaves holes inside of you’: graphic novel aims to remember the history and horror of genocideDana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to PalestineDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe artistDana Mashoian Walrath’snew book honours the Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust. But she also expects it to get her banned from Israel.That is becauseThe Book of Genocidesalso contains a chapter that portrays Palestinians forced to live as second-class citizens and watch their homes bulldozed or bombed. “What does it mean to be starved?” the narrative asks. “To know that perpetrators have themselves experienced genocide and now commit genocide against you?”‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to GazaRead moreThere are many more questions posed by Walrath’s graphic history, which is quite unlike any other book about humanity’s periodic descents into the abyss of mass extermination and ethnic cleansing over the past five centuries.In an experimental blend of anthropology, memoir and visual art, which encourages readers to cut the pages and create three-part interactive figures, she offers 10 case studies ranging from the killing of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and theenslavement of Africansto the Armenian genocide, Holocaust, Cambodia, Rwanda, Bosnia, Palestine and the persecution of the Rohingya.Walrath, 66, an artist, writer and anthropologist, travelled to all 10 places represented in the book and has a personal connection with genocide. She is Armenian-American, the granddaughter of survivors who fledthe systematic destructionof the Ottoman empire’s Armenian population during the first world war. For decades, her family’s survival story was condensed into a single narrative fragment.When she asked her mother about her own mother’s childhood in western Armenia,she replied: “After her parents were killed, she hid during the day and ran at night with Uncle Benny and Aunt Alice from their home in Palu to the orphanage in Aleppo.”It was only recently that deeper, more horrifying layers of that journey were revealed. When her mother, Alice, was diagnosed with dementia and moved into her home, Walrath took a leave of absence from her academic career to engage in full-time creative work, eventually publishing a verse novel about the Armenian genocide, Like Water on Stone.View image in fullscreenThe Genocide of Black Americans.Photograph: Harvard University Press“After that novel came out my older relatives started telling me more details of what happened,” Walrath says from her studio near Burlington in Vermont, adorned with towering draft pages of The Book of Genocides and a monumental portrait of her mother. “I did not know about my grandmother hiding in an urn while her father was dismembered until about five years ago.“She was taken into enslavement with her son. I also learned that my grandmother, at one point probably after sex, hit her enslaver on the head with a stone and the two of them fled. This is what my aunt told me. Can I verify it? Can I find these facts? I don’t know.”This inheritance of violence and survival has haunted Walrath’s life and given her a personal connection to genocide, wherever it happens. She reflects: “It’s knowing what it does to people and knowing how it leaves holes inside of you and that you have to figure out how to overcome the desire to get even.“You have to figure out how to transform the anger and the hurt into something productive and I feel like I’ve spent much of my adult life trying to figure out how to do that. Writing the novel let me exorcise a lot of demons and then writing this book was so gratifying because I could literally bring people together.”Walrath committed herself to traveling to every location depicted in the book, seeking out survivors and descendants to sit with them in their grief. She spoke with survivors ofPol Pot’s killing fields in Phnom Penh, met with perpetrators and survivors of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and visited Rohingya refugees in the sprawling camps of Bangladesh.This deep exposure to human suffering took a severe toll on her physical health. The 66-year-old recalls via Zoom: “I got physically sick at various times and it would usually take the form of a terrible chest cold. Grief is supposed to live in the lungs and I got very sick after Auschwitz. I got very sick in 2013 when I crossed into the West Bank through the wall to go to Bethlehem with a bunch of Armenian pilgrims.”View image in fullscreenDana Mashoian Walrath in her studioPhotograph: Harvard University Press“I remember right after I came back from Auschwitz I was reading [Polish lawyer and Holocaust scholar]Raphael Lemkin’s autobiography. It starts out great and then he comes unravelled in the last couple of chapters. I had a spell where I was thinking, oh no, what if I lose my mind?“Then I went through no, no, I have very good supports and live in nature and, at this moment in time, as America is well on its way into a very scary place, I felt like I could get up every morning and have something concrete to do to push back. When I reread the book recently it was even more shocking how many elements of USA 2026 are present in all these genocides.”To convey these heavy histories, Walrath turned to a medium distinctively suited to representing the unrepresentable: comics. In the tradition ofArt Spiegelman’sMaus andJoe Sacco’sPalestine, The Book of Genocides uses the graphic form to bridge the gap between abstract history and raw empathy.“Comics are very active. I love cinema and it’s a very powerful medium for learning about things that might be outside of your experience but it is passive. You sit in your seat and you take it in. Comics are probably closer to cinema than anything else but they’re active. They’re created by a series of fragments that the reader has to take in and process and put together in an active way and because of that it gave me a vocabulary to talk about these horrors without making people run away from them.”Walrath deliberately avoided drawing explicit, realistic acts of violence, opting instead for metaphorical representations. “I left out drawing most of the horror and was always walking the line between making sure the image was gonna draw people in, even if it was talking about something horrible,” she says.The book’s unsettling interactive design aims to force readers to confront the systemic patterns of dehumanisation that make such horrors possible. Readers are invited to cut certain portrait pages into thirds, creating a “turn-the-flap” sequence – a structural device reminiscent of the surrealist game of “exquisite corpse”. As the reader flips the segmented pages, the illustrated human subjects transform back and forth between recognisable faces and non-human creatures – beasts, predators, vermin and parasites.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian Genocide.Photograph: Harvard University PressFor Walrath, this physical interaction is not a gimmick but an exercise in moral philosophy. She explains:“I wanted people to try and get inside the mind of someone else and also to make it so that they would feel their potential complicity. Have I always spoken up when I’ve heard somebody call someone else a monster? Have I always spoken up if someone is called a parasite? I don’t know. A lot of times we let things slide.“We’ve invited people to cut the pages to get people thinking about how we’re taught: what’s allowed and what isn’t allowed. We’re not supposed to desecrate books. We love books and yet we’re taught that war is OK, that it’s OK to kill other people. I wanted it there in an interactive, metaphorical but also subconscious way, rather than saying, this is what we do. People take it in differently when they’re interacting with it.”The Book of Genocides relies on the concept of genocide developed by Lemkin and enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention: ‘acts committed with the intent to destroy in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group” and marked by a process of dehumanisation of the targeted group.As an anthropologist, Walrath finds a common thread running through half a millennium of genocidal violence. She argues that they are often less spontaneous outbursts of tribal hatred than highly planned, bureaucratic operations, with material interests – particularly land – playing a central role.“Land theft almost always. The only exception is not really an exception; it’s enslavement. The Europeans stole Africa but then also stole African people and then put them into thetransatlantic slave tradeso, even though the land stealing was going on within the Americas, it was dependent upon European colonisation. Settler colonialism is nearly always there.“Dehumanisation is part of that and then systemic injustices within the societies. These are precursors to massacre. What’s the difference between prisons in the US and many other countries where strictly disenfranchised people are the majority of the prisoners, andthe Warsaw Ghetto?”Perhaps the most controversial decision in The Book of Genocides is its chapter that addresses the history of Palestinian displacement and the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks andIsrael’s subsequent war in Gaza. The inclusion of Palestine underthe banner of genocideis a move that Walrath knew would draw fierce criticism and potentially severe professional consequences.View image in fullscreenDana Mashoian Walrath in her studio.Photograph: Harvard University Press“I decided that was the right thing to do because the goal of the book is to spark conversations, to put it out there, to talk about Palestine, call it a genocide, and let people start speaking with each other about it.“It would be great for someone to try and say why it is and isn’t genocide, and at the same time. I think that the way I’ve employed the term is aligned with Raphael Lemkin’s intention about what genocide was. It’s aligned with the convention, withthe Rome statute, and what we’re watching is political machinations making the convention useless.”Walrath adds: “Indiscriminate bombing of any place is a war crime for sure. When we’re killing babies and killing children and keeping people from healthcare and selectively bombing hospitals and journalists, I have no doubt in my mind that this is a systemic attempt to eliminate a people.”She is clear-eyed about the fallout of this stance in Israel. “I probably won’t be allowed to visit again, which would be sad because I have respect for the real peace activists there. Honestly, going to Jerusalem as an Armenian was incredibly powerful. But maybe this will change and in my lifetime maybe I’ll live long enough that I will be able to go back but I know right now after this book comes out I will no longer be able to arrive at the airport.”Despite the harrowing terrain of her subject matter, Walrath remains fundamentally an optimist. She rejects the jaundiced view that human violence is an evolutionary inevitability. “I am sure that’s not true. I am sure that we’re hardwired to care for one another. Every time we see dehumanisation get undone in the midst of a war it’s because someone’s heart has been touched.“It’s governments that perpetrate genocides and it’s baked into our systems and structures and because those systems and structures and governments are all human-made creations, we can make better ones. A rugged as the content is, the message is an underlying message of hope and that we can change this. It’s not inevitable.”The Book of Genocides is out on 8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsComics and graphic novelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Annie Wobbler (Revisited) review – Arnold Wesker’s moving women live again  | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Nichola McAuliffe returns to the roles Wesker tailored for her in 1981, in a trio of wistful and insightful soliloquies about working-class women’s inner thoughts
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Nichola McAuliffe returns to the roles Wesker tailored for her in 1981, in a trio of wistful and insightful soliloquies about working-class women’s inner thoughts
Content: Universal sadness … Nichola McAuliffe in Annie Wobbler (Revisited).Photograph: Ella Carmen DaleView image in fullscreenUniversal sadness … Nichola McAuliffe in Annie Wobbler (Revisited).Photograph: Ella Carmen DaleTheatreReviewAnnie Wobbler (Revisited) review – Arnold Wesker’s moving women live againFinborough theatre, LondonNichola McAuliffe returns to the roles Wesker tailored for her in 1981, in a trio of wistful and insightful soliloquies about working-class women’s inner thoughtsArifa AkbarSun 6 Sep 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome years before Alan Bennett spawnedTalking Heads, his celebrated televised monologues on the inner lives of solitary women,Arnold Weskercreated a trio of short soliloquies for women who speak their thoughts and vulnerabilities aloud in the same wistful manner.His three-character series, written in 1981 and tailored especially for the actor Nichola McAuliffe, originally began with elderly, homeless Annie Wobbler, who wanders around London’s Waterloo station ruminating on her life in service, the changing world, and what she sees as the ever-rising tide of “foreigners” in it. Younger women follow, their names variations on Annie’s, and each incorporating a specific question or inquiry into their life.This rejigged show, staged at the Edinburgh fringe festival last month, sees McAuliffe reprise the roles more than four decades on, and play out the series in the opposite order from the original, so the youngest woman, Anna, comes first.Anna’s monologue comprises an awkward mix of feminist commentary and self-loathing. She speaks of her critical mother, her establishment boyfriend (a disembodied voice played by Alex Jennings) and men in general. A university graduate with a French degree (albeit from a former polytechnic, she repeats in what seems like imitation of her boyfriend’s snobbish judgment), she bears a distinct sense of imposter syndrome. If you didn’t know the play, you might think of Anna as a mature student, likeWilly Russell’s Educating Rita. Some of her phrasing and insecurities sound over-egged and artificial (“I’ve got brains and black underwear”), while updated references to Chat GPT and the TV comedyAnn Droiddo not prevent it from feeling dated.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ella Carmen DaleThe next woman is Annabella, a celebrated novelist being interviewed by an offstage male (voiced by James Naughtie), about her artistic process and the effects of fame. There are some striking moments and McAuliffe creates pools of reflection, but confusingly the character morphs from a Dubliner in a floaty gown to a Scotswoman in lycra and then a posh Englishwoman.Arnold Wesker: the radical bard of working BritainRead moreThe destitute Annie of the final monologue is the most haunting. She seems like a figure risen from London’s past, with an old-fashioned cockney accent, and thinks of herself as a seller of “bags of coal”. But there is also the universal sadness of a drunk woman living somewhere between her better past and this foggy present. She speaks of foreigners and Jews around her but seems less critical or xenophobic than confused by time and social change. (Wesker was himself Jewish.) She cuts a moving figure who could be from Dickens’ time or found wandering around Waterloo station today.The three parts do not seem contemporary nor particularly enlightening about the female condition but they are curios and certainly show Wesker’s compassion for, and insight into, working-class women.AtFinborough theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreArnold WeskerFinborough theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Biopsies, aerial drills and a personal pizza: a day in the life of a shark scientist | Well actually | The Guardian
