description: Jasmin Graham, a shark scientist and science communicator, also makes time in her day to practice her hobbies and play music bingo with friends
Author: Jaya Saxena
Headline: Jasmin Graham, a shark scientist and science communicator, also makes time in her day to practice her hobbies and play music bingo with friends
Content: ‘Sharks are not monsters, they just need better PR,’ Graham writes on her website.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Sharks are not monsters, they just need better PR,’ Graham writes on her website.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesA day in the lifeWell actuallyBiopsies, aerial drills and a personal pizza: a day in the life of a shark scientistJasmin Graham, a shark scientist and science communicator, also makes time in her day to practice her hobbies and play music bingo with friendsJaya SaxenaSun 6 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Sharks are not monsters, they just need better PR,”writes Jasmin Graham. And she should know: Graham is a shark scientist and science communicator.Here’s what a day in Graham’s life in Sarasota,Floridalooks like.Do you have a morning routine?I usually wake up around 8am, but I woke up at 7am because I had to go to the dentist. I got a head start on some emails and took a fundraising phone call in the car.After the dentist, I got home and did my drills. I’m an aerialist, which is basically all the things you see in Cirque du Soleil: lyra [aerial hoop], pole and silks. Breakfast was Honey Nut Cheerios.I went to the office to meet with an artist in residence [with Graham’s nonprofitMinorities in Shark Sciences]. They’re helping build props and sets for our theater shows. One is an immersive experience about the mass extinction of sharks. It’s a combination of a whodunit and an escape room.What did you do for lunch?I get delivered meals because I don’t have time to cook – it was some sort of pasta thing. After that, I was working on a grant for grassroots organizations working on the environment in the south-east. I’m co-chair of the Priorities, Projects, and Campaigns committee of theAmerica the Beautiful for All Coalition, a coalition of organizations that want to protect nature and also center justice and access. Then I worked on prepping for our shark survey next week.What does a shark survey entail?Surveys have different goals, with the overall mission of understanding our local shark populations and assessing their health and stability.We are targeting bonnethead sharks, but we also get stingrays. We bring them on board and measure them. Then we take a little fin clip, which is like taking a fingernail, so we can see who’s related to who. We also take a little muscle biopsy to look at the toxin load in their body. We’re particularly interested in brevetoxin, which comes from red tide, a harmful algal bloom that we unfortunately have here in Florida a lot.For the bonnetheads, we make a quick incision and we put a transmitter inside them and suture them up. That transmitter can track their movements for up to three years. Then we release them, and they swim off.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat did you do to unwind?I came home and had a little personal pizza. Then I drove to Beerbusters, a Blockbusters-themed bar, for music bingo. One of my friends hosts, and it’s always fun – our prizes are just things that people want to get rid of. I ended up winning a printer and a 3D puzzle. Someone brought a fire pit. On the way home, I listened to the KPop Demon Hunters soundtrack.What time did you get to bed?I usually go to bed between 11pm and midnight. It’s very important for me to get eight hours of sleep. Otherwise, I become a monster of a person. I usually pet my dog and watch silly things likeKevin Languevideos in bed. I check my Google Calendar for tomorrow so that I can mentally prepare, and make sure I don’t need to wake up any earlier.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyA day in the lifeSharksFloridaAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a sweet, tender voice’: the pilot who fell for his air traffic controller – before ever seeing her | Relationships | The Guardian
description: Alfredo Bravo had a job he loved and was determined never to be grounded by marriage and kids. Then a voice from the control tower changed everything
Author: Jonathan Franklin
Headline: Alfredo Bravo had a job he loved and was determined never to be grounded by marriage and kids. Then a voice from the control tower changed everything
Content: On the same wavelength … Alfredo and Carolina, who have been together for 25 years.Photograph: Benja Villela/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOn the same wavelength … Alfredo and Carolina, who have been together for 25 years.Photograph: Benja Villela/The GuardianRelationships‘It was a sweet, tender voice’: the pilot who fell for his air traffic controller – before ever seeing herAlfredo Bravo had a job he loved and was determined never to be grounded by marriage and kids. Then a voice from the control tower changed everythingJonathan FranklinSun 6 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlfredo Bravo had landed aeroplanes in a lot of sticky situations – as a bush pilot in Chilean Patagonia and as a commercial pilot in rural China – but it was a singular voice floating over the radio waves from air traffic control in Santiago,Chile, that set his heart aflutter, upended his concentration and reshuffled his life.It was the 1990s and, although he was still young, Bravo had held pretty much every low-level flying gig possible. He had dumped plumes of orange chemicals on to forest fires and flown surveillance missions to detect illegal fireplaces polluting the already smoggy Santiago airspace. He had completed hundreds of flights with photo crews operating a big Hasselblad camera as they mapped tree farms, calculating the heights of trees in a forest owned by a timber company involved in a low-level guerrilla war with the Indigenous Mapuche. As a pilot for the company, Bravo was a conspicuous outsider who slept in the fields amid the Indigenous communities, and worked alone in the hangar. But Bravo had a pair of aces up his sleeve.His first was that he was not Chilean. Bravo was born in Montevideo, Uruguay, a quietly functional socialist democracy with a mass middle class, an erudite populace, and a fleet of dilapidated motorcars – a bit like Cuba might have become had things worked out. Thus he avoided the vitriol directed towards the Chilean government for its three-centuries-long campaign of repression of Indigenous peoples.Bravo’s second ace was his generous nature. On his days off, the young pilot began offering free flights, and spent his Saturdays and Sundays twirling local kids into the air. “Soon after, the community adopted me, they sent me food all the time,” says Bravo.Flying was Bravo’s game, and he promised himself never to let children or a family get in the way of his free-flying lifestyle. “When I saw people on the highway with bicycles in the car and three kids inside, I would think: ‘Poor guy. That guy is crazy.’”Then, in 1999, while preparing to land at a small airfield in the Vitacura neighbourhood of Santiago, Bravo heard her voice for the first time. He has never forgotten that first heart-thumping moment. “‘OK’, I told myself, ‘Alfredo, come on. Yeah, her voice is very nice but …’”View image in fullscreen‘Her voice transmitted warmth’ … Alfredo and Carolina.Photograph: HandoutBravo began to invent reasons to talk to the air traffic controllers. How could he match a face to that voice? It took him weeks. Pilots and air traffic controllers had mismatched schedules; controllers worked for three to five days, then had two or three days off. There were few routines, few fixed schedules.Bravo invented excuses to visit the control tower. “I got into the tower, officially on some stupid tour,” says Bravo, of his first visit. He had waited until it was winter and air traffic at the small field was reduced to fewer takeoffs and landings, with plenty of downtime to plot his approach.As often as he could, Bravo obtained access to the tower, listening intently for a cadence, a certain lilt as the air traffic controllers on duty answered his invented queries. Was it her? He failed, and failed again to identify her. “It was a very sweet voice, a tender voice. It transmitted warmth,” says Bravo, who only after weeks of trial and error, finally matched the voice to a woman who introduced herself as Carolina Provoste.Provoste took one look at Bravo and freaked out. From her low desk, all she could see above the partition were his Caribbean-blue eyes and a gaze that she instantly felt she recognised – because she had fallen in love with it in a dream she had when she was a teenager. “The dream was shocking, because I felt so much love that I broke up with my boyfriend,” she now says with a laugh.The normally loquacious air traffic controller clammed up. “My friends knew I liked deadpan jokes, so they told me to tell him one,” she says. “But I couldn’t. I was too nervous.” She grabbed her belongings and sped off to a meeting room, too unnerved to speak to the man her colleagues glowingly referred to as El Uruguayo.But there was no denying the instant chemistry between them. Bravo decided to up the ante, so he baked a cake, placed it in the cockpit and invented a flight plan that would end with him landing at the airport where Provoste worked.But the weather was bad and just as he was approaching the landing strip, Provoste ordered him to return to the airport from which he had come.Their first date was also a disaster. Having little cash, Bravo had got hold of two free cinema tickets, but when he handed them to the usher he was told they had expired a week earlier. At this, Bravo thought it was all over, but Provoste didn’t hesitate to pay and keep the flame alight. That night, they shared their first kiss and soon the slow, wintry afternoons provided a perfect excuse for flirting in the control tower during long hours between occasional takeoffs and landings. After work, they travelled together on the bus home – by coincidence, they lived just eight blocks apart.View image in fullscreenTheir special place … Alfredo and Carolina.Photograph: Benja Villela/The GuardianAfter a few months of this, an overseas assignment that Bravo had long sought finally came through. Flying for an NGO in the national parks of Mozambique, it would have been safari bush-pilot heaven. But Bravo turned it down immediately. He realised that what he really wanted was to be more grounded, more able to devote himself to this single mother with a three-year-old daughter.The relationship continued. Bravo was regularly piloting the last scheduled flight to land at Provoste’s airport. The airport would be nearly shut down and already darkened, but when he radioed the tower, it was Provoste’s turn to impress. “At the last minute, when the sun was setting, she would wait for me and she would turn on the lights,” said Bravo.Bravo finally asked Provoste to marry him as he descended in an Airbus jet on a flight back to Chile from Brazil. It had taken three months for his landing to coincide with Provoste’s shift in the control tower. When the moment finally arrived, Bravo panicked. “First, I had to make sure I was actually talking to her,” he says. ”“Carolina? Is this you?” asked Bravo, who had a meticulous script at the ready. She was petrified. She knew the proper use of language from air traffic control was strictly Papa Tango Alpha. No one ever uttered personal names or broadcast personal messages. She confirmed her identity, and Bravo, the co-pilot, announced that he had a question. As the captain gave him a side-eye, Bravo asked Provoste to marry him.Her silence was long and brutal. “I would appreciate your answer,” he drawled. “Before landing.”All she could do was stick to protocol, and utter a single word – “Afirmativo.”View image in fullscreenAfirmativo … the couple, with Provoste’s daughter, on their wedding day.Photograph: HandoutThis private conversation was mistakenly broadcast to a dozen pilots, the entire control tower listening live and a class of 15 up-and-coming air traffic safety planners who happened to be taking a tour of the tower. Everyone was astonished by the proposal, the dramatic delay, then Provoste’s eventual acceptance, which unleashed a whooping, tear-filled celebration – the tower staff as one collective witness. Pilots high above the clouds broadcast heartfelt congratulations.For their wedding, Bravo and Provoste went to Morro de São Paulo, a village on an island off the coast of Brazil. “We bought tropical Hawaiian-style clothing on the beach,” says Provoste. “We got married in Havaianas flip-flops.”Their witnesses and guests were the 12-person flight crew. The only priest on the island married them after motoring across a lagoon in a fishing boat namedSonho de Icaro– The Dream of Icarus.Today, they live with their three children in Santiago, Chile, and recently celebrated 25 years together. Bravo revels in a story he can barely believe is true. Provoste describes their original encounter with the astonishment of someone who just yesterday felt a dream come true. Sometimes, for fun, they listen to the old cassette recording of his bumbling cockpit proposal and laugh.Explore more on these topicsRelationshipsChileMarriageFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry – recipe | Curry | The Guardian
description: There are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation of kukul mas bears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavours
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: There are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation of kukul mas bears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavours
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfecct Sri Lankan chicken curry.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfecct Sri Lankan chicken curry.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...CurryHow to make the perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry – recipeThere are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation ofkukul masbears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavoursFelicity CloakeSun 6 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Every family in our sunny little island craves this creamy chicken,”says Sri Lankan journalist Zinara Rathnayake, “devouring each morsel with carbs of choice: string hoppers, thin rice noodle mats; hoppers, bowl-shaped pancakes; andkiribath, slender rice cooked with coconut milk. All our family recipes may slightly vary, but this glorious dish pins down the labour and love that goes into every Sri Lankan curry.”After all, Sri Lanka is a country that’s “rich in spices”, chef Peter Kuruvita explains. “Most Sri Lankan cooking,” he writes inLands of the Curry Leaf, “features unapologetically punch-you-in-the-face, get-the-adrenaline-pumping flavours. But [in part thanks to tropical crops such as coconut, lemongrass and pandan leaf] the heat is more an intensity of spice than actual physical ‘chilli heat’.” Boldly aromatic rather than delicately fragrant, rich and light at the same time,kukul mas, whichSH Fernando Jr’s book Rice & Currycalls “a mainstay of Sri Lankan cuisine”, is surprisingly quick to make once you’ve prepared, or bought, the spice blend, yet it tastes as if it’s been simmering for hours.The meatView image in fullscreen‘Unapologetically punch-you-in-the-face’ spices: SH Fernando Jr’s Sri Lankan chicken curry. All thumbnail photographs by Felicity Cloake.“Choosing a chicken is a fine art,” Kuruvita writes inhis book Serendip, “and there are two types: a curry chicken and a broiler … The chickens were always sold skinless, as it was a lot quicker for the men to rip the feathers off with the skin rather than to pluck them. The meat was cut up for us and placed in a large ‘elephant ears’ leaf. When we got home, all we had to do was add the spices and cook the curry.” Most recipes indeed call for whole chickens, cut up on the bone – a good cleaver should make this easy, or, if you’re buying from a butcher, they’ll do this for you even quicker. That said, I’m withFernando, who writes: “I use thighs with the bone in when I make this dish as breast meat tends to dry out.” If, likeKaran Gokani of Hoppers, you use thigh fillets, you may wish, as he does, to replace the water with chicken stock; I also favour removing the skin, but that’s up to you.The marinadeMany recipes, as Kuruvita notes, simply add the chicken to the pot as it is, but Gokani, Kuruvita andJeffrey Alford and Naomi Duguid in their book Mangoes & Curry Leavesall marinate the meat first: Gokani in ginger, garlic, turmeric, curry powder and salt; Kuruvita in vinegar and curry powder; and Alford and Duguid in curry powder and garlic. Though all the curries taste great, the marinated chicken comes out a clear winner with my testers and I, “because it seems to marry better with the sauce”. If you’ve bought, or already made your curry powder, there’s no need to delay cooking for too long, but it’s well worth blending it while you prepare the rest of the dish, or indeed if you want to get ahead.The baseAll the curries I try are based on onions in some form. Alford and Duguid go for shallots and Rathnayake red onion, both of which mirror the smaller, sweeter and fierier pink onions used in Sri Lanka. Everyone also adds garlic, and ginger is fairly common, too, a combination that echoes the sweet heat of the onions. Kuruvita’s is the only curry not to include tomatoes – fresh in most cases, though Fernando stirs in tomato paste in the end – which feels a shame, because they add a pleasantly fruity note to the sauce.View image in fullscreenZinara Rathnayake’s ‘emblematic’ Sri Lankan chicken curry.Curry leaves are almost mandatory – only Alford and Duguid leave them out – and I can’t resist the transporting perfume of lemongrass and pandan leaves. The latter, long green leaves sometimes referred to as screwpine, though they has nothing to do with the pine family, can usually be found in the freezer section at south-east Asian food specialists. If you can’t track any down, leave them out, but I adore their haunting flavour that, to me, combines toasty notes of dulce de leche with a grassy freshness; they also make incredible desserts.This sweet, zesty freshness can be underlined with a cinnamon stick and some cardamom pods (some recipes also add cloves), with chilli powder and fresh green chillies bringing the heat (though Fernando adds cayenne pepper and Kuruvita black mustard seeds). Many of these spices are also present in the roasted curry powder that’s the backbone of the dish, so adding a little extra during cooking simply nudges them a little higher in the overall flavour profile.The roasted curry powderIn Sri Lanka, Fernando explains, “spices are usually bought whole, raw and in bulk. They are dried out in the sun in hand-woven palm frond baskets before roasting and grinding.” Using ready-made blends, he suggests, is like swapping freshly ground beans for instant coffee – though Rathnayake, whose mother’s recipe is featured on the website of Kolamba, a Sri Lankan restaurant in London’s Soho, suggests that the stuff sold in Sri Lankan supermarkets (it may be labelled “meat curry powder”) is perfectly acceptable. If you don’t already have an arsenal of individual spices at your disposal, you may well find this the most convenient option.View image in fullscreenCashews add a sweet nuttiness to Jeffrey Alford and Naomi Duguid’s Sri Lankan chicken curry.If you have a wealth of spices to hand, however, it’s really not hard to make the roasted powder that’s usually paired with meat dishes, which, in this survey at least, always contains coriander, cumin, fenugreek, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, pandan and curry leaves, and often turmeric, fennel, black pepper and mustard seeds as well.There’s usually some toasted rice in there, too; not only, Gokani explains, for its nutty flavour, but to act as a thickener, though Kuruvita also includes a thickening powder made from extra rice, desiccated coconut and more spices, which gives his sauce considerably more body than many of the others. Alford and Duguid add cashew nuts on top, which supply a sweet nuttiness, while Kuruvita calls for a startling number of dried chillies, which may be something to consider if you find you’d like a little more fire. I’ve based my curry on the Hoppers version, because I like its sweet, peppery warmth, but, as with all such blends, I suspect there’s a lot of room for tinkering around the edges, particularly heat-wise.Liquid and cookingThe gravy is usually diluted with a mixture of coconut milk and water, though Kuruvita, who includes solid coconut in his thickening powder and tips in an unusual amount of oil, doesn’t bother with the milk. If, as mentioned earlier, you’re using boneless chicken, I’d recommend replacing the water with good, jellied chicken stock.View image in fullscreenPeter Kuruvita’s Sri Lankan chicken curry ‘uses an unusual amount of oil’.Cooking the onions until they’re soft and sweet is vital, but there’s no real need to fry most of the spices here, because they’ve already been toasted.Chickenon the bone takes some time to cook through, so most recipes cover the pan and leave it to simmer gently for 30-40 minutes; bear in mind that the coconut milk will split and separate during this time, but it will still taste just as good as it did when it was emulsified. If you’d prefer a thicker gravy, by all means reduce it further after removing the meat, or thicken by stirring in some extra ground rice mixed with a little water to make a paste.ServingGokani recommends serving this curry with rice or bread, plus a freshsambol, or turning it into akottu, a Sri Lankan favourite involving curry, chopped roti, eggs, onions and chillies (which is also a very good vehicle for leftovers, should you have any!)Perfect Sri Lankan chicken curryPrep35 minMarinate30 min+Cook50 minServes4-6For the roasted curry powder (or use 3 tbsp shop-bought Sri Lankan roasted curry/meat curry powder)4g green cardamom pods4 tbsp coriander seeds2 tsp cumin seeds1 tsp fennel seeds½ tsp fenugreek seeds¼ tsp black peppercorns2 cloves5g cinnamon stick8g rice3g fresh curry leaves(use a little less if you have only dried ones)5cm piecepandan leafFor the curry1 tbsp grated root ginger2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated1 tsp fine salt1 whole chicken, or 6 chicken legs or thighs, skinned, if you prefer, chopped into on-the-bone pieces2 tbsp coconut oil, or neutral oil1 red onion, peeled and thinly sliced2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced1 tbsp grated root ginger1 lemongrass stalk, trimmed and lightly bruised4 cardamom pods, squashed1 cinnamon stick1 tsp chilli powder½-1½ tsp roasted curry powder(see above and method), to taste1 sprigfresh curry leaves2 ripe plum tomatoes, roughly chopped2 green finger chillies10cm piecepandan leaf100ml coconut milkRice and a lime wedge, to serveRub the ginger, garlic and salt all over the chicken, then leave to marinate while you prepare the other ingredients (and for up to four hours).View image in fullscreenFor the curry powder, stir the dried spices in a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium heat until browned and aromatic, then tip out and leave to cool.View image in fullscreenToast the rice until lightly browned, add to the cooling spices, then toast the curry leaves and 5cm piece of pandan until they’ve dried out and add those to the mix, too.View image in fullscreenOnce everything is cool, put all the spices and rice in a blender or mortar, then whiz or pound to a powder.View image in fullscreenNow for the curry. Put the oil in a wide, heavy-based pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the onion for five or six minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic, ginger, lemongrass, cardamom, cinnamon and chilli powder, fry for a minute or so, then stir in the curry leaves and tomatoes and fry until the tomatoes soften.At this point, unless your pan is very large, you might find it easiest to scoop out the contents before you cook the chicken.View image in fullscreenToss three tablespoons of curry powder with the marinated chicken, then add to the pan with a little more oil, if necessary. Turn to coat, then, if necessary, return the tomato mix to the pan and add the chillies and 10cm piece of pandan leaf.View image in fullscreenMeasure out 200ml water, stir in a splash to help dislodge anything that’s stuck to the base of the pan, then pour in the rest of the water and bring to a simmer. Cover, turn down the heat and leave to cook for 15 minutes.Turn over the chicken pieces, stir in the coconut milk, cover the pan again and leave to cook for another 15 or so minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool slightly, then adjust the seasoning if required, just before serving with rice and perhaps a wedge of lime.How do you make yourkukul mas? Is this homely dish an emblem of Sri Lankan cuisine, as Zinara Rathnayake suggests, or would you make the case for something else entirely? And please, do share your recommendations for Sri Lankan restaurants around the world – I’d love to hear them.Explore more on these topicsCurryHow to cook the perfect ...FoodSri Lankan food and drinkChickenMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty
Content: Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘When a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenKintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘When a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewKintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant reviewThoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tastyGrace DentSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid all the bunting and hoopla of the platinum jubilee back in 2022, you may well have missed that Colchester, Britain’s oldest recorded settlement, got an upgrade from town to city status. And, as we all know, no true city is complete without at least one fancy restaurant that serves the likes of duck liver mousse on lattice tuiles. Well, in Colchester,Kintsutakes that slot.Or at least it did until May 2025, when chef Paul Wendholt abruptly shut up shop, citing financial pressures. The name Kintsu plays on the termkintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold, silver or platinum or, more commonly, of embracing imperfection and making something pleasing out of bad luck. So it’s rather fitting that Wendholt, a two-time winner of the Essex Chef of the Year gong, managed to reopen Kintsu just four months later, and a year on is now offering eight courses, plus a few extras, for £90 a head in a Grade II-listed building, albeit one that’s down a back lane beside a multi-storey NCP car park. The setting will win no beauty contests, but when a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him. Come for the secure parking, stay for the treacle-curedDingley Dellpork from nearby Suffolk and the Colchester cherries with amaretto.View image in fullscreen‘Cooked precisely’: Kintsu’s Suffolk bass with courgette, chorizo and XO sauce.Even the very idea of a tasting menu will deter some customers: too faffy, too fiddly. But here, from the first warm-up snack – whipped Montgomery cheddar in a fluted tartlet casing under a blanket of crunchy yeast and yet more cheese – even the hardest of the “I just want me dinner” brigade might find their hearts softening. This is followed by that duck liver mousse-topped tuile with glossy, amber beads of onion gel piped on top and a fat, postage stamp-sized chunk of bread pudding piled with ricotta, lemon, and raw peas and shoots. Style as well as substance.Hunks of warm sourdough arrive, clearly fresh from the oven and reminding you how sweet and fragrant sourdough can be, especially when it’s spread with gloriousFen Farmbutter. A plague upon all that hard, spongy nonsense served up and down the land as a plinth for scrambled eggs. While we work our way through these opening snacks, Lionel Richie’sDancing on the Ceilingplays in the background, and the bread turns up toShattered Dreamsby Johnny Hates Jazz. By the time theBraxtedtomatoes arrive, we are deep intoLiving in a Boxterritory, which feels about right for a Saturday lunchtime in a listed barn. Why can’t all restaurants play mid-1980s chart music?View image in fullscreen‘The strongest course’: Kintsu’s Herdwick lamb with turnip and mint.Those first course tomatoes are a rhapsody of very good fruit arranged strategically on silky whipped pecorino with a wicked green basil oil. It is 1pm on a Saturday and we are on one of only two tables occupied. The minimal staff – two in the kitchen and one on the floor – couldn’t be lovelier, ferrying thick, chunky and squat Cornish crab tarts that look almost like mince pies. There’s lots of brown meat layered under the white, and very good, crunchy pastry. This is good, thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty rather than flippant. I wish more people were here to taste it, but they are probably all at a bottomless brunch somewhere, eating ethylene-ripened avocado mush on fumaric acid-injected bread that tastes of old flip-flops. More fool them.We, meanwhile, are having wild Suffolk bass, its skin all crisp and blistered, cooked precisely and served on a foamed sauce flecked with chives and beads of orange oil. Next up, that treacle-cured pork, which is hot, juicy, pitch-black around the edges, and comes layered with sweet raw and cooked apple. At this point, a third booking arrives, which is great for Kintsu but curtails my enthusiastic crooning along toThe Closest Thing to Heavenby the Kane Gang. The strongest course comes next in the form of Herdwick lamb, and features a moist, well-seasoned medallion with a dark, rich jus, tiny nests of shredded turnip, and yet more lamb, roasted, pulled and compacted on to a metal skewer, and topped with cream and shredded mint.View image in fullscreenKintsu’s cherry dessert ‘doesn’t look much on the plate, but it is utterly fabulous’.A pre-pudding of yoghurt, raspberry and lemon resets the mouth. Then an inventive dessert of Colchester cherries, both cooked and preserved, and served on something biscuity, something creamy and something with a whiff of amaretto. It doesn’t look like much on the plate – a collapsed Jenga of dessert ideas – but it is utterly fabulous. We pay the bill over slices of homemade fig-leaf fudge that I would happily hand out in boxes at Christmas. Or eat alone on the sofa.Kintsu is a huge example of a small regional indie doing its very best in rather weird times. Use these places or lose them. Right now, Kintsu is open: beautifully restored, with shimmers of gold.Kintsu11a North Hill, Colchester, Essex, 01206 574361. Open lunch Fri & Sat, noon-1.30pm (last orders); dinner Weds-Sat, 6.30-8pm (8.30pm Fri & Sat; last orders). Tasting menus only, five courses for £65 or eight for £90, both plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I’ve always supported my dysfunctional siblings, but I’ve had enough. How can I divorce myself?  | Family | The Guardian
description: You feel guilty because you’ve done ‘better’ in life, but you can’t rescue them. Listen to your resentment and learn to let go
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: You feel guilty because you’ve done ‘better’ in life, but you can’t rescue them. Listen to your resentment and learn to let go
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyI’ve always supported my dysfunctional siblings, but I’ve had enough. How can I divorce myself?You feel guilty because you’ve done ‘better’ in life, but you can’t rescue them. Listen to your resentment and learn to let goAnnalisa BarbieriSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m a 66-year-old widowandthe middle of three siblings.They are struggling with mental health,financial issues, or both. I’m the only onewho is doing well in both areas. I’m the only one who graduated high school and college; the only one who hasn’t spent time in jail; the only one who had a successful careerand has a comfortable retirement. I helpthem when asked and appropriate, and do my best to be supportive, even when they continue to make bad decisions.Recently, myolder sister mistakenly texted meintimatepictures meant for the new man in her life. It’s one more disturbing thing in a very long line of disturbing things she’s said and done over the years andI’ve had enough.My world is so different frommysiblings’– it always has been.I feelas if I’m carrying this family, but don’t feel a part of it. I never have, because my choices have always been different, evenwhen we were children.Our parents are deceased, and I’ve become the de facto and very reluctant mother, I’m the responsible one. How can I divorce myself fromthem and not feel guilty? How can I shield myself from their dysfunction, and protect my own sense of peace? I know they will never change.When one sibling seems to have a “better” life than the others, that can bring up guilt, and guilt is a strong tether to behaviours we’d rather not demonstrate. If you could get to the bottom of why you feel it’s your job to carry the family, it may help you start to unshackle yourself.The guilt was the first thing psychoanalytic psychotherapist Susanna Abse picked up on. “Your letter,” she said, “made me think about survivor guilt, which people can feel when they’ve been through something like a very big trauma. [You gave no indication that you had been through trauma, but it might have been useful to know more about your childhood.] I can see you are struggling with rage at being misused by your siblings, and being made to feel responsible.”Abse said that sometimes, when one sibling has a better life than the others, it can feel that something they did caused the others to have that sub-optimal life. I stress we are not saying you did, but often this is the narrative: either their birth took attention away from an older sibling or maybe they got more attention, or more something, at the expense of the others. It’s important to realise that if this was the case it is neither your fault nor your responsibility.double quotation markIf we do better it’s usually because we’ve got a good dollop of competitiveness and we direct it effectivelyThe reality, said Abse, is that “if we do better it’s usually because we’ve got a good dollop of competitiveness and we direct it effectively. Particularly for women, when they direct their energy and ambition and succeed, they can sometimes feel quite ashamed. They don’t want to boast about it.“You can’t help your siblings,” said Abse. “Their situation is very sad, but there’s something a bit omnipotent about your feeling that you can make them better. You have to mourn the fact that you’ve had your own losses. You need to step back and accept your own limitations. We tend to go on trying to rescue others when we don’t accept our own limitations. If you keep doing this you’ll end up feeling more resentful and misused, and it will poison any loving feelings left. Love them for who they are.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI haven’t dated for years and want to try again. How do I prepare for the storm | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreYour most successful shield is to let go. Help them – but not to your own detriment. It’s not easy, but it gets easier with practice. Your resentment is a useful feeling: it reminds you that you are doing too much. When you feel resentful, stop, look and learn from what just happened and try not to repeat it. I don’t think divorce from family members is possible or easy unless you have no other relatives at all who will “loop you in”, in some way.Who was there for you when you were widowed? Refocus your energies on to those people. You deserve to be looked after. And repeat regularly: “I am not responsible for my siblings.”Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions.
