title: This is how we do it: ‘As carers, we have to be responsible. During sex, we relinquish control to each other’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Betsy and Felix have sex once a week when they are alone in the house – it frees up their minds just to be together
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: Betsy and Felix have sex once a week when they are alone in the house – it frees up their minds just to be together
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘As carers, we have to be responsible. During sex, we relinquish control to each other’Betsy and Felix have sex once a week when they are alone in the house – it frees up their minds just to be togetherHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 6 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBetsy, 55double quotation markI used to kick guys out of bed after any sexual encounters. But with Felix it was totally different from the startFelix and I have separate caring responsibilities. I look after my adult son, who has disabilities, and Felix is his elderly mother’s full-time carer. We live in separate suburbs of the same city, and see each other three set evenings a week. We often feel stressed and preoccupied, and so we have a rule: for the first hour, we do a shared trauma dump, where we talk about the sad feelings weighing on our minds.We have sex once a week because it’s the only time we are alone at mine without the people we care for. Felix tends to initiate more than I do because in the last year menopause has really dampened my sex drive. I worry about him feeling rejected. His love language is touch and I want to be able to give him that – so I hold his balls as we go to sleep, which makes him feel comforted.double quotation markOur first sexual encounter was slow, intimate and caring. He really dissolved my boundariesWhen we met at a house party three years ago, we had an instant connection. Felix is covered in tattoos, with lots of earrings and a mohawk. He gave me a gentle kiss on the cheek. After that, I was on a trip for 10 days and kept thinking about that kiss. We spent that time texting and covered so much ground that by the first date, I felt I already knew him really well. He confided in me that he was creating a science fiction pornographic comic strip based on his own fantasies – in a universe where women dominate men – and invited me into his sexual desires.I used to be quite cynical about sex. It was an itch I needed to scratch. I don’t find that intimacy comes very naturally to me. I hated sharing a bed and used to kick guys out after any sexual encounters. But with Felix it was totally different from the start. Our first sexual encounter was slow, intimate and caring. He really dissolved my boundaries. Unlike previous guys, I find him worth sharing a bed with, even if he disturbs my sleep. He’s always called me Lil Betzy – as though I am a rapper – which is hilarious, because I’m a middle-aged woman. I think of him as a gentle part of my life I can cosy into.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreFelix, 58double quotation markBetsy seemed genuinely interested in what excited me, so I felt safe to share it for the first timeI met Betsy at a party and we spoke all night about culture and philosophy. Although it was a meeting of minds, I do recall she had cute little red shoes on and was very busty – I wasn’t too highfalutin to notice those aspects. We texted for a while because she went away and I found myself opening up to her, sharing things I would have never told other folks. For six years, I had been secretly creating a sexy comic strip based in a fantasy world where women dominate men. Betsy seemed genuinely interested in what excited me, so I felt safe to share it for the first time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markEven if we don’t have sex, we’ve found if we kiss, cuddle or hold hands, I don’t feel as rejected by our mismatched libidosWe have sex once a week on a set day. I live with my ageing mother and so when Betsy is here, we don’t have sex. We also don’t have sex at hers when her son is there, which leaves the one day a week I am at Betsy’s and her son is with his father. I think it works best for us to be intimate when we are completely alone, as it frees up space in our minds to just be together. In our sex life, we like to relinquish control to one another. I think that is because in our separate lives we both have to be responsible and make the decisions all the time.This is how we do it: ‘Sex was our glue – now if we fight, we can’t just screw and come out glowing’Read moreSome of my favourite times have been when we were fooling around on the sofa and it evolved into something more. Those moments are harder to come by nowadays because of our caring responsibilities, which is a little sad. The other factor is that my sex drive is now higher than hers, because she’s going through menopause. I try to spend more time on slow foreplay to get her in the mood. Even if we don’t have sex, we’ve found if we kiss, cuddle or hold hands, I don’t feel as rejected by our mismatched libidos.Betsy is not naturally a cuddly person. I know she used to kick other blokes out the bed, and I feel pretty special that she lets me stay over. I think of our time together as very important and never enough.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The student loan scam looking to dupe already anxious students | Scams | The Guardian
description: With about £2.6bn in funds paid out each September, scammers are targeting student anxiety over the loan funding process
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: With about £2.6bn in funds paid out each September, scammers are targeting student anxiety over the loan funding process
Content: The Student Loan Company says it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media, so be suspicious if you are contacted via either.Photograph: Reeldeal Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Student Loan Company says it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media, so be suspicious if you are contacted via either.Photograph: Reeldeal Images/AlamyScam watchScamsThe student loan scam looking to dupe already anxious studentsScammers hope to siphon off some of the £2.6bn in student maintenance funds paid out each SeptemberShane HickeySun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou are about to start university and can’t wait but then you receive a worrying text message. It is a few days before the first student loan payment is due to land in your account and apparently someone has tried to alter your bank details.“Our records indicate that your bank details on your student finance account were changed on Friday 16th. If you did not do this please contact us immediately,” says the text.You click on the web link in the message and go to what you think is the website of theStudentsLoans Company (SLC), the government body that administers loans and grants. You log in to check that everything is OK, put in your bank details and the screen says: “Thanks for confirming.” But what you have done is supply this important information to criminals.Acting quickly, the scammers then use your log-in details to access your real account and change the bank account so that your student loan payment is diverted to them.View image in fullscreenStudents are often stressed enough without dealing with scam texts trying to steal their precious loan payments.Photograph: Prasit Rodphan/AlamyThe government is making a fresh push to raise awareness of this fraud as the new academic year starts.This month, about £2.6bn is being paid out in maintenance support to 1.1 million students. The first of three loan payments will be deposited in the accounts of students in England and Wales. Students from Northern Ireland and Scotland get their loan instalments every month.In the last academic year, £519,000 was lost to scammers who defrauded 168 students, according to the SLC. More than 1,100 people had their details changed but in most cases the fraud was stopped before money was lost.What the scam looks likeScammers are using several methods including text message, email or phone calls to target students.The messages can claim that a payment is at risk because bank details need to be updated. Or it may say that an account has been closed unless the student acts immediately to log in to their “account” through the link provided.The link supplied in the message leads to a clone of the SLC site and students are asked to input their details.“It’s a race against time because the criminals then use those details to log into our genuine site to change the bank account on the genuine student account to divert the maintenance loan payment before we spot it,” said Alan Balanowski, the risk director at SLC.Criminals know that billions of pounds will land in students’ accounts this month and have timed their approach to coordinate the fraud with a sense of urgency that people may not get their money when they need it. This is a common tactic used by criminals to get people to act in haste.View image in fullscreenIn England and Wales, students are paid their loan instalments each September, January and April.Photograph: Kumar Sriskandan/AlamyWhat to doBe aware of when you could be the target of scams – September, January and April are the months when the student loan instalments are paid in England and Wales.SLC says it won’t ask you to confirm personal or financial information by email, text or on social media. Don’t click on any links provided, instead log in to your account through the Gov.uk website.Students are also urged to not publicise when they are getting their payment by refraining from putting it on social media.SLC says that it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media. So immediately be suspicious if you are contacted in either of these ways.Any fraudulent emails can be sent on toreport@phishing.gov.ukwhile scam text messages can be forwarded to 7726.If you suspect your account has been compromised, change the password immediately and contact SLC. Victims should be able to get a replacement payment so there is no financial loss to them.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchStudent financeCrimeConsumer affairsStudentsHigher educationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why the Met’s John Galliano reversal shocked the fashion world: ‘There hadn’t been this much excitement since camp’ | John Galliano | The Guardian
description: Despite Anna Wintour’s years-long redemption campaign on his behalf, the Dior designer’s controversial past got him booted as the 2027 Met Gala honoree
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Despite Anna Wintour’s years-long redemption campaign on his behalf, the Dior designer’s controversial past got him booted as the 2027 Met Gala honoree
Content: John Galliano poses at the end of the presentation of the Dior Haute Couture spring/summer 2010 fashion collection on 25 January 2010, in Paris, France.Photograph: Jacques Brinon/APView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano poses at the end of the presentation of the Dior Haute Couture spring/summer 2010 fashion collection on 25 January 2010, in Paris, France.Photograph: Jacques Brinon/APJohn GallianoWhy the Met’s John Galliano reversal shocked the fashion world: ‘There hadn’t been this much excitement since camp’Despite Anna Wintour’s years-long redemption campaign on his behalf, the Dior designer’s controversial past got him booted as the 2027 Met Gala honoreeAlaina DemopoulosSun 6 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced it was dedicating its 2027 costume exhibition to designerJohn Galliano, vintage dealer Johnny Valencia figured it would be a red carpet for the ages. Celebrities would show up in full Marie Antoinette drag, or squeeze into tightly bound corsets showcasing hourglass figures, recreating the pageantry of Galliano’s over-the-top runway shows.What does Met’s U-turn on John Galliano augur for him, the gala and Anna Wintour?Read more“There was a lot of excitement around this theme,” said Valencia, whose customers include the likes of Beyoncé and Rihanna. “There had not been this much excitement since camp” – the institution’s fete of outrageous and questionable taste in 2019.Valencia runs Pechuga Vintage, a Los Angeles showroom where he sources rare archival fashion pieces from houses such as Chanel, Vivienne Westwood and Versace. With the Galliano theme set, he got to work pulling dresses for the rarefied and beautiful few who would be handpicked to attend the corresponding gala by Vogue doyenne and Met Gala co-chairAnna Wintour.“I located a gorgeous 2004 gown by Galliano,” Valencia said. (That year the designer staged a gold-dripped, Egyptian-themed runway show.) “I had people on the line in Paris to purchase [Dior] couture. There was definitely pressure to find the best of the best.”The pressure evaporated this week, after the Metannouncedthe exhibition honoring Galliano “will not proceed as planned”. This came after a wave of criticism from Met patrons, New York politicians and prominent Jewish leaders who objected to a public institution celebrating a man best-known outside fashion circles for antisemetic and racist remarks.View image in fullscreenJohn Galliano, Naomi Campbell, Helena Christensen and Kate Moss during Galliano runway show on 15 October 1996 in Paris, France.Photograph: Pool Arnal/Pat/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesIn 2010, Galliano was caught on camera saying, “I love Hitler” at a Parisian cafe and telling patrons that their ancestors would have been “gassed”. Months later, he called someone a “fucking Asian bastard” at the same cafe. A swift downfall followed. Galliano lost his creative director post at Dior, where he had worked since 1996, entered rehab and wasfound guiltyin a Paris court of a hate crime. (Galliano, who has been sober for 15 years, said he was living with a “triple addiction” to alcohol, sleeping pills and Valium during his bigoted outburst.)But he would not be fashion’s persona non grata for long. Wintour, a longtime champion of the British designer’s work, brokered his comeback. First came a temporary residency with Oscar de la Renta. Then Vanity Fair published a2013 profileof the embattled designer, who posed for Annie Leibovitz’s camera in front of a dramatic waterfall. (Headline: “Galliano in the Wilderness”.) The piece centered its subject’s “efforts to atone”, including meeting with rabbis and the Anti Defamation League to learn more about Jewish history and the Holocaust. It posited that Galliano’s addiction came at a time of personal crisis that was partly due to the demands of his career and the recent death of his longtime friend and business partner.double quotation markWintour was easing him back to the mainstream, but in the end, everyone was not OK with thatDana ThomasWintour spoke passionately about her friend in the piece. “We need the dreamers,” she said. “We need those designers who create a magic moment, a world that changes the way you look at clothes.”And, for the most part, fashion forgave Galliano, under the pretense of second chances. He ended up leading Maison Margiela from 2014 to 2024,staging a triumphantly flamboyant runway show during his final year that was near universally praised for itsbody-morphing corsetry.This year, Zara announced a collaboration with the designerto be released later this month. But no event would be as visible as “fashion’s biggest night”: the Met Gala.However, despite Wintour’s attempts to get ahead of any scandal – which included inviting Jewish leaders to meet with Galliano, with a rabbitellingthe New York Times the designer seemed “sincere” in his remorse – the rest of the world was not so charitable.View image in fullscreenAnna Wintour and John Galliano at the Dior fashion show as part of Haute Couture spring/summer 2026 held at the Musée Rodin on 26 January 2025 in Paris, France.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesWintour is known for her steely resolve and fearsome reputation. Some fashion insiders are shocked by this rare, public and messy instance when she did not get her way.Lauren Sherman writes Line Sheet, a Puck newsletter about fashion’s power players, and is one of the best-sourced style reporters in the US. But even she “didn’t see” the Met’s Galliano reversal coming. “I think that’s a reflection of being too sheltered by the fashion industry,” she said. “I didn’t speak to one person who ever thought this could happen. I would say [Wintour] was really adamant that [Galliano] be honored while he was alive and working.”Dana Thomas, a Paris-based reporter who wrote God and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano, noted a decades-long “rehabilitation campaign” spearheaded by Wintour. “There was a master plan,” Thomas said. “This was Project Galliano. Wintour was easing him back to the mainstream, but in the end, everyone was not OK with that.”Part of the plan was a documentary about Galliano. According to Thomas, Wintour spoke with three potential directors who all turned it down because they felt that her presence and demands loomed largely over the project. “She personally shopped that documentary for years,” Thomas said.Eventually director Kevin Macdonald took the gig, releasing High & Low – John Galliano, a nuanced look at the designer’s fall from grace, in 2023. The Scottish director is not a fashion person; he is perhaps best known for One Day in September, an Academy Award-winning film about theMunich Olympics massacre. He said he had full creative control over the film, in which Gallianoreferredto his hate crime as “a disgusting thing, foul thing I did”. (Galliano also reports having no memory of the incident.)“Wintour was incredibly helpful and wanted the documentary to be made,” Macdonald said. “She expended a lot of political capital on Galliano. She didn’t need to and has nothing to gain from it. I think she genuinely thinks he’s a great talent. There’s no other reason I can think of why she’d want to spend as much capital on him.”View image in fullscreenA passerby wears a Dior monogram saddle bag.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesThis is the man who created the Dior saddle bag, one of the most popular accessories of all time, and one of the few handbags to have its ownWikipedia page. Galliano’s runway shoes – especially those that came before his outburst – are beloved by professional and armchair critics alike, referenced as the height of fashion-as-art. He designed the newspaper print dress worn by Carrie Bradshaw in a pivotal Sex and the City scene; this piececamefrom a controversial 2000 collection inspired by homeless people, quickly dubbed “hobo chic”. (The collection inspired a scene in the fashion world parody Zoolander.) Galliano’s signature bias cut dresses cling to women’s bodies and ooze a timeless Hollywood glamour. His vintage pieces remain in demand for a new generation of (well-heeled) shoppers, regularly going for thousands of dollars on eBay or in high-end vintage shops – and will probably continue to do so, Met Gala or not.“I would call the Galliano girl a sexy nerd,” said Valencia, the vintage dealer. “She knows her shit and the history around why a piece was made. And she’ll pay the price for it.”double quotation markIf anything, more people know the name Galliano than they did last weekLauren ShermanGalliano is far from the only scandal-plagued fashion designer. The industry rewards those with inflated egos, bad tempers and questionable ethics, and most people who cherish fashion are used to keeping a selective memory when it comes to the past misdeeds of a favorite designer. In 2020 several peopleaccusedAlexander Wang of sexual assault and drugging drinks; his clothes are still stocked at Nordstrom, Bloomingdales and other big retailers. (Wang denied the allegations.) Stefano Gabbana, one half of Dolce & Gabbana, promptedpublic outragein 2018when he appeared to make anti-Asian statements on Instagram after the brand released a video where a model ate pizza with chopsticks that viewers deemed insensitive. Sarah Jessica Parker, Naomi Osaka, Madonna and Jennifer Lopez have all worn the brand since then.Insiders like Valencia consider Galliano’s past words abhorrent and make no excuses for his behavior. But they also fret over what they see as cancel culture run amok. “I just want to ask how many times are we going to reprimand a person and how many times are we going to punish someone?” Valencia said. “[He made] strides in his own recovery, mental health [and] a very public apology.”The devil owns Amazon: big tech has infiltrated the fashion world – will we see a revolt?Read moreCritics, however, publicly decried the Met’s choice. In alettersent to Wintour and other members of the Met’s board last week, Julie Menin, the first Jewish speaker of the New York city council, called Galliano’s antisemetic and racist outbursts “deeply troubling”, and argued that cultural institutions which receive public funding “have a responsibility to demonstrate that hatred and bigotry carry consequences”. She also referred to the account of Lauren London, a publicist who came forward this summer to allege that in 2019, Galliano yelled “Merry Christmas!” at her friend while she spoke on the phone in Hebrew. Galliano denies this account, which Londonfirst sharedon Instagram.If the GallianoMet Galahad gone ahead, Sherman said his work would have seen a boom in interest. “Next summer he would have been everywhere because people have had way more exposure to Galliano and Dior pieces,” she said. “I’m sure [that not happening] means that future sales could be muffled.”It seems Zara still plans to release its Galliano collaboration, for which the designer has reimagined his past runway looks for the fast fashion retailer. It’s Galliano for the masses, though his storybook clothes have never been made with real life in mind.“I know people who have seen the collection,” Sherman said. “They say it’s pretty unique. It’s not super commercial.” Does the Met dustup threaten any interest? Sherman thinks not. “If anything, more people know the name Galliano than they did last week.”Representatives for the Met, Condé Nast and Zara did not respond to requests for comment.View image in fullscreenA dress designed by John Galliano for Christian Dior from the Haute Couture fall/winter 2006-2007 collection is displayed at the exhibition Louvre Couture. Art and fashion: statement pieces at the Louvre Museum in Paris, France, on 23 January 2025.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersFor now, the Met Gala remains without a theme. Wintour has made clear that the fabled “first Monday in May” goes on. Still, there have been calls to cancel it outright, the most prominent one coming from Pulitzer prize-winning fashion critic Robin Givhan in a New York Times opinioncolumn. That’s not so easy to do: this year’s Met Gala, with the theme “costume art”,raised$42m for the Costume Institute.In the week since the Galliano theme was nixed, a new favorite parlor game among the glitterati (or wannabes) is dreaming up alternate ideas. Social media users have suggested a glitter-soaked Dolly Parton tribute, though that seems farfetched. “My recommendation is that they focus on sports,” Sherman said, pointing to the 2028 summer Olympics in Los Angeles. “That’s not going to offend anyone.”More likely the 2028 theme, already in the planning stages but not yet publicly revealed, will be pushed up a year, Sherman said.Thomas, the fashion writer, posted a callout to her Instagram followers for suggestions. “I got Armani, who recently died,” she said. “But they would never do that because [Wintour] doesn’t like him.” (Giorgio Armani onceclaimedthat Wintour said “the Armani era is over”.) Other options from followers: “Christian Lacroix, Issey Miyake, Oscar de la Renta. First lady fashion.”Thomas’s pick would be Ralph Lauren: “If anyone should be celebrated in New York, it’s Ralph Lifshitz, who got his start selling ties out of an office in the Empire State Building.” After all, Vogue oncecomparedthe Bronx-born designer’s rags-to-riches backstory to The Great Gatsby – and Gatsby knew how to throw a party.Explore more on these topicsJohn GallianoAnna WintourMet GalafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe | City breaks | The Guardian
description: From the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspots
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspots
Content: The Grand Éléphant takes a stroll past the Jules Verne-inspired carousel in Nantes.Photograph: Olrat/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Grand Éléphant takes a stroll past the Jules Verne-inspired carousel in Nantes.Photograph: Olrat/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.City breaks‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in EuropeFrom the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspotsSun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNantes, FranceAs dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on theCarrousel des Mondes Marins(marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun.On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project,Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks.double quotation markJules Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art project that has breathed life into the abandoned docksThis is now the stomping ground of theGrand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearbyGalerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life.View image in fullscreenThéo Mercier’s ‘Fossil Opera’, one of the temporary art installations of Le Voyage à Nantes 2026 festival.Photograph: Martin ArgyrogloThe Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival,Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegantGraslin districtare busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste.Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserieLa Cigaleweave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. TitledFossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic.Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, fromLes Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’sBelvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff.View image in fullscreenLa Cigale, an art nouveau brasserie on Place Graslin.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyAll of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by theLigne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through thePassage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposingChâteau des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellentMusée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peacefulJardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to theLieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits.And there’s more to come.The Jardin Extraordinaireis a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and theLittle Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, theCité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve.Joanne O’ConnorThe trip was supported byLe Voyage à Nantes.OceaniaHôtelde France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioneddoubles from€101room-onlyWinter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January.Basel, SwitzerlandView image in fullscreenSwimmers in the Rhine beside Basel Cathedral.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyUnless you’re a professional who makes their way to theArt Basel fairevery year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend.Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine.double quotation markBasel bills itself as ‘the city of art and culture on the Rhine’, and it lives up to its boastOnce you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, theKunstmuseumholds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, whileMuseum Tinguelyis home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines.But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city.Fondation Beyelerin the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currentlyPierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein istheVitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design.View image in fullscreenMiniatures of designer chairs at the Vitra Design Museum near Basel.Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyBefore you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; theVitra Schaudepot– which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’sformer fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is abeautiful gardenbythe Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently addedDoshi Retreatfor a moment of quiet reflection designed by theIndian architectBalkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023.That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch.Max BenatoTheVolkshaus, aboutique hotel in the old town, hasdoubles from152swiss francs (£138)room-onlyLübeck, GermanyView image in fullscreenThe ‘wonky’ Holsten Gate in Lübeck.Photograph: SW Travel Imagery/AlamyUnless you’ve readBuddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem.The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired anelectric boat(€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires.Back on dry land, we set off on a guidedwalking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky –Holsten Gate. We took in thefive red brick churchesthe spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them,St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-oldtown hallon the marketplace.But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hiddenalleyways and courtyardsthreaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore.double quotation markBehind the gothic splendour is a labyrinth of flower-filled, cobbled alleys to exploreTo better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited theEuropean Hansemuseumin the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937.In a nearby palace, theMuseum Behnhaus Drägerhausdisplays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted itssalt warehouses. Just round the corner is theGünter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015).We visited in June during theHanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annualmuseum, theatre and literature nights, andpopup live musicin the summer.Lübeck has three naturalopen-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip toTravemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back.View image in fullscreenThe old town of  Lübeck is encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz.Photograph: Acnakelsy/Getty Images/iStockphotoIn town, the medievalSchiffergesellschaft(Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions oflabskaus, a sort of hash.Sadly, we couldn’t visitBuddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort.Rachel DixonThe trip was provided bygermany.travelandluebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided byLiho Lübeck, doubles from £73room-onlyParma, ItalyView image in fullscreenParma Cathedral and the octagonal baptistery.Photograph: Peter Adams/Getty ImagesParma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordabletrattorieandosterieshowcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimateTeatro Regio.The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesquecathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothicBattistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medievalMonastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free.double quotation markAppreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Tintoretto and Canaletto without being surrounded by crowdsParma’s big must-see is the monumentalPalazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. TheTeatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmarkGalleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds.View image in fullscreenAntonio Correggio’s Assunzione della Virgine in the cupola of Parma’s Duomo.Photograph: Gordon Sinclair/AlamySightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking intotagliere– wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famousprosciuttocrudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect.This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such asDa Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen thecucinafor more than 50 years, or the 120-year-oldTrattoria Corrieri,serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15.John BruntonPalazzo Dalla Rosa Pratihas doublesfrom€80room-onlySantander, SpainView image in fullscreenEl Sardinero beach, Santander.Photograph: Miguel Moya/AlamyOften dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map.Leading the way on 8 September isFaro Santander– a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times.double quotation markThere’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedralWith its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architectDavid Chipperfield.Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house theArchivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America.Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017Centro Botíncontemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half.View image in fullscreenRenzo Piano’s Centro Botin.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamySpaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeledMadrileñosdiscovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre.The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazasand narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars servingpinchos– the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas.After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, atMesón Rampalayon a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours atMupac– the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander.The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too.Eddi FiegelThe trip was provided by Faro Santander.Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín,has stylish doubles from€66room-onlyExplore more on these topicsCity breaksEurope holidaysWeekend breaksItaly holidaysSpain holidaysSwitzerland holidaysGermany holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: Police received information nearly immediately after the killing. It took Las Vegas police 27 years to make an arrest
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: Police received information nearly immediately after the killing. It took Las Vegas police 27 years to make an arrest
Content: Tupac Shakur poses for a portrait on 7 January 1992 in Oakland, California.Photograph: Gary Reyes  /Oakland Tribune Staff Archives via GettyView image in fullscreenTupac Shakur poses for a portrait on 7 January 1992 in Oakland, California.Photograph: Gary Reyes  /Oakland Tribune Staff Archives via GettyThe Sunday readTupac ShakurTupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the casePolice received information nearly immediately after the killing. It took Las Vegas police 27 years to make an arrestLois BeckettSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTShareFor years, US law enforcement officials blamed their failure to solve hip-hop starTupac Shakur’s murder on the lack of cooperation from key witnesses, and on gang members’ “snitches get stitches” culture.But testimony in a much-delayed murder trial, whichconcluded this week, almost 30 years after Shakur’s death, highlighted just how much law enforcement officials knew about the shooting, and how early.On Monday, a Southside Compton Crips gang leader and drug dealer, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, wasconvictedfor orchestrating Shakur’s killing. Davis told investigators in 2008 that it was his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, who pulled the trigger. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998.The lack of resolution in Shakur’s murder had resonated painfully not just with the artist’s own family and friends, but with many Black Americans.View image in fullscreenFans, friends and family attend the posthumous unveiling ceremony of hip-hop legend Tupac Shakur’s star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles in 2023.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersEven though Shakur was one of the most famous Black men in the world, a star whose movements attracted enormous media attention, his killing remained officially unsolved for almost three decades, said Jody Armour, a law professor at the University of Southern California. “If even he could be murdered on a major Las Vegas boulevard and the case could sit around and languish, one naturally wonders what happens when the victim is just a 19-year-old Black man in Compton, or South Central, or Chicago.“Tupac spent much of his career insisting that America did not adequately value Black life,” Armour added. “His own homicide became another exhibit in that argument.”The fact that the Las Vegas jury reached a verdict in the Shakur case so swiftly – after less than three hours – “suggests that the evidence that had existed for some time was persuasive enough for them to convict, and calls into some question why it didn’t happen sooner”, Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor, said.And indeed, witnesses in the trial put a new spotlight on allegations of police corruption and incompetence, the mixed motivations of investigators, and law enforcement turf wars that went on for years behind the scenes of the homicide investigation.What the police knew, and whenThough it would take Las Vegas police 27 years before theymade their first arrestin Shakur’s murder, testimony at Davis’s trial revealed that police received information almost immediately about what prompted the killing, and who might be behind it.View image in fullscreenChief deputy district attorney Marc DiGiacomo questions Jeffrey Scott, a senior crime scene analyst for the Las Vegas Metropolitan police department, during the trial for Duane Davis in Las Vegas on 25 August.Photograph: John Locher/Pool via ReutersSurveillance footage played at the trial showed Shakur, the Death Row Records founder, Marion “Suge” Knight, and their associates, some affiliated with the Mob Piru Bloods, assaulting Anderson at the MGM hotel in Las Vegas, an attack that Davis would later say prompted him and his nephew to seek revenge on Shakur.Reggie Wright Jr, the former head of security for Shakur’s record label, testified that in the hours immediately after Shakur was shot in Las Vegas, he made multiple phone calls to a police lieutenant in Compton, California, warning him that Shakur and Knight had “got into it at the MGM with some guys from the Southside Crips” and “There’s going to be trouble in Compton.”The immediate communication between the Death Row Records security chief and the Compton police on the night of Shakur’s shooting was no surprise: Wright Jr had been a Compton police officer until he retired earlier that year, and he was calling his father, Reginald Wright Sr, then the head of Compton’s gang unit.The elder Wright quickly passed on the information about Shakur’s Las Vegas shooting to then-Compton gang homicide detective Robert Ladd, who testified that police in Compton immediately braced for retaliatory violence on their streets. “We expected war,” he said.The violence that exploded over the next 10 days – three killings and 10 attempted murders, including a shooting that left a 10-year-old girl in critical condition – left Ladd convinced that the information Compton police had received about who shot Shakur had been accurate.“There was no doubt in my mind that the Southside Crips were responsible, because the Mob Piru had to retaliate, and they had 54 other gangs to choose from, but they went right after the Southside Crips,” Ladd testified.In response to the violence in Compton, Ladd testified, police “rounded up” a large number of local gang members on both sides of the conflict in October 1996, including Anderson, Davis’s nephew. They also invited the Las Vegas police to interview the arrested men. The alleged gang members were “all the players that we heard about that were involved in the shooting of Tupac Shakur”, with the goal “to try to help Las Vegas PD with their investigation”, Ladd testified. Compton officers also collected a large number of firearms, hoping to find the weapon used to murder Shakur, he said.While Las Vegas sent two detectives to Compton and they did interview Anderson, nothing came of the interview, Laddtestified.The trial was not the first time the former Compton detective has spoken publicly about the Shakur case: Laddwent public about his frustrationswith how Las Vegas police handled the case in a 2002 Los Angeles Times investigation, saying that Compton police had told Las Vegas police a week after the attack that they believed Anderson was the shooter, but that the Las Vegas police rejected the theory.When Compton police gave Las Vegas police a chance to interview Anderson and other gang members they believed to be involved in Shakur’s murder, “Las Vegas expressed no interest whatsoever in talking to any of them,” Laddsaid in 2002, saying that their interview with Anderson lasted only 20 minutes.View image in fullscreenThis photo provided by the Las Vegas Metropolitan police department shows the bullet-riddled car in which rapper Tupac Shakur was fatally shot in September 1996.Photograph: Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department/Via APAnderson waspublicly identifiedas a potential suspect in Shakur’s killing less than a month after the shooting, and was widely rumored within Compton to be the one who killed the hip-hop icon. Anderson, his lawyer and his family repeatedly denied he was involved in the killing, but those close to himtold the Guardianafter his death that theallegations that he shot Shakur shaped his daily life, and that strangers would sometimes recognize him as Shakur’s killer.In 1997, while Anderson was still alive, Tupac’s mother, Afeni Shakur, filed a civil lawsuitaccusing him of murdering her son.In an audio recording heard in a Las Vegas courtroom 29 years later, DavisdescribedAnderson as the one who fired the shots that killed Shakur.Police mistrust, gang connectionsThere were reasons, of course, that Las Vegas police might be skeptical of Compton police, and particularly about information they were sharing about Shakur’s killing.It wasn’t just that Compton itself had a reputation for political corruption, and that Compton’s police department, battered byscandalsand conflicts with the city’s mayor, would soon be disbanded by the city council.The fact that a former Compton police officer was in charge of security for Death Row Records, and that he had been paid to protect Knight, Shakur and the label’s other artists while they engaged in high-profile gang disputes, concerned Las Vegas detectives because they feared that his father, the head of Compton police’s gang unit,might pass informationalong to Knight. Knight himself was known for associating with Mob Piru gang members. He would also continue to make headlines for hisdonations to Compton city officials.At the trial, Wright Jr himself testified that he had grown up in a Compton neighborhood that was considered Mob Piru territory, had known many gang members since childhood, and that he had already been employed by Knight as the head of security for Death Row Records during “my last year or two of being a police officer”.As his private security business grew, Wright testified, he would hire off-duty and retired police officers daily to provide security for Death Row Records’ studio and to accompany the label’s artists to events. He had “about ten officers working a day”, he testified.View image in fullscreenReggie Wright Jr, security chief for Death Row Records, testifies during the murder trial of Duane Davis related to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas on 18 August.Photograph: John Locher/AFP/Getty ImagesThe testimony of “Mob James” McDonald, a 61-year-old who said he had done security and enforcement for Knight, reinforced just how closely Wright and the officers he employed worked alongside the Mob Piru gang members that surrounded Suge Knight.“His security did, like, the right thing. My security did what they ain’t going to do. You get what I’m saying?” McDonald testified.It was two Mob Piru gang members who first told Wright that Shakur had been shot, he testified.In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis accused Knight, the then Death Row Records executive, as having “police hitmen”, and “crooked ass police on his payroll”, and named Reggie Wright Jr and his father specifically. Wright and his father would later beindicted on federal drug-traffickingand money-laundering charges.When it came to the Shakur homicide investigation, Las Vegas detectives had feared that Wright’s father, the gang lieutenant, or other Compton officers might pass along information to Knight, or try to protect him,the Los Angeles Times reported in 2002. Compton’s police chief at the time removed Wright Sr from the case and replaced him with another officer to address these worries, the Times reported, but it did not assuage the concerns.As conspiracy theories flourished in the absence of any official narrative of Shakur’s death, the police, and Reggie Wright Jr himself, were regarded as potential suspects in the star’s death, something Wright denied on the stand this past month.Hostile witnesses, law enforcement turf warsTestimony in Las Vegas left no doubt that some witnesses to Shakur’s killing did not want to work with law enforcement to convict the hip-hop star’s assailant, and that they preferred to seek street justice instead.Garry Dale, a former Las Vegas police officer,testifiedthat Shakur himself, lying wounded inside the ambulance, would not identify his shooter when asked, saying only something to the effect of, “No, we’ll take care of it.”View image in fullscreenGarry Dale, a former Las Vegas Metro police officer, is being questioned by Michael Sanft, attorney for Duane Davis, on 17 August.Photograph: Steve Marcus/ReutersOther witnesses described a fear of being perceived as snitches, and even facing violent retribution, if they cooperated with police or prosecutors. “Mob James” McDonald repeatedly told prosecutors, “You better treat me as a hostile witness”, and refused to answer some questions, saying “Me or anybody else bringing up the dead is wrong.”But as they investigated the ongoing conflict between the Southside Crips and Mob Piru, law enforcement officers also found themselves caught in their own bureaucratic turf wars.One of the most outspoken retired officers on the Shakur case is former Los Angeles police detective Greg Kading, who served on the law enforcement taskforce that heard Davis’s 2008 confession to his involvement in Shakur’s killing.The Los Angeles-based taskforce was originally set up to solve a different murder: the 1997 shooting of Christopher “Biggie Smalls” Wallace, which, like Tupac’s murder, languished for decades without any official resolution.Wallace’smother, Voletta, eventually sued the LAPD, alleging that police officers had been involved in the murder. “Desperately trying to cover its ass,” the LAPD set up a multi-agency taskforce to investigate the Wallace murder, Kading wrote in his 2011 memoir, Murder Rap: The Untold Story of the Biggie Smalls & Tupac Shakur Murder Investigations.In an account that largely mirrors the one Las Vegas prosecutors brought to trial, the book describes how, in a 2008 interview with the taskforce, Davis unexpectedly confessed to his role in Shakur’s murder. The book also alleges a motive and a gunman for Wallace’s murder, which remains officially unsolved. The book ends with Kading’s removal from the taskforce, which eventually shut down without bringing the evidence it had gathered in either hip-hop killing to trial.View image in fullscreenA 1996 photo of Tupac Shakur and Marion ‘Suge’ Knight is displayed during the Duane Davis murder trial on 17 August.Photograph: Steve Marcus/AFP/Getty Images“It’s my belief that the LAPD carefully weighed its options and decided that, all things considered, it best suited them to let sleeping dogs lie,” Kading wrote.It wasn’t that the LAPD wanted to hide the identity of the killers, Kading argued – it was that the specifics of the murder trials in the cases, and the accompanying media coverage, might be messy and difficult for the department’s reputation. In the end, it was more bureaucratic ass-covering, not conspiracy, that stood in the way of justice, he argued. “Rather than manning up to bring these killers to justice, it chose to hedge its bets, letting the investigation die an unnatural death rather than risk the potentially damaging, but ultimately insubstantial, flak that would surely come its way.”Kading did not testify in the Las Vegas trial. Daryn Dupree, a career Los Angeles police detective who served with Kading on the taskforce, did, and suggested a different motivation for the apparent law enforcement priorities in the case: Davis was a relatively small fish to federal law enforcement officials involved in the taskforce, which had tried, and ultimately failed, to hook a much bigger fish.After Davis’s initial confession in 2008, the taskforce focused on trying to verify allegations by Davis thatSean “Diddy” Combs, who ran the rival record label Bad Boy Records, had commissioned the hit on Shakur and offered payment, Dupree testifiedDespite flying Davis to New York to attempt to verify his link to Combs, the investigators were unable to get the evidence they needed, Dupree said.The higher-level officials overseeing the Los Angeles taskforce also made the decision to delay sharing intelligence from their investigation with Las Vegas police, Dupree testified. That choice would probably have “led to a lot of frustration” once Las Vegas learned about it, Chutkow, the former federal prosecutor, said.At the federal level, law enforcement officials on the taskforce were “chasing the money”, and trying to build a racketeering case against both Suge Knight’s Death Row Records, which had signed Shakur, and Combs’s Bad Boy Records, Dupree testified. The FBI, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Drug Enforcement Administration were trying to solidify that both record companies had been originally funded by drug sales.“I’m from the hood,” Dupree said. “Everybody knows that those record companies were started with narcotics. So the feds were looking at a Rico [a case using the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act]. We cared about the murders.”‘The defendant implicated himself’In finally bringing Davis to trial for orchestrating Shakur’s murder, Las Vegas prosecutors relied heavily on two fairly old pieces of evidence: Davis’s 2008 confession to the Los Angeles taskforce, and his public description of the shooting in his 2019 memoir,Compton Street Legend.In the end, the only reason the case was solved was “because the defendant implicated himself”, said Shirin Bakhshay, an assistant professor at UCLA law school. “This is not amazing police work that uncovered, after 30 years, the facts of the case. This was a guy who thought he was out of the window of any sort of danger – who didn’t understand the legal implications of what he was doing.”When Davis was finally arrested and indicted for murder in 2023, Steve Wolfson, the Clark county, Nevada district attorney, told reporters, “In this case, justice has been delayed, but justice won’t be denied.”View image in fullscreenThe Clark county district attorney, Steve Wolfson, and Lt Jason Johansson of Las Vegas Metropolitan police look on as the Clark county sheriff, Kevin McMahill, speaks about the arrest and indictment of Duane Davis on 29 September 2023.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesBut the delay in securing any official justice in Shakur’s murder “festered for a long time”, Armour, the USC law professor said, and a guilty verdict after 30 years “isn’t going to repair America’s deplorable record of racial injustice in the criminal justice system”.“It will give at least some sense of closure,” he said. “It will put to rest some of the conspiracy theories that have cropped up around this case.”While Shakur’s killing had acquired an almost mythical status, and the theories around it were sweeping and dramatic, Armour said, the case prosecutors ultimately made in court was not: Shakur was “a 25-year-old artistic genius, who died largely because one group of young men beat another young man in a casino lobby, and the humiliation demanded retribution”.
