title: Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Slavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of state
Content: Olivia Grange (right) said the petition’s request for Charles to seek legal advice from the privy council was critical to advancing Jamaica’s reparations claim.Composite: PA, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOlivia Grange (right) said the petition’s request for Charles to seek legal advice from the privy council was critical to advancing Jamaica’s reparations claim.Composite: PA, Getty ImagesCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaicaJamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King CharlesSlavery’s legacy continues ‘to deprive our country and our people’, says minister, as group prepares to appeal to Jamaica’s head of stateNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentSun 6 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTShareA landmark petition is to be handed to King Charles by Jamaica over slavery reparations, aiming to confront historical crimes that still disadvantage former British colonies, theCaribbeannation’s culture minister has said.The petition will be lodged with Charles, Jamaica’s head of state, on Monday.“We’re a resilient people. We were able to bounce back from [Hurricane] Melissa, for example,” said Olivia Grange, who arrived in London at the weekend with members of Jamaica’s National Council on Reparations.“But we still have a lot of work to do, and you can imagine if we did not have those inherited problems, the legacy that came out of slavery, how much better we would have been able to do so,” she told the Guardian.First announcedin June last year, the petition asks the monarch to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.It wants Charles to ask whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, if it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.Grange said that these questions and a privy council response were critical to progressing the country’s reparations claims.Between the 15th and 19th centuries, more than 12.5 million Africans were kidnapped, forcibly transported to theAmericasand sold into slavery.Grange said that Jamaica had been the first Caribbean nation to create a national reparations mechanism, establishing it in 2009. She said the aim was to address the enduring impacts of slavery that put countries such as Jamaica at a grave economic disadvantage and affected its ability to respond to modern-day challenges in the Caribbean, such as the climate crisis.“We have inherited systems that continue to deprive our country and our people. The legacy in education, even in health, the way we eat, our diet because of what we were fed, our ancestors were fed,” she said.Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines who was instrumental in setting up theCaribbean Community Reparations Commission, echoed Grange’s sentiments.“The present is very much the past, because what we are dealing with is the legacies of underdevelopment which you can source, and we do source, to native genocide and enslavement of African bodies,” he said on Sunday.“People must remember this: that European nations were enriched because of the enslavement of African bodies.” Gonsalves is an elder and adviser forthe Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.He said Jamaica’s visit was a critical milestone among a number of upcoming events, including a Caribbean reparations conference in Barbados later this month, and planned advocacy at the upcoming UN general assembly in late September and the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua in November, which King Charles is scheduled to attend.There are growing global calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to recognise hundreds of years of transatlantic slavery that treated African people as chattel as a crime, and to engage in a process of reparatory justice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slaveryas the gravest crime against humanity. In June, the Caribbeanlaunched a manifestooutlining the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations”. And last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries werelegally obliged to consider reparationsfor the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the March UN resolution, and in October 2024, the former British prime minister Keir Starmerresisted pressure from member statesto include reparations in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting agenda.Grange said she hoped the visit would facilitate a unifying response to the complicated history.A palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.”Later on Sunday, the delegation hosted a remembrance church service in Brixton, and later in the week they are due to meet UK members of parliament. Grange said there would also be a visit to the British Museum to discuss repatriation of Jamaican artefacts.She said: “We may have different history, different heritage, different skin colour, but it’s about humanity. It’s about, as a people, being able to live together, to work together, and to respect each other.“And in our efforts to seek reparatory justice, we will use the opportunity to also promote and encourage what Jamaica is known for, One Love, because we have the song of the century through Bob Marley.”Explore more on these topicsJamaicaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceSlaveryKing Charles IIICaribbeanAmericasMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending
Content: Stanley in the Falkland Islands. Ministers in the UK have condemned Javier Milei’s comments.Photograph: Rob Carter/AlamyView image in fullscreenStanley in the Falkland Islands. Ministers in the UK have condemned Javier Milei’s comments.Photograph: Rob Carter/AlamyDefence policyFalklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chairExclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spendingKiran StaceyPolicy editorSun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJavier Milei’s threats to theFalkland Islandsmake it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.Tan Dhesi said thecomments by the Argentinian presidentthis week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for thedrone incident[in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. TheLabourMP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year.During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”.He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment.The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035.View image in fullscreenTan Dhesi asked Andy Burnham whether he backed the 2030 commitment to defence spending at Wednesday’s PMQs.Photograph: House of Commons/PA“There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.”Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran.“Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJavier Milei threatened oil sanctions against firms planning to exploit oil close to the islands.Photograph: Mariana Nedelcu/ReutersHis comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”.He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows thatArgentinahas a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina.Ministers in the UKcondemned Milei’s commentson Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyFalkland IslandsArgentinaAmericasLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war? | Australian military | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here
Content:
Australian facilityAustralian facility with US military accessAustralian facility with US access unresolvedUS facility with Australian accessUS corporate accessRAAF Base AmberleyRAAF Base AmberleyRAAF Base TindalHarold E. Holt Communication StationPine GapScroll downVideo credit: The Australian Ministry of DefenceIn the near pitch blackness of a wet June morning, a US B-2 Spirit stealth bomber 
                swoops from the sky, touching down on the outskirts of Brisbane to swiftly refuel – 
                engines still running – at one of the US air force’s key allied bases. 
                Before the sun is up, the nuclear-capable warplane is back in the air.RAAF Base Amberley, about 50km south-west of Brisbane, is a vital staging point for 
                US military operations across the region. But it is hardly alone.This map shows every military base in Australia, which includes US- and Australian-run bases.Analysts warn of a “saturation” of the continent by the US military, and argue that Australia’s 
                most important security ally could drag the country unwillingly into war.Amid the red dirt of Katherine, the runway at RAAF Base Tindal is being expanded to be able to better accommodate massive American B-52 bombers, the so-called “Stratofortresses”. These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask.On the remote coast of Western Australia, a cluster of highly technological assets – deep space radar, space surveillance telescope, and the Harold Holt naval communication station – provide vital information to enable US submarine and space warfare.The naval communication station is designed to reach submerged submarines. Its antenna array broadcasts on very low frequency radio.The US-run Pine Gap, in the centre of the country, is regarded by some as the US military’s most valuable intelligence site outside the continental United States.The satellite tracking and signals intelligence base detects missile launches, intercepts military communications and provides targeting information for US forces around the world.Essentially incorruptible – difficult to access, physically or otherwise – in a desert valley in the centre of a massive continent, it downloads and transmits masses of data from powerful US satellites constantly monitoring vast swathes of the globe.For the US military, Australia represents, in the words of one now-retired general, “location, location, location”.Australian militaryThe US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?Exclusive:US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them hereUS military presence in Australia, mapped – videoWhy can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcastBen Doherty,Andy BallandNick EvershedSun 6 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTShareUS militaryinterests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. TheUS militarycontrols 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”The US military-industrial complex in AustraliaEach square represents one facilityUnited States-controlled facilities with Australian access (17)Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access (24)Australian facilities with US military access (51)Australian facilities with US corporate access (18)Australian facilities with no significant US access (41)Australian facilities with US access unresolved (17)US access to Australian defence facilitiesAccess levelFacilitiesUnited States-controlled facilities with Australian access17Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access24Australian facilities with US military access51Australian facilities with US corporate access18Australian facilities with no significant US access41Australian facilities with US access unresolved17Guardian graphic‘Aligning ourselves completely’The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.Training, including for2,500 marines on dry-season rotationin the Northern Territory.Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth ofpre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.7:00US military presence in Australia, mapped – videoBeyond the military’s presence, at least 42Australian militaryfacilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.Lockheed Martinassembles guided missilesin Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to buildrocket motors for guided weaponsat Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperabilityand provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access,Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.View image in fullscreenWorkers with a missile at the Port Wakefield facility.Photograph: Lockheed MartinThe Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.TheForce Posture agreement– “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base –rather a “rotation”– but there is little contestation of its actual implication.double quotation markThis is a massive institutional failure in AustraliaProf Richard TanterArguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence ministerChristopher Pynetold a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it:Aukusis also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and anhonorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.Is Australia at war with Iran? The fine line between ‘defensive operations’ and complicityRead more“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations withChina, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”View map of military facilities by the numbers‘Waltzing its way into a war’At apress conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.View image in fullscreenUS defense secretary Pete Hegseth meets Australia’s defence minister Richard Marles at the Pentagon.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAMarles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.Earlier,the minister toldthe Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s2026 national defence strategyreiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.Australians’ fragile faithGovernment ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship isbroader, deeper and more enduringthan thetenures of prime ministers and presidents.But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.ALowy Institute pollshowed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.a graphicJust more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.Other findings are more damning: apoll for the Australia Institutefound more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.Explore the US military's footprint in AustraliaAustralian facilityAustralian facility with US military accessAustralian facility with US access unresolvedUS facility with Australian accessUS corporate accessAll basesAustralianUSFacility type: All types▾Guardian graphicThis represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that theTrump administrationhas repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you canliterally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”Secret documents reveal preferred Australian nuclear submarine base – and warn it could be a military targetRead moreShe cites theMarch attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”Scappatura says the phrase“empire by invitation”was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”TheAustralian bases & US involvementdatabase is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth | China | The Guardian
description: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
Content: A Chinese national flag raised outside a bank’s headquarters in the financial district of central Beijing.Photograph: Kim Kyung Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Chinese national flag raised outside a bank’s headquarters in the financial district of central Beijing.Photograph: Kim Kyung Hoon/ReutersChinaChina prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growthBeijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reservesRob DaviesSun 6 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth.A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly.The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy isstruggling to escape weak growth.The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn.China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry ElliottRead moreThe People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry ​of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital.The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies.The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health.“The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk.Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year.The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share ​placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco ​Corp and its subsidiaries.The two lenders said the ​proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them ​sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks ​to support growth despite weak demand for loans.Explore title: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities
Content: Anak Krakatau’s eruption sent ash as high as 15,000 metres (50,000ft).Photograph: Indonesian Geological Agency/EPAView image in fullscreenAnak Krakatau’s eruption sent ash as high as 15,000 metres (50,000ft).Photograph: Indonesian Geological Agency/EPAAir transportVolcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airportsAsh cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and  fishing activitiesGuardian staff and agenciesSun 6 Sep 2026 10.51 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 00.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano.Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing. Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday.Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday.The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, according to the airport operator, Angkasa Pura.SingaporeAirlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday.MapThe Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”.“Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement. “Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.”Volcanic ash can damage jet engines, baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens.View image in fullscreenPassengers wait in the check-in lounge at Soekarno-Hatta international airport.Photograph: Faisal Ramadhan/EPAAsh ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000ft) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said.Several ​schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents ​suffered eye irritation, and fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported.The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could ​include cloud-seeding to promote rain.El Niño-fuelled wildfires destroy precious Indonesian forests – in picturesRead more“If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference.More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said.Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed.Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited from going within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant.With Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsAir transportIndonesiaSingaporeAir pollutionAsia PacificVolcanoesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian first | Australia news | The Guardian
description: The casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the process
Author: Jack Larkin
Headline: The casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the process
Content: The mushroom coffin, created by Loop Biotech, pictured at Sydney Harbour.Photograph: Loop BiotechView image in fullscreenThe mushroom coffin, created by Loop Biotech, pictured at Sydney Harbour.Photograph: Loop BiotechAustralia newsWoman laid to rest in coffin made from mushrooms in Australian firstThe casket, grown from mycelium and hemp fibres, takes just 45 days to break down, enriching the soil in the processFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJack LarkinSun 6 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has been buried in a coffin made from mushrooms inNew South Walesin an eco-friendly first for Australia.Carolyn, whose surname was withheld for privacy reasons, was laid to rest on Friday by friends and family at Springwood Cemetery in the Blue Mountains. She was aged in her 70s.The mushroom coffin, created by the Dutch firm Loop Biotech, was grown from mycelium – the root network of fungi – and hemp fibres.The coffin is grown in mould in a climate-controlled room, taking just a week to fully form. Once buried, it takes about 45 days to become part of the soil.The process is akin to composting, as the body and coffin gently biodegrade and transform into nutrient-rich soil in far less time than a traditional wooden casket, which can take up to 50 years to break down.View image in fullscreenThe biodegradable coffins weigh about 30kg.Photograph: Loop BiotechCarolyn’s husband, Donald, said picking the mushroom coffin aligned with his wife’s values of giving back.“She was always there to help others. It feels very true to who she was that even after her death, she can still do something for others while giving something back to nature,” he said.While Carolyn is the first to be buried in the coffin in Australia, Loop Biotech’s founder Bob Hendrikx said there had been thousands of others across Europe and the US.“Five years ago when I started, there was lots of interest from Australia,” Hendrikx said. “It was a little bit harder to ship overseas [at the time].”Hendrikx hopes the mushroom coffins, which weigh about 30kg each, could improve the sustainability of the Australian funeral sector by shortening the decomposition process.“It’s about giving back to nature: we have the mushroom, which is grown and dissolves into nature, but the actual benefit is that … it’s enriching the soil,” he said.“The body needs to just return to nature and let nature do what it’s done best forever.“If a kangaroo dies in the forest, it’s just going to be part of the cycle of life.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s enriching the soil’: Loop Biotech founder Bob Hendrikx in Sydney.Photograph: Loop BiotechDr Hannah Gould, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Melbourne, believes people are becoming increasingly interested inenvironmentally friendly farewells.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As people perhaps become less religious, other kinds of values or community groupings become more important, and one of those that we’ve seen is eco-death.Gone to a wetter place: the Queenslanders disrupting the death industry with water cremationsRead more“This idea that perhaps that you don’t go up to heaven after you die, you return to the earth, has been an increasingly popular narrative around death and dying.”While about 70% of Australians choose to be cremated, it has a substantial environmental impact: the emissions from a typical cremation are estimated to be equivalent to125kg of carbon dioxide.View image in fullscreenLoop Biotech’s mushroom coffin can be lined with moss.Photograph: Loop BiotechIn recent years options such asalkaline hydrolysis(a cremation-like process that uses water instead of fire), natural burials without embalming, and even shallow burials have become available. A natural burial uses a cardboard coffin with rope handles and will emit less than 10kg of carbon dioxide equivalent, according toPlanetMark analysis.Gould believes that as Australians are living longer and more people are dying from prolonged illnesses, more time is being spent thinking about how to depart and farewell loved ones.“They’ve maybe seen or organised a funeral for their parents and it hasn’t gone so well,” she said. “And they’re now deciding that they want to do things differently. So we’re seeing a huge rise in funeral planning.”This story was amended on 7 September 2026 to correct the name of Carolyn’s husband, Donald.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsNew South WalesConsumer affairsDeath and dyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens criticise Labor after former IDF officer’s ‘reprehensible’ comments on Zomi Frankcom strike | Australian foreign policy | The Guardian
description: David Shoebridge says ‘words are just distractions’ until government takes action
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: David Shoebridge says ‘words are just distractions’ until government takes action
Content: Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, one of the seven World Central Kitchen colleagues killed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza.Photograph: World Central Kitchen/PAView image in fullscreenAustralian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, one of the seven World Central Kitchen colleagues killed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza.Photograph: World Central Kitchen/PAAustralian foreign policyGreens criticise Labor after former IDF officer’s ‘reprehensible’ comments on Zomi Frankcom strikeDavid Shoebridge says ‘words are just distractions’ until government takes actionFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updates‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrikeGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen DohertySun 6 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 18.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greens have criticised inflammatory statements from the formerIsraelDefense Forces officer who ordered the attack that killed Zomi Frankcom, accusing the Albanese government of weakness over its failure to halt military exports and impose new sanctions.Australian aid worker Frankcom andsix of her colleagues were killed in 2024while bringing food to the people ofGaza. Former IDF reserve colonel Nochi Mendelhas saidhe would do “exactly the same thing” again and that those killed in the World Central Kitchen (WCK) humanitarian convoy in Gaza were “not innocent”.The statements have been condemned as “utterly disgraceful” by Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, and as an “outrageous smear” by WCK’s humanitarian chief.Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workersRead moreBut the Greens’ defence spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said the government’s response was insufficient in the face of Mendel’s “reprehensible” statements. He said the comments “reflect the rhetoric and policy of the Israeli government, where collective punishment of aid workers, doctors and innocent civilians is occurring daily”.“I do not care what minister Wong’s personal feelings are, I don’t care about her outrage, I care about the actions taken as foreign minister,” Shoebridge told Guardian Australia.“Anyone can condemn the actions of the Israeli military, but only the government can impose the sanctions and material responses needed. Until they do their words are distractions.”He called for material reprimand for members of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and for the sale of parts for the F-35 fighter jet to be immediately halted.View image in fullscreenGreens defence spokesperson David Shoebridge said on Sunday he could not fathom the pain and distress facing Zomi Frankcom’s family.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPJosé Andrés, the WCK founder, said Mendel had smeared Frankcom and her colleagues.“Now, one of the officers involved says he isn’t sorry for what happened. He said we are not a neutral organisation,” he said in astatement published onlinethis week.“Really? Let me be very clear, to him and to the whole world. We are humanitarians. We are friends of humanity. We believe that food is a universal human right.”Mendel, then the chief of staff of the Nahal brigade, said he gave the order to attack a humanitarian convoy delivering hundreds of tonnes of food to Gaza on the night of 1 April 2024.Three vehicles in the convoy were attacked along Gaza’s coast road, in successive drone strikes, each about two minutes apart.One after another, the three vehicles were bombed, as survivors from the initial strikes ran to the untouched cars, seeking sanctuary.An IDF investigation found the attack was a grave mistake, identifying specific errors made by a handful of officers, in particular Mendel, who was removed from his position. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect the food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.‘An insult’: Zomi Frankcom’s family issues strongly-worded statement as Israel rejects criminal investigation into her killingRead moreLast month, Israel’s advocate general declined to press charges against anyone for the deaths, saying there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”.Mendel has given interviewsto the ABCand the Guardian saying he did not regret the attacks. He told the Guardian he was following IDF protocol, and the humanitarians were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishingguilt by association.Mendel was referring to a general policy ofhaflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion in designating a person a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association.Mendel told the Guardian that while he didn’t plan to kill aid workers, those killed “were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas”.He did not support this assertion with any evidence. Investigations by the IDF itself and the former head of the Australian military have found no suggestion of any connection between Hamas and World Central Kitchen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA destroyed car from the World Central Kitchen convoy in the southern Gaza Strip.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAMendel said he fought in the war in Gaza “to defeat Hamas”, and dismissed the seriousness of the killing of seven humanitarians.“If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing,” he told the Guardian.“I think it’s an idiotic side event. It really isn’t a serious event.”Wong, asked about earlier comments from Mendel that he was unapologetic over the strikes, said his statements were extremely distressing for Frankcom’s family.“I thought those comments were disgraceful, utterly disgraceful,” she told the ABC. “I don’t even want to go into some of the detail of them because I don’t want to give them any credence.”Wong said theAustralian government was dissatisfied with Israel’s decisionnot to lay criminal charges against those responsible, and would continue to “press for justice”.“We do want to see full accountability for the deaths of Zomi Frankcom and her colleagues. They were humanitarian workers working to deliver aid and they are protected under the Geneva conventions.”Wong ‘outraged’ at Israeli decision to not criminally investigate Zomi Frankcom killing – videoRestaurateur Andrés, whose charity has provided more than 600m meals to people affected by natural disasters, climate emergencies and conflict around the world, said the deaths of humanitarian workers who were just trying to feed hungry people was inexcusable.“Enough with the outrageous smears. Enough with excuses. Enough with the shifting of blame.“From the start, we have demanded truth, truth and justice for our friends and their families. We want an independent investigation with all the video and audio released in public so the world can know the truth, because we continue to grieve for our friends. We will never forget them or stop fighting for them.”Frankcom’sfamily issued a statement following Israel’s decision not to lay criminal charges, saying they were “deeply disappointed” by the decision.“The families of the victims deserve transparency and an independent judicial assessment of the criminal responsibility for the international humanitarian law violations that took place on that day,” the said.Shoebridge said on Sunday he could not fathom the pain and distress facing the Frankcom family.“I think most people are in shock at the inaction of the Labor government when an Australian has been murdered and the killers walk free. At some point the Albanese government is going to have to get their head out of sand and start taking action.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian foreign policyIsrael-Gaza warAustralian GreensIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Victoria police hunt for man on run after allegedly attacking brother and parents with axe | Victoria | The Guardian
description: Police say they believe argument took place before three people critically injured in Gippsland town of Tyers on Saturday
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Police say they believe argument took place before three people critically injured in Gippsland town of Tyers on Saturday
Content: Peter O’Ryan allegedly attacked three people with an axe or hatchet on Saturday afternoon in Victoria, leaving them critically injured.Photograph: Victoria policeView image in fullscreenPeter O’Ryan allegedly attacked three people with an axe or hatchet on Saturday afternoon in Victoria, leaving them critically injured.Photograph: Victoria policeVictoriaVictoria police hunt for man on run after allegedly attacking brother and parents with axePolice say they believe argument took place before three people critically injured in Gippsland town of Tyers on SaturdayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated Press andAndrew MessengerSun 6 Sep 2026 05.07 EDTFirst published on Sat 5 Sep 2026 20.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictoria police have urged the public to remain vigilant as they search for a man who allegedly attacked his brother and parents with an axe or tomahawk.Police issued an arrest warrant on Sunday for Peter O’Ryan, 48, whose last known location was his family’s home in the Gippsland town of Tyers.He is alleged to have entered the Cowies Road property about 12.30pm on Saturday before attacking his brother and turning on his mother and father.The alleged attack is believed to have occurred after an argument.O’Ryan’s father and brother, aged 77 and 47, were airlifted to hospital with life-threatening injuries and were in a critical condition.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHis mother, 74, was transported to hospital with critical injuries and was in a stable condition.Det Sen Sgt Rodney Findlay said police had conducted a widespread search for O’Ryan, who was alleged to have fled the scene on foot and was likely still armed.“We are working furiously to try and bring him into custody so that we can make sure everyone’s safe and he’s held to account,” he said.Detectives are still working to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, limited by the serious condition of O’Ryan’s alleged victims.O’Ryan’s father and brother required immediate surgery and were in intensive care at the Alfred hospital. They have not regained consciousness.His mother, meanwhile, had only been able to provide sparse details in between treatments, Findlay said.Police released images of O’Ryan on Sunday in the hope people would recognise him and provide information about his whereabouts.O’Ryan was of no fixed address and was known to frequent the Morwell area, police said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey said he had been known to take refuge in abandoned properties and outhouses.Members of the public are cautioned not to approach him and to call triple zero if they see him.Police have also directly appealed to O’Ryan to turn himself in, saying it would be in his and the public’s best interests.“Give yourself up, come and see us,” Findlay said.O’Ryan was last seen wearing a black and mustard coloured jacket and carrying a black backpack.He is Caucasian and described as being of medium build with dark grey hair.Explore more on these topicsVictoriaMelbournenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengers  | Sydney | The Guardian
description: Passenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issue
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Passenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issue
Content: According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down in Christchurch shortly before 5pm local time.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenAccording to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down in Christchurch shortly before 5pm local time.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPSydney‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengersPassenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issueGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSun 6 Sep 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when herQantasflight ran into trouble.The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island’s mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound forSydney, when a bang shook the cabin.A passenger seated near the left wing soon shouted “the engine’s on fire”, Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane’s left engine in a series of rapid bursts.“I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible,” Loch said.“There was a lot of screaming at the time.”As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“That’s what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine,” she said.“But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming.”Qantas flight QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off fromQueenstownon Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, butQantassent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff sought to comfort passengers.“The crew were all terribly, terribly calming,” Loch said.Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, with passengers allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.“There were massive cheers when we landed,” Loch said.A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.“Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely,” they said.“We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support.”Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch international airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.“I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney,” Loch said.“It was quite traumatic.”Explore more on these topicsSydneyQueenstownNew ZealandQantasAirline industryTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: US envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talks | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Witkoff says he hopes trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Europe will be announced ‘in short order’
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Witkoff says he hopes trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Europe will be announced ‘in short order’
Content: Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, welcomes Jared Kushner, centre, and Steve Witkoff, right, in Kyiv on Sunday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, welcomes Jared Kushner, centre, and Steve Witkoff, right, in Kyiv on Sunday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkraineUS envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talksWitkoff says he hopes trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Europe will be announced ‘in short order’Amy Hawkinsin KyivSun 6 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Ukraine for the first time on Sunday for talks withVolodymyr Zelenskyyin an attempt to end the war with Russia.The Ukrainian president announced plans to widen peace discussions to include European countries in the near future, saying he wanted to do “everything to ensure that trilateral meetings take place” withUkraine, the US and Europe.Witkoff said he was hopeful such meetings would be announced “in short order”. The British, French and German national security advisers briefly joined Sunday’s talks.Witkoff said the talks with Zelenskyy had been “very constructive and substantive”. Kushner said the conflict betweenRussiaand Ukraine was “a long, hard and emotional war”.There were otherwise few details from the highly anticipated talks between Washington and Kyiv, which came a day after the US envoys met Russia’s president,Vladimir Putin, in Moscow.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy greets Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv’s Sophia Square.Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/APKushner and Witkoff were forced to arrive in Kyiv by train after Russia bombed the city’s two main airports on Friday. Both countries pledged to refrain from attacking each other’s capitals over the weekend to ensure the US envoys’ safe passage.Zelenskyy joked that the delegation should come more often to “protect our citizens who are in the capital”.But the president’s mood was generally sombre. He said Ukraine was “really counting on a winter package” from the US andEuropeto enable it to withstand another war-torn winter.“We specifically discussed this with Steve and Jared, as well as with our European partners: air defence, energy support, and as you know we are counting on the serious use of LNG, American LNG,” he said, referring to liquefied natural gas.Zelenskyy greeted the US envoys earlier in the day in Sophia Square, in front of Kyiv’s historic cathedral.The cathedral is a few hundred metres away from the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency, which washit by a Russian droneon Friday afternoon, marking an escalation in a conflict that has dragged on for more than four and a half years.View image in fullscreenJared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held talks with Vladimir Putin, right, in Moscow on Saturday.Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/ReutersKushner said his team was in almost daily contact with Ukrainian officials. “Just because we haven’t travelled out, it doesn’t mean we haven’t … been communicating,” he said.Expectations going into the talks were low. US-backed mediation has stalled over the past few months as Washington has been focused on the war with Iran. Many Ukrainians are also sceptical that Trump is committed to a peace agreement that is acceptable to Kyiv. “People don’t trust the Russians and people don’t trust Trump personally,” said Artem Bronzhukov, a political analyst.Talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending the war have focused on a20-point peace planput forward by Washington and Kyiv in December. But the two sides have failed to reach common ground on several sticking points, including control of territory in east Ukraine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Nobody will win’: Zelenskyy adviser warns of mutual destruction if war with Russia continuesRead more“People mostly understand that if you step back from the Donbas, the next day or the next week, Putin will push for another condition,” Bronzhukov said.A White House officialsaidon Saturday that the talks with Moscow “discussed substantive plans for next steps” for ending the war and that an announcement would follow in the coming weeks.The senior Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the talks as “extremely frank” and said there was an acknowledgement of the need to address “the root causes of the conflict”.Kyiv and the surrounding areas have been hit by a barrage of daily drone strikes for more than a week, the most sustained attack on Ukraine’s capital in months.The capital is now enjoying a reprieve from strikes and air raid alerts that had become a daily occurrence, but other parts of the country are still being hit. Ukrainian authorities reported on Sunday that at least eight people were killed and 69 injured across Ukraine in the past day.Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-modeljet-powered dronesthat can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.Many Ukrainians are worried about the war dragging on into a fifth year and are anxious about the winter ahead. This week, Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov,told the Guardianthat the government should consider evacuating elderly people from Kyiv as Putin had ordered the Russian military to “prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities.Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent weeks in an effort to sap morale in each other’s countries.Additional reporting by Illia DyadikExplore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyJared KushnerUS foreign policyVladimir PutinRussiaTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majority | Germany | The Guardian
description: Projections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Projections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being counted
Content: Ulrich Siegmund, pictured arriving to vote on Sunday, had said his goal was to gain 45% or more.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund, pictured arriving to vote on Sunday, had said his goal was to gain 45% or more.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersGermanyFar-right AfD wins key German state election but may fail to secure majorityProjections show Alternative für Deutschland on 44.4% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt after huge turnout, with votes still being countedKate Connollyin BerlinSun 6 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has emerged as the winner in a crucial state election in Germany, exit polls have projected, securing a historic result and more than doubling its support. The AfD now appear on the brink of becoming the first far-right party to gain power in Germany at state level since the second world war.Germany’s far-right AfD thanks Elon Musk as France warns state election win a ‘serious moment’Read moreInitial exit polls showed the party to have secured 44.4% of the vote, a larger share than predicted, anddecisively larger than that of the Christian Democrats (CDU) of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in a contest that was being followed across the world. However, it still remains unclear as to how and whether the AfD will be able to form a government, having ruled out entering a coalition and being refused any form of cooperation by the mainstream parties.The CDU was trailing massively on around 18.4% and the far-left Die Linke was third with 9.3%, with the Social Democrats on 8.4% and the Greens on 8.7% by around early evening. The smaller BSW reached the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament, against expectations. The party, an offshoot of Die Linke, has agreed to cooperate with the AfD on issues such as energy price reform.Participation was at a record high of 76.5%.Votes are still being counted, but it appeared initially that the AfD might have failed to secure an absolute majority – the condition it has said is central to it taking power, given its refusal togovern with another party.The CDU and all other mainstream parties have also refused to collude with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as aBrandmauer,or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.Addressing jubilant supporters, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said: “We have made history in this country”. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD, he said his party was ready to ⁠reach out ​to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change.“We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue ​better policies,” a beaming Siegmund,35, said after ⁠exit polls had been published. He said themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with the AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Siegmund on Sunday evening called Merz “a very good campaigner for the AfD”.Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how the AfD could rule.About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents.Final polls had shown the AfD to have around 40-41% of support,and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSiegmund celebrating with the AfD’s co-leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right) after polls closed on Sunday.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersThe Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.Explore more on these topicsGermanyAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warns | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: Protest using 10 coffins to symbolise struggling manufacturing industry to take place in Brussels
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Protest using 10 coffins to symbolise struggling manufacturing industry to take place in Brussels
Content: A steelworker in Germany. In June the EU introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersView image in fullscreenA steelworker in Germany. In June the EU introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersManufacturing sectorEU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warnsProtest using 10 coffins to symbolise struggling manufacturing industry to take place in BrusselsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 6 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJob losses in EU manufacturing will rapidly increase unless Brussels stops the “colonisation” of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry trade body has warned.Eurometal predicts 300,000 job losses in manufacturing in the rest of 2026 because of expanding competition from China, which is now enjoying a record€1bn-a-day trade surpluswith the bloc.On Monday, Eurometal will bring its concerns to decision-makers in Brussels, staging a protest using 10 symbolic coffins in a procession around the European Commission headquarters.The coffins will be marked with phrases such as “EU competitiveness”, “industrial jobs” and “European factories”.European manufacturers fear that the commission is not fully alive to thecannibalisation of their industriesas China becomes embedded in supply chains through the sale of components.Alexander Julius, the president of Eurometal, told the Guardian: “China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan.“China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.” He wants the commission to understand fully the impact of Chinese exports at component level, including metals and chemicals used in 90% of manufacturing.The EU has already taken action on electric vehicles by imposing tariffs on Chinese imports in 2024, and in June introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel. The bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, has also said the EU’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance with China is “not sustainable”, with both sides agreeing to hold three months of talks, ending in October,to try to avert a trade war.“You look at the job losses stacking up in industries in places like Germany. The media, the politicians can see the consequences, but they don’t go after the virus that is causing it,” Julius said. “They don’t see why it is happening or ask why companies are either relocating to China or India or going bust.”Among the conditions allowing the “virus” to spread is the increasing costs borne by European metal manufacturers with tariffs on steel imports and carbon emissions taxes for those high-energy sectors.Components manufactured in China face none of those levies, said Julius, and that, combined with the undervaluation of the Chinese currency, the yuan, makes it challenging to compete with Chinese rivals, he added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCompanies have to satisfy shareholders and will continue to buy from China, whatever the political rhetoric coming out of Brussels, he said.“When manufacturing leaves Europe, Europe not only loses production but investment, knowhow and long-term economic resilience,” Eurometal said ahead of the protest.Analysis by the European Commission in June projected potential job losses of more than 1m on the back of high energy costs and global competition, which will include the100,000 job cuts at Volkswagenconfirmed by the German carmaker last week.China has repeatedly accused Europe of protectionism. It threatened “resolute countermeasures should the EU further target Chinese companies or products”, according to the state-owned Xinhua agency earlier this year. Since then, the EU and China have agreed a three-month truce.Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorEuropean UnionInternational tradeChinaEuropeJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe | Aerospace industry | The Guardian
description: Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market
Content: The uncrewed Spectrum rocket successfully entered orbit after its launch from Arctic Norway.Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe uncrewed Spectrum rocket successfully entered orbit after its launch from Arctic Norway.Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/ReutersAerospace industryGerman startup sends first commercial rocket into space from EuropeIsar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch marketReuters in OsloSun 6 Sep 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continentalEurope, a milestone for Europe’s efforts to secure independent access to space.Isar Aerospace
