said on Sunday that it would rapidly ⁠expand satellite deployments after the ⁠first orbital launch of ​its uncrewed Spectrum rocket from ArcticNorway, marking a ⁠breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches.“Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry,” Isar’s co-founder and chief executive, Daniel Metzler, told reporters.Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, hailed Saturday’s launch in a ​statement, calling it “the beginning of a new era”.Merz visited Isar’s ‌launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s ‌efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under the administration of country’s president, Donald Trump.The EU defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, wrote on the social media platform X: “Europe’s independent access to space just got a major boost.”Blasting off from Andøya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment.It was Isar’s second launch, 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site.Isar has said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting about 40 launches a year.The German company ​is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.Global players ⁠in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the US, and the French firm ArianeGroup, ​a joint venture between Airbus and Safran ​that uses a spaceport in French Guiana, South America.Explore more on these topicsAerospace industrySpaceEuropeNorwayGermanySatellitesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons
Content: The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US energy secretary, Chris Wright, in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranEnergy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with IranChris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weaponsMaya YangSun 6 Sep 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement withIranthat would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and theUS-Israel war on Irancontinues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare thestrait of Hormuzsafe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflictdrags on.How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedRead moreThis came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’sinsistencelast week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed byfurther strikesfrom both sides in the area.Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Timesreportfound that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warnsRead moreNuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to havestalledafter a June interim agreement to end military operationscollapsedwithout producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after USstrikes last summercausedhuge damage.Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vancesaidat a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump thendefendedVance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.“Probably not,” he said.The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warnedin an interviewwith the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyIranTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests | Iran | The Guardian
description: Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession
Content: It took four months for the mother of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 19, to find out where they were being detained.View image in fullscreenIt took four months for the mother of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 19, to find out where they were being detained.IranBroken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protestsTaraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confessionDaniel BoffeyChief reporterSun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities duringthe January protestsagainst the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May.The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed.View image in fullscreenTaraneh Rahimi, who has a love of horses.Photograph: Taraneh RahimiThe visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in centralIran,was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing.View image in fullscreenRomina Rahimi.Photograph: RominaThe difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime.“They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.”Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’”Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January.At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent.Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from footage of anti-government protests in Tehran in early January.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersThe two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’”Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.”Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before.“My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”Explore more on these topicsIranProtestMiddle East and north AfricaHuman rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens | Bristol | The Guardian
description: Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute
Content: Redevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRedevelopment of the Temple Quarter of Bristol including the Sloane Robinson Building, an addition to the University of Bristol.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianBristol‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opensTemple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commuteSteven MorrisSun 6 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone.On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of thatcrumbling Royal Mail sorting officenext door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public.The proximity ofthe Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC)to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot affordBristol’s expensive property and rental marketto commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings.The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been.View image in fullscreenThe former Bristol Royal Mail sorting office next to Bristol Temple Meads train station was demolished in 2019.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes,Bristol Temple Quarter, which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’sfirst prime minister’s questions.Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city.“We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students.“It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.”View image in fullscreenThe Sloane Robinson building is the £241m centrepiece of the University of Bristol’s Temple Quarter campus.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThe site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies.It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space.But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens.A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added.Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations.Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised.View image in fullscreenThe Sloane Robinson building is named after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student Hugh Sloane.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianMembers of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.”The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m.The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths.The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m.Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market.View image in fullscreenMembers of the public will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianThough the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it.Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said.Martin Booth, editor of the independent magazine and websiteBristol 24/7and author of111 Places That You Shouldn’t Miss in Bristol, said the new site looked as if a “gigantic spaceship” had crash-landed next to the station. “But it is a manifestation of the university’s efforts to be a more visible part of our city – not just in their privileged position on top of a hill in Clifton,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBristolUniversitiesHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision
Content: Activists staged a demonstration in Westminster, London last September in anticipation of the government’s changes to the Send system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenActivists staged a demonstration in Westminster, London last September in anticipation of the government’s changes to the Send system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianSpecial educational needsPupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for supportSchools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provisionRichard AdamsEducation editorSun 6 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools and councils acrossEnglandare expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes.Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs.The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029.Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets.School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications.One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month.Some parents of special school pupils in England spending £5,000 on EHCPsRead moreBill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February.“Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded.“This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.”EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million haveidentified special needs, according toofficial data.The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid manylocal authorities becoming technically bankrupt.Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to itswhite paper, which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030.During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries.“I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Gould, the schools minister, on a visit to a school in Colchester, said she families have been let down by the system.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian“That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.”Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.”Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”.Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.”Send plan for England gets cautious welcome amid workload concernsRead moreIpsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced.Madeleine Cassidy,Ipsea’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.”The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029.William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures.Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsSchoolsSchool fundingLocal governmentChildrenEducation policyEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black-clad Dover vigilantes will return if police do not act, say campaigners  | Far right | The Guardian
description: Far-right linked group able to mobilise at scale due to police ‘inaction’, says founder of Hope Not Hate
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Far-right linked group able to mobilise at scale due to police ‘inaction’, says founder of Hope Not Hate
Content: The peaceful protest appears to have been claimed by a group called Patriot Platform.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreenThe peaceful protest appears to have been claimed by a group called Patriot Platform.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeFar rightBlack-clad Dover vigilantes will return if police do not act, say campaignersFar-right linked group able to mobilise at scale due to police ‘inaction’, says founder of Hope Not HateRachel HallSun 6 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 06.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe group of masked, black-clad vigilantes who blockaded roads in Dover could repeat the disruption unless police step up efforts to stop them, politicians and campaigners have said.Responsibility forthe demonstrationhas been claimed by Patriot Platform, an anti-immigration group with links to the far right, which styles itself as having a “fierce love for our homeland”.The campaign group Hope Not Hate, which has been monitoring Patriot Platform, said that despite its founder, Daniel Thomas, nicknamed Danny Tommo, posting on social media about his plans to cause disruption, the authorities had “failed to act”.Thomas, a far-right social media influencer who was Tommy Robinson’s bodyguard, was able to mobilise a large group for the demonstration on Saturday. Hope Not Hate’s founder, Nick Lowles, said that this was “clearly the consequence of the inaction from the police”.He added: “We fear that without decisive action things will only get worse from here.”Thomas posted that Saturday’s gathering had been the group’s “warning”, suggesting it could be the first step in a wider plan. On Instagram, he wrote that he was switching off for a few weeks as he was “mentally exhausted”, but that he would subsequently resume “updated meetings and vetting”.“A message was sent! Now imagine how powerful the next message will be,” he wrote.Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, shared his concerns about the need for greater police support “when Dover is targeted again” in a piece for the Mirror. He suggested that he would like additional officers, including mutual aid from forces such as the Met, available to be mobilised quickly.He wrote: “The Port of Dover is not just another road junction. It is critical national infrastructure.“Wilfully obstructing a highway can be a criminal offence. New legislation also means police can designate protest areas where concealing your identity with a balaclava or other face covering becomes an offence.”Tapp posted on X that Kent police appeared to have had “little advance warning”, and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he wrote.“A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by police. We can and must do better.”Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said that although peaceful protest was an “essential part of British life”, this differed from “dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives”.He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “I would condemn it, but I’d condemn the disruption it caused for local people as well. Clearly, that’s not something we would want or expect to see on the [streets] of Britain.”When pressed on the apparent unpreparedness of the police, he said that “on the whole, the police handled it very well”.Kent policeengaged with the protest on Saturday, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Protesters had dispersed by lunchtime, and no arrests were made during the incident.Social media videos showed a large number of demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20, chanting “stop the boats” and “England till I die”. The police did not give an official estimate of the number of people involved.The PatriotPlatform was formed in June from smaller localised anti-migrant groups, and describes itself as an “army of patriots” that believes “Britain belongs to the British”. Before the demonstration on Saturday, it had held several recruitment days across England.The group has been built up through Thomas’s social media following, with his content containing false or unevidenced claims, such as that Birmingham city council has banned English flags, as well as unsourced statistics claiming that rape has ballooned in the UK relative to other European countries.Hope Not Hate has previously revealed theviolent history of key members of the group, including records of violence against women. Thomas also has multiple criminal convictions.In late 2025 and early 2026, he collaborated with Raise the Colours – the flag campaign group that put up hundreds of union and St George flags across England in 2025 – to run a series of trips to Calais in which he filmed asylum seekers and hounded the charity workers assisting them, resulting in a ban from France.He has since targeted migrants arriving by small boat along the English south coast, and was banned from Dover, Ramsgate and Folkestone in August.Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said that although he understood that people were “extremely frustrated” by the small boats crisis, he has “always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life”.He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that.“The police should take whatever action they can to stop this happening again.”Kent police declined to comment. A government spokesperson said:“The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.”Explore more on these topicsFar rightImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: No bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says minister | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government
Content: The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg the focus should be on making the carmaker ‘as ⁠competitive as possible’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenThe business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg the focus should be on making the carmaker ‘as ⁠competitive as possible’.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAJaguar Land RoverNo bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says ministerCarmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and governmentRob DaviesSun 6 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job losses at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), after it emerged that the UK’s biggest carmaker isplanning up to 4,000 redundancies.Before crunch talks on Tuesday between JLR, union leaders and government officials, the business secretary,Jonathan Reynolds, said it was not his job to “intervene and run businesses”.JLR, owned by the Indian conglomerateTataMotors, told staff on Friday to expect a voluntary redundancy programme, as it tries to shore itself up against tough conditions with £1.7bn in cuts over two years.The Coventry-based company is expected to provide further details on job cuts as soon as Monday, which could include an admission that compulsory job losses are possible.The expected cuts, which represent almost 12% of JLR’s 34,000-strong UK workforce, threaten to provide an early reality check on Andy Burnham’s pledge to “reindustrialise” Britain.View image in fullscreenJaguar Land Rover staff check Range Rover bodies at the carmaker’s factory in Solihull.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersSources said they expect the redundancies, first reported in the Sunday Times, to be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shop floor production workers.JLR is understood to be responding to pressure from Tata to offset a slump in sales, exacerbated by thefallout from last year’s cyber-attackand the impact of Donald Trump’s tariff wars.Speaking on the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg show on Sunday, Reynolds signalled that the government was unwilling to put money into the business to limit job losses.Which UK carmakers will be hit hardest by Trump’s latest import tariffs?Read moreAsked if there could be financial support to protect the jobs, he said: “Not if it’s to bail people out.“If this is about making sure over time that workforce is right to make the business as ⁠competitive as possible, that’s the conversation we need to have,” Reynolds said, referring to the wider “challenging” environment for the auto sector.“We need to adapt to evolving global market conditions,” a spokesperson for JLR, which has its largest plant in Solihull in the West Midlands, said.Reynolds is expected to come under pressure to help staunch the number of job cuts from the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, during crunch talks with the JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, scheduled for Tuesday. Union officials will push for JLR to swerve compulsory job losses in favour of retraining or voluntary redundancy where possible.While Reynolds indicated that no bailout would be available, he hinted at other options to support carmakers.He refused to rule out watering downgovernment targets for UK automakersto reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035, pointing to an open consultation on the issue.Carmakers and unions have lobbied hard for a slower transition, saying the targets outpace actual customer demand.Reynolds also said that the government was sometimes prepared to invest “alongside” industry.In 2024, the new Labour government under Keir Starmer agreed to invest £500m in another Tata business, the Port Talbot steelworks, to build greener electric arc furnaces. However, the investment did not prevent 2,500 job losses at the south Wales site.View image in fullscreenStephen Kinnock, the secretary of state for Wales, and Andy Burnham at Tata Steel in Port Talbot – Keir Starmer’s investment in 2024 did not prevent job losses there.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetThe prospect of a jobs purge at JLR poses a challenge for Burnham, who has placed plans to “reindustrialise” Britain at the heart of his offer to voters since taking office less than two months ago.Last year, after JLR suffered the crippling cyber-attack, the government agreed to provide the company with a guaranteed loan facility of £1.5bn to help battle the impact on its supply chains and production.None of the loan has been drawn down.Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival planRead moreAs well as the cyber-attack, which halted production for several weeks anddented the UK economy, JLR has suffered the fallout from tariffs imposed by Trump, affecting the key American market for models such as the Range Rover and Defender.Trump initially slapped tariffs of 27.5% on British cars before reducing the figure to 10% as part of aUS-UK trade deal unveiled by Starmerto great fanfare at a press conference held at JLR’s Solihull plant in May last year.Competition from Chinese models such as ​the Jaecoo 7 – ​ranked third among Britain’s top-selling cars – ​has also eaten into sales at JLR, which makes more than 400,000 vehicles a year.JLR is not alone in being affected by these external factors. The German carmaker Volkswagen said last week itplans to cut a further 50,000 jobsas part of its turnaround plan as it faces US tariffs and Chinese competition.The Guardian has approached the department for business and trade for comment.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryJob lossesManufacturing sectorTataHackingJonathan ReynoldsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Assailant lunged at Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, campaign says | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Armed suspect Patrick Havas allegedly attacked Amy Acton during a campaign stop at a fair, injuring several people
Author: Diana Ramirez-Simon
Headline: Armed suspect Patrick Havas allegedly attacked Amy Acton during a campaign stop at a fair, injuring several people
Content: Amy Acton speaks with a reporter in Columbus, Ohio, on 15 April.Photograph: Sue Ogrocki/APView image in fullscreenAmy Acton speaks with a reporter in Columbus, Ohio, on 15 April.Photograph: Sue Ogrocki/APOhioAssailant lunged at Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, campaign saysArmed suspect Patrick Havas allegedly attacked Amy Acton during a campaign stop at a fair, injuring several peopleDiana Ramirez-Simonand agenciesSun 6 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmy Acton, Democratic candidate forOhiogovernor, was the target of an attack on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, campaign officials said. Several people were injured when the armed assailant lunged at Acton.The suspect knocked volunteers to the ground before he was arrested and was “discovered to have weapons”, Mahoning county Democratic party chairperson Chris Andersonsaid in a statement.Sheriff Jerry Greene told a local NBC outlet, 21 News, that the suspect, Patrick Havas, knocked down two older ‌adults during the incident.Havas is expected to be charged with assault and disorderly conduct, Greene ​told 21 News.Acton was not injured, but campaign officials said multiple people were hurt.She is “grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another,” said Addie Bullock, communications director for the campaign.Aphoto sharedto social media by a fair attendee after the incident showed Acton checking on one of those injured in the incident.“What happened at our tent today during today’s visit from Dr Acton is reprehensible and should be condemned by leaders on all sides of the aisle,” Anderson said.Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton, the state’s former public health director.Ramaswamy called the incident Sunday unacceptable.“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement on Sunday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbdul El-Sayad, Michigan’s Democratic US Senate candidate, also denounced the attack.“There’s no place for political violence in America,” El-Sayad said in asocial media post. “Our prayers go out to Dr. Acton and her team, and we hope that this moment is yet another wake up call regarding how important it is to make sure that democracy is a process by which we address our political differences peacefully.”The fairground’s police department referred inquiries to the Mahoning county sheriff’s department, which didn’t immediately return a message seeking comment. The Ohio state highway patrol didn’t immediately respond to a request for information.Explore more on these topicsOhioDemocratsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport | Florida | The Guardian
description: Three people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a halt
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Three people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a halt
Content: An Amazon cargo plane after it crashed at Miami international airport on Sunday, in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Amazon cargo plane after it crashed at Miami international airport on Sunday, in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesFloridaAt least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airportThree people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a haltMaya YangSun 6 Sep 2026 17.49 EDTFirst published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami international airport inFloridaon Sunday afternoon after the flight, which was arriving from Puerto Rico, overshot the runway, striking several vehicles and resulting in at least five deaths.The plane erupted in flames as dark smoke billowed into the sky, bringing operations at one of the busiest airports in the US to a halt. The pilot and copilot were trapped in the cockpit as a result of the crash, said the Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah.The mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade county said at a news conference on Sunday that in addition to the five people who were killed, five others were injured. Miami-Dade fire rescue confirmed during the same conference that ten total people were involved, with five deaths, three people in critical condition and two taken to a local hospital.Jadallah, described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.The National Transportation Safety Board has assembled a team to investigate, the agency said in asocial media poston Sunday evening. They are scheduling a media briefing for Monday.Videos posted online show heavy plumes of smoke surrounding an aircraft bearing theAmazonarrow logo on its tail. Unconfirmed reports suggest there may be casualties, but details about injuries or fatalities remained unclear.The plane was a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Prime Air.The Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) confirmed the crash in a statement to the Guardian, saying: “21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 pm local time on Sunday, September 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.”The plane overran the airport’s diagonal runway and was disabled at the north-west end of the airport, a spokesperson for Miami international airport said.An air and ground stop has been issued at the airport, preventing all other flights from landing or taking off at the busy south Florida hub. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said.“All runways and taxiways at MIA are currently closed as of 3pm and a ground stop is in effect,” the airport said, adding: “Miami-Dade Fire Rescue has responded to the scene.”About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.More than 60 units from the Miami-Dade fire rescue services appeared on scene, with units arriving “to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”, the fire departmentsaid, with the post adding that the plane had struck multiple vehicles near the airport.Firefighters were “working on extinguishing the fire and assessing patients”, the post said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS transportation secretary Sean Duffysaidon social media that responders would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.“If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,” he added.Meanwhile, the Miami-Dade sheriff’s officeannouncedstreet closures due to the crash, saying: “NW 67th Avenue between NW 25th Street – NW 36th Street is currently closed. Expect delays and seek alternate routes.”Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today.”Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”Explore more on these topicsFloridaMiamiAmazonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands | Hawaii | The Guardian
description: Storm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane season
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Storm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane season
Content: A satellite image shows three storms, from left: Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie, in the Pacific Ocean on Wednesday.Photograph: CIRA/NOAA/APView image in fullscreenA satellite image shows three storms, from left: Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie, in the Pacific Ocean on Wednesday.Photograph: CIRA/NOAA/APHawaiiHawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islandsStorm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane seasonMarina DunbarSun 6 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHawaii has declared a state of emergency as powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands, with the first impacts expected as soon as Monday.The storm is the third system in just over three weeks to threaten Hawaii during an active hurricane season in the central Pacific. Lowell remained a category 3 hurricane early on Sunday morning, packing winds of 125 miles per hour while moving north-west at six miles per hour.According to the forecast, Lowell will reach Hawaii as a category 2 hurricane. Its center could pass roughly 130 miles west of Ni’ihau or 170 miles west of Kauai between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.The threat comes amid unusually intense hurricane activity across the Pacific.As of Saturday, Hurricanes Karina, Lowell and Marie were all churning in the Pacificat the same time, marking the region’s first triple-hurricane stretch in a decade. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) was also monitoring afourth potentialsystem off the coast of Mexico.The Pacific averages only eight hurricanes per year, according to the NHC, making three simultaneous hurricanes highly unusual.Lowell’s projected offshore path is expected to keep the storm’s most dangerous winds away from Hawaii’s islands. But heavy rain, high surf and dangerous coastal conditions are still expected.A tropical storm warning is in effect for Kauai and Ni’ihau, where wind gusts above 39 miles per hour are possible over the next 48 hours.Lowell is the third storm in a matter of weeks to hit Hawaii as the climate crisis continues to increase the intensity and frequency of storms and other weather events.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTropical Storm Moke poised to slam into Hawaii just days after Hurricane LalaRead moreTropical Storm Mokestruck the southern partof Hawaii’s islands two weeks ago, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. That came just days after Hurricane Lala hit the region.The Hawaii governor Josh Green said Lala alone had caused at least $43m in infrastructure damage on the Big Island, along with another $4.6m in damage to homes.The escalating storm activity comes as the UN warns that this year’s El Niño is forecast to become the strongest on record in four decades.Astatementreleased on Thursday described El Niño as being “supersized before our eyes”, adding that the world is in “the danger zone of extreme weather”.The latest data on the natural climate phenomenon shows a near 100% likelihood that the latest El Niño will continue through February 2027, the statement said. The stronger an El Niño becomes, the greater the chance it will significantly alter rainfall and temperature patterns around the world and help fuel extreme weather.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) haspreviously warnedthere is a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in 70 years.Explore more on these topicsHawaiiExtreme weatherHurricanesEl Niño southern oscillationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom | US voting rights | The Guardian
description: Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections
Content: A USPS collection box stands next to a Snohomish County ballot drop box stands at the edge of a parking lot in Bothell, Washington, on 1 September 2026.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA USPS collection box stands next to a Snohomish County ballot drop box stands at the edge of a parking lot in Bothell, Washington, on 1 September 2026.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUS voting rightsTrump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loomLegal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm electionsMarina Dunbarand agencySun 6 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Trump administration renewed its appeal to theUS supreme courton Sunday to allow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judgehad blockednew limits on such ballots, just ahead of November’s midterm elections.The latest filing follows a decision by US district court judge Indira Talwani on Friday toextend a court orderpreventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Donald Trump’s executive order.The legal fight was continuing as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail – giving the administration little time to make major changes to the rules.“Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more states will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place – including Alabama on September 9 and at least five states the week of September 13,” the solicitor general, John Sauer, said in the filing to the supreme court on Sunday.“Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them. And while the injunction allows the Postal Service and the states to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements … each day the injunction is in place risks sowing confusion and chaos because the injunction makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer continued in the emergency application.It is the third time the administration has asked the highest court in the US to step into the dispute and that court has allowed the plan to move forward but has not decided whether it was legal.The outcome of the wrangling could have significant consequences for this year’s elections, with control of Congress on the line. Nearlyone-thirdof US voters cast their ballots by mail.The US president signed anexecutive orderin March that would prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots – ie only to voters on approved lists.Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the ordered changes areunconstitutional, while state election officials who run the elections say there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives.TheTrump administrationhas called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” which are aimed at protecting voting security, and further called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”.Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite having often used the method himself. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, while promotingbaseless claimsof fraud.The USPS has said itstands readyto implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS voting rightsTrump administrationUS politicsDonald TrumpUS supreme courtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Air conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or not | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis
Content: ‘Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.’Photograph: Ay Moments/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.’Photograph: Ay Moments/Getty ImagesClimate crisisAir conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or notEduardo PorterGlobal AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisisSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareThe greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to“degrow”the economy and tocurb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation overair conditioning.If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts toreduce carbon emissions, one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to theWorld Resources Institute. Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world,according to the International Energy Agency(IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they aregenerally poorerand they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today,according to the IEA. In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of40% to 50%of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.This is going to requirea lot of energy. Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciencesestimated thatin India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to aUnited Nations report, about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.So what does one do? Apparently,58% of the Frenchwould rather “suffer from the heat than install an air conditioner in order to protect the environment”. But these sentiments cannot drive the world’s response to a warming world. To fight the battle against climate change requires, in fact, facilitating access to AC for billions of people who are now at risk of facing a hotter planet without the technology to protect themselves and their economies.This proposition doesn’t rest only on arguments from ethics – although there are plenty of those. For starters, there is substantial evidence that air conditioning reduces heat’s impact on health.One study of US datafound that the lethality of days hotter than 80F (27C) declined by about 75% from 1900 to 2004, almost entirely due to the adoption of residential air conditioning. Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.Another powerful reason is that limiting access to air conditioning will set back economic growth. There is abundant evidence that excessive heat in the workplacereduces labor productivityand that air conditioningmitigates the decline. Heat can also stymiestudent achievement,eroding human capital.Those living in India, Bangladesh, Indonesia or other unbearably hot places wherever will not heed the call to resist AC. Demanding unrealistic policies that are detrimental to their development is a straightforward strategy to ensure these countries do not cooperate with the effort to slow climate change.Campaignsfrom the west to stophydropowerin Africa, (even as westerners also called tostop developing fossil fuelson the continent) delivered little and engendered ill will. Trying to limit their access to AC would do the same.Whether it is to power industries, improve transportation, or cool homes and workplaces, achieving faster economic growth will require poor hot countries around the world to consume more energy. Their economic development is indispensable for the global battle against climate change.Just as fans of depopulation must understand that innovationneeds people, fans of shrinking humanity’s footprint on the planet to prevent climate change misunderstand how humanity has prospered despite environmental constraints: through innovation. The path to decarbonization requires figuring out how to produce zero-carbon energy on a vast scale everywhere. It will be easier to do thisin a rich worldwith AC and refrigeration than in a poor hot one.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisExtreme heatEconomicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Wild opening salvo against Chelsea hints at exciting times for Arsenal fans | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: The home side’s response to Chelsea’s early goal was to play breathless attacking football
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: The home side’s response to Chelsea’s early goal was to play breathless attacking football
Content: Arsenal fans taunt Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers as he leaves the pitch after being substituted.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArsenal fans taunt Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers as he leaves the pitch after being substituted.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesArsenalAnalysisWild opening salvo against Chelsea hints at exciting times for Arsenal fansBarney Ronayat the Emirates StadiumThe home side’s response to Chelsea’s early goal was to play breathless attacking footballSun 6 Sep 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWe’re back, baby. So, so back. Well, OK, not exactly back. But back down the time tunnel, for a while at least, as on a powder blue afternoon at the Emirates Stadium, Arsenal andChelseaproduced an opening half-hour that felt like a throwback to prime Barclays of the early 2000s.In that period this really did feel like a twist on a classic: spells of midfield murder-ball, stretched and flustered full‑backs, players hurling themselves at the defensive lines like the fall guys in a cowboy western being tossed out through the saloon-bar doors.Ødegaard fires winner as Arsenal complete comeback win over ChelseaRead moreArsenal had 10 shots in that period and played breathless, physically overwhelming attacking football. The game settled after they scored their equaliser. In the second half it became simply gripping and episodic, broken up by subs and stoppages, which is the current dynamic. Second halves: these are a problem. ButArsenalnever really looked like losing their 2-1 lead.The key to the day was that agreeably wild opening half‑hour, evidence that both teams have will and the energy to progress this season. Which will, in turn, be good news for the Premier League.About last season. It was OK, wasn’t it? Quite a lot of demo-mode football. Games that were like watching someone knitting a scarf. Teams with such elite levels of defensive organisation the experience is like watching one of those police motorbike display teams doing a pyramid, while a group of men on laptops furiously study the data.All very orderly, and disciplined. Just lacking in colour and fire. And more significantly, the higher gears that mean you might actually be able to run step for step with Paris Saint-Germain, or blow away, rather than slowly strangle, an opponent.It is about balance of course, about releasing the urge for total control. There was a moment on 87 minutes that captured both sides of this. Chelsea were awarded a free-kick 25 yards out in front of goal: high drama, a moment to be seized, necks craned forward in the seats. At which point Danny Welbeck, on as a late sub, sprinted straight to Reece James as he prepared to shoot, looking like a man in a state of high alert, some vital mission being run. Welbeck’s mission turned out to be handing James a piece of paper and urging him to read it. What was this? Expected 87th-minute free-kick numbers? Forty-seven per cent scoring chance uplift high and to the left? Maybe it just said “Score, dufus”, in which case, more of this please. James studied it dutifully, then paced out his run again. And to be fair, if the note did say hammer it straight into Declan Rice’s head, then job done, great process everyone. But the overriding feeling was: no, thank you. Away with you, interventionist wonks, tracksuited control freakery. This is art. This is play, this is drama. Whatever it is, it’s definitely not time for a briefing.View image in fullscreenKai Havertz equalises for Arsenal in a whirlwind opening half-hour.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe other thing, simultaneous to this, was Morgan Rogers walking off around the pitch and being barracked relentlessly by the Arsenal fans – “You should have signed for a big club” – but looking spent, exhausted and emotionally drained, after giving everything to that part of the spectacle that felt like the counterpoint to Welbeck’s note, the wildness and the energy that feeds this thing.There really was nothing not to like about that start, which was all jam, all sugar rush. First there was the manager match‑up, a kind of Basque childhood romcom revenge drama. The league needs rivalries and sibling symmetry. It feeds off this stuff. Hmm. They might have to start jabbing each other in the chest a bit more. But it was still fascinating to seeXabi Alonso on the touchline. This was fresh meat for the eye: jawline, pecs, tan, elite smart-casual styling, and above all an effortless sense of aura. There’s a new sheriff in town. Even the sun had appeared, giving off a weird, dead September heat, the sky behind the stand a pale Hockney blue. And Chelsea scored with 1min 17sec gone, Rogers finishing on the volley with a measured, very deliberate grubber into the corner.For a while these two teams just ran into each other. Emi Martínez was kicked in the head but got up and was still booed relentlessly. Arsenal had a goal disallowed. They produced one flowing full-length move, set up by a lovely roll and spin by Myles Lewis‑Skelly. On 25 minutes it was 1-1, the goal all Kai Havertz’s own work as he drifted inside like a gangling, bookish Arjen Robben then shot low inside the near post.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHavertz was also involved in the decisive moment, producing a lovely, and indeed deeply unfashionable dummy to put Martin Ødegaard in space in front of goal. It wasn’t even really a dummy, Havertz just dribbled his foot away, with no real feint or shoulder dip in the classic dummy style.Arsenal’s fans are sometimes frustrated by Ødegaard. He’s not direct enough, doesn’t shoot, always gilding the lily, regilding it, taking it back to the gilders for another look. Maybe this is how you get him to shoot. Put him right in front of goal with time to see every option, run the numbers, and conclude, ‘oh, well, I really am going to have to do this?’The finish was emphatic. After that the game became snarling and mean for a bit. Arsenal did enter one of their slow periods, taking the air out of it, killing the game a bit. But this was an excellent win against a very promising Chelsea.A final thought. The question will be asked: why don’t Arsenal always play like this? Why stop with the rage and forward gallops? The answer is that you can’t. It’s physically very hard. This is not a computer game. They’re humans, with 90 minutes to run. The real question is, can you raise it again, take that 30-minute spell and store it away, keep it ready in your repertoire? If so, and on the evidence here, we really might have an Arsenal upgrade on our hands.Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetaChelseaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: US overcome poor shooting and Italy’s eye-poke claims in edgy Fiba World Cup win | USA women's basketball team | The Guardian
description: The Americans escaped with a 55-52 win over Italy in the Fiba Women’s World ⁠Cup on Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Americans escaped with a 55-52 win over Italy in the Fiba Women’s World ⁠Cup on Sunday
Content: Jackie Young came through when it mattered against Italy.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJackie Young came through when it mattered against Italy.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockUSA women's basketball teamUS overcome poor shooting and Italy’s eye-poke claims in edgy Fiba World Cup winUSA edge into quarter’s with nervy 55-52 winCecilia Zandalasini claims she was poked in eyeCaitlin Clark shoots 0-6 from the fieldAgenciesSun 6 Sep 2026 17.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJackie Young had a big fourth quarter and Breanna Stewart made her only basket of the game to put ⁠the United States up for good, helping the Americans escape with a 55-52 win over Italy in the Fiba Women’s World ⁠Cup on Sunday.The ​US (2-0), who clinched a quarter-final berth with the victory, led only 42-39 after three quarters and fell behind by two points on three occasions in the fourth. Stewart’s jumper, assisted by Young, gave the Americans a 51-50 lead with 3:20 to go, and Young hit a ⁠floater on their next possession. Chelsea Gray made a pull-up with 1:07 left for an ​important cushion, but Italy hit a quick ‌two-pointer in response to ‌cut it to 55-52. Gray missed a shot on the next US trip but Young ‌corralled the rebound to help her team bleed more clock.Italy’s Cecilia Zandalasini, who missed a three-pointer to tie the game with three seconds left, was seen shouting at the referees after the buzzer as she argued she had been poked in the eye on the play. She expressed contrition after the game.“I would like to apologize for how I reacted in the end,” said Zandalasini. “To the opposing team, it was a lot of emotions today, but I should have kept them inside of me a little better. I want to apologize to the referees. It’s just when I wear this jersey, it’s just a different beast that comes out of me, and now I feel embarrassed for how I reacted.”Young scored six of her team-high 10 points in the fourth quarter. ‌Angel Reese scored eight points, Stewart grabbed 11 rebounds to help offset her 1-of-9 shooting day, and Paige Bueckers added seven points, five boards, ​two assists, two steals and two blocks for the US. Caitlin Clark shot 0-for-6 from the floor and scored one point.The Americans won despite shooting a woeful 16 of 56 (28.6%) overall and 1 for 12 on 3-pointers. They outscored the Italians 22-14 at the foul ⁠line.Zandalasini of the WNBA’s Golden State Valkyries had 14 points and ​seven boards to guide Italy (1-1).The ​US narrowly avoided ​their first World Cup loss since the 2006 semi-finals. It marked their ​closest World Cup ‌game in 20 ​years, per NBC Sports.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ​Americans conclude Group D play on Monday against the Czech Republic (0-2). The other game will pit Italy against China (1-1) with both teams still holding a chance to advance.Explore more on these topicsUSA women's basketball teamFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026BasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton rules out world title challenge after Italian Grand Prix setback | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Briton, who could only finish sixth at Monza after a clash with teammate Charles Leclerc, questioned the strategy of Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The Briton, who could only finish sixth at Monza after a clash with teammate Charles Leclerc, questioned the strategy of Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur
Content: Lewis Hamilton said of Ferrari’s strategy: ‘If we continue to travel the same path, we’ll get the same result.’Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton said of Ferrari’s strategy: ‘If we continue to travel the same path, we’ll get the same result.’Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFormula One 2026Lewis Hamilton rules out world title challenge after Italian Grand Prix setbackBriton finishes sixth after clash with teammate LeclercHamilton questions Ferrari chief Fred Vasseur’s strategyGiles Richardsat MonzaSun 6 Sep 2026 16.16 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has conceded theFormula Oneworld ­championship this year is all but out of reach after a bruising Italian Grand Prix. ­Hamilton’s afternoon included a clash with his Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc, which he thought was the result of the team’s failure to listen to his entreaties to manage their drivers and execute races better.The race at Monza waswon by Kimi Antonelliafter a remarkable comeback by the Mercedes driver from 19th on the grid. Hamilton could manage only sixth. Having been 59 points back he now trails Antonelli by 76 with 10 meetings remaining and he felt that Ferrari not ­prioritising his title chances, coupled with operational failures, had finally cost him a shot at the drivers’ championship.Antonelli ends Italy’s 60-year wait for home F1 win with Monza triumph from 19thRead more“From today, we’ve just lost so much ground to them on points. It’s far too late for those decisions to come,” he said of giving him priority over Leclerc. “It’s many, many weeks too late. All I can do is just try and turn up. I’ll get up tomorrow morning and I’ll give it my best. I don’t know how many points it is now but it’s an amount and with the pace that they [Mercedes] have, it is a very, very difficult amount to close up.”Leclerc did not finish the race after a huge crash on lap two from which he emerged unhurt. Before that on the first lap at the first ­chicane, Hamilton looked to go past his teammate but was squeezed wide, went off and dropped to 10th place.The seven‑time champion said imme­diately that Leclerc had driven him off track and noted pointedly that the incident demonstrated where Ferrari had been going wrong and that the team principal, Fred ­Vasseur, had to bear responsibility.“Look I don’t race dirty, I have always raced clean and fairly and always left space, so I don’t think they should be worried about me,” he said. “I’ve come into the team and tried to be respectful of space but ultimately it comes from the top. It trickles down.
