Twice a week, dozens of men and women gather at a local gym where they punch pads, practise their gait, laugh together and cheer each other on.On the surface, it looks like a regular exercise class but I know that it is so much more than that. It is a community built around the conviction that even when our bodies become weaker, our capacity to strengthen another person’s spirit does not diminish.For the duration of the classes, no one is sick or feeling sorry for themselves. They are all fighters who support one another through their difficult neurological illness.One of my favourite verses in the Torah encapsulates the dogged determination that my dad exemplifies: “I have set before you life and death, a blessing and a curse. Therefore, choose life.”As humans, we do not choose so many of the things that shape our lives. We do not choose illness or grief or disappointment.But choosing life is not about choosing our circumstances. It is about choosing our response to them. We choose life when we refuse to surrender to bitterness. We choose life when we build community instead of retreating into isolation. We choose life when we use whatever strength we still possess to make someone else’s burden a little lighter.Watching my dad has made me grateful for many things that some may take for granted. I am grateful for my legs that carry me where I need to go, I am grateful for the ability to work a day job, even though sometimes work is tiring. I am grateful to be a present mum who can hug my children, run after them in the park and sit with them on the floor and read them books. I know that having a body that works properly is a huge blessing.More than anything, my dad has taught me that life is not defined only by what happens to us. It is defined by the choices we make in response.Parkinson’s disease has taken things from my dad but it never took away his kindness, his faith and his desire to help those around him.Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish communityExplore more on these topicsParkinson's diseaseMaking sense of itJudaismReligionHealth (Australia news)Health (Society)commentShareReuse this content

title: It felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquiet | John Harris | The Guardian
description: This young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edge, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: This young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edge, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Geese at the End of the Road festival in Dorset, 3 September 2026.Photograph: End of the Road festivalView image in fullscreenGeese at the End of the Road festival in Dorset, 3 September 2026.Photograph: End of the Road festivalOpinionGeeseIt felt as if the world had tired of rock music, yet Geese are the perfect soundtrack for this age of disquietJohn HarrisThis young American band, led by Cameron Winter, make music for a generation on the edgeSun 6 Sep 2026 06.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShare“If you want me to pay my taxes,” sang the 23-year-old man on the stage, loudly accompanied by the thousands in front of him, “You better come over with a crucifix/ You’re gonna have to nail me down.”Last Thursday night, I stood in a field in Dorset, and watched the headlining attraction on the first night of the End of the Road festival. Geese are a rock group from New York, led by the extremely talentedCameron Winter,who has a lot to say, and an often gnomic, veiled way of saying it. But the meaning of the most celebrated lines on his band’s most recent album – Getting Killed – might be clearer than a lot of the rest.There are hundreds ofdifferent interpretationsonline of a song simply called Taxes, from death and martyrdom to the avoidance of responsibility.He may just, I suppose, be telling the Internal Revenue Service to go away in the cause of small-state libertarianism. But at the risk of ridicule, I’ll opt for the most literal and crowd-pleasing reading: that Winter is inspirationally updating the idea of rock music sneering at the powers that be and rejecting whatever it is they want. When I first heard those lines, in fact, I imagined him being cornered by Donald Trump, JD Vance and some or other Maga goon squad, wearily exhaling and sending them on their way.For at least a decade now, rock – which is to say, stuff largely made with guitars and mostly delivered by bands – has been in an increasing state of cultural eclipse. Its presence in what remains of the singles chart is usually minimal-to-nonexistent; it tends to fare better in the albums rankings, but chronically lacks its old ability to push itself to the forefront of its era.It’s striking, then, that Geese’s somewhat belated rise has been powered by an album that consummately embodies its time, has received praise to match and is evidently loved by younger people who were supposed to have long ago become largely rock-phobic (for proof,see the footageof Geese’s performance at this year’s Reading festival). Their current high profile has been powered not just byGetting Killed, but Winter’s much more intimate solo album – titled Heavy Metal – and a one-man performance at Carnegie Hall in New York, about to be released as a film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson. Seemingly as a matter of contractual obligation, all four members of his group (including guitarist Emily Green) have hairstyles like those of the early-1970s Rolling Stones, but the music they now make – their first album came out in 2018 – usually suggests something immeasurably more contemporary.It is variously tender, soothing, angry and explosive, prone to tumble into lengthy improvisation, and sometimes shot through with knowingness that can be maddening, but is presumably the result of working in an artistic field now full of cliches that either have to be acknowledged or swerved around. But when they play live, power, ferocity and sudden snaps between loudness and calm take precedence. Some moments are redolent of Led Zeppelin, but taken somewhere completely different by the lyrical content. Radiohead are another oft-cited reference point, which feels more satisfactory, but only in the sense thatGeeselargely stay true to the idea that they should sound like no one but themselves and damn the consequences.This is an age in which a huge amount of popular music is tailor-made for audiences assumed to be in a constant state of distraction, so songs often have the briskest of intros and the crassest, most earworm-ish hook lines. Geese’s music, by contrast, is often gnarly and difficult, and entails friction between the musicians and their listeners. It took me six or seven plays to even start to get my head around Getting Killed, but in an occasionally masochistic way, I enjoyed every minute.And this, I think, is why. From its title onwards, Getting Killed is full of flickers and flashes of the volatile and frightening condition of both Geese’s home country and the wider world. Among the first words on the album, repeated five times, are “There’s a bomb in my car”, quickly followed by “My daughter is dead.” Otherlyrics seem – seem – to reference the crazed ringmaster who has led the US into both internal conflict and disastrous entanglements abroad: “All people/In times of war/Must go down to the circus,” Winter sings on a piece titled 100 Horses, following that up with “There is only dance music in times of war/But we have danced for too long.” What you really yearn for is a zinger akin to Bob Dylan’s “even the president of the United States/Sometimes must have to stand naked.” But Winter’s facility with words suggests he will soon get there, even if he is currently too keen on bathetically bursting his own lyrical bubble and thereby avoiding the “spokesperson for a generation” deadweight that Dylan found so irksome: “There were hundred horses dancing/Maybe 124,” he sings at one point, which isn’t even that funny.View image in fullscreenGeese performing on the Canopy stage at the Reading festival, 28 August 2026.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PABut such slip-ups are rare. At the core of what Geese do is something that is also sharply generational. It’s surely one of the identifying features of people their age that even comparative material comfort (all four were privately educated) doesn’t make the anxiety that comes with being the canaries in the coalmine of digital capitalism unavoidable. The title track puts this point plainly: “I’m getting killed by a pretty good life,” wails Winter. “Getting killed by a pretty good life/I have been fucking destroyed by the city tonight.” A track titled Half Real suggests twentysomethings so understandably confounded that they just want to switch off. On Thursday, Winter sang with such ferocity that any lingering suspicions about archness or humour instantly vanished: “I’ve got half a mind/To just pay for the lobotomy/And tell ’em get rid of the bad times/And get rid of the good times too/I’ve got no more thinking to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn the face of it, there may be reasons to keep your distance: their comparatively privileged backgrounds, or aspurt of controversyabout the ubiquity and craftiness of their (very common) online marketing. But their empathetic kind of excellence makes those things almost irrelevant. What they excel at is reflecting their audience’s experiences, feelings, passions and furies back at them. At End of the Road, evidence of that connection was consistently there on the giant screen next to the stage. The younger members of the audience pressed against the barrier at the front rejoiced in every note of Taxes, and sang along most loudly to that eternal rebuke to the hypocrisies of power and influence: “Doctor, heal yourself.” But what was most telling was the ecstatic exchange between the band and their core crowd triggered by asimple linefrom one of Winter’s love songs, which seemed to take on quite another meaning: “I see myself in you.”They would doubtless hate me for saying so, but still: right now, Geese sound like the accidental representatives of a global demographic that may look sensitive and gentle, but that – in response to the impossibility of just about everything – may yet explode. In that sense, the simplest of messages is woven into what they do: look out.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGeeseOpinionPop and rockFestivalsIndiecommentShareReuse this content

title: Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom | Nell Frizzell | The Guardian
description: I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect, says journalist and author Nell Frizzell
Author: Nell Frizzell
Headline: I’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospect, says journalist and author Nell Frizzell
Content: ‘I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic chairs as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders.’Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreen‘I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic chairs as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders.’Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAOpinionCareersAged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroomNell FrizzellI’m one of many creatives turning to teaching mid-career, but that’s no bad thing. I’m thrilled by the prospectSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTShareYou know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.View image in fullscreenNell Frizzell in a homemade ladybird fancy dress costume, made while she was at school.Photograph: Nell Frizzell/The GuardianBut as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometresback home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the namethe Strokes, and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.I’m also far from the only person I knowhole-punching their way into a new careerafter decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years andthenwent into creative fields –Romesh Ranganathan,Philip Pullman,Joanne Harris,Greg Daviesand so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd this time I don’t even need to bring in my PE kit.Nell Frizzell is a journalist and authorExplore more on these topicsCareersOpinionTeacher trainingTeachingWork & careersSchoolscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold on to hope | Ezra Collective | The Guardian
description: The bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. He shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. He shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks
Content: Femi Koleoso … ‘There’s power in a happy story – it brings hope.’Photograph: Sergio PontierView image in fullscreenFemi Koleoso … ‘There’s power in a happy story – it brings hope.’Photograph: Sergio PontierEzra Collective‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold on to hopeThe bandleader, drummer, DJ and broadcaster is guest-editing this week’s Saturday magazine Culture features. In his editor’s letter, he shares why he’s optimistic for the future. Plus: his bandmates offer their cultural picks‘Things work out for the good people’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso meets his inspirations‘Like painting with light’: photographer Temi Adegbayibi on capturing the energy of musicMy cultural awakening, featuring Ezra CollectiveFemi KoleosoSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy first thought when contacted about guest editing the culture section in today’s Saturday magazine was: this will elevate me into an intellectual bracket far beyond my wildest dreams. The first person I told was my dad. The second was my secondary school English teacher, Mr Pickering. I guess it was a subtle way of letting them know that the student is now in charge.It’s a truly wonderful feeling. Even if this entire takeover is trash, I’m still proud to have been given this wonderful opportunity. That said, I did get an A in my GCSE English and English Lit!To give some context: I am not a writer, nor an intellectual or a journalist. I am Femi Koleoso, a musician from north London. Born to Nigerian parents and raised in Enfield, a corner of London paved with gold, I started playing the drums at church (I know, typical). This became more than a hobby; it was a deep-set love, nurtured in the UK’s wonderful state school system and polished in powerful youth clubs. Today, I travel the world with my band,Ezra Collective, playing and producing music, DJing and broadcasting on BBC Radio 6 Music for a living. If there were a version of the “British-Nigerian dream” that didn’t involve becoming a lawyer, accountant or doctor, you could say my family and I got pretty close.double quotation markThere is reason to have hope for the future; perhaps in this guest edit, I’m building a case for a more positive outlookThere’s power in a happy story; it brings hope. Normal school, amazing career. That’s the dream, right? That said, joy is at the centre of who I am, and every day I am filled with hope for the future.But is there really reason to have hope for the future? Though I often only want to talk about Arsenal football club and playing the drums, I am well-informed enough to see the many reasons to lose all hope, not just for the future of the UK but the world. But while I acknowledge that, I believe there is a counter argument. I believe there is reason to have hope for the future of the UK and beyond; perhaps in this guest edit, I’m building a case for a more positive outlook on things.The word “hope” has many definitions, but as my dear friend, the actor Letitia Wright, wonderfully phrases it via spoken-word interludes on our new album, Here Because of Hope, hope also captures the belief that on the other side of pain there can be renewal. There’s joy after mourning. Beauty from the ashes. Even when you don’t know how or when things will change, there can still be something inside you that believes your feet will eventually land on solid ground.So on one side, you have pain; on the other, there will be joy. And hope is a marker on that spectrum that brings you from one end to the other; it makes you feel like getting to joy might be possible.Being a musician, I see that hope most eloquently articulated in songs. Songs born out of pain bring joy. Fela Kuti wrote a song about his mother being executed by the Nigerian government – and its bassline became a club anthem. The pain and hardship of life in poverty-ridden council estates gave us grime music, which has people sweating and smiling in clubs. Calypso even emerged out of the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade.The fuel for this wide-ranging artistic output, across continents and centuries is, for me, hope. In these features, you’ll be able to read about some people and stories that bring me out of pain and into joy; stories that bring me hope.Collective decisions: Ezra’s cultural picksView image in fullscreen‘Wagner Moura is incredible’ … The Secret Agent.Photograph: APFilm: The Secret AgentI watched The Secret Agent recently while on a long drive to a show in Italy. It’s an intense story and Wagner Moura is incredible. I love the way director Kleber Mendonça Filho so immersively takes you into 70s Brazil.TJ KoleosoAlbum: Rosa Passos – RecriaçãoRecriação by Rosa Passos is a beautiful album, with minimal instrumentation but used in the most perfect way. Especially the drumming. It’s often just kick drum, rather than the full kit, and it works incredibly well. Also, if anybody knows what synth they used on the record, please let me know.Joe Armon-JonesView image in fullscreen‘It was a “Best of London” feeling’ … Steelpans, as celebrated recently at the Southbank Centre.Photograph: Tomprout/Getty ImagesLive music: Southbank CentreRather than go the traditional album-film-TV-show route, I’m picking the Southbank Centre. As part of its 75th-anniversary celebrations, it chose to celebrate the steelpan, and I had the privilege of watching loads of young bands play. It was a “best of London” feeling just seeing so many different generations, cultures and people all dancing and celebrating the joy that togetherness and music can bring.Femi KoleosoView image in fullscreen‘It felt so raw and had so much cultural depth’ … My Father’s Shadow.Photograph: Mubi /PAFilm: My Father’s ShadowMy pick is Akinola Davies Jr’s 2025 film My Father’s Shadow, a Nigerian coming-of-age tale. I watched it recently and loved it. The storytelling was great and it felt so raw. It had so much cultural depth, which I could resonate with as a Nigerian.Ife OgunjobiView image in fullscreen‘She’s not confined to one thing’ … KeiyaA.Photograph: Jessica FoleyAlbum: KeiyaA – Hooke’s LawI’m really into Hooke’s Law by KeiyaA at the moment. Ife put me on to this record when we were on tour in Italy and I haven’t put it down since. I love it when artists take us on a journey through different sound worlds within one album, as I think it creates such a rich and beautiful piece of art. Throughout this album it feels as if she’s not confined to one thing, which gives it a really original energy and makes it a truly unique and captivating listen. She produced it all as well and, sonically, it’s really tasty.James MollisonExplore more on these topicsEzra CollectiveBlack British culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of Thrones | Maisie Williams | The Guardian
description: After her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourself
Author: Simran Hans
Headline: After her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourself
Content: Maisie Williams: ‘I’m in love! That’s all I’ll say.’ All portraits: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaisie Williams: ‘I’m in love! That’s all I’ll say.’ All portraits: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianMaisie WilliamsInterview‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of ThronesSimran HansAfter her role in the fantasy series, the actor felt lost. Now she’s getting relationship advice from Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, and following a Sex and the City star’s mantra: never be anywhere you aren’t enjoying yourselfSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaisie Williams has dabbled in witchcraft exactly once. The actor was getting ready to audition for a part in a film. “I wanted it so badly that I went on to Etsy, and I paid a witch to manifest me the role,” she says, poker-faced.“It didn’t work, and that was where my days of witchcraft ended,” she adds, breaking into an infectious cackle.The spell may not have worked that time, but Williams will soon try her own hand at witchcraft on screen in Practical Magic 2. The sequel to the beloved 1998 romcom, about two supernatural sisters played by Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, it features Williams as Antonia, the youngest daughter of Bullock’s Sally Owens. She never did get her money back from her Etsy witch. “It was maybe, like, £16.50? Which is not going to break the bank, but good for her. Good for her, to be making money doing nothing!” Williams laughs again.We meet on a sweltering afternoon at a posh pub in Belgravia in London where women in expensive-looking sundresses are drinking Aperol spritzes on the terrace. Williams arrives from a busy day of appointments. She removes a pair of oversized grey headphones and sets them down on the table (she was listening to the US singer-songwriter Slayyyter on the walk over). “I’m in my business outfit because I’ve hadbusinessmeetings,” she explains. (It’s arguably a very gen Z take on corporate dressing: long, dark hair worn in a practical ponytail, white T-shirt, smart grey trousers with a matching grey miniskirt attached, chunky, don’t‑mess-with-me Prada boots.)Today’s agenda has included two jewellery fittings for a red carpet event, an “important producing meeting, with me as the producer” and lunch with her former Game of Thrones co-starHannah Murray. The pair were catching up and discussing Murray’s recent memoir,The Make-Believe, about her devastating experience with a wellness cult. The group promised spiritual healing through expensive, elaborate rituals; Murray experienced a psychotic episode and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder. “I knew something was going on, but I didn’t know it was that,” Williams says. “I felt really upset with myself for not asking sooner.”View image in fullscreenMaisie Williams as Arya Stark in Game of Thrones (above) and with Florence Pugh in The Falling (right). Photographs: Helen Sloan/HBO; AlamyView image in fullscreenWilliams says she hasn’t always been a sceptic regarding magic. “I used to indulge in the whimsy of the patterns of the universe and think, ‘Oh, it’s a sign that everything’s going to work out.’” She says, taking a sip of Diet Coke. But after reading Murray’s book, Williams decided that searching for symbols in daily life might not be so wholesome after all. “I realised it leaves your mind slightly malleable to seeing a sign because you think it’s a divine intervention, and not just a good, fun coincidence.”The 29-year-old actor is probably still best known as Arya Stark from Game of Thrones, the baby-faced assassin who shot her to stratospheric levels of fame at age 12. I remember first seeing her in Carol Morley’sThe Falling, in which she stood out as a prickly, stiff‑backed schoolgirl opposite a then unknown Florence Pugh. In the seven years since Game of Thrones ended, Williams has landed roles in Marvel spin-offThe New Mutants, in Danny Boyle’s miniseriesPistolas punk icon Jordan, and in Apple TV’sThe New Look, a glossy drama about Christian Dior and Coco Chanel in Nazi-occupied Paris. She has started her own production company, and co-hosts theFrank Film Clubpodcast with two of her friends. It has been a period of trying different things, of searching for light relief, after a long stretch dealing with some much darker stuff. Last year, she even got a new agent. “He was bringing me fun things and was calling me every day,” she says. One of those fun, unexpected things was Practical Magic 2.Williams had seen the original once or twice, but rewatched it before her audition. “The first movie has a lot of different beats to it,” she says diplomatically. That’s one way to put it: tonally, the film is all over the place. Based on an Alice Hoffman novel, it tells the story of the Owens sisters, two witches doomed by an ancestral curse: any man who falls in love with an Owens woman is destined to die. It is a cult classic, with fabulous 90s costumes, Bullock and Kidmandrunkenly dancing around their kitchento Harry Nilsson’s Coconut and a jarringly dark domestic violence subplot. The sequel is much slicker. Directed by Susanne Bier, it sends Sally’s more rebellious eldest daughter Kylie (Joey King) to England as she tries to break the family curse. Bullock and Kidman go after her, bickering the whole way, while Williams’s character, a trainee neurosurgeon, holds the fort at home.View image in fullscreenMaisie Williams as Jordan in Danny Boyle’s Pistol.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/FX“Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman are real movie stars – from a time in cinema that is escaping us,” says Williams matter-of-factly. “I went into this film seeing them as otherworldly.” She recalls meeting the actors for the first time at the read-through. Later that day she was heading to Glastonbury festival. “I got back in my car, and I wound the windows up, and I was just like … ” Williams claps both French-manicured hands to her face and lets out a high-pitched shriek. “I had my dog in the car. He was probably thinking, ‘What is going on?!’ And then I drove to Glastonbury.” On set, in between takes, the veteran Hollywood actors imparted important wisdom to their younger co-stars. But it wasn’t about the industry. “We spoke about how being friends with your ex is a fallacy,” she says. Who said that? Was it Kidman, who is recently divorced? “We all said that!” Williams demurs.In the film, Williams and King are an inseparable sister duo, snuggled under the covers at their mum’s house and whispering as if they’re at a sleepover. In real life, Williams has three siblings, including one sister who is five years her senior. “When we’re together it’s like no time has passed but we’re not … ” She pauses. “We don’t call every day,” she says. “We’ve had waves in our life when we’re a lot closer, but a lot of our connection now comes through the kids.” Williams takes her niece and nephew on camping trips. “We never went out partying together,” she says. And, anyway, when she would have been the right age, Williams was busy filmingGame of Thrones. “I was away most of the time, and I’d moved out as well.”Williams’s route to child stardom came via a curiously X Factor-themed school nativity play. “I played Sharon Osbourne, and had done such a good job that my friend’s mum felt compelled to tell my mum, ‘You should put her into classes.’ That was when I started taking it seriously, because they were taking me seriously.” Then things got very serious, with Williams barely in secondary school when she landed a role on Game of Thrones. The speed at which her career took off shaped her expectations of the film industry, she says. “I thought, oh! Whatever you want, you can get. Like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “That was how I thought the industry was.” Her naivety, she reckons, was a good thing. “It informed the way I see life, and the way I threw myself into what turned out to be a huge responsibility.”Those early positive experiences, she says, gave her the confidence to pursue her dreams. “I wasn’t knocked down as a child. I wasn’t knocked down by my mum. I wasn’t knocked down by teachers at drama school, and I wasn’t knocked down by the industry when I did start auditioning.” Williams wonders if she would have still been resilient if she hadn’t enjoyed early success. “I think that a lot of people have a gift, but they just don’t get cast in a huge TV show when they’re 12.”double quotation markI could access anger and fear because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of timeView image in fullscreenWilliams claims not to know about an Arya Stark spin-off movie that is reportedly in development with HBO. “I saw that, too! I was like, huh?” Would she be interested in returning to that character? “I don’t know, really. She would have to be developed in some way because I feel like I’ve changed so much, and I feel like what people loved about Arya is that she was always a child doing things that were quite grownup.”In person, Williams is warm but somewhat guarded; she sits next to me on the leather banquette but maintains a cautious distance. She is good company, with a beaming smile and a glorious, trilling laugh, but several times in our conversation I sense her weighing up her words. When asked about her early life growing up between Bristol and Somerset she becomes visibly uncomfortable. She settles on an honest, abridged answer. “My mum and my siblings and I spent a lot of time with my auntie,” she says, adding that she was mostly raised by the two women. “My auntie was a childminder with loads of other kids, so my life was vibrant and silly and fun and playful.”Williams describes herself as “not coming from a hugely privileged background”. I wonder how, on the brink of 30, she reflects on growing up with less. “When I reflect on myself as a child, I wish I could just tell her it’s going to be fine. It’s going to work out. I think the fear that I felt at that time was so defining for many years of my childhood. I didn’t know. I was so ambitious as a small child, and I think maybe that did come from wanting my life to be different.”In 2022, Williams spoke about the difficulties she faced back then on theDiary of a CEOpodcast. Her parents split up when she was a baby, and her father is no longer in her life. “I had a traumatic relationship with my dad, and ever since I can remember I have struggled sleeping,” she told host Steven Bartlett. She described a teacher noticing her struggling at school and asking if she ate breakfast in the mornings. Williams said she didn’t. She was eight. The teacher called her mum. “I would look around at other kids and be, like, ‘Why don’t they seem to understand this pain or dread or fear? Joy – when does that come for me?” she said on the podcast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markMy relationship to success was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?View image in fullscreen“I have very close friends that I had not told,” Williams says today. “What I said on that podcast was all I’ve said about it to a lot of people, other than my family and my therapist. I even had boyfriends who didn’t know. So my reluctance to want to talk about it again is because my relationship to fame, and my relationship to success, was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?” She winces.“I think it reached a lot of people who were in the same position, and I’m really happy that it did.” I’m curious to know why she chose that moment to finally speak about what had happened to her. “I always wanted to,” she says. “I think part of the reason why I was so good at playing Arya was because of how I’d grown up.”She says journalists would often ask her how she was able to access such difficult emotions as a younger, less experienced actor. “I always felt like it was something I couldn’t say. I could access these emotions because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of time.” What emotions? “Anger and fear.” She lets out a bitter laugh. “Stonewalling. I know that feeling of shutting down. These things that you don’t really start to understand about yourself until a lot later.” Being a teenager, she says, is already so fraught with emotion.By the time she recorded that podcast, “I had done a lot of therapy,” she says, “and so was feeling a lot clearer about a lot of things.” It was Bartlett’s initial question that cracked them open for her. “He said, ‘What happened to you as a child that defines how you are?’ or something. It’s literally the only question that someone would have to ask me for me to answer honestly.” I was struck by her candour and vulnerability in that interview, I tell her. “I just thought that by releasing it, it was the last step in being free from it. Which kind of turned out to be true,” she says.I wonder what she makes of Bartlett now. “Mmm,” she says, eyebrows raising, her mouth tightening into a horizontal line. In recent years, Bartlett has become a controversial figure, who has been criticised for amplifying medical misinformation and platforming manosphere-adjacent guests such as fellow podcaster Chris Williamson, who blamed declining birthrates on “women’s socioeconomic emancipation into the workforce”. Bartlett has aired the views of “experts” who claimed that Covid vaccines were “a net negative for society” and that cancer could be treated by a keto diet. It’s not a show that seems particularly aligned with liberal values.View image in fullscreenStyling: Magdalena Bryk at Art Dept, assisted by Vienna Divens. Hair: Clayton Hawkins at Frame Agency. Makeup: Kindra Mann at Frame Agency. Dress and shoes: Alexander McQueen. Tights: Los Angeles Apparel. Knit: Shushu Tong. Headpiece: Piers Atkinson. Blazer, skirt and shoes: Shushu Tong. Coat: Marc Jacobs“At the time, it felt like he had a podcast that felt fresh and different,” Williams says. “After, I felt slightly like I had been part of a podcast that gets a lot of views based on uprooting trauma. When I saw the trailer to the episode, I felt slightly icked out by how he had clipped it. But ultimately I can’t control that. Now I just feel like it’s quite dangerous, some of these conversations that are being had and taken out of context.”Still, speaking about her experiences publicly was “a huge, defining moment of change” for Williams. “The first half of my 20s was just hell, but I think maybe it is for a lot of people,” she says. “I think that has more to do with the fact that Game of Thrones was ending, and I didn’t know what I was going to do next, and I just needed a break, to be honest with you. And then it also has to do with delayed teenage awkward years, and figuring a lot of things out that I felt like maybe I couldn’t do much earlier than that. And also Covid, and also an industry strike,” she adds with a shrug. The pub is getting noisy, filling up with finance bros who have just finished work.“But post-2023, every day has been getting better,” she says. What happened in 2023? “I started seeing my friends again. I moved out of London. I was living alone. I was back with my dog. Everything was different,” she says. Williams is too discreet to confirm whether this change was sparked by the breakup of her long‑term relationship with fashion designer Reuben Selby. “At that point, it was time to … ” She smiles as if she’s got a secret. “Just choose myself,” she says. “What always comes into my mind is Kim Cattrall,” she adds, paraphrasinga quote the actor gave to the Guardianthat became a popular meme. “‘I don’t want to be anywhere, not even for an hour, where I’m not enjoying myself.’ That’s truly how I’ve been the last three years.”For Williams, choosing herself means “a lot of quiet, a lot of reading, and writing, and yoga, and running, and exercise, and swimming, and cycling, and walking the dog. Walking the dog for, like, hours a day.” In other words, being in her body. “Exactly, because then I know what I want. And that can be going out with my friends all weekend, or it can be a fun dinner in London where you miss your last train home, or it can be going to the cinema alone.” This summer, it has meant going to Primavera Sound and seeing singer Ethel Cain play, having barbecues with her friends and watching the World Cup in her local pub.When I ask Williams what her career ambitions are now, a misty, faraway look comes over her. She does say her dreams out loud, but she’d rather not say them in print, she says. “My ambition is to work with people who have proven themselves to be really talented,” she says. “I’ve worked in the industry for quite a long time, and even though I love working with debut directors, there’s a stark difference in our experience now, which is noticeable. Working with people who are more experienced brings a different atmosphere on set.” She’s also been pouring her time into her production company, Rapt. It has meant reading a lot of scripts. “I cannot tell you the amount of postpartum horrors that people are making,” she says. “Whenever there’s one great movie, you’ll get seven scripts like that on your desk.” She and her co-founder, Lowri Roberts, are having fun writing their own feature film, too. “It’s a dark comedy. It’s a satire about the end of the world,” she says.Williams has frequently been cast in dark, dramatic roles: “But I don’t really think that’s how I am most of the time,” she says. “I think when I’m in bad situations, I’d be more likely to laugh than to cry. I don’t know if I’m really in the camp of ‘plan for the worst’. I’ve had periods of my life where I’ve been so overcome by the fear of what could go wrong that, particularly now, I’m more in a phase of ‘anything can be fixed’.”Not that there’s much that needs fixing. She is dating and “so happy” about it, though she is coy when pressed about the details. Has she been enjoying playing the field? “No! I’m in love,” she says, smirking. “That’s all I’ll say.” Does it feel different from other times she’s been in love? “Yes, which is good. There’s lots of laughter,” she says, giggling. The vibe this summer, she says, has been “hot, in all senses of the word”. She grins. “I got myself a fan. I am a late adopter of the fan.” Before that, she says, she was “just sweating”. These days, she’s too busy enjoying herself a la Kim Cattrall to be constantly bracing for the worst. “Life is actually quite fun, but we all torture ourselves over the agony of what could be.”Practical Magic 2 is out in cinemas on 11 September.Explore more on these topicsMaisie WilliamsGame of ThronesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It leaves holes inside of you’: graphic novel aims to remember the history and horror of genocide | Comics and graphic novels | The Guardian
description: Dana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to Palestine
Author: David Smith
Headline: Dana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to Palestine
Content: An image from Dana Mashoian Walrath’s studio.Photograph: Dana WalrathView image in fullscreenAn image from Dana Mashoian Walrath’s studio.Photograph: Dana WalrathComics and graphic novels‘It leaves holes inside of you’: graphic novel aims to remember the history and horror of genocideDana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to PalestineDavid Smithin WashingtonSun 6 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe artistDana Mashoian Walrath’snew book honours the Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust. But she also expects it to get her banned from Israel.That is becauseThe Book of Genocidesalso contains a chapter that portrays Palestinians forced to live as second-class citizens and watch their homes bulldozed or bombed. “What does it mean to be starved?” the narrative asks. “To know that perpetrators have themselves experienced genocide and now commit genocide against you?”‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to GazaRead moreThere are many more questions posed by Walrath’s graphic history, which is quite unlike any other book about humanity’s periodic descents into the abyss of mass extermination and ethnic cleansing over the past five centuries.In an experimental blend of anthropology, memoir and visual art, which encourages readers to cut the pages and create three-part interactive figures, she offers 10 case studies ranging from the killing of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and theenslavement of Africansto the Armenian genocide, Holocaust, Cambodia, Rwanda, Bosnia, Palestine and the persecution of the Rohingya.Walrath, 66, an artist, writer and anthropologist, travelled to all 10 places represented in the book and has a personal connection with genocide. She is Armenian-American, the granddaughter of survivors who fledthe systematic destructionof the Ottoman empire’s Armenian population during the first world war. For decades, her family’s survival story was condensed into a single narrative fragment.When she asked her mother about her own mother’s childhood in western Armenia,she replied: “After her parents were killed, she hid during the day and ran at night with Uncle Benny and Aunt Alice from their home in Palu to the orphanage in Aleppo.”It was only recently that deeper, more horrifying layers of that journey were revealed. When her mother, Alice, was diagnosed with dementia and moved into her home, Walrath took a leave of absence from her academic career to engage in full-time creative work, eventually publishing a verse novel about the Armenian genocide, Like Water on Stone.View image in fullscreenThe Genocide of Black Americans.Photograph: Harvard University Press“After that novel came out my older relatives started telling me more details of what happened,” Walrath says from her studio near Burlington in Vermont, adorned with towering draft pages of The Book of Genocides and a monumental portrait of her mother. “I did not know about my grandmother hiding in an urn while her father was dismembered until about five years ago.“She was taken into enslavement with her son. I also learned that my grandmother, at one point probably after sex, hit her enslaver on the head with a stone and the two of them fled. This is what my aunt told me. Can I verify it? Can I find these facts? I don’t know.”This inheritance of violence and survival has haunted Walrath’s life and given her a personal connection to genocide, wherever it happens. She reflects: “It’s knowing what it does to people and knowing how it leaves holes inside of you and that you have to figure out how to overcome the desire to get even.“You have to figure out how to transform the anger and the hurt into something productive and I feel like I’ve spent much of my adult life trying to figure out how to do that. Writing the novel let me exorcise a lot of demons and then writing this book was so gratifying because I could literally bring people together.”Walrath committed herself to traveling to every location depicted in the book, seeking out survivors and descendants to sit with them in their grief. She spoke with survivors ofPol Pot’s killing fields in Phnom Penh, met with perpetrators and survivors of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and visited Rohingya refugees in the sprawling camps of Bangladesh.This deep exposure to human suffering took a severe toll on her physical health. The 66-year-old recalls via Zoom: “I got physically sick at various times and it would usually take the form of a terrible chest cold. Grief is supposed to live in the lungs and I got very sick after Auschwitz. I got very sick in 2013 when I crossed into the West Bank through the wall to go to Bethlehem with a bunch of Armenian pilgrims.”View image in fullscreenDana Mashoian Walrath in her studioPhotograph: Harvard University Press“I remember right after I came back from Auschwitz I was reading [Polish lawyer and Holocaust scholar]Raphael Lemkin’s autobiography. It starts out great and then he comes unravelled in the last couple of chapters. I had a spell where I was thinking, oh no, what if I lose my mind?“Then I went through no, no, I have very good supports and live in nature and, at this moment in time, as America is well on its way into a very scary place, I felt like I could get up every morning and have something concrete to do to push back. When I reread the book recently it was even more shocking how many elements of USA 2026 are present in all these genocides.”To convey these heavy histories, Walrath turned to a medium distinctively suited to representing the unrepresentable: comics. In the tradition ofArt Spiegelman’sMaus andJoe Sacco’sPalestine, The Book of Genocides uses the graphic form to bridge the gap between abstract history and raw empathy.“Comics are very active. I love cinema and it’s a very powerful medium for learning about things that might be outside of your experience but it is passive. You sit in your seat and you take it in. Comics are probably closer to cinema than anything else but they’re active. They’re created by a series of fragments that the reader has to take in and process and put together in an active way and because of that it gave me a vocabulary to talk about these horrors without making people run away from them.”Walrath deliberately avoided drawing explicit, realistic acts of violence, opting instead for metaphorical representations. “I left out drawing most of the horror and was always walking the line between making sure the image was gonna draw people in, even if it was talking about something horrible,” she says.The book’s unsettling interactive design aims to force readers to confront the systemic patterns of dehumanisation that make such horrors possible. Readers are invited to cut certain portrait pages into thirds, creating a “turn-the-flap” sequence – a structural device reminiscent of the surrealist game of “exquisite corpse”. As the reader flips the segmented pages, the illustrated human subjects transform back and forth between recognisable faces and non-human creatures – beasts, predators, vermin and parasites.View image in fullscreenThe Palestinian Genocide.Photograph: Harvard University PressFor Walrath, this physical interaction is not a gimmick but an exercise in moral philosophy. She explains:“I wanted people to try and get inside the mind of someone else and also to make it so that they would feel their potential complicity. Have I always spoken up when I’ve heard somebody call someone else a monster? Have I always spoken up if someone is called a parasite? I don’t know. A lot of times we let things slide.“We’ve invited people to cut the pages to get people thinking about how we’re taught: what’s allowed and what isn’t allowed. We’re not supposed to desecrate books. We love books and yet we’re taught that war is OK, that it’s OK to kill other people. I wanted it there in an interactive, metaphorical but also subconscious way, rather than saying, this is what we do. People take it in differently when they’re interacting with it.”The Book of Genocides relies on the concept of genocide developed by Lemkin and enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention: ‘acts committed with the intent to destroy in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group” and marked by a process of dehumanisation of the targeted group.As an anthropologist, Walrath finds a common thread running through half a millennium of genocidal violence. She argues that they are often less spontaneous outbursts of tribal hatred than highly planned, bureaucratic operations, with material interests – particularly land – playing a central role.“Land theft almost always. The only exception is not really an exception; it’s enslavement. The Europeans stole Africa but then also stole African people and then put them into thetransatlantic slave tradeso, even though the land stealing was going on within the Americas, it was dependent upon European colonisation. Settler colonialism is nearly always there.“Dehumanisation is part of that and then systemic injustices within the societies. These are precursors to massacre. What’s the difference between prisons in the US and many other countries where strictly disenfranchised people are the majority of the prisoners, andthe Warsaw Ghetto?”Perhaps the most controversial decision in The Book of Genocides is its chapter that addresses the history of Palestinian displacement and the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks andIsrael’s subsequent war in Gaza. The inclusion of Palestine underthe banner of genocideis a move that Walrath knew would draw fierce criticism and potentially severe professional consequences.View image in fullscreenDana Mashoian Walrath in her studio.Photograph: Harvard University Press“I decided that was the right thing to do because the goal of the book is to spark conversations, to put it out there, to talk about Palestine, call it a genocide, and let people start speaking with each other about it.“It would be great for someone to try and say why it is and isn’t genocide, and at the same time. I think that the way I’ve employed the term is aligned with Raphael Lemkin’s intention about what genocide was. It’s aligned with the convention, withthe Rome statute, and what we’re watching is political machinations making the convention useless.”Walrath adds: “Indiscriminate bombing of any place is a war crime for sure. When we’re killing babies and killing children and keeping people from healthcare and selectively bombing hospitals and journalists, I have no doubt in my mind that this is a systemic attempt to eliminate a people.”She is clear-eyed about the fallout of this stance in Israel. “I probably won’t be allowed to visit again, which would be sad because I have respect for the real peace activists there. Honestly, going to Jerusalem as an Armenian was incredibly powerful. But maybe this will change and in my lifetime maybe I’ll live long enough that I will be able to go back but I know right now after this book comes out I will no longer be able to arrive at the airport.”Despite the harrowing terrain of her subject matter, Walrath remains fundamentally an optimist. She rejects the jaundiced view that human violence is an evolutionary inevitability. “I am sure that’s not true. I am sure that we’re hardwired to care for one another. Every time we see dehumanisation get undone in the midst of a war it’s because someone’s heart has been touched.“It’s governments that perpetrate genocides and it’s baked into our systems and structures and because those systems and structures and governments are all human-made creations, we can make better ones. A rugged as the content is, the message is an underlying message of hope and that we can change this. It’s not inevitable.”The Book of Genocides is out on 8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsComics and graphic novelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herself | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: The Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in music
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: The Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in music
Content: ‘It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.’Photograph: Roam ArtistsView image in fullscreen‘It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.’Photograph: Roam ArtistsBlack US culture‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herselfThe Infinity Song artist is embracing uncertainty as she launches her solo career, while challenging the assumptions placed on Black women in musicMorgan JerkinsSun 6 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be, but at the same time enjoying the fact that there’s nowhere I’m supposed to be.” This admission might seem like the beginning of an existential crisis, but it’s a welcome, liminal space for the rising singer and songwriter Momo Boyd. Between her recently released debut EP, a second EP in the works, and two tours, the 27-year-old is being pulled in many directions. But she’s also enjoying the emotionally ambiguous position she’s currently in – it’s what characterizes much of her work.Boyd, who’s a part of Infinity Song, a pop rock sibling quintet that debuted in 2015, confesses that she’s nervous about striking out on her own as a solo artist. The demands are high: Her debut MissMichigantour just finished its US leg this past August and she will continue on throughout Europe in the fall, with a stop in London in November. She said that in comparison to Infinity Song’s sound, which can be characterized by guitar-driven melodies full of romanticism. “I’m doing my own thing and it’s a bit folksy, emotional and personal.” One might expect that Boyd being both a solo artist and an ensemble group member means that she runs the risk of producing indistinguishable bodies of work. But her moodier sound could not be more different from the family band’s more optimistic tunes. Nevertheless, the young singer is quick to say that the balance between the two lanes has been “pretty easy”.The challenge so far has been trusting herself to explore different sounds in an industry where Black women’s artistry is often flattened into categories. The alternative and indie rock artist Santigoldspoke about the industry’s narrow view of “Black music”during her 2022 Tiny Desk performance, and theGrammy award-winning artist SZA once saidthat her own music was only categorized as R&B because she’s Black. Being Black, female and gifted is often accompanied with being misunderstood–a consequence that Boyd has learned early on in her career.View image in fullscreen‘I’m doing my own thing and it’s a bit folksy, emotional and personal.’Photograph: Jakubaszek/RedfernsHer musical origins began with her father, John Boyd, who started multiple choirs in Michigan, where the family is from, so that the younger people of their community would have an activity after school. By the time Momo was seven, her family relocated from the midwest to the north-east. While going to school in the Bronx, Boyd recalled, a blonde-haired, blue-eyed girl said to the singer: “Where you from? You talk like a white girl.” The comment made Boyd acutely aware of the cultural shift from her slower, midwestern roots to a faster, city life. The suspicion that she was cosplaying whiteness would resurface years later when she released her debut single, American Love Song.Boyd’s melancholic, haunting voice about an ill-fated romance in American Love Song has made some listeners call her the BlackLana Del Rey, which Boyd considers a compliment. “She’s so emotionally interesting,” Boyd says about Del Rey. “I was drawn to her.” Boyd said that working through her own deep-seated sadness has allowed her to protect her inner child and to present herself to the world with intentionality and sensitivity. As the seventh of nine children who, Boyd said, didn’t get much attention growing up, she spent a lot of her formative years experiencing anxiety and temperamental attitudes. She decided to channel those feelings from childhood into her music.After high school, Boyd chose not to attend college and remained at home with her parents, where she learned and practiced the guitar and bass for hours daily. She describes the isolation of that period as “tough” but crucial. When Infinity Song’s Hater’s Anthem, a quirky, acoustic number about jealousy and prideful laziness, went viral in 2023, her family knew that their dedication came full circle. “We always knew something would happen,” Boyd said. “We were feeling a bit discouraged and very unsure. Around that time we were just coming together to see what could happen.”View image in fullscreenMomo Boyd of Infinity Song performs during the Boston Calling music festival at Harvard Athletic Complex on 23 May 2025.Photograph: Astrida Valigorsky/Getty ImagesThough Infinity Song has developed a cult following as a group, each member intends to go solo. So when Boyd released Miss Michigan in April, her siblings were in full support of her endeavors. Boyd’s velvety vocals float over the seven tracks as she processes her self-doubt, avoidant tendencies and lovelorn experiences. Fader called hervoice “moisturized”and The Sourcecalled Miss Michigan “reflective and deeply personal”.This emotional interiority of her music manifests through the visuals for the aforementioned American Love Song, where Boyd sings about the inability to love due to being too “independent” and “American” for commitment. The music video captures Boyd with a delicate touch that complements her soft vocals. She is introduced wearing two-tone chaps-style denim jeans as she pets a horse and stares off into the distance. The fashion is pure rockabilly and Americana – her softly coiffed curly hair, the fit-and-flare silhouettes, a vintage style wedding gown, and an American flag sweater.Boyd alternates between playing the guitar amidst wild grass and brush and running through an open pasture. The ease that Boyd exudes as she frolics through a pastoral landscape might seem incongruent to how such settings, which recall plantations and fields, would have been the historical sites of violence against Black people. “People were assuming that I was catering to a white audience. They were questioning my right to make a song on Americanism because of my race. For it to be twisted as if I’m sinister or an agent of propaganda, when I tell you–” Her voice trails off before continuing. “Sometimes I’m like, should I even bring it up?”The truth, Boyd said, is that American Love Song is not propaganda or even a product of her own imagination. It was her life. Boyd lived with her large family in Shay Lake,a rural oasis for working class and upwardly mobile Black peopleseeking rest away from their homes in Detroit and Flint. Her home was the renovated lobby of an old motel with huge pine trees wrapped around the entrance. She reminisced on her family’s crabapple tree, picnics and bonfires, the small Black church her family frequented, and the countless stars that illuminated the evening skies. “This is where my home is. Do I not exist? Is this not where my family has put in all these hours of work? It’s just the truth. But the truth was controversial.”View image in fullscreen‘This is where my home is. Do I not exist? Is this not where my family has put in all these hours of work? It’s just the truth. But the truth was controversial.’Photograph: Jeremychanphotography/Getty ImagesBoyd operates within a tradition of Black female artists who dare to center their experiences as integral to the American landscape as anyone else’s.In 2016,Beyoncé performed with The Dixie Chicks at the Country Music Awards and online communities argued whether or not she belonged in the genre. Despite her 2024 album Cowboy Carter topping the Billboard charts,she received no CMA nominations.In 2020, Mickey Guyton triggered a shockwave throughout the country music scene withBlack Like Me,a song that addressed systemic racism in the industry. Country music star Tanner Adellspoke about the underrepresentationof Black women in her genre and staked her claim as a glamorous Black woman of the south with her song, Buckle Bunny. Adell toldGrammy.com:“We, as Black women, have been fighting our whole lives. We’ve been fighting for space. I’m purposely trying to bring softness into the picture.”Although Boyd emphasizes that she doesn’t want to over-intellectualize her music, her sound and aesthetic choices are inherently political. “I had some not so pretty experiences in high school with colorism–how you’re perceived, how you’re ranked on the scale of desirability, and whether or not you’re seen. It lowkey radicalized me … My goal is to be a representation for Black women who desire freedom.”Freedom, to her, is the refusal to allow the fear of failure to eclipse one’s courage and the ability to be one’s self. When Boyd created She’s a Sweetheart, a tongue-in-cheek song about a woman who’s too accessible to others, she said she wanted to create a world where Black women were the moment and nothing else existed besides those who looked like her. Despite once feeling invisible because of the color of her skin, Boyd professes that she’s always been a lover of beauty and feminine archetypes. She’s a devotee of classic rom-coms like Love Jones, Brown Sugar, and Pretty Woman. She loves the effortlessness of women from the 1970s and 1990s. And though her wide-ranging interests may confuse some people, Boyd enjoys the variety. “It takes a lot of work to have gratitude and peace. I have done a lot of work to protect my heart and who I am at the core and maintain this joy.”Explore more on these topicsBlack US cultureMichiganPop and rockBeyoncéLana Del ReyprofilesShareReuse this content

title: King Lear review – Ian McDiarmid is a titanic, heartbreaking wonder | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive production
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive production
Content: From emperor to king … Ian McDiarmid as Lear at the Crucible theatre.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenFrom emperor to king … Ian McDiarmid as Lear at the Crucible theatre.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewKing Lear review – Ian McDiarmid is a titanic, heartbreaking wonderCrucible theatre, SheffieldThe 82-year-old actor gives a performance of absolute authenticity and clarity as the erratic demagogue in a uniformly impressive productionMark LawsonSun 6 Sep 2026 08.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “nothing” is spoken four times in four lines in the opening scene of King Lear, among 30 uses across the play. This feels the key to Titus Halder’s Sheffield Crucible staging, which really makes something of nothingness, crowned by an unusually age-appropriate performer as the “fourscore and upward” English king: 82-year-oldIan McDiarmid.The dark pit of Richard Kent’s design might be a nuclear after-blast. Like Peter Brook’s mid 20th-century stage and film versions, in a previous era of existentialist international tension, the interpretation radiates terminal uncertainty. Characters address pleas and prayers to “the gods” in the direction identified with heaven but with a growing knowing that nothing is there.It is also clear that the kingdom Lear ruinously tries to divide between his three daughters is already past its rule-by date, probably due to his eccentric leadership. In a moment of apparent clarity during his mental decline, Lear says, “I will be jovial”, and this often unremarked line seems the base note to McDiarmid’s titanic performance.View image in fullscreenFode Simbo as Edmund and Katie Wimpenny as Goneril.Photograph: Johan PerssonGiggling dirtily when speculating about his daughters having “issue”, he grins manically out of sync with situations. His threat to inflict “terrors” on the world even though he “does not know yet” what they are is not, as often, the forgetfulness of dementia but political bullshitting that wins a knowing laugh from the audience. Leaving his court unsure what he will say or do next, the erratic head of state is also transactional, giving real chill to the dismissal of the banished Cordelia: “Her price has fallen.”But, while it might be no surprise if this Lear suddenly imposed tariffs on France, the portrait of power is much broader: this demagogue, unfashionably, admits fault and reaches forgiveness.The acting paradox of Lear is that the textual extreme physical frailty must co-exist with the ability to carry Cordelia’s corpse and the vocal depth to serve the dense poetry. Because of this, middle-aged actors are often cast.View image in fullscreenSimbo as Edmund with Harry Redding as Edgar.Photograph: Johan PerssonWhile birth-date realism raises obvious risks, McDiarmid perfectly combines bodily authenticity (the problem of transporting the dead daughter cleverly sidestepped) with absolute verbal clarity on the required range from explosion to self-reflective emotion. When Lear’s heart broke, so did mine.Fool – also seemingly a chief of staff cum carer to Lear – is Max Revell, a dancer with a background in breaking and popping. The result is a spectacularly gymnastic Fool, backflipped by the storm winds and illustrating the jester’s metaphor about a crab by twisting himself into one. Dramaturg Sophie Duncan’s skilled elision of variant texts emphasises Edmund, played by Fode Simbo with a manipulative charisma suggesting Gloucester’s bastard son as a cousin of Iago in Othello. Bebe Sanders’ dignified, wounded Cordelia highlights the bravery of this character in the dramatic scheme. Mark Holgate is powerful as a site-specific Yorkshire Kent.The production is uniformly impressive but the wonder is McDiarmid, topping a remarkable career that combines a popular culture summit – Emperor Palpatine in the Star Wars movie franchise – with, now, this classical peak.At theCrucible theatre, Sheffield, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWilliam ShakespeareIan McDiarmidreviewsShareReuse this content
