title: TV tonight: laughter and horror in a dark new Aussie crime comedy  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Fans of Guilt will enjoy this thriller about two siblings who accidentally kill a man. Plus: more claustrophobic action in Vigil. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Fans of Guilt will enjoy this thriller about two siblings who accidentally kill a man. Plus: more claustrophobic action in Vigil. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Risky business … Reckless on ITV1.Photograph: SBSView image in fullscreenRisky business … Reckless on ITV1.Photograph: SBSTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: laughter and horror in a dark new Aussie crime comedyFans of Guilt will enjoy this thriller about two siblings who accidentally kill a man. Plus: more claustrophobic action in Vigil. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellSun 6 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReckless10.15pm, ITV1The cover-up is always riskier than the crime. This darkly comic Australian thriller is loosely based on the excellent BBC drama Guilt and involves a pair of bickering siblings who accidentally run over and kill a man. Cue a slow-motion meltdown as the perps flee the scene, the police sit on their hands and the victim’s niece decides to investigate. A convincing balance of laughter and horror.Phil HarrisonAmerican Classics at the Proms6pm, BBC TwoUS conductor Marin Alsop marshals a rousing selection of 20th-century favourites, with numbers from West Side Story and On the Town bringing urban clatter, while excerpts from Aaron Copland’s ballet Appalachian Spring and Jerome Moross’s soundtrack to The Big Country take us into America’s wide open spaces.Jack SealeVigil9pm, BBC OneMore claustrophobic thriller action in the Arctic Circle. Rose Leslie’s Kirsten has annoyed the Russians but, fortunately, the cavalry is on the way in the shape of her formidable other half, Amy (Suranne Jones). But the more Amy digs, the murkier the circumstances around Hodge’s murder seem. Are they looking in the right place?PHTrigger Point9pm, ITV1A precision-tooled terror campaign by enemies unknown has turned London into a literal boom town. Stressed bomb disposal officer Wash (Vicky McClure) is about ready to blow her top. Will chasing down a surprise lead get her team off the back foot? Or is it all part of a sinister master plan? Continues on Monday.Graeme Virtue24 Hours in Police Custody: The Ambush9pm, Channel 4The disturbing case, which began last week, concludes as police continue to investigate the circumstances that left a 17-year-old boy with potentially fatal head injuries. As the young man fights for his life, the officers follow a trail of evidence that leads them to a territorial dispute between two drug gangs. Bleak.PHThe Terror: Devil in Silver9pm, Sky AtlanticThe unsettling horror anthology wraps up its third season with a double bill. In a shabby psychiatric hospital, Iron Maiden-loving inmate Pepper (Dan Stevens) is girding himself to take down an insidious demon. But before that we get the tragic backstory of Dorry (Judith Light), the facility’s longest-serving patient.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceSteel Magnolias, 6.40pm, Film4View image in fullscreenIconic … Dolly Parton in Steel Magnolias on Film4.Photograph: Zade Rosenthal/Tri-Star/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockA double-bill tribute to the late Dolly Parton includes Seriously Red, a romcom about a Dolly impersonator, but the real McCoy is here in Herbert Ross’s 1989 weepie. The drama revolves round a Louisiana beauty parlour run by Parton’s plain-talking Truvy, where a group of close female friends gather to gossip, mark major life changes and set the world to rights. The prime movers are Julia Roberts as bride-to-be Shelby and Sally Field as her mother M’Lynn, but Shirley MacLaine sweeps all before her as the gloriously sour Ouiser (try saying it out loud).Simon WardellLive sportPremier League Football: Everton v Man United, 1pm, Sky Sports Main EventArsenal v Chelsea follows at 4pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe | City breaks | The Guardian
description: From the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspots
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspots
Content: The Grand Éléphant takes a stroll past the Jules Verne-inspired carousel in Nantes.Photograph: Olrat/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Grand Éléphant takes a stroll past the Jules Verne-inspired carousel in Nantes.Photograph: Olrat/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.City breaks‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in EuropeFrom the Renaissance treasures of Parma to offbeat creativity in Nantes, these cities offer world-class art, great food and a laid-back alternative to Europe’s hotspotsSun 6 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNantes, FranceAs dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on theCarrousel des Mondes Marins(marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun.On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project,Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks.double quotation markJules Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art project that has breathed life into the abandoned docksThis is now the stomping ground of theGrand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearbyGalerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life.View image in fullscreenThéo Mercier’s ‘Fossil Opera’, one of the temporary art installations of Le Voyage à Nantes 2026 festival.Photograph: Martin ArgyrogloThe Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival,Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegantGraslin districtare busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste.Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserieLa Cigaleweave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. TitledFossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic.Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, fromLes Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’sBelvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff.View image in fullscreenLa Cigale, an art nouveau brasserie on Place Graslin.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyAll of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by theLigne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through thePassage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposingChâteau des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellentMusée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peacefulJardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to theLieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits.And there’s more to come.The Jardin Extraordinaireis a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and theLittle Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, theCité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve.Joanne O’ConnorThe trip was supported byLe Voyage à Nantes.OceaniaHôtelde France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioneddoubles from€101room-onlyWinter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January.Basel, SwitzerlandView image in fullscreenSwimmers in the Rhine beside Basel Cathedral.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyUnless you’re a professional who makes their way to theArt Basel fairevery year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend.Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine.double quotation markBasel bills itself as ‘the city of art and culture on the Rhine’, and it lives up to its boastOnce you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, theKunstmuseumholds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, whileMuseum Tinguelyis home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines.But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city.Fondation Beyelerin the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currentlyPierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein istheVitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design.View image in fullscreenMiniatures of designer chairs at the Vitra Design Museum near Basel.Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyBefore you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; theVitra Schaudepot– which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’sformer fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is abeautiful gardenbythe Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently addedDoshi Retreatfor a moment of quiet reflection designed by theIndian architectBalkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023.That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch.Max BenatoTheVolkshaus, aboutique hotel in the old town, hasdoubles from152swiss francs (£138)room-onlyLübeck, GermanyView image in fullscreenThe ‘wonky’ Holsten Gate in Lübeck.Photograph: SW Travel Imagery/AlamyUnless you’ve readBuddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem.The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired anelectric boat(€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires.Back on dry land, we set off on a guidedwalking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky –Holsten Gate. We took in thefive red brick churchesthe spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them,St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-oldtown hallon the marketplace.But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hiddenalleyways and courtyardsthreaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore.double quotation markBehind the gothic splendour is a labyrinth of flower-filled, cobbled alleys to exploreTo better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited theEuropean Hansemuseumin the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937.In a nearby palace, theMuseum Behnhaus Drägerhausdisplays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted itssalt warehouses. Just round the corner is theGünter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015).We visited in June during theHanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annualmuseum, theatre and literature nights, andpopup live musicin the summer.Lübeck has three naturalopen-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip toTravemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back.View image in fullscreenThe old town of  Lübeck is encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz.Photograph: Acnakelsy/Getty Images/iStockphotoIn town, the medievalSchiffergesellschaft(Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions oflabskaus, a sort of hash.Sadly, we couldn’t visitBuddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort.Rachel DixonThe trip was provided bygermany.travelandluebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided byLiho Lübeck, doubles from £73room-onlyParma, ItalyView image in fullscreenParma Cathedral and the octagonal baptistery.Photograph: Peter Adams/Getty ImagesParma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordabletrattorieandosterieshowcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimateTeatro Regio.The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesquecathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothicBattistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medievalMonastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free.double quotation markAppreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Tintoretto and Canaletto without being surrounded by crowdsParma’s big must-see is the monumentalPalazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. TheTeatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmarkGalleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds.View image in fullscreenAntonio Correggio’s Assunzione della Virgine in the cupola of Parma’s Duomo.Photograph: Gordon Sinclair/AlamySightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking intotagliere– wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famousprosciuttocrudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect.This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such asDa Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen thecucinafor more than 50 years, or the 120-year-oldTrattoria Corrieri,serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15.John BruntonPalazzo Dalla Rosa Pratihas doublesfrom€80room-onlySantander, SpainView image in fullscreenEl Sardinero beach, Santander.Photograph: Miguel Moya/AlamyOften dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map.Leading the way on 8 September isFaro Santander– a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times.double quotation markThere’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedralWith its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architectDavid Chipperfield.Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house theArchivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America.Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017Centro Botíncontemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half.View image in fullscreenRenzo Piano’s Centro Botin.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamySpaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeledMadrileñosdiscovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre.The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazasand narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars servingpinchos– the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas.After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, atMesón Rampalayon a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours atMupac– the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander.The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too.Eddi FiegelThe trip was provided by Faro Santander.Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín,has stylish doubles from€66room-onlyExplore more on these topicsCity breaksEurope holidaysWeekend breaksItaly holidaysSpain holidaysSwitzerland holidaysGermany holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry – recipe | Curry | The Guardian
description: There are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation of kukul mas bears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavours
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: There are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation of kukul mas bears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavours
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfecct Sri Lankan chicken curry.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfecct Sri Lankan chicken curry.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.How to cook the perfect ...CurryHow to make the perfect Sri Lankan chicken curry – recipeThere are as many variations are there are cooks, but every interpretation ofkukul masbears the country’s classic bold aromatics and adrenaline-pumping flavoursFelicity CloakeSun 6 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Every family in our sunny little island craves this creamy chicken,”says Sri Lankan journalist Zinara Rathnayake, “devouring each morsel with carbs of choice: string hoppers, thin rice noodle mats; hoppers, bowl-shaped pancakes; andkiribath, slender rice cooked with coconut milk. All our family recipes may slightly vary, but this glorious dish pins down the labour and love that goes into every Sri Lankan curry.”After all, Sri Lanka is a country that’s “rich in spices”, chef Peter Kuruvita explains. “Most Sri Lankan cooking,” he writes inLands of the Curry Leaf, “features unapologetically punch-you-in-the-face, get-the-adrenaline-pumping flavours. But [in part thanks to tropical crops such as coconut, lemongrass and pandan leaf] the heat is more an intensity of spice than actual physical ‘chilli heat’.” Boldly aromatic rather than delicately fragrant, rich and light at the same time,kukul mas, whichSH Fernando Jr’s book Rice & Currycalls “a mainstay of Sri Lankan cuisine”, is surprisingly quick to make once you’ve prepared, or bought, the spice blend, yet it tastes as if it’s been simmering for hours.The meatView image in fullscreen‘Unapologetically punch-you-in-the-face’ spices: SH Fernando Jr’s Sri Lankan chicken curry. All thumbnail photographs by Felicity Cloake.“Choosing a chicken is a fine art,” Kuruvita writes inhis book Serendip, “and there are two types: a curry chicken and a broiler … The chickens were always sold skinless, as it was a lot quicker for the men to rip the feathers off with the skin rather than to pluck them. The meat was cut up for us and placed in a large ‘elephant ears’ leaf. When we got home, all we had to do was add the spices and cook the curry.” Most recipes indeed call for whole chickens, cut up on the bone – a good cleaver should make this easy, or, if you’re buying from a butcher, they’ll do this for you even quicker. That said, I’m withFernando, who writes: “I use thighs with the bone in when I make this dish as breast meat tends to dry out.” If, likeKaran Gokani of Hoppers, you use thigh fillets, you may wish, as he does, to replace the water with chicken stock; I also favour removing the skin, but that’s up to you.The marinadeMany recipes, as Kuruvita notes, simply add the chicken to the pot as it is, but Gokani, Kuruvita andJeffrey Alford and Naomi Duguid in their book Mangoes & Curry Leavesall marinate the meat first: Gokani in ginger, garlic, turmeric, curry powder and salt; Kuruvita in vinegar and curry powder; and Alford and Duguid in curry powder and garlic. Though all the curries taste great, the marinated chicken comes out a clear winner with my testers and I, “because it seems to marry better with the sauce”. If you’ve bought, or already made your curry powder, there’s no need to delay cooking for too long, but it’s well worth blending it while you prepare the rest of the dish, or indeed if you want to get ahead.The baseAll the curries I try are based on onions in some form. Alford and Duguid go for shallots and Rathnayake red onion, both of which mirror the smaller, sweeter and fierier pink onions used in Sri Lanka. Everyone also adds garlic, and ginger is fairly common, too, a combination that echoes the sweet heat of the onions. Kuruvita’s is the only curry not to include tomatoes – fresh in most cases, though Fernando stirs in tomato paste in the end – which feels a shame, because they add a pleasantly fruity note to the sauce.View image in fullscreenZinara Rathnayake’s ‘emblematic’ Sri Lankan chicken curry.Curry leaves are almost mandatory – only Alford and Duguid leave them out – and I can’t resist the transporting perfume of lemongrass and pandan leaves. The latter, long green leaves sometimes referred to as screwpine, though they has nothing to do with the pine family, can usually be found in the freezer section at south-east Asian food specialists. If you can’t track any down, leave them out, but I adore their haunting flavour that, to me, combines toasty notes of dulce de leche with a grassy freshness; they also make incredible desserts.This sweet, zesty freshness can be underlined with a cinnamon stick and some cardamom pods (some recipes also add cloves), with chilli powder and fresh green chillies bringing the heat (though Fernando adds cayenne pepper and Kuruvita black mustard seeds). Many of these spices are also present in the roasted curry powder that’s the backbone of the dish, so adding a little extra during cooking simply nudges them a little higher in the overall flavour profile.The roasted curry powderIn Sri Lanka, Fernando explains, “spices are usually bought whole, raw and in bulk. They are dried out in the sun in hand-woven palm frond baskets before roasting and grinding.” Using ready-made blends, he suggests, is like swapping freshly ground beans for instant coffee – though Rathnayake, whose mother’s recipe is featured on the website of Kolamba, a Sri Lankan restaurant in London’s Soho, suggests that the stuff sold in Sri Lankan supermarkets (it may be labelled “meat curry powder”) is perfectly acceptable. If you don’t already have an arsenal of individual spices at your disposal, you may well find this the most convenient option.View image in fullscreenCashews add a sweet nuttiness to Jeffrey Alford and Naomi Duguid’s Sri Lankan chicken curry.If you have a wealth of spices to hand, however, it’s really not hard to make the roasted powder that’s usually paired with meat dishes, which, in this survey at least, always contains coriander, cumin, fenugreek, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, pandan and curry leaves, and often turmeric, fennel, black pepper and mustard seeds as well.There’s usually some toasted rice in there, too; not only, Gokani explains, for its nutty flavour, but to act as a thickener, though Kuruvita also includes a thickening powder made from extra rice, desiccated coconut and more spices, which gives his sauce considerably more body than many of the others. Alford and Duguid add cashew nuts on top, which supply a sweet nuttiness, while Kuruvita calls for a startling number of dried chillies, which may be something to consider if you find you’d like a little more fire. I’ve based my curry on the Hoppers version, because I like its sweet, peppery warmth, but, as with all such blends, I suspect there’s a lot of room for tinkering around the edges, particularly heat-wise.Liquid and cookingThe gravy is usually diluted with a mixture of coconut milk and water, though Kuruvita, who includes solid coconut in his thickening powder and tips in an unusual amount of oil, doesn’t bother with the milk. If, as mentioned earlier, you’re using boneless chicken, I’d recommend replacing the water with good, jellied chicken stock.View image in fullscreenPeter Kuruvita’s Sri Lankan chicken curry ‘uses an unusual amount of oil’.Cooking the onions until they’re soft and sweet is vital, but there’s no real need to fry most of the spices here, because they’ve already been toasted.Chickenon the bone takes some time to cook through, so most recipes cover the pan and leave it to simmer gently for 30-40 minutes; bear in mind that the coconut milk will split and separate during this time, but it will still taste just as good as it did when it was emulsified. If you’d prefer a thicker gravy, by all means reduce it further after removing the meat, or thicken by stirring in some extra ground rice mixed with a little water to make a paste.ServingGokani recommends serving this curry with rice or bread, plus a freshsambol, or turning it into akottu, a Sri Lankan favourite involving curry, chopped roti, eggs, onions and chillies (which is also a very good vehicle for leftovers, should you have any!)Perfect Sri Lankan chicken curryPrep35 minMarinate30 min+Cook50 minServes4-6For the roasted curry powder (or use 3 tbsp shop-bought Sri Lankan roasted curry/meat curry powder)4g green cardamom pods4 tbsp coriander seeds2 tsp cumin seeds1 tsp fennel seeds½ tsp fenugreek seeds¼ tsp black peppercorns2 cloves5g cinnamon stick8g rice3g fresh curry leaves(use a little less if you have only dried ones)5cm piecepandan leafFor the curry1 tbsp grated root ginger2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated1 tsp fine salt1 whole chicken, or 6 chicken legs or thighs, skinned, if you prefer, chopped into on-the-bone pieces2 tbsp coconut oil, or neutral oil1 red onion, peeled and thinly sliced2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced1 tbsp grated root ginger1 lemongrass stalk, trimmed and lightly bruised4 cardamom pods, squashed1 cinnamon stick1 tsp chilli powder½-1½ tsp roasted curry powder(see above and method), to taste1 sprigfresh curry leaves2 ripe plum tomatoes, roughly chopped2 green finger chillies10cm piecepandan leaf100ml coconut milkRice and a lime wedge, to serveRub the ginger, garlic and salt all over the chicken, then leave to marinate while you prepare the other ingredients (and for up to four hours).View image in fullscreenFor the curry powder, stir the dried spices in a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium heat until browned and aromatic, then tip out and leave to cool.View image in fullscreenToast the rice until lightly browned, add to the cooling spices, then toast the curry leaves and 5cm piece of pandan until they’ve dried out and add those to the mix, too.View image in fullscreenOnce everything is cool, put all the spices and rice in a blender or mortar, then whiz or pound to a powder.View image in fullscreenNow for the curry. Put the oil in a wide, heavy-based pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the onion for five or six minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic, ginger, lemongrass, cardamom, cinnamon and chilli powder, fry for a minute or so, then stir in the curry leaves and tomatoes and fry until the tomatoes soften.At this point, unless your pan is very large, you might find it easiest to scoop out the contents before you cook the chicken.View image in fullscreenToss three tablespoons of curry powder with the marinated chicken, then add to the pan with a little more oil, if necessary. Turn to coat, then, if necessary, return the tomato mix to the pan and add the chillies and 10cm piece of pandan leaf.View image in fullscreenMeasure out 200ml water, stir in a splash to help dislodge anything that’s stuck to the base of the pan, then pour in the rest of the water and bring to a simmer. Cover, turn down the heat and leave to cook for 15 minutes.Turn over the chicken pieces, stir in the coconut milk, cover the pan again and leave to cook for another 15 or so minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool slightly, then adjust the seasoning if required, just before serving with rice and perhaps a wedge of lime.How do you make yourkukul mas? Is this homely dish an emblem of Sri Lankan cuisine, as Zinara Rathnayake suggests, or would you make the case for something else entirely? And please, do share your recommendations for Sri Lankan restaurants around the world – I’d love to hear them.Explore more on these topicsCurryHow to cook the perfect ...FoodSri Lankan food and drinkChickenMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier life | Food | The Guardian
description: We all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshed
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: We all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshed
Content: Choosing the ideal diet can be a minefield, especially when you’re tired.Illustration: Moritz Wienert/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChoosing the ideal diet can be a minefield, especially when you’re tired.Illustration: Moritz Wienert/The GuardianFoodThe sleeping x eating secret: 15 ways to better rest, a healthier diet – and a happier lifeWe all know tiredness can lead to hunger, and vice versa. But there are so many other ways our habits in these areas are linked. Here are some easy tweaks to help us feel properly refreshedRachel DixonSun 6 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstudy published in the journal Nature Healthlast month found that food choices and meal timings have “immediate and measurable effects” on sleep. It was just the latest in a growing body of research into the link between diet and rest. Here is the latest science on what to eat for better sleep – and how sleep deprivation can affect your dinner the next day.What should I eat for a good night’s sleep?While there isn’t “a special sleep diet” that will guarantee eight undisturbed hours, a Mediterranean-style diet comes closest, says Dalhia Campbell, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for theBritish Dietetic Association. She describes it as “a balanced, varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, lean proteins and healthy fats to help stabilise energy and support the hormones involved in sleep”.Prof Marie-Pierre St-Onge is the director of theCenter of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Researchat Columbia University in New York, and the author ofEat Better, Sleep Better. Her research into“plant-forward” diets, includingthe Mediterranean diet, is investigating why they are beneficial for sleep. She says this could be due partly to the phytonutrients in plant foods, which have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds, and partly to nutrients that feed the gut microbiome and are involved in gut-brain communications. “That could play a role in improving sleep through helping people quiet their minds,” St-Onge says.Are there any specific sleep-promoting foods?View image in fullscreenGive kiwi fruit a try.Photograph: Flavia Morlachetti/Getty Images“It is best to look at your overall diet rather than focusing on one particular food,” says Campbell. “The latest UK diet and nutrition survey shows that fewer than 17% of adults meet the ‘five a day’ recommendation. Improving fruit and vegetable intake supports general healthandsleep.”But once you’ve nailed your five a day, are any fruit and veg better than others? “There’s quite a bit of research showing tomatoes, tropical fruits such as bananas and pineapples, and oranges have benefits for sleep,” says St-Onge. “Nuts and seeds, especially pistachios and walnuts, and wholegrains can contribute to better sleep as well.”Emerging studies show that kiwis may have some benefits, says Dr Sammie Gill, a senior nutrition scientist at theBritish Nutrition Foundation,but the evidence is limited so far. There is also early research into tart cherries: “A recentsystematic reviewindicated that consumption may help improve sleep duration, sleep efficiency or sleep onset time,” she says. “That said, the science remains limited and inconsistent.”Do I need more protein?View image in fullscreenGet your protein from a range of sources.Photograph: fcafotodigital/Getty ImagesDiets higher in protein have alsobeen associated with better sleep. “Proteins are important because they provide a source of tryptophan, which is essential for producing serotonin and melatonin, which are important for sleep,” says St-Onge. Tryptophan is one of the nine essential amino acids that your body can’t make on its own, so it has to come from your diet. All animal proteins and many plant proteins contain tryptophan. “In the US, people talk about turkey all the time, like, ‘That’s why you fall asleep at dinner on Thanksgiving,’” says St-Onge. “But food is not an instantaneous process – it’s not like you pop a pill and two hours later it gets to exactly where it needs to get.”If you do want to try tryptophan-maxxing, Gill says other sources are “dairy, eggs, fish, seafood, meat, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and legumes. Tryptophan-containing foodshave been linkedwith improved sleep outcomes – such as total sleep time and sleep efficiency – compared with controls.” So having a warm milky drink before bed makes sense? “There isn’t strong research showing thatwarm milk helps with sleep, but that shouldn’t stop you from having milk as a bedtime option,” says Gill.What foods will keep me awake?“Foods that are low in nutrients and high in fats and sugars are less likely to support good sleep,” Campbell advises.St-Onge conducted research on this topic in France. “We showed that people who consumed more ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of insomnia symptoms. We’ve also shown that women who consume foods that have a higher glycemic index – the types of foods that tend to raise your blood sugars to a greater extent than others – have a higher risk of developing insomnia.” According to Diabetes UK,high GI foodsinclude refined carbohydrates such as white bread, potatoes, doughnuts, bagels, sweets, sugar-sweetened breakfast cereals and sugar-sweetened drinks. As well as added sugars, St-Onge would avoid foods high in salt.Does caffeine help or hinder?View image in fullscreenCaffeine tolerance can decrease with age.Photograph: Curly_photo/Getty Images“Caffeine is a double-edged sword,” says Gill. “Plenty of studies have shown that caffeine in moderate doses [up to 400mg/four cups of coffee a day] can have a positive effect on cognitive performance, memory and alertness. But at higher doses, it can trigger anxiety, irritability and restlessness.”Four coffees may sound an awful lot to some. “The effects of caffeine vary from person to person – some people are more sensitive to its effects. How you respond to caffeine is partly determined by your genetics,” she says. But however much you drink, the main thing is to do so in the morning. “Caffeine has a quarter-life of around 10-12 hours, meaning that if you consume it at lunchtime, a quarter of the caffeine is still in your body close to midnight, which can disrupt sleep.” Cutting it out by lunch “can lead to noticeable improvements in sleep quality and quantity”.As you get older, you may find the after-dinner espresso you once enjoyed is now keeping you awake. “Your ability to metabolise caffeine changes as you age,” says St-Onge. “It’s important to keep track and evaluate every so often. If you’re starting to see that your sleep is changing, you might want to make adjustments related to intake of caffeine or timing of the last caffeinated beverage.”How about alcohol?View image in fullscreenAvoid ‘one for the road’ …Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesMany people think a drink or two helps them fall asleep – and they are right. But that doesn’t mean it’s a sleep aid. “Alcohol is a sedative – it does not prompt natural, ‘true’ sleep,” says Gill. “While it may help you fall asleep faster, it significantly disrupts the quality of your sleep. Alcohol, even in low amounts,reduces REM sleep, which is important for emotional processing and memory consolidation.”What’s more, “alcohol interacts with several neurotransmitters that are important in the regulation of sleep and can trigger awakenings during the night, which can make you feel tired the next day”. It can also make acid reflux worse, adds Campbell. So much for the trusty nightcap.How long should I leave between dinner and bed?View image in fullscreen… and the late-night cuppa.Photograph: Daniel de la Hoz/Getty Images“Studies have foundthat later meals are generally linked to lower-quality sleep,” says Gill. “A recent trialfound that eating dinner one hour before bedtime was linked with reduced sleep continuity and stability.” And you may find it harder to drop off in the first place, says Campbell, as your body is busy digesting your meal.St-Onge cautions that going to bed on a full stomach also increases your risk of heartburn and acid reflux. “As a general rule, wait two to three hours after a meal,” she says. If you already suffer from acid reflux,NHS adviceis to avoid food for up to four hours before bed. Beware of that late-night cuppa, too, says St-Onge: “If you’re drinking much too close to bedtime, you’ll need to wake up to use the bathroom.”But I hate going to bed hungry!“It’s OK to have a light snack after an early dinner if you’re feeling hungry – going to sleep on an empty stomach can disrupt sleep, too,” says Gill. “The key message is: don’t go to bed too full or too hungry.”“Choose a light, nutritious option such as yoghurt with fruit and nuts, or wholegrain toast with nut butter and banana,” says Campbell. “That’s better than grazing on biscuits and chocolate.”Why am I ravenous when I haven’t slept well?View image in fullscreenSugary cereal is tempting when you’re tired, but it’s not ideal.Photograph: Kinga Krzeminska/Getty ImagesThis is partly down to your body’s hunger signals. “Some research suggests that sleep loss can alter appetite hormones such as leptin [which signals fullness] and ghrelin [which stimulates appetite],” says Gill. “One study showedthat one night of inadequate sleep can increase ghrelin levels and decrease leptin levels.” As a result, “poor sleep is associated withincreases in energy intake, mainly from snacking, especially on foods higher in fat and carbohydrates.One review foundthat people who are sleep-deprived consume an average of 385 calories extra the following day compared with controls.”St-Onge’s research has found this hormone effect varies by sex: “Ghrelin tends to rise before a meal, signalling hunger. We’ve shown that it increases to a greater extent in men who haven’t had sufficient sleep.” In sleep-deprived women, on the other hand, leptin – “the satiety signal” – is suppressed. But the result is the same: overeating.It’s not just about ghrelin and leptin. “I always tell people that we don’t necessarily eat because we’re hungry, right? People have many reasons to eat, and eat despite lack of hunger,” says St-Onge. She says our brain reward centres are affected by how much sleep we’ve had the night before, and the “hedonic signals – the things that make food more appealing – tend to be more intense after a period of short sleep. So you’re more susceptible to reaching for appetising or pleasurable foods.” Who hasn’t chosen the pain au chocolat over the porridge after a bad night?Does this mean poor sleep will make me gain weight?In the long term, it certainlyincreases the likelihood. “Studies showthat people who regularly sleep less than six hours tend to gain more weight over time, and increasing sleep to seven or eight hours can help with appetite regulation,” says Campbell. As well as disrupted hunger hormones, there are a number of explanations. “Observational studies show those who don’t get enough sleep tend to eat less fruit and vegetables, more sugar, less protein and less fibre. Staying up late at night also means that you might get peckish and be more tempted to snack. And when tired, we may be less motivated to be active and to cook from scratch, relying more on quick, less nutritious foods and fizzy, sugary drinks.”Does the time I go to bed affect what I eat the next day?View image in fullscreenEarly birds may have it easier than night owls.Photograph: Flashpop/Getty Images“Most ofthe research focusis on chronotype [your body’s natural preference of when to sleep and wake] – if you have a late chronotype versus an earlier chronotype,” says St-Onge. So is it better to be an early bird or a night owl? “Typically, people with earlier chronotypes tend to have more healthful diets and exercise more,” she says. Plus, “people who have an earlier chronotype have an easier time getting adequate sleep duration because their sleep is more aligned with the societal clock”. Unfortunately for late risers, chronotypes are thought to be largely genetic.I do shift work – how can I eat and sleep well?“Shift workersreport less healthy dietscompared with day workers, andshift work is associatedwith increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes,” says Campbell. She suggests “eating the main meal before a night shift, and choosing lighter, nutrient-rich foods overnight”. This is easier said than done, says St-Onge. “It’s difficult because it’s a whole culture that needs to change – people tend to bring in treats to have in the middle of the night.”Should I take magnesium?View image in fullscreenSome studies show supplements help.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty Images“Try science-backed sleep strategies first, focusing on regularity, timing, temperature and lighting,” says Gill.Campbell agrees: “Rather than looking to supplements, it’s more helpful to look at the bigger picture. Take a look at sleep routine, stress levels, alcohol and caffeine intake, activity levels, and any underlying health issues that might be affecting rest, such as sleep apnoea, menopause symptoms or frequent night-time waking.”If you’ve sorted your diet, exercise, sleep hygiene and general health, however, there is some weak evidence that magnesium may help. “Observational studieshave linked magnesium with sleep-promoting effects, whereas limitedgold-standard trialsreport mixed results,” says Gill. “A recentrandomised controlled trialin adults with self-reported poor sleep quality supplemented with magnesium glycinate found modest improvements in insomnia severity.Another studyshowed that supplementation with magnesium threonate improved sleep quality and daytime alertness in people with self-reported sleep problems.”Do I need added vitamins?B vitamins and vitamin D are also commonly believed to help with sleep – are supplements advisable? “B vitamins are abundant in the diet – typically, people don’t have any deficiencies in those,” says St-Onge. “Vitamin D is something that could be problematic, especially if you don’t drink fortified dairy products. We can produce vitamin D from sunlight, but in some populations the sun is not sufficient, so that could be something that could be supplemented.” In the UK,government adviceis to consider taking vitamin D in autumn and winter.What about melatonin?“Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles,” says Gill. “It’s often called the ‘hormone of darkness’ because its levels increase as evening approaches, signalling to your brain and body that it’s time for sleep. Rather than acting like an on-off switch, melatonin works more like a dimmer switch – preparing your body for sleep without directly causing it.” So should insomniacs take supplements? “Melatonin supplements are most effective for shifting the timing of your sleep, rather than as a routine, everyday sleep aid,” says Gill. “Melatonin can also be really helpful for managing jet lag. When used at the right time, melatonin can help fool the brain into thinking it’s night-time.”Explore more on these topicsFoodSleepHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty
Content: Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘When a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenKintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘When a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him.’Photograph: Amy Heycock/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewKintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant reviewThoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tastyGrace DentSun 6 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid all the bunting and hoopla of the platinum jubilee back in 2022, you may well have missed that Colchester, Britain’s oldest recorded settlement, got an upgrade from town to city status. And, as we all know, no true city is complete without at least one fancy restaurant that serves the likes of duck liver mousse on lattice tuiles. Well, in Colchester,Kintsutakes that slot.Or at least it did until May 2025, when chef Paul Wendholt abruptly shut up shop, citing financial pressures. The name Kintsu plays on the termkintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold, silver or platinum or, more commonly, of embracing imperfection and making something pleasing out of bad luck. So it’s rather fitting that Wendholt, a two-time winner of the Essex Chef of the Year gong, managed to reopen Kintsu just four months later, and a year on is now offering eight courses, plus a few extras, for £90 a head in a Grade II-listed building, albeit one that’s down a back lane beside a multi-storey NCP car park. The setting will win no beauty contests, but when a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him. Come for the secure parking, stay for the treacle-curedDingley Dellpork from nearby Suffolk and the Colchester cherries with amaretto.View image in fullscreen‘Cooked precisely’: Kintsu’s Suffolk bass with courgette, chorizo and XO sauce.Even the very idea of a tasting menu will deter some customers: too faffy, too fiddly. But here, from the first warm-up snack – whipped Montgomery cheddar in a fluted tartlet casing under a blanket of crunchy yeast and yet more cheese – even the hardest of the “I just want me dinner” brigade might find their hearts softening. This is followed by that duck liver mousse-topped tuile with glossy, amber beads of onion gel piped on top and a fat, postage stamp-sized chunk of bread pudding piled with ricotta, lemon, and raw peas and shoots. Style as well as substance.Hunks of warm sourdough arrive, clearly fresh from the oven and reminding you how sweet and fragrant sourdough can be, especially when it’s spread with gloriousFen Farmbutter. A plague upon all that hard, spongy nonsense served up and down the land as a plinth for scrambled eggs. While we work our way through these opening snacks, Lionel Richie’sDancing on the Ceilingplays in the background, and the bread turns up toShattered Dreamsby Johnny Hates Jazz. By the time theBraxtedtomatoes arrive, we are deep intoLiving in a Boxterritory, which feels about right for a Saturday lunchtime in a listed barn. Why can’t all restaurants play mid-1980s chart music?View image in fullscreen‘The strongest course’: Kintsu’s Herdwick lamb with turnip and mint.Those first course tomatoes are a rhapsody of very good fruit arranged strategically on silky whipped pecorino with a wicked green basil oil. It is 1pm on a Saturday and we are on one of only two tables occupied. The minimal staff – two in the kitchen and one on the floor – couldn’t be lovelier, ferrying thick, chunky and squat Cornish crab tarts that look almost like mince pies. There’s lots of brown meat layered under the white, and very good, crunchy pastry. This is good, thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty rather than flippant. I wish more people were here to taste it, but they are probably all at a bottomless brunch somewhere, eating ethylene-ripened avocado mush on fumaric acid-injected bread that tastes of old flip-flops. More fool them.We, meanwhile, are having wild Suffolk bass, its skin all crisp and blistered, cooked precisely and served on a foamed sauce flecked with chives and beads of orange oil. Next up, that treacle-cured pork, which is hot, juicy, pitch-black around the edges, and comes layered with sweet raw and cooked apple. At this point, a third booking arrives, which is great for Kintsu but curtails my enthusiastic crooning along toThe Closest Thing to Heavenby the Kane Gang. The strongest course comes next in the form of Herdwick lamb, and features a moist, well-seasoned medallion with a dark, rich jus, tiny nests of shredded turnip, and yet more lamb, roasted, pulled and compacted on to a metal skewer, and topped with cream and shredded mint.View image in fullscreenKintsu’s cherry dessert ‘doesn’t look much on the plate, but it is utterly fabulous’.A pre-pudding of yoghurt, raspberry and lemon resets the mouth. Then an inventive dessert of Colchester cherries, both cooked and preserved, and served on something biscuity, something creamy and something with a whiff of amaretto. It doesn’t look like much on the plate – a collapsed Jenga of dessert ideas – but it is utterly fabulous. We pay the bill over slices of homemade fig-leaf fudge that I would happily hand out in boxes at Christmas. Or eat alone on the sofa.Kintsu is a huge example of a small regional indie doing its very best in rather weird times. Use these places or lose them. Right now, Kintsu is open: beautifully restored, with shimmers of gold.Kintsu11a North Hill, Colchester, Essex, 01206 574361. Open lunch Fri & Sat, noon-1.30pm (last orders); dinner Weds-Sat, 6.30-8pm (8.30pm Fri & Sat; last orders). Tasting menus only, five courses for £65 or eight for £90, both plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
